And there is no other basis for this awareness apart from the body and such; or even if there were, it would fall on the side of the knowable. Nevertheless, a Self distinct from consciousness (<s>saṃvit</s>) and the knowable (<s>saṃvedya</s>) is not established — this is indicated by the word 'api' (even). Thus, no Self exists that is distinct from consciousness and the knowable, because of the non-apprehension of that visible [entity]. // 1 // // 2 //
One might say: that to which this succession is attached — that too shines — to that [the reply is]: since both this — whether non-conceptual or conceptual in nature — is not related to any other
Here, the proponent of the Self raises an inference:
Now, when experience is destroyed, how can there be memory that conforms to it?
The Self must be permanent if it is the experiencer.

children.text: iha smṛtikāle susmūrṣito 'rtho bhavatu , dhvaṃsatāṃ vā ---- iti kintena(KSS: kimanena) , anubhavastāvat dhvastaḥ ---- ityatra sarvasya avivādaḥ , tameva ca anurundhānā smṛtirjāyate / tathā hi ---- smṛtau na arthasya prakāśaḥ , na adhyavasāyaḥ , nāpi anubhavasya arthasya ca aṅgulidvayavat , nāpi anubhavaviśiṣṭasya arthasya daṇḍivat , sarvatra ayam ---- iti pratyayaprasaṅgāt ; kiṃtu anubhavaprakāśa eva smṛtau pradhānam , anubhavasya tu arthaprakāśātmakatvāt anubhavaprakāśanāntarīyako 'rthāvabhāsaḥ iti / sarvathā yadi anubhavo dhvastaḥ , tadā tatprakāśarūpā kathaṃ smṛtistaddvāreṇa arthaviṣayā syāt , tayā ca sarvo vyavahāraḥ kriyamāṇo dṛṣṭaḥ ityasau svarūpeṇa anapahnavanīyā satī anubhavasya nāśe kiṃcit avinaṣṭam āvedayati / tadeva ca anubhavakartṛ ---- anubhavitṛrūpam , ātmā anubhāvako nityaḥ ---- iti / iyadeva ca ātmasiddherjīvitam / tattu na adhikam ihaiva unmīlitam ācāryeṇa , vaktavyaśeṣavivakṣayā pūrvapakṣo mā tāvat samāpat ityāśayena /

children.translated_text: how could it come about?

children.text: iti / arhtastāvat tasyām akiṃcitkaraḥ , anubhavaśca dhvastaḥ iti na kenacitprakāreṇa smṛtiḥ syāt , tadabhāve ca saṃketaśabdasmṛtyāyattā api astaṅgatāḥ sarve vikalpāḥ , nirvikalpaṃ ca andhabadhiramūkaprāyam iti hanta nirākrandam avasīdet viśvam ---- iti //3//
children.translated_text: Thus. As for the object, it is ineffective in that [memory], and experience has been destroyed—therefore memory could not arise by any means; and in the absence of that, all conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpas</s>), which depend on the memory of conventional words, would also be extinguished; and the non-conceptual state would be like being blind, deaf, and mute—alas, the universe would sink into a state beyond lamentation. //3//

Here, whether the object that is to be remembered exists at the time of memory or has perished — what of it? But experience at least has been destroyed — on this there is no dispute for anyone — and it is memory that conforms precisely to that [experience] that arises. For thus: in memory, there is neither the manifestation of the object, nor the determination, nor [are they] like [two] separate fingers — one being the experience and the other the object, nor like a staff-bearer — the object qualified by experience; for in all those cases, the cognition 'this is the same' would follow. Rather, in memory, the illumination of experience is primary; and since experience is of the nature of illuminating the object, the manifestation of the object is necessarily entailed by the illumination of experience. In every case, if experience has been destroyed, then how can memory — which is of the nature of illuminating that [experience] — and through it, having the object as its content, come about? And since all practical activity is seen to be carried out through memory, memory, being undeniable in its own nature, when experience has been destroyed, testifies to something that has not been destroyed. And that is the agent of experience — the experiencer-nature — the Self is the permanent experiencer. And this alone is the life of the proof of the Self. But the master did not develop this further here, with the intention that the prior position should not conclude just yet, wishing to express the remainder [of the opponent's arguments].

children.text: iha kāryātirekeṇa tādṛk kalpanīyaṃ yat kāryasiddhaye paryāpnoti , na caivam ātmā , artho hi tāvat smaryate , sa ca anubhavaprakāśamukhena , anubhavaśca dhvastaḥ ---- ityuktam ; yadi ātmā kaścidasti , kiṃ tena / etadapi hi vaktavyam ---- ākāśamapi asti ---- iti / atha ucyate ---- na kevalena ātmanā etat siddhyati , api tu anubhavasaṃskāro 'pi atra upayogī ---- iti , tarhi sa evāstu , kim anena ? ---- tadetat darśayati
children.translated_text: Here, beyond the effect, that which is to be postulated must be sufficient for the accomplishment of the effect—and the self is not like that; for the object is indeed remembered, and that through the medium of the light of experience, and experience has been destroyed—thus it has been stated. If there is some self, what use is it? For this too must be said—space also exists. Now if it is said that this is not accomplished by the self alone, but that the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of experience is also useful here—then let that alone suffice, what need is there of this [self]? This he shows:
Even if the self exists, since perception is destroyed, memory of objects perceived through it—
by what means [could it arise]? And where experience itself occurred, that alone is its ground.
'Dṛṣṭeṣu' (of those perceived):
of those experienced,
'vastuṣu' (objects):
'yā' (which):
'smṛtiḥ' (memory):
in that [memory], experience, whose nature is perception,
'dvāram' (is the door):
for contact with the object; and that [experience],
'even if the self exists' (satyapy ātmani):

children.text:
naṣṭo'nubhavaḥ ,
tasya hi anāśe idam ---- ityeṣa eva atruṭitaḥ prakāśaḥ iti kā smṛtiḥ , tadanubhavitā kiṃ smṛteḥ kuryāt ---- iti /
children.translated_text:
the experience is destroyed;
for if it were not destroyed, this very unbroken light would continue as 'this'—then what need of memory? What would the experiencer do with memory?
'Yatraiva' (in that very):
object,
'anubhavo' (experience):
has occurred,
'tadeva' (that alone):
of that memory,
'padaṃ' (is the ground):
what is remembered. 'Tatpadā' is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> (possessive compound),
'sā' (that):
means memory. //4//

children.text: nanu jñānāntarasya viṣayeṇa kathaṃ tasyāḥ viṣayitvābhimānaḥ ---- ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Now, objecting—how can there be a claim of subjecthood for a cognition that is different from the object—he says:
Since memory arises from the impressions of prior experience,
if so, what use is there of a permanent self that is like a tumor within?

children.text: anubhavena hi saṃskāro janyate svocitaḥ , saṃskāraśca prātanarūpāṃ sthitiṃ sthāpayati , ākṛṣṭaśākhādeścirasaṃvartitasya vivartyamānasya bhūrjādeḥ / tena atrāpi saṃskāraḥ tāṃ smṛtiṃ pūrvānubhavānukāriṇīṃ karoti ---- iti tadviṣaya eva smṛterviṣayaḥ /
children.translated_text: For experience generates an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) appropriate to itself, and the impression establishes a subsequent form of persistence, like a birch bark or the like that has been long rolled when bent, which retains that shape when released. Thus here too the impression produces that memory which resembles the prior experience—and so the content of memory is precisely the content of that [experience].
'antargaḍuḥ' (an internal tumor):

children.text: yathā āyāsāya param , tadvat ātmā sthiraḥ kalpanāyāsamātraphalaḥ iti kiṃ tena , sarvaṃ hi saṃskāreṇa jagadvyavahārakuṭumbakaṃ kṛtakarāvalambam ---- iti //5//
children.translated_text: just as [a tumor] serves only to cause pain, likewise the self, being permanent, yields only the fruit of the effort of postulation—what use is it? For the entire family of worldly transactions rests upon the support of impressions alone. //5//
If so, then

children.text: nanu tasmaiva saṃskārasya āśrayo vaktavyaḥ , sa hi guṇatvād āśrayamapekṣate , ya āśrayaḥ sa ātmā syāt ---- ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Now, objecting—a substratum for that very impression must be stated, for being a quality it requires a substratum, and that substratum would be the self—he says:
Then, since there is no distinction in its own nature among the distinct properties,
if memory is established from impression alone, the rememberer would be postulated like the perceiver.

children.text: iha saṃskāre jāyamāne , yadi ātmano viśeṣaḥ , sa tarhi avyatiriktaḥ iti na nityaḥ syāt ; atha na kaścit asya viśeṣaḥ , tena tarhi kim / atha saṃskāra eva asya viśeṣaḥ , tarhi na vyatirikto 'sau iti punarapi anitye jñāne saṃskāraḥ ---- ityāyātam / anubhavādviśiṣṭaṃ viśiṣṭasmrṭyākhyakāryakāri jñānaṃ paramparayā jāyate ---- iti iyāneva saṃskārārthaḥ / atha saṃskārātmā vyatirikto viśeṣaḥ , tasya tarhi kimasau / saṃbandhaśca vyatirikto nirākariṣyate / evaṃ jñānasukhaduḥkhecchādveṣaprayatnadharmādharmā api vikalpanīyāḥ / etadāha ----

children.translated_text: 'Tataḥ' (then):
means 'of the self';
'bhinneṣu dharmeṣu' (when the properties are distinct):
even when those are accepted as existing,
'svarūpe' (in the essential nature):

children.text: viśeṣābhāvāt sa tāvat ātmā smrṭau na vyāpriyeta , asmatṛrūpāsaṃskṛtarūpādiprācyarūp|anapāyāt , iti
children.translated_text: of the self, due to the absence of any distinction, the self would not be operative in memory, since there is no departure from its prior nature of being unmodified by memory and the like; therefore
memory is established from impression alone—
thus. 'I remember'—he who is the
'smartā' (rememberer):
is also determined to be the bodily continuum and the continuum of cognitions,
just as the perceiver is.
For it was stated earlier:

Here, when an impression arises, if there is a modification of the self, then it is non-different [from the impression] and thus would not be permanent. If there is no modification of it whatsoever, then what use is it? If the impression itself is its modification, then it is not different [from the impression], and so we return to the position that the impression resides in the impermanent cognition. A cognition that is distinct from experience and that produces an effect called distinct memory arises through a series—this alone is the meaning of impression. If, however, the modification that constitutes the impression is different [from the self], then what is it to the self? And a separate relation will be refuted. Thus knowledge, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, <s>dharma</s> (merit), and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) are also to be similarly analyzed. This he states—
{This awareness of 'I' too is a determination regarding the body.} (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.2.2)

children.text: iti / evam ātmani sādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ pratyakṣamanumānaṃ ca parākṛtam , bādhakaṃ ca sūcitaṃ ---- dharmayoge nityatāhāni , anyathā kiṃ tena / taduktam
children.translated_text: Thus. In this way, both <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference) as valid means of knowledge regarding the self have been refuted, and a counter-argument has been indicated—if properties are conjoined, permanence is lost; otherwise, what use is it? As it has been stated:

children.text:
{carmopamaścetso'nityaḥ svatukyaścedasatsamaḥ /
varṣātapābhyāṃ kiṃ vyomnaścarmaṇyasti hi tatphalam //}
children.translated_text: {If it is like leather, then it is impermanent; if it is equal to itself, it is like the non-existent. What do rain and heat mean for space? For that result exists only in leather.}
Thus. //6//

children.text: ittham ātmānaṃ nirākṛtya , tasya aiśvaryamapi nirākartuṃ jñānaśaktimeva parīkṣitumāha
children.translated_text: Having thus refuted the self, in order to refute its sovereignty as well, he proceeds to examine the power of knowledge:

children.text: jñānaṃ ca citsvarūpaṃ cet tad anityaṃ kimātmavat /
children.translated_text: If knowledge is of the nature of consciousness, is it then impermanent like the self?
And if it is insentient, how could it have the capacity to illuminate objects?

children.text: parābhyupagamena prasaṅgāpādanam etat pūrvapakṣavādī karoti ---- prasaṅgaviparyayalābho me bhaviṣyati ---- iti / tatra ātmavādī nityatvam ātmana itthaṃ brūte ---- iha kālo nāma idaṃbhāvaviśiṣṭasya viśeṣaṇatām avalambamānaḥ taṃ viśiṣṭīkurvan tatsaṃkocāt anityaṃ saṃpādayati / ātmanaśca citsvabhāvatvāt idam ---- iti prathanābhāvena viśeṣyatvaṃ nāsti , viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvo hi yojakāyattaḥ , na ca svaprakāśe yojakāntaram asti / sa itthaṃ bruvāṇaḥ paryanuyujyate ----

children.translated_text: Knowledge too

children.text:
tarhi svaprakāśam iti tatrāpi eṣaiva vārtā iti tadapi kasmāt na nityam ? na ca dvayornityayoḥ kaścit saṃbandhaḥ , kāryakāraṇabhāvo hi asau nānyaḥ , tata ātmano jñānaṃ śaktiḥ iti avasannam adaḥ / atha na svaprakāśaṃ jñānaṃ tarhi parasyāpi ado na prakāśaḥ ,
svaprakāśarūpāveśanaṃ hi asau parasya vidadhat bodhaḥ prakāśo bhavati parasyāpi , tataḥ svaprakāśatāśūnyo na asau arthasya prakāśaḥ syāt , bhāvāntaravat //7//
children.translated_text:
is then self-luminous, so the same argument applies to it as well—why then is it not also permanent? And between two permanent entities there can be no relation, for that would be nothing other than a cause-effect relation; therefore the proposition that knowledge is a power of the self collapses. If, on the other hand, knowledge is not self-luminous, then it is not a light even for another,
for it is by bestowing the form of self-luminosity upon another that cognition becomes light for the other as well; therefore, being devoid of self-luminosity, it would not be an illumination of objects, just like any other thing. //7//

The opponent of the prior position makes this reductio argument based on the other's own premises—'I shall gain the reverse of the reductio.' Therein, the proponent of the self states its permanence thus: here, what is called time, assuming the role of qualifier of something qualified by 'this-ness,' makes it qualified and thereby, through the limitation of that, produces impermanence. But since the self is of the nature of consciousness, there is no objecthood through manifestation as 'this,' and hence no status as something qualified; for the relation of qualifier and qualified depends on a connector, and in what is self-luminous there is no other connector. He, speaking thus, is challenged—

children.text: jaḍo'pyasau ittham arthasya prakāśo bhaviṣyati ---- iti sāṃkhyamatam āśaṅkate
children.translated_text: Anticipating the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> view that even though insentient, it could illuminate objects in this manner, he says:
Now, just as the intellect bears the form of the object, so too
it bears the consciousness of the self...

children.text: iha tāvat arthaṃ jānāmi ----ityasti vyavahāraḥ / tatra arthasya prakāśaḥ ---- ityetāvāneva paramārthaḥ / tat na arthasya svaṃ rūpam , sarvaṃ prati tathātvaprasaṅgāt , na kaṃcitprati vā iti sarvajñam ajñaṃ vā jagat syāt / nāpi arthe anyata etadrūpam upanipatitam , eṣa eva hi doṣaḥ syāt / tat nūnam anyatraiva ayaṃ dharmaḥ tattvāntare , tatrāpi katham arthasya prakāśaḥ syāt iti nūnaṃ tatra tattvāntare so'rthaḥ pratibimbatvena upasaṃkrāmati / tat tattvāntaraṃ sattvaprādhānyāt pratibimbagrahayogyaṃ tamasā''cchāditatvāt sakalapratibimbanato vyāvartitam , bhāge rajasā tamaso'pasāraṇāt kiṃcideva pratibimbakaṃ gṛhyāti , tadeva buddhitattvam ucyate / arthapratibimbagrahaśca jñānam asya vṛttirūpaṃ pūrvavyapadeśatirodhāyakadadhyādipariṇāmavilakṣaṇapariṇativiśeṣātmakam / evam

children.translated_text: 'arthasya' (of the object):
first of all,
'rūpaṃ buddhiḥ' (the form is held by the intellect):

children.text:
dhārayati / iyaśca sattvādīnāṃ sukhaduḥkhamoharūpatayāṃ bhogyatvāt jaḍam iti darpakṣavat aprakāśam / na ca bhogyasya aprakāśasya tadviruddhabhoktṛtārūpaprakāśātmakasvabhāvasaṃbhavo yuktyanupātī iti tadvilakṣaṇena bhoktrā bhavitavyam / sa ca prakāśaḥ ---- ityetāvatsvabhāvaḥ , svabhāvāntaraṃ hi aprakāśarūpaṃ bhogyaṃ kathaṃ bhoktuḥ svabhāvatayā saṃbhāvyeta / sa ca prakāśamātrasvabhāvatvenaiva yadi viśvasya prakāśaḥ ,
tarhi yugapadeva prakāśeta , ghaṭaprakāśo'pi paṭaprakāśaḥ syāt iti viśvaṃ saṃkīryeta / sa ca arthāt arthapratibimbāt tadādhārācca buddhitattvāt anyaḥ katham arthasya prakāśaḥ syāt , asaṃbandhāt / tasmāt buddhireva svacchatvāt prakāśapratibimbamapi gṛhṇāti / tataḥ prakāśapratibimbaparigrahamahimopanataprakāśāveśabuddhitattvāveśitapratibimbakanīlādyarthaparyantasaṃkrānteḥ prakāśāveśasya arthaḥ prakāśate iti siddho vyavahāraḥ / tadevaṃ jñānaṃ jaḍabuddhitattvāvyatirekāt jaḍamapi citpratibimbayogāt viṣayasya prakāśaḥ ---- iti /
children.translated_text:
it holds. And since this [intellect], being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion due to <s>sattva</s> and the other [guṇas], is an object of enjoyment, it is insentient—like a mirror, non-luminous. And since it is not reasonable that an object of enjoyment, being non-luminous, could have the nature of the enjoyer, which is the very form of luminosity and is opposed to it—therefore there must be an enjoyer who is distinct from it. And he is of such a nature as to be just 'luminosity,' for how could another nature, which is of the form of non-luminosity and is an object of enjoyment, be conceived as the very nature of the enjoyer? And if he, by being merely of the nature of luminosity, is the illuminator of everything,
then everything would be illuminated simultaneously; the illumination of a pot would also be the illumination of a cloth—and the entire universe would be confused. And how could he, being other than the object, the object's reflection, and its substratum the <s>buddhi-tattva</s>, be the illuminator of the object, given the absence of relation? Therefore, it is the intellect itself that, due to its transparency, grasps the reflection of luminosity as well. Then, through the glory of absorbing the reflection of luminosity, the luminosity-infusion extends down to the objects such as blue that are reflected in the intellect-principle, which has been infused with luminosity through the absorption of the reflection of luminosity—and thus the object is illuminated, and ordinary usage is established. In this way, knowledge, being non-different from the insentient intellect-principle, though insentient, illuminates objects through the conjunction with the reflection of consciousness—thus [says the Sāṃkhya].

Here, first of all, there is the ordinary usage 'I know the object.' Therein, 'the illumination of the object'—this alone is the ultimate truth. That is not the object's own form, for otherwise it would apply to everything, or to no one—and the world would be either omniscient or entirely ignorant. Nor has this form descended upon the object from elsewhere, for the same fault would apply. Then surely this property belongs to something else, to another principle; but how could the object be illuminated there, in that other principle? Surely the object migrates to that other principle in the form of a reflection. That other principle, due to the predominance of <s>sattva</s> (purity), is capable of receiving reflections; being covered by <s>tamas</s> (darkness), it is prevented from reflecting everything; through the partial removal of <s>tamas</s> by <s>rajas</s> (activity), it grasps only some reflections—and this is called the <s>buddhi-tattva</s> (intellect-principle). And the grasping of the object's reflection is its <s>vṛtti</s> (modification), a particular transformation distinct from the prior designated states such as curd and the like. Thus,

children.text: etadeva tāvat anucitam ---- yat prakāśātmā pumān buddhau pratibimbam arpayati , samānaguṇe bimbakāpekṣayā ca vimale pratibimbasaṃkrāntidarśanāt , rūpavati ādarśe ghaṭarūpapratibimbavat ; ātmabuddhyośca ativailakṣaṇyam , ātmāpekṣayā ca na buddhirvimalā tat bahvatu tāvat etat ---- iti

children.translated_text: 'atha' (now):
he indicates with this word.

But even this much is inappropriate—that the self, whose nature is luminosity, deposits a reflection in the intellect; for the transmission of reflection is seen in a mirror that shares similar qualities with respect to the original and is clear; like the reflection of the form of a pot in a mirror that possesses form. But between self and intellect there is extreme dissimilarity, and the intellect is not clear in comparison to the self. But let that be for now—thus

children.text: kiṃtu pratibimbavādenāpi na kiṃcit pratisamāhitaṃ bhavet ---- iti darśayati
children.translated_text: He shows that even with the reflection theory, nothing is properly accounted for:
...being non-insentient [it becomes so]; in insentience there would be no illumination of objects. // Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.2.8 //

children.text: caitanyapratibimbayoge yadi tāvat tatpratibimbakamapi mukhyaṃ prakāśarūpameva na bhavati , tenāpi na kiṃcit kṛtaṃ syāt , na hi pratibimbatavahnipuñja ādarśo dāhyaṃ dahet / atha mukhyaprakāśarūpameva tatpratibimbakam , tat tarhi buddheravyatiriktam iti mukhyaprakāśarūpaiva buddhirjātā iti / yato viruddhadharmādhyāsāt bhīrubhiḥ etat kalpitam / sa eva punaḥ jājvalyamānaṃ nijam ojo jṛmbhayati , tataśca sā buddhireva cinmayī syāt , kiṃ puruṣeṇa / evam arthapratibimbakadvāreṇa arthamayī ---- ityapi āyāto vijñānavādaḥ / kuta etasyāḥ tadrūpatvam ---- iti , pūrvakāraṇaparamparātaḥ ---- iti utaraṃ vācyam / evaṃ saiva cet cidrūpā , prāgvat nityatāprasaṅgaḥ ; na ceta cidrūpasyāpi nityatā , tarhi ātmā na nityaḥ kaścidasti , yasya jñānaṃ nāma śaktiḥ syāt iti jñānamātrameva asti / yo 'rthaprakāśarūpo bodho yaśca vikalpasmṛtyādirūpaḥ tāvatā arthavyavahārasiddheḥ ---- iti prasaṅgaviparyayalābhaḥ

children.translated_text: 'If knowledge is of the nature of consciousness'—
this is the import of these two verses. //8//

If, through the conjunction with the reflection of consciousness, even that reflection does not become principally of the nature of luminosity, then nothing is accomplished by it either—for a bundle of reflected fire in a mirror does not burn a combustible. But if that reflection is indeed of the nature of principal luminosity, then being non-different from the intellect, the intellect itself has become of the nature of principal luminosity. For this [theory of reflection] was devised by the timid due to the superimposition of contradictory properties. That very [luminosity] then causes its own innate splendor to blaze forth, and so the intellect itself would be of the nature of consciousness—what need then of the <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit)? Similarly, through the medium of the reflection of the object, [the intellect] being of the nature of the object—thus the <s>vijñānavāda</s> (idealist doctrine) is also arrived at. Whence does it have that nature?—from the chain of prior causes—such would be the reply. If it is thus of the nature of consciousness, there follows the consequence of permanence as before; and if even what is of the nature of consciousness is not permanent, then there is no permanent self whose power could be called knowledge—and so knowledge alone exists. That cognition which is of the nature of illuminating objects and that which is of the nature of conceptual construction, memory, and the like—with just that much, ordinary usage is established. This is the reverse of the reductio—
Having thus examined knowledge, he examines action:
Action too is merely the arising of the body and such in various places and the like, with respect to the object.
There is nothing other, as it is not perceived...

children.text: iha parispandarūpaṃ tāvat gavcchati , calati, patati ---- ityādi yat pratibhāsagocaram , tatra gṛhaseśagatadevadattasvarūpāt anantaraṃ bāhyadeśavartidevadattasvarūpam ---- ityetāvat upalabhyate , na tu tatsvarūpātiriktāṃ kāṃcit anyāṃ kriyāṃ pratīmaḥ /

children.translated_text: <s>Devadatta</s> stands for a day.

children.text: ityatra tu prabhātakālāviṣṭadevadattasvarūpaṃ tataḥ praharakālāliṅgitatatsvarūpam ---- ityādi bhāti ,
children.translated_text: But here, the form of <s>Devadatta</s> pervaded by the morning-time, then the same form embraced by the afternoon-time — and so on — appears;
"Milk transforms" —

children.text: ityatra madhuravasturūpam amlavasturūpam dravarūpaṃ kaṭhinarūpam ---- ityādi / evaṃ sādṛśyācca tatra pratyabhijñā bhinne'pi kāyakeśanasvādāviva / deśākārānyatve tu kālānyatvam avaśyaṃbhāvideśakālānyatve 'pi , svarūpasyaiva deśatvāt , kālabhede ca svarūpabhedāt , deśakālākārā ākāra eva yadyapi paryavasmanti , tathāpi sthūladṛṣṭyā asti bhedaḥ iti te hi bhedena bauddhairucyante ---- iti tātparyam / evaṃ pratyakṣeṇa na dṛśyate kacit kriyā , tadbhāvāt na tatpūrvakeṇa anumānena , kāryaṃ ca prāmaprāptyādyuttarakṣaṇarūpaṃ taddeśavasturūpādi iti kāryānyathānupapattyāpi na sā kalpyā / evaṃ pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ tasyā adṛṣṭiḥ ---- iti sādhakapramāṇābhāva uktaḥ /
children.translated_text: here, the sweet-substance form, the sour-substance form, the liquid form, the solid form — and so on. And through similarity, there is recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) even in difference, as in the case of body, hair, and taste. When there is difference of place and form, there is necessarily difference of time also; even when place and time are necessarily different, since the essential nature itself is place, and since with difference in time there is difference in essential nature, and although spatial, temporal, and formal aspects ultimately resolve into form alone, still from a gross perspective there is difference — and thus they are spoken of as different by the Buddhists: this is the purport. Thus, no action is perceived by direct perception; due to its non-existence, not by inference based on it either; and the effect, being of the nature of the next moment such as obtaining or not obtaining, or of the nature of things at that place, etc. — action cannot be postulated even through the impossibility of explaining the effect otherwise. Thus, through both perception and inference, its non-apprehension has been stated — the absence of establishing means of knowledge.

Here, as for what appears as movement in perception—'goes,' 'moves,' 'falls,' and so on—therein, what is apprehended is merely that the form of <s>Devadatta</s> in the external location [comes] immediately after the form of <s>Devadatta</s> inside the house; but we do not perceive any action that is distinct from those forms.
He also states the invalidating argument:
................... Nor is that single [action] sequential, and what is proper for a single [agent]... // <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.2.9 //

children.text: tatra pūrvāpararūpatā kṣaṇānāṃ vikalpabudvyānusaṃdhānāt , na tu svātmani kiṃcit pūrvam aparaṃ vā , vastumātraṃ hi tat / ato vikalpaprāṇitaṃ pūrvāparībhūtatvaṃ kramarūpatā kriyāyāḥ kiṃcit kṣaṇaṃ na vastu spṛśati , te hi kṣaṇā na anyonyasvarūpāviṣṭāḥ iti katham

children.translated_text: a single

children.text: kriyā , kramo hi bhedena vyāptaḥ abhiśne tadabhāvāt , bhedasya viruddham ekyam iti kathaṃ
children.translated_text: action? For sequence is pervaded by difference universally, and in its absence [of sequence there is no action]; since unity is contradictory to difference, how could there be
both sequential and single

children.text:
iti syāt ? atha ekatra āśraye'vasthānāt ekā , tatrāpi tatkṣaṇātirikto na kaścit āśrayo'nubhūyate , kṣaṇā eva hi prabandhavṛttayo bhānti / kiṃ ca tathābhūtairbhinnadeśakālākāraiḥ kriyākṣaṇairāviṣṭa āśrayaḥ kathamekaḥ syāt ?
ata eva
children.translated_text:
[action]? If [it be said] that it is single due to abiding in one substrate, even there no substrate separate from those moments is experienced, for moments alone appear as having a continuous existence. Moreover, how could a substrate pervaded by action-moments of different place, time, and form be single?
Therefore,
"This is <s>Devadatta</s>, he himself has arrived at the village" —

children.text: iti sādṛśyāt bhavantī pratyabhijñā na aikyaṃ vāstavaṃ gamayitumalam //9//
children.translated_text: such recognition arises from similarity, and is not capable of conveying real identity. // 9 //

Therein, the prior-and-posterior nature of moments is due to conceptual cognition and recollection, but in their own nature, nothing is prior or posterior — for that is mere being. Therefore, the sequentiality that constitutes the nature of action, being animated by conceptual thought, having become prior and posterior, does not touch any momentary reality; for those moments are not pervaded by each other's nature — so how can there be

children.text: evaṃ jñānaṃ kriyāṃ ca parīkṣya , yasmin sati te saṃbaddhe sarvajñatvasarvakartṛtārūpaiśvaryaprasādhanāya prabhavataḥ , taṃ saṃbandhaṃ dhvaṃsayituṃ tadviṣayaṃ pramāṇābhāvaṃ tāvadāha
children.translated_text: Having thus examined knowledge and action, in order to demolish the connection — upon whose existence they, being related, would be capable of establishing sovereignty in the form of omniscience and omnipotence — he first states the absence of a means of knowledge regarding that connection:
When this is present, that arises — this alone is observed;
there is no other, nor any other connection, beyond the relation of cause and effect. //

children.text: mṛtppiṇḍe sati stūpakaḥ , tatra sati śiviko yāvat ghaṭaḥ ityevaṃ bhāvakṣaṇā eva upalabhyante , na adhikaṃ kiṃcit pratyakṣeṇa avabhāsate , nāpi anumānena ---- iti kriyāyāmiva vācyam / sarvatra ādhārādheyabhāvādau ayameva panthāḥ ---- pṛthagrūpakuṇḍavadarakṣaṇānantaraṃ nirantarātmakaviśiṣṭakuṇḍavadarodayaḥ ---- iti / ayameva ca bhāvo bhāvāntareṇa saha niyatapūrvāparatayā vikalpena vyavahiyamāṇaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ ---- iti abhidhīyate / na ca jñānakriyābhyāṃ saha ātmanaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ ātmanastatkāryatvābhāvāt , jñānasya ca svasāmagrokāryatvāt , kriyāyāśca abhāvāt iti na jñānakriyāsaṃbandho yato jñātṛtvakartṛtve syātām //10//
children.translated_text: When a clay lump is present, a stūpaka arises; when that is present, a śivikā; and so on up to a pot — thus only momentary existences are apprehended; nothing more is manifest through direct perception, nor through inference — as should be stated just as in the case of action. Everywhere, in the relation of container and contained, this alone is the path: after the moment of the distinct pot of a particular form, there arises the distinct pot of an uninterrupted nature — thus. And this very existence (<s>bhāva</s>), when spoken of through conceptual thought as having a fixed prior-posterior relation with another existence, is called the cause-and-effect relation. But the self has no cause-and-effect relation with knowledge and action — because the self is not their effect; knowledge arises from its own aggregate of causes; and action is non-existent — therefore, there is no connection of knowledge and action [with the self] from which the states of being a knower and an agent would follow. // 10 //

children.text: evaṃ pramāṇaṃ parākṛtya , saṃbandhe bādhakaṃ sāmānyaviśeṣamukhena nirūpayati
children.translated_text: Having thus set aside the means of valid knowledge, he demonstrates the invalidating argument regarding connection, both in its general and particular aspects:
Because what abides in two has many forms, because what is already established needs no other,
because of the impossibility of dependence and such — by that, even the agent is a mere construct. //

Connection, to begin with, has the general definition: it is of the nature of mutual attainment; [but] it abides in one of the two parties that partake of attainment — how is that? For surely, one whose entire essential body rests in one [locus] cannot rest in another without the consequence of a split in its essential nature. By this, <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), as well as other connections rooted in them, should be understood as having been placed on a platform devoid of invalidation. As for the connection that is of the nature of dependence, spoken of in the case of sentient beings and, by analogy, in the case of insentient things — therein, for what is already established there is no dependence, precisely because it is already established; for what is not established, even less so, since what has no essential nature cannot possess such a property. The same should be said regarding mutual requirement. And how do two forms coalesce? Since the identity of two is impossible; or if they are one, what coalescence is there? Therefore, from the connection with knowledge, the [notion of]

children.text: iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptaviracitāyāṃ pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinyāṃ jñānādhikāre pūrvapakṣavivṛtirnāma dvitīyamāhnikam // 2 //
children.translated_text: Thus concludes the second chapter (<s>āhnika</s>), entitled 'Exposition of the Opponent's View' (<s>pūrvapakṣa-vivṛti</s>), in the Knowledge Section (<s>jñānādhikāra</s>) of the <s>Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 2 //
Now begins the third chapter (<s>āhnika</s>).
{Without whom nothing would exist, even all perceptions —
Him, whose essential nature is unextinguished perfect awareness, <s>Śiva</s>, we praise. //}

children.translated_text: up to that — seven verses. The refutation regarding action and connection will come in the second, the Action Section (<s>kriyādhikāra</s>). As for the opponent's rejection of knowledge as distinct [from the self] in the <s>Kāśa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, and other views — that is indeed accepted by the author of the treatise, so that itself constitutes another refutation. Therein, in two verses, the non-manifestation of experience in memory is shown, even when born of latent impressions, because knowledge has the nature of self-awareness. Then, in two verses, after first raising the doubt and refuting the notion that memory is erroneous, in a third verse the incidental suspicion that all determinate cognitions are erroneous is pacified. Then, even when latent impressions exist, the impossibility of memory [without a self] would result in the cessation of all practical activity — this is stated in one verse; and in one's own position its possibility — this is stated in one verse: such is the purport. The meaning of the text is now examined.
It is true; however, the knowledge that is memory, born from the latent impression of prior experience,
even though arisen, being self-referential, is not a cognizer of the original experience. //

tasmāt saṃskāra eva bhavatsaṃbhāvitadoṣabhaṅgāya prabhavet / naitat , yato hi asau tatsaṃskārasaṃskṛtāt samanantarapratyayāt utthitaḥ smṛtibodhaḥ , tena tatsadṛśo bhavatu śāsvāsaṃniveśa iva pūrvasaṃniveśatulyaḥ , na tu yo yatsaṃskārāt jātaḥ sa tasya vedanasvabhāvo bhavati ---- iti yuktam / sadṛśatvasyāpi gatiravagamaḥ katham ? na hi anubhavajñānaṃ sādṛśyaṃ gamayati , nāpi smṛtijñānam , parasparam asaṃvedane dvayaniṣṭhasādṛśyādhyavasāyāyogāt , abhyasya ca tadubhayavedanarūpasya abhāvāt iti saṃskārāt paraṃ saviṣayatāmātraṃ smṛteḥ siddham , na tu anubhavaviṣayatvam , nāpi asya viṣayasya pūrvānubhavaviṣayīkṛtatvam ---- iti niścayaḥ eṣaḥ //2//
children.translated_text: — the knowledge having taste as its object — is not known; for otherwise, taste would effectively be grasped by the eye alone. But if experience does not shine forth in memory, then what would the latent impression accomplish? The cognition of form is not born from the latent impression born of the cognition of taste — so how is this consequence applicable? Therefore, the latent impression itself should be able to overcome the defects you attribute to it. Not so, for this memory-cognition, having arisen from the proximate condition conditioned by that latent impression, may be similar to that [experience], like a later arrangement [of things] being similar to a prior arrangement — but it is not correct that whatever is born from whatever latent impression becomes the awareness of that [original experience]. And how is the apprehension, i.e., the cognition, of similarity itself possible? For the experiential knowledge does not convey similarity, nor does the memory-knowledge — since when neither knows the other, the determination of similarity residing in both is impossible; and since a third [cognition] that would know both is absent. Therefore, from the latent impression, only the having-an-object-ness of memory is established, but not its having the experience as object, nor the certainty that this object was the object of prior experience — this is the conclusion. // 2 //

He presents this as something to be objected to:
But even if memory does not have that as its [real] object, because it determines it as such,
it has a previously-seen basis through error... //

children.translated_text: The non-loss — the non-removal — of an object that has been experienced, that is, illuminated by experience, [meaning] its being illuminated in the same way — that which is the essential nature of memory, that would be destroyed if such illumination were absent. Moreover, in error, either a non-existent thing or a self-form appears, but the object is not appropriated by it, since that [object] is not illuminated by it; therefore, the object is simply not established by error. For establishment is of the nature of illumination. And thus, how could there be practical activity regarding the object through memory and desire? Nor does the fact that it arises from impressions accomplish anything when the object is not illuminated, for that [impression theory] is relied upon to obtain similarity; and there is no similarity whatsoever between experience — which is of the nature of illuminating the object — and error, which is called memory, since error does not touch the object in any way. //4//

children.translated_text: Here, in memory or any other erroneous cognition, insofar as the self-awareness aspect shines, there is no erroneousness, since there is no distortion there. And that aspect, characterized as the object, is not touched by memory or any other error; therefore, regarding that, it is silent — and so forcibly, in that aspect, insentience has befallen it, like the cognition of a pot with respect to a cloth. And the insentient has nothing to do with the object; therefore, practical activity regarding the object would be destroyed.

exists as one, whose body is consciousness, possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion. //
That consciousness shines —

children.text: iti tāvat na kecit apahnuvate / sā tu saṃvit yadi svātmamātraviśrāntā arthasya sā kathaṃ prakāśaḥ ? sa hi arthadharma eva tathā syāt ; tataśca arthaprakāśaḥ tāvatyeva paryavasita iti galito grāhyagrāhakabhāvaḥ / ato 'rthaprakāśarūpaṃ saṃvidam icchatā balādeva artho'pi tadrūpāntargata eva aṅgīkratavyaḥ ; sa ca arthaprakāśo yadi anyaśca anyaśca , tat na smaraṇam upapannamityata eka eva asau ---- iti / ekatvāt sarvo vedyarāśiḥ tena kroḍīkṛtaḥ ---- ityetadapi anicchatā aṅgīkāryam / evamapi satatameva unmagnena nimagnena vā viśvātmanā prakāśeta , tathā svabhāvatvāt / na caivam , ataḥ svarūpāntarbruḍitam artharāśim aparamapi bhinnākāram ātmani parigṛhya , kaṃcideva arthaṃ svarūpāt unmagnam ābhāsayati ---- iti āpatitam / saiṣā jñānaśaktiḥ / unmagnābhāsabhinnaṃ ca citsvarūpaṃ vahirmukhatvāt tacchāyānurāgāt navaṃ navaṃ jñānamuktam / evamapi navanavābhāsāḥ pratikṣaṇam udayavyayabhāja iti saiva vyavahāranivahahāniḥ / tena kvacit ābhāse gṛhītapūrve yat saṃvedanaṃ bahirmukham abhūt , tasya yat antarmukhaṃ citsvarūpatvaṃ tat kālāntare 'pi avasthāsnu svātmagataṃ tadviṣayaviśeṣe bahirmukhatvaṃ parāmṛśati iti eśā smṛtiśaktiḥ / yacca tat navaṃ bhāsayati smarati vā tat vastutaḥ saṃvidā viśvamayyā tādātmyavṛtti iti viśvamayaṃ pūrṇameva iti navaṃ na kiṃcit ābhāsitaṃ smṛtaṃ vā syāt / idamapi pravāhapatitam urīkāryam ---- yat kila tat ābhāsyate tat saṃvido vicchiidyate , saṃvicca tataḥ , saṃvicca saṃvidantarāt , saṃvedyaṃ ca saṃvedyāntaraāt ; na ca vicchedanaṃ vastutaḥ saṃbhavati , iti vicchedanasya avabhāsamātram ucyate / na ca tat iyatā pāramārthikam , nirmīyamāṇasya sarvasya ayameva paramārthaḥ / yataḥ eṣa eva paritaśchedanāt pariccheda ucyate , tadavabhāsanasāmarthyam apohanaśaktiḥ / anena śaktitrayeṇa viśve vyavahārāḥ / tacca bhagavata eva śaktitrayam ---- yat tathābhūtānubhavitṛ-smartṛ-vikalpayitṛsvabhāvacaitramaitrādyavabhāsanam / sa eva hi tena tena vapuṣā jānāti , smarati vikalpayati ca / yathoktam ācāryeṇaiva
children.translated_text: this much at least no one denies. But if that consciousness rests in its own self alone, how could it be the illumination of the object? For that [illumination] would then be a property of the object itself; and so the illumination of the object would terminate in just that much, and the relation of apprehended and apprehender would dissolve. Therefore, by one who accepts consciousness as being of the nature of illuminating objects, the object too must forcibly be accepted as included within the form of that [consciousness]. And if that illumination of the object were one thing and another, then memory would not be possible — therefore it is one and the same. From its oneness, the entire mass of objects is embraced by it — this too must be accepted even unwillingly. Even so, it would always manifest with the universal nature either emerged or submerged, since that is its nature. But it is not so; therefore, having internally embraced the mass of objects concealed within other forms, as well as [objects of] different forms, it illuminates only some particular object as emerged from its own nature — this follows. And this is the power of knowledge (<s>jñāna-śakti</s>). And the nature of consciousness, differentiated from the emerged appearance, being outward-facing and tinged with its coloring, is called ever-new knowledge. Even so, the ever-new appearances, partaking of arising and cessation at every moment — that same destruction of the totality of practical activities [would follow]. Therefore, regarding some appearance previously apprehended, the awareness that was outward-facing — its inward-facing nature of consciousness, which persists even at another time and abides in the self, reflects upon outward-facing-ness with respect to that particular object — this is the power of memory (<s>smṛti-śakti</s>). And that which newly illuminates or remembers, in reality, being identical with consciousness that is of the nature of the universe, is complete and universal — and so nothing new would be illuminated or remembered. This too, falling into the stream [of experience], must be accepted — namely, that what is being illuminated is delimited from consciousness, and consciousness from that, and consciousness from another consciousness, and the knowable from another knowable. But delimitation is not in reality possible; therefore, delimitation is said to be mere appearance. And that is not real to that extent, for this itself is the ultimate reality of everything that is being produced. Since this very cutting-off from all sides is called delimitation (<s>pariccheda</s>), the capacity to make that appear is the power of exclusion (<s>apohana-śakti</s>). Through this triad of powers, all practical activities [function]. And that triad of powers belongs to the Blessed One alone — for the appearance of <s>Caitra</s>, <s>Maitra</s>, and others whose nature is such as to be experiencers, rememberers, and conceptualizers [is His manifestation]. For it is He alone who knows, remembers, and conceptualizes through each of those forms. As stated by the master himself:

children.text:
{yadyapyarthasthitiḥ prāṇapuryaṣṭakaniyantrite /
jīve niruddhā tatrāpi paramātmani sā sthitā //}
children.translated_text: {Even though the establishment of objects is confined to the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) controlled by <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and <s>puryaṣṭaka</s> (subtle body), even there it rests in the Supreme Self. //}

children.text: ityādi / etāsāṃ ca jñānādiśaktīnām asaṃkhyaprakāro vaicitryavikalpa iti tatsāmarthyaṃ svātantryam aparādhīnaṃ pūrṇaṃ mahadaiśvaryaṃ tannirmitabrahmaviṣṇurudrādyaiśvaryāpekṣayā ucyate / tadevaṃ

children.translated_text: 'Whose body is consciousness' (<s>cidvapuḥ</s>) —
taking this as one, this much has been arrived at:
'Whose form is the universe' (<s>viśvarūpaḥ</s>) —

children.text: iti / tata eva ca pariniṣṭhitaikarūpajaḍabhāvavailakṣaṇyāt jñānādiśaktiyuktatāmāheśvaryam upasaṃprāptaḥ / etadanupagame na kiṃcit idaṃ bhāseta ---- iti prasaṅgaḥ / bhāsate tu , tasmāt etat avaśyāṅgīkartavyam ---- iti prasaṅgaviparyayaḥ / naśyejjanasthitiḥ , yadyevaṃ na syāt ---- iti prāktanena ślokena saha saṃbandhaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. And from that very fact, being distinct from the insentient entity whose single form is fully established, He has attained sovereignty characterized by possession of the powers of knowledge and the rest. If this is not accepted, then nothing whatsoever would manifest — this is the unwanted consequence. But it does manifest; therefore this must necessarily be accepted — this is the reverse of the unwanted consequence. 'The stability of people would perish' — if it were not so — this is the connection with the previous verse.
'If' (<s>cet</s>) —
by this, the reverse [of the stated consequence] is indicated. //7//

And so forth. And the variety of modes of these powers of knowledge and the rest is of innumerable kinds; therefore their capacity — the freedom that is independent, complete, and of great sovereignty — is spoken of in comparison with the sovereignty of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Rudra</s>, and others created by that [Supreme Lord]. Thus —
Thus, auspiciousness! From the beginning, 23 [verses]. //

children.text: iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptaviracitāyāṃ īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinyāṃ jñānādhikāre paradarśanānupapattirnāma tṛtīyamāhnikam // 3 //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the third chapter named 'The Impossibility of Other Views' in the Section on Knowledge, in the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 3 //
Now begins the fourth chapter.
{The multitude of jewels of meaning gathered in the treasury of His own heart,
stringing them with the thread of memory — we praise <s>Śiva</s> with [this] continuous [garland]. //

children.text: evaṃ jñānapūrvikā smṛtiḥ , tadubhayānugrāhiṇī apohanaśaktiḥ ---- iti tāvat vastusaṃbhavakrameṇa pradarśitam / upakramānusāreṇa smṛtireva sūcitaprasaṅgaviparyayasamarthanadṛśā vivecyā /
children.translated_text: Thus, memory is preceded by knowledge, and the power of exclusion assists both — this has been demonstrated in accordance with the order of actual occurrence. Following the introduction, memory itself is to be examined from the perspective of establishing the reverse of the stated consequence.
{'True, but the knowledge that is memory...' /}

children.text: iti hi upakrāntam / tatra saṃskāramātrāt tāvat mā nāma udapādi smṛtiḥ , idaṃ tu vaktavyam ---- tathābhūtabhavadabhyupagatabhagavatprabhāvo'pi katham enāṃ kuryāt ---- iti śaṅkāṃ śamayituṃ smṛtitattvanirūpaṇāya
children.translated_text: Thus it has been introduced. Therein — let memory not arise from mere impression alone; but this must be stated: how could even the power of the Blessed One, of the nature accepted by you, produce it? To dispel this doubt, for the examination of the true nature of memory —
{'For he, as the apprehender of the previously experienced object...' /}
and so forth, up to
{'...the object shines in the knowing subject.' /}

children.text: ityantaṃ ślokāṣṭakam / tatra ślokena svapakṣe smṛtirupapannā ---- iti kathitam / dvitīyena smṛteḥ pūrvānubhavaviṣayīkṛtasvalakṣaṇaprakāśanasāmarthyamuktam / tṛtīyena anubhavena tadviṣayeṇa ca ekībhāvaparyanta āveśaḥ smaraṇasya uktaḥ / turyeṇa anubhavasya na viṣayatayā smṛtyā prakāśanam ---- iti nirūpitam / pañcamena yogijñānamapi anubhavaṃ pṛthagbhāvena na viṣayīkaroti ---- iti baḍatā turyaślokārtha eva upodvalitaḥ / ṣaṣṭhenāśaṅkyamānam anubhavasya smṛtyā pṛthagviṣayīkaraṇaṃ kākpanikam ---- ityavāstavīkṛtam / saptamena smṛtiprasaṅgāt vikalpe'pi pūrvānubhavena aikyātmāveśo darśitaḥ / aṣṭamena smartavyasya smṛteḥ smartuśca ekacittattvaviśrāntiḥ uktā , prasaṅgācca dṛśyasya darśanasya draṣṭuśca ---- iti tātparyārthaḥ / atha krameṇa ślokārtha ucyate /
children.translated_text: — a group of eight verses. Therein, by the [first] verse, it is stated that memory is accounted for on our position. By the second, the capacity of memory to illuminate the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) that was the content of prior experience is stated. By the third, the absorption of memory reaching up to the point of unification with the experience and its object is stated. By the fourth, it is determined that the experience is not illuminated by memory as an object. By the fifth, the meaning of the fourth verse itself is reinforced by the stronger [argument] that even the knowledge of <s>yogins</s> does not objectify experience as a separate entity. By the sixth, the anticipated separate objectification of experience by memory is rendered unreal — as a mere fiction. By the seventh, in connection with memory, the absorption into unity with prior experience is shown even in conceptual construction. By the eighth, the resting of the object to be remembered, the memory, and the rememberer in a single principle of consciousness is stated; and by extension, [the same applies to] the seen, the seeing, and the seer — this is the import. Now the meaning of the verses is stated in order:
For he, the apprehender of the previously experienced object, even though being subsequent [in time],
reflecting [upon it], that autonomous one is designated as 'he remembers.' //
'Of the object that was previously experienced' —
he who is the
'apprehender' (<s>upalabdhā</s>) —
the inward-facing awareness — he, even now,
'subsequently' (<s>parataḥ</s>) —

children.text: smṛtikāle'pi astyeva , saṃvinmātrasvarūpasya kālakṛtasaṃkocarūpaviśeṣātmakāvacchedāyogāt / anubhavasya ca antaḥ artho'pi apṛthagbhāvena avasthitaḥ ---- ityetadapi ayatnasiddham / iyat tu cintyam ---- akālakalite saṃvedane tadantarvartini ca viśvatra bhāvajāte yadi tāvat cinmayatāparāmarśaḥ , tat
children.translated_text: Even at the time of memory, [that content] certainly exists, since the essential nature of mere consciousness (<s>saṃvinmātra</s>) cannot be delimited by a particular form consisting of contraction produced by time. And the fact that the object also subsists within experience in a state of non-difference — this too is established without effort. But this much is to be considered: if, regarding awareness unconditioned by time and the entire host of entities subsisting within it, there is the apprehension of their being of the nature of consciousness (<s>cinmayatā</s>), then

children.text:
iti etāvataiva pūrṇena vimarśena bhāvyam ;
atha idamtayā pṛthagbhāvāvabhāsanena , tathāpi tatra dvayī gatiḥ /
children.translated_text: with just this much, the full awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) is to be realized. But if through manifestation as separate, as 'this,' then even so there are two possibilities.

children.text:
ityaṃśe yadi viśrānyati idantā , tadā ahamidamitisadāśivādidaśayā bhāvyam /
atha na rohati , tat
children.translated_text: if 'this-ness' comes to rest in the aspect of 'I,' then the state is that of <s>Sadāśiva</s> and the like, experienced as 'I am this.' But if it does not take root, then
'this' —

children.text: ityeva ābhāsanena bhavitavyam ; apūrvatābhāsanācca tat anubhavanameva syāt na smaraṇam ---- ityāśaṅgyāha
children.translated_text: there would be manifestation only as 'this'; and since it would be a manifestation of something novel, it would be experience, not memory — anticipating this objection, he says:
<s>svairī</s> (the independent one) —
thus.

children.text: ātmīyam upakaraṇam īrayati svakartavyeṣu avaśyaṃ tacchīlaśca ;

'svam' (oneself) —

<s>svairī</s> —
means independent (<s>svatantra</s>). Therefore, being independent,
'sa' (that) —
