'sa' (that) —

children.text:
iti vimarśanasya ca iyadrūpam ---- yat sarvathā akālakalitasvarūpaparāmarśanameva na ,
nāpi atyantaṃ bhedena vimarśanameva api tu yo bhāvaḥ pūrvamanubhavakāle taddeśakālapramātrantarasācivyena pṛthakkṛto na ca ahantāyāmeva līnīkṛtaḥ , sa tādṛgeva tamaseva ācchādya avasthāpitaḥ saṃskāraśabdavācyaḥ , tasya tamācchādakam apahastayati ; tatra apahastite sa pūrvavat pṛthakkṛte evāvabhāti / nanu ca idantayā avabhāset pūrvavadeva , naivam / tadānīntanāvabhāsanapṛthakkṛtaśarīrādisaṃbandhamanavadhūyaiva hi tatprakāśaḥ ; tataśca idānīntanāvabhāsanasmaraṇakālaparāmarśo'pi na nimīlati iti tatparāmarśabhittiprādhānyena pūrvakālaparāmarśaḥ iti viruddhapūrvāparaparāmarśasvabhāva eva
children.translated_text: and the reflective awareness expressed by 'that' has this nature: it is not entirely an apprehension of one's nature unconditioned by time, nor is it entirely a reflective awareness in complete separation; rather, that entity which at the time of prior experience was differentiated through the accompaniment of the place, time, and another knower of that [experience], and was not dissolved into 'I-ness' alone — it was, as it were, covered by darkness and deposited in a state designated by the word <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression), and [the reflective awareness] pushes aside the covering darkness of that [impression]; when that [covering] is pushed aside, it appears differentiated just as before. But would it not appear as 'this-ness' just as before? No, for its luminosity occurs without shaking off the connection with body and such that was differentiated in that earlier manifestation; and therefore the apprehension of the present time of manifestation — the time of memory — does not close down either; and so the apprehension of the earlier time occurs with the predominance of the wall of present apprehension — thus
'sa' (that) —

children.text: iti parāmarśa ucyate / evaṃ ca sa eva parameśvaraḥ
children.translated_text: this reflective apprehension is said to be of the very nature of apprehending contradictory earlier and later [temporal] aspects. And thus it is the Supreme Lord Himself who
remembers.

children.text: / etadeva hi tasya smartṛtvam ---- yat evaṃprakāraparāmarśocitakālakalādisparśasahiṣṇumāyāpramātṛbhāvaparigrahaḥ iti māyāvidyādvayādvayamayam / tata eva sakalasiddhivitaraṇacaturacintāmaṇiprakhyam āgamikāḥ smaraṇameva mantrādiprāṇitaṃ manyante / tathā ca
children.translated_text: For this is precisely His nature as rememberer — namely, the assumption of the status of a <s>Māyā</s>-knower capable of bearing the touch of time, parts, and the like appropriate to such a mode of apprehension — and thus it consists of the duality-non-duality of <s>Māyā</s> and <s>Vidyā</s>. Therefore, the <s>Āgama</s> (scriptural tradition) followers consider memory itself, animated by <s>mantras</s> and the like, to be like a <s>cintāmaṇi</s> (wish-fulfilling jewel) skilled in bestowing all <s>siddhis</s> (accomplishments). As it is said:
{Memory, having attained the state of meditation and such, being a <s>cintāmaṇi</s>, manifests Your glory.}

children.text: iti / alaṃ tāvat / anena tṛnnantasamāsena yatnato 'nubhavasyārthamukhena kālasparśam arthaviśrāntatāṃ dvayorapi pramātari nirūḍhiṃ bhedābhedābhyāṃ darśayati , vṛtto ekārthībhāvāt / tasya ca bhedābhedamayatvam ---- iti vakṣyāmaḥ //1//
children.translated_text: Thus. Enough for now. By this compound ending in a present participle, he deliberately shows that experience has contact with time through the aspect of the object, and that the object rests in experience, and that both are rooted in the knower, through both difference and non-difference — since in the <s>vṛtti</s> (commentary), being of one meaning [with the verse]. And that it is of the nature of difference-and-non-difference — we shall explain. //1//

children.text: etadeva smṛtitattvamupapādayituṃ ślokāntarāṇi / tatra yadi kaścid brūyāt ---- iha smṛtirvikalpaḥ , na ca anenārthaḥ prakāśyate , arthāsaṃsparśino hi vikalpāḥ , anubhavena ca yena so'rthaḥ prakāśatāṃ nītaḥ sa idānīṃ kīrtimātramūrtirjātaḥ , na ca so'pi smṛtyā prakāśyate ---- jñānasya jñānāntareṇāsaṃvedyatvāt asattvācceti arthasya prakāśanābhāvāt

children.translated_text: 'I remember this' —

children.text: iti jñānaṃ bhrāntimātrameva ---- iti punarapi āpatitam ---- iti , tadā taṃ prati ucyate
children.translated_text: such knowledge is nothing but delusion — thus the [opponent's] objection has been raised again — to that [opponent] it is said:

In order to establish this very truth of memory, further verses [follow]. There, if someone should say: here, memory is a <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), and the object is not illuminated by it, for <s>vikalpas</s> do not contact the object, and the prior experience by which that object was brought to light has now become a mere phantom of fame, and that [experience] too is not illuminated by memory — since a cognition cannot be cognized by another cognition, and since [the prior cognition] is non-existent — and therefore, since the object is not illuminated,
And it illuminates in its own time, apprehending what was previously manifested from the object —
whether its particular characteristic, the mere appearance of a pot, or else in its full nature.

children.text: iha smṛtivikalpe tāvat artho 'vasīyate , anyathā suptamūrcchitakalpatāpatteḥ / evaṃ ca yāvat adhyavasāyo'rthasya tāvat

children.translated_text: 'from the object' —

children.text: iti sāmarthyāt iyat abhyupagantavyam ---- yat so'rthaḥ prakāśate , aprakāśamāne 'dhyavasātavye 'dhyavasāyo'ndhaprāyaḥ syāt / prakāśanaṃ ca na tadānīntanakālasya tyāgena , nāpi dvīkāreṇa , idam ityevāvabhāsanaprasaṅgāt / tasmāt atītānubhavakālaḥ pūrvānubhūtabhāvasvālakṣaṇyākṣepakatvenāpekṣaṇīyo vedyabhāge prakāśātmakāvabhāsābhiniveśitayā , smartṛdehaprāṇādyavabhāsakālaścāvalambanīyo vedakabhāge vimarśāṃśābhiniveśitvena / ābhāsamātraṃ hi bhāvasya svarūpam , pratyābhāsaṃ pramāṇasya vyāpārāt / tadeva ābhāsāntaravyāmiśraṇayā dipasahasraprabhāsaṃmūrcchanavat sphuṭībhavati / ābhāsāntaravyāmiśraṇābhāve 'pi tu kālābhāsasaṃbhedenaiva svālakṣaṇyaṃ tasya ābhāsasya karoti , kālaśaktereva bhedakatvāt iti vakṣyate / evaṃ tāvat svalakṣaṇībhāvaḥ prāktanadehābhāsasācivyābhyuditakālābhāsayā ghaṭābhāsasya iti / tāvatyeva vā smṛtiḥ ābhāsāntarairapi vyāmiśrā atisphuṭeti / atyantasphuṭībhāve 'pi tadānīntanakālatā na truṭyati anyasādhāraṇyānavabhāvāt / tathāvabhāse tu yoginastannirmāṇameva / brahmabhāṣitādau tu navameva avabhāsanam iti / atra tu āgamādimānāntarānubhūtabrahmādisvarūpasmaraṇaparamparā abhyupāyaḥ /
children.translated_text: by implication this much must be conceded — that the object is illuminated; for if what is to be determined is not illuminated, determination would be as though blind. And the illumination is not by abandoning the time of that [prior experience], nor by duplicating it, since then it would appear merely as 'this.' Therefore, the time of past experience must be taken into account as being capable of evoking the particular characteristic of the previously experienced entity, placed within the knowable aspect with its manifestation of the nature of illumination; and the time of manifestation of the rememberer's body, vital breath, and such must be relied upon, placed within the knower aspect in the portion of reflective awareness. For the manifestation alone is the entity's own form, since the operation of a means of knowledge occurs with each manifestation. And that very [manifestation] becomes clear through intermixture with other manifestations, like the merging of the light of a thousand lamps. But even without intermixture with other manifestations, the intermixture with the manifestation of time alone produces the particular characteristic of that manifestation, since it is time-power alone that produces differentiation — as will be stated. Thus, the particular characteristic arises from the manifestation of the pot accompanied by the manifestation of time conjoined with the accompaniment of the prior body-manifestation. Or memory, mixed with other manifestations as well, is to that extent extremely clear. Even in extreme clarity, the character of belonging to the present time is not severed, due to the impossibility of there being no commonality with others. But when the manifestation occurs in that way for a <s>yogin</s> (practitioner), it is nothing but creation by him. In the case of divine speech (<s>brahmabhāṣita</s>) and such, however, it is entirely a new manifestation. But here [in ordinary memory], the succession of remembering the nature of <s>Brahman</s> and the like previously experienced through <s>Āgama</s> (scripture) and other [means] is the method.
'bhāsayet' (it illuminates) —

children.text: iti vidhirūpeṇa niyogena niyamo lakṣyate , na bhāsayati ityetat na , api tu bhāsayatyeva iti /
children.translated_text: by the injunctive form, a rule with the force of necessity is indicated — not that it does not illuminate, but rather that it certainly does illuminate.
'svakāle' (in its own time) —
means at the time of memory.
'āmṛśan' (apprehending) —
the present tense indicates [the aspect] placed within the knower-portion, referring to the present time.
'pūrvābhāsitaṃ svalakṣaṇam' (the particular characteristic previously manifested) —

children.text: iti vedyāṃśasparśī bhūtakālo ghaṭābhāsasyāpi kevalasya svālakṣaṇyāpattiheturdarśitaḥ / iyadeva smṛteḥ avyavhicāri vapuḥ , arthitātiśayāt tu sphuṭatvam iti
children.translated_text: the past tense, touching the knowable aspect, has been shown as the cause of even the mere pot-appearance attaining its particular characteristic. This alone is the invariable nature of memory; but clarity [arises] from the intensity of desire — thus
'atha' (or else) —
this word indicates. He states this very thing:
'akhilātmanā' (in its full nature) —
means with a form intermixed with all manifestations. //2//

Here, first of all, in the <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) of memory, the object is certainly determined; otherwise the absurd consequence of being like one asleep or unconscious would follow. And to the extent that there is determination of the object,

children.text: nanu evaṃ svalakṣaṇasya prakāśane bhedena bahistadavabhāseta / etadeva hi bahiravabhāsanam ---- yat svalakṣaṇaprakāśanam iti śaṅkāśamanāya nirūpayati
children.translated_text: But if the particular characteristic is thus illuminated, it would appear externally, in separation. For external manifestation is precisely this — the illumination of the particular characteristic. To remove this doubt, he determines:

children.text: na ca yuktaṃ smṛterbhede smaryamāṇasya bhāsanam /
children.translated_text: It is not reasonable that in memory, in separation, the remembered should appear;
by that [memory], the unity of cognitions of different times — this is known as 'he, that one.'

children.text: smaraṇajñānāt bhinnatvena bahīrūpatayā yadi so 'rtho bhāseta

children.translated_text: 'of the remembered' —
the
'appearance' —

children.text: tadeva na syāt smaryamāṇameva tat na syāt , anubhūyamānameva tat bhavet iti yāvat / nanu caivaṃ kathaṃ svalakṣaṇasya prakāśanam uktam ? etat na idāṇīṃ prakāśanam api tu pūrvakāle eva , tadā cāsau bahiravabhāsata eva / nanu cedānīṃ tarhi kim ? vimarśanam iti brūmaḥ / nanu prakāśanavimarśanayoḥ bhinnakālatvam āpatitam / tataḥ kim ? ubhayamapi na kiṃcit syāt , anyonyajīvitatvāt asya / maivam , yasya hi saṃvedanānyeva bhinnāni tattvam , tasya idam apratisamādheyameva , asmaddarśane tu bhinnakālā api saṃvidaḥ tatkālātyāgenaiva ekatāvabhāsanena svatantraḥ pramātā yāvadantarmukhatayā tāvatyaṃśe vimṛśati tāvat prakāśasya tātkālikabahirbhāvābhāso vimarśasya idānīntanāntarmukhā sthitiriti / etadeva vedanādhikaṃ veditṛtvaṃ ---- vedaneṣu saṃyojanaviyojanayoḥ yathāruci karaṇaṃ svātantryam , kartṛtvaṃ ca etadeva ucyate / ghaṭamahamanvabhūvam iti vā sa ghaṭaḥ iti vā
children.translated_text: that itself would not exist; it would not be something remembered at all — it would rather be something being experienced — that is the import. But then, how was the illumination of the particular characteristic stated? This is not illumination occurring now, but rather at the prior time itself — and then it did appear externally. But then what is happening now? We say: reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>). But then the difference in time between illumination and reflective awareness has been incurred. What of it? Neither would exist at all, since both depend on each other for their life. Not so — for one whose view is that cognitions are themselves truly distinct entities, this is indeed irresolvable; but in our view, even cognitions of different times, without abandoning their respective times, through appearing as one, the independent knower — to the extent that he reflects inwardly — to that extent the externality of illumination belonging to its time [obtains], and the reflective awareness has its stance of being directed inward at the present — thus. This very thing, being more than mere sensation, is the nature of being a knower — the freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) to conjoin and disjoin sensations as one wishes is called agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>). 'I experienced the pot' or 'that is the pot' —
'unity' —

children.text: anusaṃdhānam anusaṃdhāturabhinnam iti darśayituṃ yadeva aikyaṃ
children.translated_text: reconnection, which is non-different from the reconnector — to show this, the very
'unity is the knower himself' —
has been shown through co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>).
'eṣa saḥ' (this is he) —

children.text: iti ācchāditasyeva pramātṛtattvasya sphuṭāvabhāsanaṃ kṛtam , idam iti , vismayagarbhayānayā uktyā pratyabhijñā eva sūcitā / yadāha granthakāra eva
children.translated_text: a clear manifestation of the principle of the knower that was, as it were, concealed, has been accomplished; 'this' — by this expression pregnant with wonder, <s>pratyabhijñā</s> (recognition) itself has been indicated. As the author of the treatise himself has said:
If, as separate from the cognition of memory, in the form of being external, that object were to appear,
{That principle of the knower which was obscured by those who, denying their own self-awareness, spoke as if [it were absent] —
that has been made manifest through clear reasoning, rendering them silent.}
Thus. //3//

children.text: nanu ca prācya eva anubhavo yadi smaryamāṇasya bahiravabhāsanarūpaḥ prakāśaḥ tarhi iyat ucyatām ---- so'nubhava idānīṃ smaraṇena viṣayīkriyate ---- iti , aikyena tu alaukikena ko'rthaḥ iti vyāmohaṃ vihantumāha
children.translated_text: But if it is the prior experience itself that is the illumination in the form of external manifestation of what is remembered, then let this much be said — that experience is now objectified by memory — and what is the point of unity, which is unordinary? To dispel this confusion, he says:
For the prior experience does not shine in memory separately, like an object;
because of the manifestation of mounting upon the self as 'I previously experienced.'
'pūrvaḥ' (prior) —
the object, such as a pot;
'pṛthak' (separately) —

children.text: iti idantayā bhāti sma naivaṃ smaraṇakāle smṛtijñānāt pṛthaktvena idaṃ pūrvamanubhavanam iti
children.translated_text: it shone as 'this-ness'; not so at the time of memory — as separate from the memory-cognition, 'this is the prior experience' — it does not
shine.

children.text: / yathā ca smṛtikāle tasmāt smṛtijñānāt so'rthaḥ
children.translated_text: And just as at the time of memory, that object does not appear from that memory-cognition in separation, as
'prior' —

children.text: iti pūrvasvabhāvo na bhedena ābhāti , smṛtikāle bahiravabhāsābhāvāt evaṃ tata eva hetoḥ
children.translated_text: that is, as having its prior nature, since there is no external manifestation at the time of memory — similarly, for that very reason,
'even the prior experience' —

children.text: na bhedena ābhāti , kathaṃ tarhi ubhayaṃ bhāti ? anvabhūvam ityevam / etat kimucyate iti cet ,
children.translated_text: does not appear in separation. How then does both [object and experience] appear? As 'I experienced' — in just this way. If [you ask] what is being said here:
the self (<s>ātman</s>), which is of this nature,
'ātmā' —
whose nature is directed inward among prior and subsequent cognitions — there, the
'mounting' —
is the repose [upon the self]; by that cause, of the self-luminous nature of the prior cognition,
'because of appearing' —
even the pot, which is submerged in that [cognition], appears by virtue of belonging to the domain of self-luminosity.
'Mounting upon the self' —

children.text: viśramaṇā anubhavasya arthasya ca / prakṛtipratyayau pratyayārthaṃ saha brūtaḥ ---- iti nyāyāt saṃkhyākṣipte tadvati vā kartṛbhūte 'smadarthe 'nubhavo bruḍitaḥ taddvāreṇa artho'pi ca , na tu svātantryeṇaiva asau , tadarthameva karma na nirdiṣṭam / ghaṭādiḥ punaḥ anubhavakāle na asmadarthamārohati ,
children.translated_text: the repose of both experience and object [in the self]. Since the nominal stem and suffix together express the meaning of the suffix — by this principle, when number is implied or when the referent [of the stem] becomes the agent, in our first-person referent, experience is expressed, and through it the object as well; but the object is not independently [expressed], and therefore has not been designated as the grammatical object.
'hi' (for) —

children.text: yasmāt naiva bhāti pūrvo 'nubhavaḥ pṛthak aparārdhoktāt hetoḥ , tasmāt saṃvidāmaikyam iti pūrveṇa saṃbandhaḥ / luṅā bhūtakālasya dyotitatvāt
children.translated_text: since the prior experience does not at all shine separately, for the reason stated in the second half [of the verse], therefore there is unity of cognitions — this is the connection with the previous [verse]. Since the past tense (<s>luṅ</s>) indicates past time,
'prāk' (before) —
is in different sequence, and in the first person, for the meaning of 'our-referent,'

children.text: ityapi / ārohaṇam iti , ruhiriti aṇijantaḥ ṇijantopi //4//
children.translated_text: likewise. 'Ārohaṇa' (mounting) — 'ruh' is a verbal root forming both <s>aṇij</s> and <s>ṇij</s> derivatives. //4//

children.text: nanu ka evamāha ---- anubhavaḥ pṛthak na bhāti iti , ghaṭavat na bhāti iti cet kiṃ tataḥ ? ghaṭo'pi hi na anubhavasakhyaḥ bhāti iti kiṃ na bhāti ? svabhāvena bhāti iti tu ubhayatrāpi samānam / tathā hi ---- atītānāgatasūkṣmādi yathā yogijñāne viṣayībhavati iti abhyupagatam , tathā paracittamapi
children.translated_text: But who says this — that experience does not shine separately? If [you say] it does not shine like a pot, then what of it? For the pot too does not shine as a companion of experience — does it then not shine? It shines by its own nature — this is the same in both cases. For — just as the past, future, subtle, and so on become objects in the cognition of a <s>yogin</s>, as is accepted, so too does the mind of another —
{Knowledge of the other's mind [comes] from [saṃyama on] the presented idea.} (Yogasūtra 3.19)

children.text: ityādau / tatra jñānavṛttipariṇatameva sattvaṃ cittaśabdenoktam , anyathā pratyayasya saṃyamaviṣayīkāryatvaṃ kathamucyeta , ālambanayogaśca kathaṃ śaṅkayeta

children.translated_text: 'and not with the support' —

children.text: iti / tasmāt parakīyamanubhavanamiva nijamapi viṣayīkriyatām ityāśaṅkya dṛṣṭānta evāsiddhaḥ iti
children.translated_text: thus. Therefore, just as another's experience is made an object, so too let one's own [past experience] be made an object — anticipating this [objection], since the very example is unestablished:
'they appear' —

children.text: ityantena , abhyupagamena vā siddhatve 'pi prakṛte 'rthe viṣamaḥ iti śeṣeṇa darśayati
children.translated_text: — up to this point; even if established by concession, the present matter is unequal — this he shows with the remainder:

and so on. There, it is <s>sattva</s> (the pure constituent) transformed into the state of the cognitive modification that is referred to by the word 'citta' (mind); otherwise, how could it be said that the presented idea is to be made the object of <s>saṃyama</s> (concentrated meditation), and how could the conjunction with a support be doubted —
Even for yogins, the cognitions [of others] do not appear in the perception of another;
they shine having only their own self-awareness as their measure, or they exist in the domain of the knowable.
'Yoginām' (of yogins):
That which is this
'darśanāntara' (perception of another) —
a special knowledge arising from <s>bhāvanā</s> (contemplative practice) and having another's mind as its object — in that,
'dṛśaḥ' (cognitions):

children.text: iti upalabdhayo na bhānti / tathā hi ---- saugatānāṃ tāvat svaprakāśaikarūpaṃ jñānam , tat cet jñānāntareṇa vedyam , tarhi yad asya nijaṃ vapuḥ ananyavedyatayā prakāśanaṃ nāma , na tatprakāśitaṃ syāt / sāṃkhyānāmapi puruṣacchāyaiva upalabdhiḥ , puruṣaśca asaṃvedya parvā iti kathaṃ vedyā syāt / vaiśeṣikāṇāmapi ātmani abhedena samavāyi saṃvedanaṃ paragataṃ manasā kathaṃ gṛhyeta antaḥśarīravṛttinā , taccharīrāntaranupraveśe tu tasyaiva aham iti śarīrīkaraṇāt ahantāvabhāsitatvāt ātmano bhedo vigalet , nityānumeyatvaṃ tu na ātmana upapadyate , jñānasya ca jñānāntaravedyatve 'navasthānādi uktam /
children.translated_text: that is, perceptions, do not shine. For thus: for the Buddhists, cognition is of a single nature of self-luminosity; if that were knowable by another cognition, then what is called its own form — its illumination as not knowable by anything else — would not be illuminated [by that other cognition]. For the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> also, perception is merely the reflection in <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness), and <s>Puruṣa</s> is of a nature that cannot be known — so how could it be known? For the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> also, awareness inhering non-differently in the self — how could it be grasped by the mind (<s>manas</s>) of another that operates within the body, being extrinsic? And if there were entry into another's body, then since that very [body] would be made one's own through 'I'-awareness, the difference of self would dissolve; and permanent inferability of the self is untenable, while the knowability of knowledge by another knowledge leads to infinite regress and so forth — as has been stated.

children.text: tasmāt yoginaḥ paracittavedanāvasare iyān prakāśaḥ ---- etaddehaprakāśasahacārī ghaṭasukhādiprakāśaḥ ---- iti / tatra ghaṭasukhādi idantayā bhāti , tadgatastu prakāśo 'ham ---- ityeva svaprakāśatayā prakāśate / pramātrīkṛtaparadehaprāṇādisamavabhāsasaṃskārāt tu tanniṣṭhām idantām eva prakāśabhāge 'pi manyamāna idaṃ parajñānam iti abhimanyate avigalitasvaparavibhāgo yogī / prāptaprakarṣastu sarvam ātmatvena paśyan svasṛṣṭameva svaparavibhāgaṃ manyate iti jñānasya na yogijñānena prakāśyatā / bhavatu vā tathāpi prakṛtaṃ na etatsamam / tathā hi ---- ayamanubhavati iti paraniṣṭha eva asau anubhave yoginaḥ prakāśaḥ , na tu ahamanubhavāmi iti ātmāroheṇa vartamānaḥ , iha tu anvabhūvam iti ahamaṃśaviśrāntiḥ anālīḍhedaṃbhāvaiva anubhavasya iti yuktamuktam ---- yasmāt anubhavaḥ pṛthak na bhāti tasmāt aikyaṃ bhinnakālānāṃ saṃvidāṃ veditā iti //5//
children.translated_text: Therefore, for the yogin, at the occasion of perceiving another's mind, the cognition is only this much: 'this illumination of pot, pleasure, and such is co-present with the illumination of that body.' Therein, the pot, pleasure, and such appear as 'this-ness,' but the light pertaining to them appears as 'I' in its self-luminous nature. However, due to the latent impression from the co-appearance of another's body, <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), and such which have been made the subject, the yogin who has not dissolved the distinction of self and other, imagining 'this-ness' even in the light-aspect, conceives 'this is another's knowledge.' But the accomplished one, seeing everything as the Self, considers even the distinction of self and other as his own creation — thus knowledge is not illuminated by the yogin's knowledge. Or, even if it were so, still it is not equal to the present case. For thus: 'this one experiences' — the yogin's illumination rests in the other's experience alone, not as 'I experience' through the ascent to the self. But here, 'I experienced' — the resting in the 'I'-aspect, without assuming the 'this'-ness of the experience — therefore it was rightly said: since experience does not appear separately, hence there is unity of cognitions at different times through a single knower. // 5 //

children.text: yadyahaṃabhāvaviśrāntivaśāt anubhavaḥ smṛtau pṛthak na bhāti iti ucyate , tadā parāmarśāntaraṃ sākṣādeva idantayā anubhavaṃ parāmṛśat yadi vā idaṃbhāvocitaghaṭādiviśrāntatām anubhavasya prathayat upalabdham , iti tadanusāreṇāpi kiṃ na vyavahriyate iti parābhiprāyaṃ pratikṣipati
children.translated_text: If it is said that experience does not appear separately in memory due to its resting in the 'I'-aspect, then — a different reflective awareness (<s>parāmarśa</s>) that directly grasps the experience as 'this-ness,' or that reveals the experience as resting in pot and such which are proper to 'this-ness,' is [also] apprehended — so why can one not transact on the basis of that too? — he refutes this view of the opponent:
What is remembered is: 'there was a perception, mine' — even thus, through distinction,
that is merely a grammatical analysis of the memory 'I saw [it].'

children.text: lokasya tāvat evaṃ na saṃvedanam , sa hi na pṛthagbhūtāṃ dṛśaṃ kāṃcit manyate ----

children.translated_text: 'There was a perception, mine' —
in this way. And even so,
'what is remembered' —

children.text: evaṃbhūtamapi yat smaraṇaṃ kasyacit vivecakaṃmanyasya , tat smṛtervyākaraṇam , padasyeva prakṛtipratyayārthanirūpaṃaṃ kālpanikaṃ vibhajya ākaraṇaṃ paratra pratipādanamātram / so 'pi yadi mūlapratīti vedayate pūrvoktakrameṇa , tadā anubhavaṃ pṛthagbhūtaṃ na veda , yata eva tat rāhoḥ śiraḥ itivat kalpitaṃ bhedaṃ manyate / anyathā sa ghaṭaḥ itivat
children.translated_text: even such a memory, if it belongs to some analytical mind, is a grammatical analysis of memory — just as a word's analysis into stem and affix meaning is an artificial division, a mere presentation to others. If even that [analytical person] experiences the root awareness in the previously described manner, then he does not know the experience as separate, which is precisely why he considers that separation as artificial, like 'the head of <s>Rāhu</s>.' Otherwise, just as in 'that pot,'
'that perception' —

children.text: ityatrāpi prāktanaṃ dṛgantaram apekṣaṇīyaṃ syāt / tat ityanena hi ghaṭasya vā dṛśo vā pūrvānubhavaviṣayāpattiḥ ucyate , anyathā dṛk ityeva syāt / tataśca dṛk mayā dṛgantareṇa anubhūtā iti āpatet / tatrāpi tathātve 'navasthā / nanu smṛteḥ maulikaṃ kiṃ rūpam ? ucyate ---- mayā dṛṣṭam iti / nanu atra dayitāvadananalinādiviśrāntaṃ darśanam uktam na tu ātmārūḍham , karmaṇi niṣṭhotpatteḥ / sa eṣa svavācameva na cetayati / kartuḥ kriyayā hi āpyaṃ karma iti dṛśikriyāyāḥ kartṛniṣṭhataiva / tathā ca kartṛsthāmeva dṛśikriyāmāhuḥ
children.translated_text: here too one would have to expect a prior perception-other [to establish 'that-ness']. For by the word 'that,' the falling of the pot or the perception into the domain of prior experience is stated; otherwise, one would simply say 'perception.' And then it would follow: 'the perception was experienced by me through another perception.' And there too, in that case, there would be an infinite regress. But what is the fundamental form of memory? It is said: 'I saw [it].' Now, here 'seeing' is said to rest in the beloved's face, lotus, and such [objects], not as ascended to the self, because the participial form is derived from the object. This person does not understand his own words. For the object is to be reached by the agent through action — hence the verb 'to see' (<s>dṛś</s>) rests in the agent. And indeed, they say that the action of seeing rests in the agent:
'The king shows [to] the servants' —

children.text: ityādau / jaiminīyairapi jñānarūpā dṛśiḥ bhāvanātmikā pramātṛviśrāntaiva uktā , kevalaṃ prakaṭatā viṣayadharmo dṛṣṭatākhyā , anyā saṃvit vā'svatantrā iti anyat etat / pramātṛviśrāntatvameva kathayituṃ mayā ityuktam / tena anvabhūvamaham , mayānubhūtam iti śabdavaicitryamātramidam , na tu arthabhedaḥ / anye tu bhinnakramatvena yojayanti ---- dṛk āsīt sā me ityevam , mayā dṛṣṭam iti ca yat smaraṇaṃ
children.translated_text: in such [usage]. According to the <s>Jaiminīyas</s> also, seeing (<s>dṛśi</s>), being of the nature of knowledge, having the nature of <s>bhāvanā</s> (contemplative force), is stated to rest in the subject alone; only the manifestness is a property of the object, called 'having been seen,' while another consciousness is dependent — but that is a separate matter. To express precisely the resting in the subject, 'by me' (<s>mayā</s>) is said. Therefore, 'I experienced,' 'it was experienced by me' — this is merely a variation in expression, not a difference in meaning. Others, however, construe it differently in sequence: 'there was a perception, that, mine' — thus, and the memory 'I saw [it]'
'is the grammatical analysis of that' —

children.text: iti anantaroktānvabhūvamityucitaparāmarśāyāḥ smṛteḥ iti / apiḥ cārthe //6//
children.translated_text: namely, of the memory whose proper reflective awareness is the just-mentioned 'I experienced.' The word 'api' is used in the conjunctive sense. // 6 //
For ordinary people, experience is not like that at all, for they do not consider any separate perception —

children.text: nanu dṛṣṭamapi nirvikalpakena yāvat na parāmṛṣṭaṃ vimarśaviśeṣaviśrāntyā tāvat na smaryate mārgadṛṣṭamiva tṛṇaparṇādi viśeṣeṇa rūpeṇa , tadidameva vicāraṇīyam , samanantarabhāvivikalpakāle taddarśanam idantayā avabhātapūrvaṃ vā na vā iti , tadetat āśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Now, even what has been seen by non-conceptual [perception], as long as it has not been reflectively grasped through a specific <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness), is not remembered — like grass, leaves, and such seen on a road, in their specific form. This very point is to be investigated: at the time of the immediately subsequent <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition), has the seeing previously appeared as 'this-ness' or not? Anticipating this, he says:
And the determination 'I see this,' 'this is a pot' —
even that considers the seeing as co-present with the determiner.

children.text:
iha darśanaṃ yādṛśaṃ nijena vapuṣā tādṛśenaiva tena bhātavyaṃ sarvadā , tacca svakāle'nanyaprakāśam aham ityetāvatā svarūpeṇa ucitaprakāśam , tadvikalpāṃśavicāraḥ tāvat na kutracit aṅgam , bhavatu vāṅgam , kiṃ tu avasāyo 'pi evaṃbhūtaḥ iti apiśabdena sūcayati / tatra samanantarabhāvinā vikalpena vastu parāmṛśyamānam anubhavaparāmarśamukhena vā parāmṛśyate ahamimaṃ paśyāmi iti vartamānatayā , imam ityanena ca pratyakṣavyāpāratvaṃ pratyakṣāyamāṇatvena darśitam / evameva vā parāmṛśyate ---- ghaṭo'yam iti / atra ayaṃśabdena pratyakṣāyamāṇatvamuktam / tatra antye vikalpe darśanasya pṛthak parāmarśa eva nāsti iti kā tatra idantāśaṅkā / tataśca pāriśeṣyāt ahantayā tasya atrāsti parāmarśaḥ , tadabhāve vikalpasya nimīlitākṣe 'pi bhāvāt svayamarthasparśe sati sphuṭamaviṣayaparyavasitaḥ kathamadhyavasāyo bhavet / ādye tu darśanaṃ parāmṛṣṭamapi asmadarthe 'ntarbhūtam ahaṃbhāvāspadam avasātari viśrāntaṃ svaprakāśameva parāmṛṣṭam iti vikalpo'pi na bodhāntarabodhyatāṃ bodhayati bodhasya /
avasāyaḥ avasā , samavetam iti apṛthagbhāvamāha / avasātari iti , svatantre'ntarmukhe bodhātmani ahantāspade ityarthaḥ / darśanam iti nirvikalpakamanubhavanam / upalakṣaṇaṃ caitat vikalpasmṛtyāderapi , jñānasya jñānāntareṇa parāmarśe hi ayameva nyāyaḥ / vikalpayāmyaham , smarāmyaham , vikalpitaṃ mayā , smṛtaṃ mayā iti ahantārūḍhyaiva vikalpādeḥ avabhāsāt / ata eva ātmano'mī vikalpādyāḥ śaktiviśeṣāḥ tadviśrāntaśarīratvāt iti darśitam

children.translated_text: 'He who possesses the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion' —
in that [verse]. // 7 //

Here, seeing, just as it is in its own nature, must always appear in that very form; and in its own time, being not illuminated by anything else, its proper illumination is just 'I' — thus far, the investigation of the <s>vikalpa</s> aspect is not relevant anywhere. But even if it were relevant, the determination too is of this very nature — this he indicates with the word 'api.' Therein, when an object is reflectively grasped by the immediately subsequent <s>vikalpa</s>, it is grasped either through the reflective grasp of experience — as 'I see this,' in the present tense, where 'this' shows the operation and being-perceived of direct perception — or it is grasped in this way: 'this is a pot.' Here, by the word 'this,' being-perceived is stated. In this latter <s>vikalpa</s>, there is simply no separate reflective grasp of seeing — so what suspicion of 'this-ness' can there be? And therefore, by elimination, seeing is reflectively grasped here with 'I-ness.' Without that, since <s>vikalpa</s> would occur even with closed eyes, and when contact with the object is present, how could a determination clearly terminate in a non-object be possible? In the former case, seeing, even when reflectively grasped, is included within the 'I'-sense, resting in the self-dependent determiner as the locus of 'I'-awareness — it is grasped as self-luminous. Thus even <s>vikalpa</s> does not reveal the knowability of cognition by another cognition.
'Avasāyaḥ' as 'avasā' — 'samavetam' means non-separately. 'Avasātari' means in the self-dependent, inward-facing, awareness-natured locus of 'I'-awareness. 'Darśanam' means non-conceptual experience. And this is illustrative also of <s>vikalpa</s>, memory, and so on — for when cognition is reflectively grasped by another cognition, this same reasoning applies. 'I conceptualize,' 'I remember,' 'conceptualized by me,' 'remembered by me' — since <s>vikalpa</s> and the like appear only through their ascent to 'I'-awareness. Hence, these — <s>vikalpa</s> and the rest — are specific powers of the Self, because their body rests in that [Self]. This has been shown
Having thus [established this much], in order to summarize the fruit of this much of the provable, he says:
Therefore, 'it is seen by me,' 'this was seen,' 'that' — he reflectively grasps thus;
the two meanings — non-different from the graspable (<s>grāhya</s>) and grasper (<s>grāhaka</s>) — shine in the knower.
'Tat' (therefore):

children.text: iti tasmādarthe pūrvoktasya prameyasya hetubhāvena upajīvanam iha sūcayati / yata evamuktam ---- anubhavasya arthasyeva smaraṇāt na bhedena avabhāsaḥ smrṭiśaktiśca parameśvarasyaiva , tata idamatra pariniṣṭhitaṃ tattvam iti / iha smṛtiḥ anubhavaṃ kroḍīkaroti ityuktam / anubhavaśca dvidhā , ---- parāmarśabhedāt kadācit svātmaparāmarśapūrvakam anubhāvyam parāmṛśati yatra asya abhisaṃdhipradhānatā
children.translated_text: By 'therefore,' the dependence of the previously stated provable in the role of a reason is indicated here. Since it has been stated thus — from the remembering of experience just like the object, there is no appearance of [experience] as separate, and the power of memory belongs to the Supreme Lord alone — therefore this is the established truth here. Here it is said that memory encompasses experience. And experience is of two kinds, through the distinction of reflective awareness: sometimes one reflectively grasps the object to be experienced with a prior reflective awareness of the self, wherein the predominance of intention [is present] —
'It is seen by me' —

children.text: iti , kadācit anubhavanīyameva pradhānatayā parāmṛśati yatra anabhisaṃdhereva sahasā vastūpanipātaḥ , arthakriyāṃ prati āgrahaviśeṣo vā
children.translated_text: thus; and sometimes one reflectively grasps primarily only the object to be experienced, wherein there is a sudden encounter with the object without prior intention, or a particular eagerness toward effective action —
'This' —

children.text: iti , tatrāpi ca prakāśaparāmarśo 'styeva , anyathā prakāśāyogāt / evamubhayathānubhave pratyekaṃ smṛtirapi dvayaparāmarśamayī udeti iti catvāraḥ smaraṇabhedāḥ , dvau anubhavabhedau / anusaṃdhānaṃ pratyabhijñānamapi etadubhayamelanātmakam atraivāntarbhūtam / tacca etadbhedāt aṣṭadhā , pūrvāparaviśrāntikṛtāt pratyekaṃ dvidhābhedācca ṣoḍaśadhā / tadete dvāviṃśatiḥ saṃvedanabhedāḥ / teṣu ca grāhyaṃ tāvat prakāśāt abahirbhūtam , anyathā prakāśanāyogāt , bahirbhūtaṃ ca tat , anyathārthatvāsaṃbhavāt , na ca tata eva , tadaiva , tadevāpṛthagbhūtaṃ atra pṛthagbhūtaṃ ca bhavati iti nūnamanyaḥ kalpitaprakāśātmā kaścit atra artho 'sti , yato 'yam artharāśiḥ pṛthagbhavan anyonyamapi pṛthaktām adhigacchet , anyathā prakāśābhinnānāṃ parasparamapi kathaṅkāraṃ pṛthagbhāvo bhavet / so 'yaṃ vedyaikadeśa eva , vicchinna eva , anujjhitavedyabhāva eva , aham iti vicchedaśūmyaprakāśocitena parāmarśena parāmṛśyamāno māyāpramātā iti vakṣyate {dehe buddhau ...................... /}(Ipv_1,6.4) ityatra / sa ca grāhaka iti ucyate / evaṃ samameva svātmani nirmalamakurasthānīye yat yugalakaṃ svasmāt prakāśarūpāt avyatiriktam avabhāsayati parameśvaraḥ tadeva etat bhagavato jñānakartṛtvaṃ smaraṇakartṛtvaṃ jñānaśaktismṛtiśaktirūpam ucyate iti tātparyārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus; and even there, a reflective awareness of luminosity does exist, for otherwise there would be no illumination. Thus, for each of the two kinds of experience, memory also arises as composed of the reflective awareness of both — hence there are four divisions of memory and two divisions of experience. Recognition (<s>anusaṃdhāna</s>) and re-cognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) too, being of the nature of the fusion of both, are included here. And these, through [the distinction of] these divisions, are eightfold; and through the twofold division resulting from resting in the prior or the subsequent, they are sixteenfold. Thus there are twenty-two divisions of awareness. And therein, the graspable (<s>grāhya</s>) is not external to luminosity, for otherwise there would be no illumination; and yet it is external, for otherwise it would not have the status of being an object. Since it is not the case that the very same, non-separate [entity] here becomes separate there, surely there is some other, fabricated-luminosity entity here as the object; for otherwise, this mass of objects, becoming separate [from luminosity], would attain mutual separateness as well; otherwise, for things non-different from luminosity, how could there be mutual separateness? This very [entity], being merely a portion of the knowable, being delimited, not having abandoned its status as knowable — when reflectively grasped through the reflective awareness proper to the luminosity devoid of limitation as 'I,' that is the <s>Māyā</s>-subject — as will be stated in {in the body, in the intellect... /} (<s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.6.4). And that is called the grasper (<s>grāhaka</s>). Thus, the pair that the Supreme Lord simultaneously manifests as non-different from His own luminous nature in His own pure-mirror-like Self — that alone is called the Lord's authorship of knowledge and authorship of memory, which is of the nature of <s>jñāna-śakti</s> (power of knowledge) and <s>smṛti-śakti</s> (power of memory): this is the purport.

children.text: akṣarārthastu ---- mayā dṛśyate iti , ayam iti ca yat āmṛśati pramātā prakāśarūpo yena anubhavati iti ucyate , tata āmarśanāt etat lakṣyate , grāhyarūpeṇa grāhakarūpeṇa yojitau ghaṭādidehādisvabhāvau arthau vedyau pramātari viśuddhaprakāśarūpe bhātaḥ prakāśete / evaṃ dṛṣṭaḥ iti sa iti ca yat parāmṛśati prakāśarūpaḥ pramātā , yato 'sau smarati iti vyapadeśyaḥ / tato 'pi etadeva lakṣyate / anubhavarūpopajīvitvaṃ pūrvoktaṃ draḍhayituṃ prasaṅgāt atra jñānaśakterapi unmīlanaṃ kṛtam / lakṣaṇe śatrādeśaḥ / apiśabdaścārthe / arthaśabdo vicchinnavedyavācī / grāhako māyīyaḥ kalpitaḥ pramātā aśuddhaprakāśasvabhāvaḥ iti śivam / āditaḥ ślo. 31//
children.translated_text: As for the literal meaning: 'it is seen by me' and 'this' — that which the knower, whose nature is luminosity, reflectively grasps, whereby he is said to 'experience' — from that reflective grasping, this is indicated: the two meanings — having the nature of pot and such (as the graspable) and body and such (as the grasper) — shine, that is, are illuminated, in the knower whose nature is pure luminosity. Likewise, 'was seen' and 'that' — that which the luminous knower reflectively grasps, whereby he is designated as 'one who remembers' — from that too, this very same [conclusion] is indicated. The dependence on experience, stated earlier, is here confirmed incidentally through the unfolding of <s>jñāna-śakti</s> (power of knowledge) as well. The <s>śatṛ</s> suffix is used in the sense of definition. The word 'api' is in the conjunctive sense. The word 'artha' (meaning) denotes the delimited knowable. The <s>grāhaka</s> (grasper) is the <s>Māyic</s>, constructed knower whose nature is impure luminosity. Thus, may there be auspiciousness. // From the beginning, [this covers] verses 31. //

children.text: iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptaviracitāyāṃīśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinyāṃ prathame jñānādhikāre smṛtiśaktinirūpaṇaṃ nāma caturthamāhnikam // 4 //
children.translated_text: Thus concludes the fourth chapter (<s>āhnika</s>), entitled 'Examination of the Power of Memory' (<s>smṛtiśaktinirūpaṇa</s>), in the Knowledge Section (<s>jñānādhikāra</s>) of the <s>Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 4 //
Now begins the fifth chapter (<s>āhnika</s>).
{He who illuminates the multitude of entities immersed in the great cave [of ignorance],

children.text: jñānaśaktipradīpena yaḥ sadā taṃ stumaḥ śivam //}
children.translated_text: with the lamp of the power of knowledge (<s>jñānaśakti</s>) — Him, <s>Śiva</s>, who is ever [such], we praise. //}

children.text: ityantayā ślokaikaviṃśatyā nirūpayati / tatrādyeva ślokena vastuni pratijñāṃ karoti evaṃbhūtā jñānaśaktiḥ iti / tataḥ ślokadvayena prakāśa evārthānāṃ svarūpa, ityāha / tato dvayena prakāśabāhyānāmarthānāṃ sadbhāvaṃ vijñānavādyupagatavāsanādūṣaṇena dṛḍhīkṛtam āśaṅkya , tṛtīyena tadanabhyupagame 'pi tāvat na kiñcit uparudhyata iti darśayati / atha ślokena svadarśane 'rthatattvam upadarśayan bāhyārthasadbhāve pratyakṣaṃ parākaroti pramāṇatvena / tato dvayena anumeyatāmapi bāhyasya nirasyati / anantaraṃ ślokena cidātmani arthānām avaśyaṃ sadbhāvaḥ parāmarśātmanā iti prakaṭayati / tato 'pi prakāśasya pramātṛrūpasya pratyavamarśa eva jīvatam iti ślokacatuṣṭayena anubhavāgamanyāyasvarūpanirūpaṇābhiḥ abhidhatte / anantaraṃ jñānaparāmarśa eva jñeyaṃ śuddhaṃ pramātṛrūpatānujjhitaṃ ca prakṣayati iti tasyaiva pradhānatve nyāyaṃ ślokatrayeṇāha / prakāśaikarūpatve ca jñānajñātrādi bhinnam iti ślokenāha / tato jñātari iva viśuddhe jñāne 'pi avikalpakasavikalpakarūpe vimarśa eva prāṇitam iti ślokadvayenāha / tato jñāturjñānasya ca pūrvapakṣe dūṣi / yat bhinnatvaṃ tat upasaṃhāradiśā ślokena samarthayate , iti tātparyam āhnikasya / ślokārthastu nirūpyate /
children.translated_text: ending with this — he establishes it through twenty-one verses. Therein, with the very first verse he makes a thesis regarding the reality: 'such is the power of knowledge.' Then, in two verses, he states that the very nature of things is luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>). Then, in two verses, having anticipated the objection — strengthened by the refutation of the <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions) accepted by the idealist (<s>vijñānavādin</s>) — that the external existence of things devoid of luminosity [is established], in a third verse he shows that even without accepting that, nothing is obstructed. Then, in one verse, while showing the nature of objects in his own system, he sets aside direct perception as a valid means for [establishing] the real existence of external objects. Then, in two verses, he also negates the inferability of the external. Next, in one verse, he reveals that objects necessarily exist in the consciousness-self through reflective awareness (<s>parāmarśa</s>). Then, that the life-breath of luminosity, which is of the nature of the perceiver, is precisely self-reflective awareness — this he states in four verses through the examination of experience, scripture, reasoning, and their essential nature. Next, that in the reflective awareness that is knowledge itself, the knowable is pure and does not abandon its nature as the perceiver — this he states in three verses, setting forth the reasoning for its primacy. And that in the unity of luminosity, knowledge, knower, and such are differentiated — this he states in one verse. Then, that in pure knowledge too, just as in the knower, whether non-conceptual or conceptual in form, reflective awareness alone is the life-principle — this he states in two verses. Then, the defect in the opponent's position regarding the separateness of knower and knowledge — he supports this in a verse in the direction of summary: such is the purport of the chapter. The meaning of the text is now examined.

Thus far, the essential nature of the power of memory has been established. Now, extending the definitive determination of the ultimate reality of the power of knowledge, which is to be relied upon by that [power of memory],

children.text: nanu smaraṇavikalpādīnām anubhava eva jīvitam , tatra yadi bhedena ābhāsānte 'rthāḥ tat teṣvapi tathaiva avabhāsa ucitaḥ , no cet anyathā , tadanubhava eva tāvat jñānaśaktirūpo vicāraṇīya ityāśayenāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Experience alone is the life of memory, conceptual construction, and such; if objects appear therein as distinct, then they should appear in those [memories, etc.] in the same way; if not, then otherwise. Therefore, experience itself, being of the nature of the power of knowledge, is to be examined — with this intention he says:
The manifestation of entities that are manifesting as present
is possible only for those that exist within, through the medium of externality.

children.text: vartamānatvena sphuṭatayā avabhāsanam idamityevamākāraṃ yeṣāṃ teṣām , yadetat

children.text: pramāṇena upapadyate , tena anujjhitasaṃvidabhedasya bhāvasya kalpitapramātrapekṣayā bhedena prakāśanaṃ bhagavato jñānaśaktirityuktaṃ bhavati //1//
children.translated_text: is established by valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>). Therefore, it is stated that the manifestation of an entity — whose non-difference from consciousness has not been abandoned — as differentiated, with reference to a postulated perceiver, is the Lord's power of knowledge (<s>jñānaśakti</s>). //1//
Of those whose manifestation is vivid, in the form of 'this' — that is, of those manifesting as present — this
Having said 'it is established by valid cognition,' he shows that valid cognition:
As before, the object would be non-luminous without having the nature of luminosity;

children.text: na ca prakāśo bhinnaḥ syādātmārthasya prakāśatā //
children.translated_text: and luminosity is not separate — the luminosity of the object is its very self.

children.text: artho nīlādiḥ , tasya nīlādirūpataiva yadi prakāśamānatā na punaḥ sāparā kācit arthaśarīrottīrṇā prakāśātmatā tarhi yathā sarvān prati nīlameva tatsaṃbhāvanayā bhaṇyate , na kaṃcit vā prati , vastuto vā svātmanyeva tat nīlaṃ parasya paraniṣṭhatvānupapatteḥ , svātmani vā na nīlaṃ na anīlam prakāśānugraheṇa vinā vyavasthānāyogāt / tathā prakāśamānatāpi asya sarvān prati na kaṃcit vā prati api tu svātmanyeva , svātmanyapi vā na syāt iti andhatā jagataḥ /
children.translated_text: The object is blue and such. If its being manifested is nothing but its being of blue and such form, and not something else — some luminous nature that transcends the body of the object — then, just as blue is posited as blue for everyone, or for no one at all, or in truth only in itself — since the belonging of something to another that is established in another is untenable — so too in itself it is neither blue nor non-blue, since without the favor of luminosity no determination is possible. Similarly, its state of being manifested would also be for everyone, or for no one, or only in itself — or even in itself it would not be — and so the world would be blind.

children.text: atha indriyālokādikṣaṇavargāt prakāśarūpo 'sau nīlakṣaṇo viśiṣṭa eva jātaḥ , evamapi sa eva prasaṅgaḥ , prakaṭatāvāde 'pi ayameva doṣaḥ , sarvathā arthaśarīraviśrāntaḥ cet prakāśo mama avabhāsate iti pramātṛlagnatayā prakāśasthitiḥ durupapādā / pramātā hi tadānīm indriyādimayo 'rtharūpaprakāśasya kāraṇaṃ bhavet bījamivāṅkurasya / na ca aṅkuro bījāpekṣo 'ṅkurātmā , tato yadi na prakāśātmā sa syāt

children.translated_text: 'prāgiva' (as before):

children.text: jñānodayāt pūrvaṃ yathā'sāvaprakāśaḥ tathā jñānodaye 'pi syāt / nanu jñānam arthaprakāśarūpameva , tat kathaṃ jñānasya udayānudayayoḥ arthasya tulyatā syāt / syāt etat yadi upapadyet , yāvatā arthāt bhinnaṃ yat jñānaṃ prakāśarūpam , tat arthasya saṃbandhitayā kathaṃ syāt / yadi tāvat arthaḥ prakāśate ityevaṃbhūtaṃ jñānasya svarūpaṃ tat arthajñānayoḥ abheda evāyātaḥ , arthasvabhāvasya jñānatvena uktatvāt , arthasvabhāvatve ca sati prakāśasya arthātmatāyām uktaṃ dūṣaṇam / atha arthaṃ prakāśayati iti jñānasya svarūpam , tarhi prakāśamānamarthaṃ karoti jñānam iti āpatite punarapi sa eva doṣaḥ / kṛtapratānaśca ayaṃ prakṛtyarthaṇyarthaviveko mayaiva bhedavidāraṇe iti tata eva anveṣyaḥ / tasmāt bhinnaḥ prakāśo 'rthasya saṃbandhī bhavati iti saṃbhāvanaiva nāsti / tacca idam upapattyā āyātam ---- arthasya svarūpaṃ prakāśamānatā prakāśābhinnatvam iti / prakāśaśca yadi ghaṭe 'nyaḥ paṭe 'nyaḥ tadā anusaṃdhānasya ayogaḥ , dvayoḥ prakāśayoḥ svātmamātraparyavasānād iti vitatya upapāditaṃ
children.translated_text: just as before the arising of knowledge, it was non-luminous, so too it would remain even at the arising of knowledge. Objection: knowledge is precisely of the nature of illuminating the object — so how can there be sameness of the object whether knowledge arises or not? That might be so if it could be established; but a knowledge that is separate from the object and is of the nature of luminosity — how could it be related to the object? If the essential nature of knowledge is such that 'the object is illuminated,' then the non-difference of object and knowledge is arrived at, since the essential nature of the object has been declared to be knowledge; and if luminosity, while being of the nature of the object, is the object's own self, the previously stated objection applies. If the essential nature of knowledge is that 'it illuminates the object,' then since knowledge makes the object manifest, the same fault arises again. This exploration of the distinction between object and luminosity has been extensively treated by me in the <s>Bhedavidāraṇa</s> — it should be sought there. Therefore, the very supposition that a separate luminosity could be related to the object does not hold. And this has been arrived at through reasoning: the essential nature of the object is its being-manifested, which is non-difference from luminosity. And if luminosity were one thing in the pot and another in the cloth, then connected awareness would be impossible, since each of the two luminosities would terminate in itself alone — this has been established at length
'naśyet janasthitiḥ' (the life of beings would perish):

children.text: ityatra / tasmāt eka eva prakāśaḥ / etadeva āvṛttyā darśitaṃ
children.translated_text: in that context. Therefore, luminosity is one alone. This very thing is shown again:
'na ca prakāśo bhinnaḥ syāt' (and luminosity cannot be separate):
thus. //2//

If, however, from the aggregate of conditions such as sense organs, light, and such, that thing of the nature of blue arises as qualified with luminosity — even so, the same consequence follows. Even in the theory of manifestation (<s>prakaṭatāvāda</s>), this same fault applies. In every case, if luminosity rests in the body of the object, the position that luminosity exists as attached to the perceiver — 'it appears to me' — is difficult to establish. For the perceiver, at that time, being constituted by sense organs and such, would be the cause of the luminosity of the object's form, like a seed of a sprout. But the sprout, depending on the seed, is not of the nature of the seed. Therefore, if it is not of the nature of luminosity,
Even accepting that knowledge, which is separate [from the object], has the nature of illuminating objects, he states another invalidating argument:

children.text: bhinne prakāśe cābhinne saṃkaro viṣayasya tat /
children.translated_text: If luminosity is separate, there would be confusion of objects; and if non-separate, then
the object to be illuminated would be of the nature of luminosity — and a non-luminous [object] cannot be established.

children.text: yadi arthāt anya eva jñānātmā prakāśaḥ ata eva bhinno 'rthataḥ tarhi svātmani tasya prakāśamātrarūpatvāt abheda eva / tathā hi nīlasya prakāśaḥ , pītasya prakāśaḥ iti yo nīlāṃśaḥ pītāṃśaśca , sa na tāvat jñānasya svarūpam bhedavādatyāgāpatteḥ / atha viṣayaḥ , tadevedaṃ vicāryate ---- iha prakāśabalāt nīlapītayoḥ bhedo 'bhyupagantavyaḥ , yenaiva ca prakāśena nīlo nīla eva iti upagamyate , tenaiva ca prakāśena pītaḥ pīta iti kathaṃ saṃgacchatām , nīlena janitaḥ , pītena janitaḥ , tena vā saha samānasāmagrīka ityādi yat ucyate tat siddhe nīlapītayorbhede syāt , sa eva vicāryaḥ / atha nīlākāro 'sau tat yadi pratibimbabalāt taddvitīyabimbānavabhāsāt ayuktam / atha abhedaḥ , tarhi tyakto bhedavādaḥ , tathā karaṇatādivāde śikharasthajñānaṃ bahutaranīlādijanyam ekatra paṭu anyatra mandam iti kathaṃ bhedaḥ prakāśaśarīrasya abhedāt / tathābhūte ca anyataradarśanodbhūte 'pi saṃskāre balādeva aśeṣasmaraṇaprasaṅga iti bhūyān saṅkaraḥ / syādetat , artha evāstu , kimanena doṣāpādakena prakāśena iti / atrāha ---- aprakāśasya prasiddhireva na kācit , svātmani hi nīlaṃ yadi pūtaṃ na kiṃcit vā , tat kiṃ duṣyet , ata eva granthakṛtaiva anyatra uktam
children.translated_text: If luminosity, being of the nature of knowledge, is indeed other than the object, and therefore different from the object, then in itself it is non-different, since it has the sole nature of luminosity. For the blue portion and the yellow portion in 'the luminosity of blue' and 'the luminosity of yellow' are not the essential nature of knowledge, since that would entail abandoning the doctrine of difference. If they are the content, then this is precisely what is being examined: here, by the power of luminosity, the difference of blue and yellow must be accepted; but how can the same luminosity by which blue is accepted as blue also [be that by which] yellow is accepted as yellow? 'Produced by blue,' 'produced by yellow,' or 'sharing the same aggregate of conditions with one or the other' — all such statements would be valid only if the difference of blue and yellow were already established, and that very thing is under examination. If it has the form of blue, then by the force of reflection, the non-manifestation of a second image would make it untenable. If there is non-difference, then the doctrine of difference is abandoned. Similarly, in the theory of causation by instruments, the knowledge at the apex, being produced by many blues and such, being sharp with respect to one and dull with respect to another — how can there be difference, given the non-difference of the luminosity-body? And in such a state, even when an impression arises from seeing one thing, there would necessarily follow the remembering of everything — thus the confusion would be great. It might be said: let the object alone be [sufficient] — what need is there of this luminosity that only produces faults? To this he replies: there is no establishment whatsoever of what is non-luminous; for if blue is purified in itself, or is nothing, what harm is there? Hence the author of the treatise himself has said elsewhere:
{Thus, these [entities], which are like non-existents in themselves, belong to luminosity alone;
the inert [entities] — luminosity alone exists, of its own nature, for itself and for others. //}

children.text: iti / tat yadi prakāśaḥ tadā bhavati arthaḥ , prakāśaśca asau katham / yadi prakāśataiva ghaṭasya vapuḥ saiva paṭasya ityādi viśvavapuḥ prakāśaḥ siddhaḥ //3//
children.translated_text: Thus. If there is luminosity, then the object exists; and how is it luminosity? If the luminosity of a pot is its very form, and that same [luminosity] is the form of a cloth — then luminosity is established as having the form of the universe. //3//

children.text: ekasyaiva prakāśasya evaṃbhūtakramākramakāryakāraṇabhāvādivicitravaiśvarūpyapradarśanasāmarthyarūpam aiśvaryam ityetāvat paryavasāyayitavyam / taccaivaṃ paryavasyati , yadi prakāśasya vicitrabhāve hetvantaram apākṛtam / tatra prakāśasya avicitrasya krameṇa vicitratākāraṇaṃ pratibimbātmakaṃ tatpratibimbasajātīyaṃ yat tadeva nīlādirūpaṃ bāhyam , tacca yadyapyanumeyam , tathāpi idaṃ nīlamiti pratyakṣeṇa adhyavasāyāt adhyavasāyaprāṇitatvācca pramāṇasthiteḥ pratyakṣavyapadeśyaṃ bhaviṣyati / bāhyārthavādokathitamiti hetvantaram anumīyamānabāhyarūpam āśaṅkyamānatvena darśayati
children.translated_text: That the sovereignty whose nature is the capacity to display the wonderful variety of sequential and non-sequential, cause-and-effect relations and such, belongs to one single luminosity — this much is to be concluded. And it concludes thus if another cause of the variety of luminosity is set aside. Therein, for luminosity which is without variety, the external, which is of the nature of reflection and is of the same kind as that reflection and is itself of the form of blue and such — that is the cause of variety through sequence; and although that is to be inferred, nevertheless, since through the determination by direct perception 'this is blue,' and since the life of valid cognition is precisely determination, it would be designated as perceptual. What has been stated by the proponent of external objects — this he presents as an anticipatable objection, the external form being inferred:
If the accidental appearance of this and that were to indicate something external,
for non-different cognition does not have the capacity to cause varied appearances.
Nor would the varied awakening of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) here serve as a cause,
for what would be the basis for the variety of the awakening of those [impressions] themselves?

children.text: iha bodhaḥ tāvat abhinnaḥ , prakāśamātrameva hi asya paramārthaḥ , prakāśādhikaṃ yadi nīlasya rūpam , tarhi tat aprakāśarūpam iti na prakāśeta / atha tathā prakāśatvameva asya rūpam , pītaprakāśaḥ kathaṃ syāt / athāpi kramikanīlapītādiprakāśarūpameva tasya svarūpam , nīlādyābhāsaśūnyo 'hamiti prakāśaḥ svāpādyavasthāsu na syāt / tasmāt prakāśaḥ prakāśa eva , aṇumātramapi na rūpāntaram asya asti iti abhinno bodhaḥ , tasya ca abhinnasya kadācit nīlābhāsatā kadācit pītābhāsatā iti ye vicitrābhāsāḥ tatra kāraṇatvam hi yasymāt na upapannam hetau abhinne kāryabhedasya asaṃbhavāt , tasmāt sa sa vicitranīlapītādirūpa ākāsmiko 'jñātapratyakṣasiddhahetukaḥ san bāhyaṃ vijñānagatapratibimbātmakasvasvabhāvasaṃpādakam aucityāt nijarūpasadṛśaṃ kramopanipatadrūpabahutarabhedātmakaṃ jñānāt sarvathā pṛthagbhūtam anumāpayati iti saṃbhāvayate bāhyārthavādī //4//
children.translated_text: Here, cognition, to begin with, is non-differentiated, for its ultimate reality is nothing but luminosity. If the form of blue is something more than luminosity, then being of the nature of non-luminosity, it would not be luminous. If its form is precisely the state of being luminous in that manner, then how could the luminosity of yellow arise? And even if its essential nature is precisely the sequential luminosity of blue, yellow, and such, then the luminosity 'I am devoid of the appearance of blue and such' would not occur in states such as deep sleep. Therefore, luminosity is just luminosity — not even an atom's worth of another form belongs to it — and so cognition is non-differentiated; and the varied appearances — sometimes as blue, sometimes as yellow — their causality cannot be established for what is non-differentiated, since difference in the effect is impossible when the cause is non-differentiated. Therefore, that varied form of blue, yellow, and such, being accidental — having a cause that is not perceived directly — the proponent of external objects postulates that it indicates an external [reality] which is of the nature of reflection in cognition, which brings about its own respective nature, which is reasonably similar to its own form, and which consists of a multitude of forms descending in sequence, being entirely separate from cognition. //4//

children.text: na ca asya idaṃ saṃbhāvanāmātram , api tu niścayaparyavasāyi eva bhavati / tathā hi vijñānavādinā yo hetuḥ vaicitrye vāsanāprabodhalakṣaṇa uktaḥ sa na upapadyate /

children.translated_text: The latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that generates memory is <s>vāsanā</s>.

children.text: iti tāvat prasiddham , iha tu anubhavavaicitryahetuḥ paryeṣaṇīyo vartate / astu vā nīlādyābhāsasaṃpādanasāmarthyarūpā jñānasya yogyatātmikā śaktiḥ vāsanā , tasyāśca svakāryasaṃpādanonmukhyaṃ prabodhaḥ , tato bodheṣu ābhāsavaicitryam iti / tatrāpi tu brūmaḥ ---- iha yadyāpi ābhāsānāṃ jñānāntarvartinām apāramārthikatvaṃ saṃvṛtisattvam ucyetāpi , tathāpi yadeṣāṃ tad vastusadeva aṅgīkāryam avastunaḥ sarvasāmarthyavirahitālakṣaṇasya kāryasaṃpādanaprāṇitasāmārtthyātmakasvabhāvānupapatteḥ / evaṃsthite yā etā vāsanā ābhāsakāraṇatvena iṣyante , tāsāṃ bodhāt yadi bhinnaṃ rūpam , tacca paramārthasat , tadayaṃ śabdāntarapracchanno bāhyārthavādaprakāra eva / atha saṃvṛtisat , tarhi tena rūpeṇa kāraṇatānupapattiḥ / tathā yena rūpeṇa āsāṃ pāramārthikatā tena kāraṇatā , tat tarhi jñānamātraṃ tacca abhinnam iti nīlādyābhāsarūpasya kāryabhedasya asiddhiḥ / evaṃ vāsanānām abicitratve tatprabodho vicitra iti kā pratyāśā / bhavantu vā vāsanā bhinnāḥ , tathāpi bodhamātrātiriktasya deśakālabhāvādeḥ prabodhakābhimatasya vicitrasya kāraṇasya abhāvāt prabodho'vicitra iti eka eva prabodhaḥ iti samameva nīlādivaicitryaṃ bhāseta / atha svasaṃtānavartīni jñānāntarāṇi vicitrāṇi prabodhakāraṇāni iti , tadasat , sukhaduḥkhanīkapīlādipūrvāparādideśakālabhedasya vijñānamātrarūpatve vijñānasya ca prakāśamātrapramārthatāyāṃ svarūpabhedāsaṃbhave tathā bodhavailakṣaṇyānupapatteḥ / parapramātṛrūpeṣu bodhāntariṣu saṃtānāntaraśabdavācyeṣvapi tulyo'yam availakṣaṇyaprakāraḥ / tatrāpi parakīyābhimatasya kṛśasthūlādeḥ kāyasya , śvāsapraśvāsādeḥ prāṇasya , sukhaduḥkhādeḥ dhīguṇasya ; anumātrabhimatasaṃbinmātrarūpābhede paratvaṃ kasya bhavet iti na vidmaḥ / bodhasya tanniṣṭhasya iti cet , so 'pi pramāṇena yadi na siddhaḥ tat asat eva , siddho 'pi prameyatayā cet tat jaḍa eva , tathāpi ca kāyādivat eva jñānamātrasvabhāvaḥ svasaṃvinmātrarūpatve paraṃ prati asya asiddheḥ / nanu vyāhārādikriyā svātmani icchayā vyāhareyam ityevaṃrūpayā hetubhāvena vyāptā dṛṣṭā tat caitrakāye'pi tayā taddhetukayā bhāvyam / na ca matsaṃtatipatitā samīhā asti iti svasaṃvedanena niścitam , tataśca parasamīhā siddhyati , tadeva saṃtānāntaram iti / atrocyate ---- iha anumātuḥ vyāhārābhāso dvidhā bhavati ---- vyāptigrahaṇakāle 'vicchedaprāṇo 'haṃ vyāharāmi ityevaṃrūpaḥ / anumānāvasare ca
children.translated_text: Thus much is well-established. But here, the cause of the diversity of experience is what needs to be investigated. Let there be a <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression), which is a power in the form of the capacity of knowledge to produce appearances such as blue etc., constituting a fitness; and let <s>prabodha</s> (awakening) be its readiness to produce its own effect; from that, the diversity of appearances in cognitions follows. But even in that case, we say: Here, although the non-ultimacy and conventional reality of appearances existing within cognition may be asserted, nevertheless, their being-ness must be accepted as a real thing, since something that has no reality at all — being devoid of all capacity and featureless — cannot have the nature characterized by the capacity for producing effects. This being the case, if these <s>vāsanās</s> that are postulated as causes of appearances have a form different from cognition, and that is ultimately real, then this is just a variant of the doctrine of external objects hidden under a different term. If, on the other hand, [the form is] conventionally real, then causality through that form is impossible. If the causality is through that form by which they are ultimately real, then that is nothing but cognition, and that is non-different — hence the difference of effects in the form of blue etc. as appearances is not established. Thus, if the <s>vāsanās</s> are non-diverse, what hope is there that their awakening would be diverse? Or even if the <s>vāsanās</s> are different, still, since there is no diverse cause that awakens them other than mere cognition — such as place, time, existence, etc. — the awakening would be non-diverse, i.e., a single awakening, and the diversity of blue etc. would appear equally. If other cognitions within one's own continuum are the diverse causes of awakening, that is wrong — because when the difference of pleasure, pain, blue, yellow, etc., and prior, posterior, etc. in terms of place and time has only the nature of mere consciousness, and when consciousness has only the ultimate reality of mere luminosity, the impossibility of difference in essential nature makes the dissimilarity of cognitions untenable. In cognitions belonging to other perceivers, designated by the term 'other continuum,' the same manner of non-dissimilarity applies. Even there, the body such as thin or stout etc. that is attributed to the other, the breath such as inhalation and exhalation etc., the quality of the intellect such as pleasure and pain etc. — when all these are non-different in nature as mere consciousness, which is held to be mere atomic [awareness], we do not know what 'otherness' could belong to. If [it be said] it belongs to the cognition residing in that [other] — even that, if not established by a valid means of knowledge, is simply non-existent; and if established, it is so as an object of knowledge, hence it is inert; and even so, like the body etc., its essential nature is mere consciousness, and being of the nature of mere self-awareness, its otherness with respect to the other is not established. Now, it may be observed that activity such as speech is seen in oneself as pervaded by desire in the form 'I wish to speak' as its cause; therefore, in <s>Caitra</s>'s body too, that [speech] must be caused by that [desire]. And it is ascertained through self-awareness that the volition does not belong to my continuum; therefore, the volition of the other is established — that indeed is the other continuum. To this we reply: Here, the appearance of speech for the one who infers is twofold — at the time of grasping the universal concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>), it is of the form 'I, of unbroken continuity, speak'; and at the occasion of inference,
"he speaks" —

children.text: iti vicchedajīvita iti anyasya vyāptiḥ gṛhītā anyaśca ābhāsaḥ katham idānīṃ hetuḥ syāt ? vyāharati iti ābhāsasya hetuḥ avidita eva iti kathaṃ tato hetoḥ samīhā anumīyeta ? kiṃ ca
children.translated_text: it is of the nature of discontinuity. Thus, the concomitance grasped is of one thing, and the appearance is of another — how then can this be a valid logical reason? The cause of the appearance 'he speaks' is entirely unknown — so how can volition be inferred from that cause? Moreover,
"he speaks" —

children.text: iti yaḥ pramātrantare 'numātṛsaṃmate vicchinnatayā avabhāsaḥ so'numeyasaṃmatāyāḥ paramīhāyāḥ kathaṃ kāryaḥ syāt ? tasyā hi vyāharāmītyābhāsaḥ kāryo yo'sau avicchedajīvitaḥ / na ca avicchedamayasya vicchedamayaḥ kāryam iti yuktaṃ tathābhūtakāryakāraṇabhāvagrahaṇopāyābhāvāt , na hi svātmani yo'yam avicchinnābhāsaḥ sa paratra vicchinnaṃ
children.translated_text: this appearance that manifests in another perceiver, accepted by the one who infers, as discontinuous — how could it be the effect of the volition of the other, which is the accepted object of inference? For the effect of that [volition] is the appearance 'I speak,' which is of the nature of unbroken continuity. And it is not proper that what is of the nature of discontinuity should be the effect of what is of the nature of continuity, since there is no means of grasping such a cause-effect relation. For it has not been established by any valid means that the unbroken appearance in oneself generates the broken
"speaks"

children.text: ityevaṃrūpam ābhāsaṃ janayati iti kenacit pramāṇena siddham , parasiddhipūrvakatvāt asya arthasya , parapramātṛsiddhaśca evaṃbhūtārthādhīnatvena itaretarāśrayāt / na ca avaśyan avicchinnāt vicchinnena bhāvyam iti niyamo 'sti vyavhicārāt / na ca vicchinno 'pi ābhāsa upadyatām iti tadanusaṃdhānāt tadutpattiḥ niyatā tatsadbhāve 'pyasyānutpatteḥ tadabhāve ca utpatteḥ , vicchinna ābhāsaḥ paratra utpadyatām iti yā samīhā tayā saha pratra utpannasya vicchinnābhāsasya kāryakāraṇabhāvagrahaṇameva parāsiddhau na yukta, iti vyāptereva asiddhiḥ /
children.translated_text: — an appearance of such a form in the other. This is because this matter presupposes the establishment of the other, and [that establishment itself] depends on matters of such a kind being established for the other perceiver — resulting in mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>). Nor is there any rule that the continuous must necessarily produce the discontinuous, due to deviation. And it is not the case that just because one has the recollection 'let the discontinuous appearance arise' [in the other], its arising is necessitated — for even when that [recollection] exists, it does not arise, and when that is absent, it does arise. The grasping of a cause-effect relation between the volition 'let a discontinuous appearance arise in the other' and the discontinuous appearance that has arisen in the other is simply unjustified when the other is not established — hence the concomitance itself is not established.

And this is not a mere supposition for him; rather, it culminates in certainty. For the cause of variety in the form of the awakening of latent impressions stated by the idealist (<s>vijñānavādin</s>) is not tenable.

children.text: pramātrantarāṇi ca yadi bhinnāni tadā tanniṣṭhānām avabhāsānāṃ bheda eva

children.translated_text: "since [the appearance] is not different from cognition" —

children.text: iti nyāyāt / tataśca ekābhāsaniṣṭhatvābhāvāt ekābhāsaviśrāntaḥ saṃbhūya pramātḥṇāṃ vyavahāro na syāt iti anyosaṃbhavaḥ ---- yat prameyaṃ bodhāt bhinnaṃ bhavati iti / sahopalambhaniyamādeḥ anaikāntikatvāt nīlapītādināpi prameyarāśinā kim apakṛtam , yena asya svarūpaviśrāntiḥ na sahyate , tasmāt pramātrantarāṇāmapi asiddhireva , siddhau vā sarvapramātrantargatā ābhāsā ekaikatra paratra ābhāsavaicitryahetuṃ vāsanodvodhavaicitryaṃ janayeyuḥ niyame hetvantarābhāvāt iti tathāpi na nīlādivaicitryasiddhiḥ / evaṃ vāsanānāṃ tadudbodhahetūnāṃ ca vicitrāṇām anupapattireva / tataśca sthitametat , abhinno bodhaḥ tasya ākasmikābhāsabhedahetutvānupapatteḥ bāhyo'rtho'numeyaḥ saṃbhāvyate iti yadi bāhyārthavādinā ucyate iti ślokadvayārthaḥ / cecchabdaḥ ślokadvayavākyārthaśaṅkādyotakaḥ / evam āśaṅkyamānatvena parasaṃbhāvanā dṛḍhā darśitā //5//
children.translated_text: by this principle. Therefore, since there is no abiding in a single appearance, the practical activity of perceivers that rests upon a single appearance, combining [their perspectives], would not be possible — and hence, there would be the impossibility of the other. This is [what follows] if the knowable object (<s>prameya</s>) is different from cognition. Since the invariable co-perception (<s>sahopalambha-niyama</s>) and such arguments are inconclusive, what harm has the aggregate of knowable objects such as blue, yellow, etc. done, that their resting in their own nature is not tolerated? Therefore, other perceivers too are simply not established; or if established, the appearances belonging to all other perceivers, being in each and every one of the others, would generate diversity of the awakening of <s>vāsanā</s> as the cause of diversity of appearances — since there is no other reason for the restriction — and even so, the diversity of blue etc. would not be established. Thus, the impossibility of diverse <s>vāsanās</s> and of the diverse causes of their awakening is clear. Therefore, this is established: since non-different cognition cannot possibly be the cause of accidental difference of appearances, an external object is inferred as a possibility — if the proponent of external objects were to say this: such is the meaning of the two verses. The word 'cet' (if) indicates the hypothetical nature of the two-verse statement. Thus, by presenting it as something being hypothesized, the strong plausibility of the opponent's reasoning has been shown. // 5 //
And if other perceivers are distinct, then the appearances residing in them are also necessarily distinct,

children.text: adhunā tu enāṃ saṃbhāvanāṃ śithilayituṃ tāvadāha
children.translated_text: Now, to begin weakening this plausibility, he says:
This may be so; but when practical activity is settled upon those very appearances alone,
what need is there for an external [object] that is impossible to establish? //
"This may be so" (<s>syādetat</s>) —

children.text: iti pūrvoktasaṃbhāvanābhyupagame yadā vyākhyāyate tadā kiṃ tu iti vākyaśeṣeṇa tacchaithilyaviṣayaṃ saṃbhāvanāntaraṃ śeṣaślokena darśayate iti vyākhyeyam / yadi tu adhyāhāro na sahyate tadā syādetaditi idamapi saṃbhāvanāntaraṃ syāt , yadanena ślokena ucyate iti ekavākyatayā yojyam / anayāpi kaṣṭakalpanayā bāhyān arthān prasādhayatā bhavatā taiḥ na kiṃcit kartavyam , ābhāsaireva taiḥ bhavatā abhyupagataiḥ vyavahārasiddheḥ , na hi nityānumeyena kaścit vyavahāra iti kiṃ bāhyena , yatra sādhakaṃ ca nāsti pramāṇam , bādhakaṃ ca prakāśāt bhede anumeyatayāpi prakāśanābhāva iti tāvat mukhyam / abhyuścayabādhakastu avayavino vṛttyanupapattiḥ , samavāyāsiddhiḥ , kampākampāvaraṇānāvaraṇaraktāraktadigbhāgabhedādiviruddhadharmayogaḥ /
children.translated_text: when this is explained as an acceptance of the aforementioned plausibility, then with the remainder of the sentence beginning 'but,' the object of its weakening, i.e., an alternative plausibility, is shown in the remaining verse — thus it should be explained. But if the ellipsis is not tolerated, then 'this may be so' would be yet another plausibility, which is stated by this verse — and thus it should be construed as a single sentence. Even by this strained reasoning, you who seek to establish external objects need not do anything with them, since practical activity is accomplished through those very appearances accepted by you. For there is no practical activity with what is always merely inferred — so what need is there of the external? Regarding which, first, there is no establishing means of valid knowledge; and second, the invalidation: since even as something inferred, when different from luminosity, it cannot be manifested — this much is primary. The accumulated invalidation, however, is: the impossibility of the existence of a composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>), the non-establishment of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), and the possession of contradictory properties such as motion and non-motion, concealment and non-concealment, colored and non-colored, difference of spatial portions, and so on.

children.text: aṇusaṃcayabāhyavāde 'pi saṃcayasya anyasya abhāve paramāṇava eva , te ca yadi saṃyujyante nirantaratayā tat avaśyaṃ digbhāgabhedaḥ , evanākṣe ṣaṭsu dikṣu saṃcīyamāneṣu ṣaṭsu aṇuṣu madhyamasya paramāṇoḥ yatraiva dhāmni eko lagnaḥ tatraiva yadi aparaḥ tat ekaparamāṇumātratā / atha anyatra ekaḥ anyatar aparaḥ tat avaśyaṃ bhāgabhedāpattiḥ , iti bhāga eva san , tasyāpi eṣaiva saraṇiḥ iti na kiṃcit avaśiṣyate bāhyaṃ tattvataḥ /
children.translated_text: Even in the doctrine of external objects as aggregates of atoms, in the absence of any other aggregate, there are only the atoms themselves; and if they combine without gaps, then there is necessarily a distinction of spatial portions. Thus, when six atoms accumulate in the six directions around a central atom, if another atom is attached at the very same point where one is attached, the result would be merely the size of a single atom. But if one is at one place and another at another, then necessarily the consequence of a distinction of parts follows — and being a mere part, for that too the same path applies, and thus nothing external remains in reality.

children.text: na caitat vācyam ---- mūrtānām ekadeśatvāyogāt , saṃyoge bhinnadeśatvāvyāvṛtteḥ tanniṣṭaṃ dvyaṇukaṃ nāma kāryadravyam aṇuparimāṇam , tebhyaḥ tribhyo mahatkāryam iti / avayavīvādo hi ayam , sa ca pūrvameva apabādhitaḥ / yacca avyāpyavṛttitvaṃ saṃyogasya ucyate tanniraṃśe kathaṃ saṃgacchatām / svāśraye hi yadi asau samavaiti kim anyāt asya avaśiṣyate yat na vyāpnuyāt iti / abhyuścayabādhakaṃ ca idam iti na atra asmābhiḥ bharaḥ kṛtaḥ / vistareṇa ca prajñālaṅkāre darśitam ācāryaśaṅkaranandanena //6//
children.translated_text: Nor can it be said that since material substances cannot be in the same location, and since in conjunction their separate spatiality is not negated, the product substance called <s>dvyaṇuka</s> (dyad), residing in those [conjunctions], is of atomic size, and from three of these the great product arises. For this is the doctrine of the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>), which has already been refuted. And as for the statement that conjunction has non-pervading existence, how can that be coherent in what is partless? For if it inheres in its substrate, what remains of it that it does not pervade? This is the accumulated invalidation — and we have not burdened ourselves with it here. It has been shown at length by the master <s>Śaṅkaranandana</s> in the <s>Prajñālaṅkāra</s>. // 6 //

children.text: nanu bādhakaṃ nāma pramāṇasiddhe vastuni na kiṃcit kartuṃ samartham , tenaiva dṛḍhena pramāṇena bādhakābhimatasya bādhitasya apramāṇatvasaṃpādanāt / darśitaṃ ca iha sādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ kāryahetuḥ

children.translated_text: "those accidental appearances" —
has been shown in that <s>kārikā</s>. Anticipating this, he says:

Objection: An invalidating argument is not capable of doing anything to an object established by a valid means of knowledge, since that very strong valid means establishes the non-validity of what is claimed to be invalidating. And the establishing means of valid knowledge — namely, causal inference —
The Lord, whose nature is consciousness, having [things] within [Himself], by the power of His will, externally,
like a <s>yogī</s>, would manifest the entire collection of objects without any material cause. //
