children.text: iha tāvat svapna -- smaraṇa -- manorājya -- saṃkalpādiṣu nīlādyābhāsavaicitryaṃ bāhyasamarpakahtuvyatirekeṇaiva nirbhāsate iti yadyapi asti saṃbhavaḥ , tathāpi tadābhāsavaicitryam asthairyāt sarvapramātrasādhāraṇyāt pūrvānubhavasaṃskārajatvasaṃbhāvanāt avastu iti śaṅkyeta / yat punaridaṃ yoginām icchāmātreṇa purasenādivaicitryanirmāṇaṃ dṛṣṭam , tatra upādānaṃ prasiddhamṛtkāṣṭha-śukra -- śoṇi -- tādivaicitryamayaṃ na saṃbhavatyeva , na hi evaṃ vaktuṃ śakyam ---- sarvagatāḥ paramāṇavo yogīcchayā jhaṭiti saṃghaṭitāḥ kāryam ārapsyante iti / yat etat lokaprasiddhakāraṇabhāvānatikramasiddhaye nirūpyate / na ca etat prasiddham ---- pramāṇubhya eva sthūlaṃ ghaṭādi jāyate iti , kiṃ tu kapālādivyavadhānena , tathāpi niyatasahakārisamavalambanam karacaraṇādivyāpāre viśiṣṭadeśakāladharmādhipatyayogaḥ śikṣābhyāsaprakarṣa iti , iyati ca āṃśrīyamāṇe yogī kumbhaṃ nirmimāṇaḥ kumbhakāraprasiddhasanastasāmagrīsanarjanapuraḥsaraṃghaṭaṃ ghaṭayan kumbhakāra eva syāt , tasmāt prasiddhakāraṇollaṅghane kim asaṃcetyamānaparamāṇvādyupādānakāraṇāntaracintayā iti / tatra yogisaṃvida eva sā tādṛśī śaktiḥ ---- yat ābhāsavaicitryarūpam arthajātaṃ prakāśayati iti / tadasti saṃbhavaḥ ---- yat saṃvit eva abhyupagatasvātantryā apratīdhātalakṣaṇāt icchāviśeṣavaśāt saṃvido 'nidhikātmatāyā anapāyāt antaḥsthitameva sat bhāvajātam idamityevaṃ prāṇabuddhidehādeḥ vitīrṇakiyanmātrasaṃvidūpāt svātantryaṃ kiṃ na abhyupagamyate svasaṃvedanasiddham , kimiti hetvantaraparyeṣaṇāprayāsena khidyate / evakāreṇa idamāha ---- sarveṇa tāvat vādinā viṣayavyavasthāpanaṃ saṃvidrūpam anapahnavanīyam ādisiddhaṃ hi tat iti uktam / tasya ca svātantryameva devaśabdanirdiṣṭaṃ cidrūpatvam iti kim aparakāraṇānveṣaṇavyasanitayā / hi yasmāt evaṃ prakāśayati deva iti saṃbhāvyate , tasmāt kiṃ bāhyena anupapattinā iti pūrveṇa saṃbandhaḥ //7//
children.translated_text: Here, to begin with, although there is the possibility that the diversity of appearances such as blue etc. manifests even without an external cause-provider in dreams, memories, fantasies, imaginations, and such, nevertheless, that diversity of appearances might be suspected to be unreal due to its instability, its being common to all perceivers, and the possibility of its being born from latent impressions of prior experience. But what has been observed — this creation of diverse cities, armies, and such by <s>yogīs</s> through mere will — there, the material cause consisting of the well-known diversity of clay, wood, semen, blood, and such is simply not possible. For it cannot be said that omnipresent atoms, suddenly assembled by the yogī's will, will commence the effect — this is examined for the purpose of establishing the non-transgression of well-known causal relations. And this is not well-established — that a gross pot etc. arises from mere atoms; rather, it arises through the intermediary of potsherds and such. Even so, it depends upon fixed auxiliary conditions; in the activity of hands, feet, and such, there is the conjunction of particular place, time, and the dominion of specific properties; and there is the excellence of training and practice. And if this much is admitted, a yogī creating a pot, having first acquired the well-known assemblage of materials in the potter's manner, and fashioning the pot, would simply be a potter. Therefore, in the transgression of well-known causes, what is the use of thinking about other material causes such as imperceptible atoms? There, the consciousness of the yogī itself is that kind of power — which manifests the collection of objects in the form of diverse appearances. That there is a possibility — namely, that consciousness itself, endowed with accepted sovereignty, through the characteristic of unimpededness, by the power of a particular will, since the non-receptacle nature of consciousness is never lost, the entire collection of entities, while existing within, [appears] as 'this' — the sovereignty established through self-awareness, going beyond the mere consciousness-form of <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), body, and such — why is this not accepted? Why does one torment oneself with the labor of searching for other causes? By the emphatic particle 'eva,' this is stated: By every philosopher, the determination of objects as being of the nature of consciousness is undeniable — for that is primordially established, as has been said. And the sovereignty of that is precisely the nature of consciousness indicated by the word '<s>deva</s>' (Lord) — so what is the use of being addicted to searching for other causes? Since the Lord plausibly manifests thus, therefore, 'what need is there of an external [object] that is impossible to establish?' — this is the connection with the preceding [verse]. // 7 //

children.text: nanu evam ubhayathāpi saṃbhāvanānumānam unmiṣati , tatra kiṃ makurapratibimbitaghaṭādidṛṣṭāntena jñānapratibimbatābhāsavaicitrye vijñānadarpaṇātiriktaṃ tata eva bāhyābhimataṃ hetuṃ kalpayema ? kiṃ vā yogidṛṣṭāntena saṃvitsvātantryameva hetubhāvena brūyāma ? tadidaṃ sāṃśayikaṃ vartate iti āśaṅkya bāhyārthānumānasaṃbhāvanāṃ sūtradvayena apākartumāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Thus, the inferential possibility opens up in both ways. Should we, by the analogy of a pot etc. reflected in a mirror, postulate a cause external to the cognition-mirror for the diversity of appearances as reflections in knowledge? Or should we, by the analogy of the yogī, declare the sovereignty of consciousness itself to be the cause? This remains doubtful. Anticipating this, to remove the possibility of inference for external objects, he says in two <s>sūtras</s>:
Inference is never accepted regarding what has never appeared before, nor is a sense organ [capable of it];
it is precisely what has appeared — from the appearance of a causal entity such as a seed etc. //
The appearance, again, of an external [object] that has never appeared — how could it have occurred somehow?
Therefore, there is no establishment of this [external object], nor even through inference. //

children.text: na kevalam anantaraślokanirdiṣṭābhiḥ yuktabhiḥ pratyakṣeṇa bāhyo'rtho na bhāsate , iyadeva hi pratyakṣaṃ tacca nīlaṃ bhāti iti svaprakāśasaṃvidrūpaṃ nādhikaṃ kiṃcit iti , yāvat anumānenāpi na asya bāhyāsya siddhiḥ iti apiśabdasyābhiprāyaḥ / tatra anumānam atra naiva pravartitum utsahate / pravṛttamapi na prakṛtasiddhim ādavyāt iti anena sūtradvayena upadarśyate / tatra anumānaṃ vikalpaḥ , sarvaśca ayaṃ vikalpo'nubhavamūla iti prasiddham / tena yat sarvathā anābhātapūrvam ananubhūtacaraṃ tatra anumānam anumitivyāpāro vikalpātmā naiva kenacit vādinā iṣyate / nanu bhavatu pratyakṣato dṛṣṭe 'numāne saṃkathā iyam , sāmānyato dṛṣṭe tu kiṃ vakṣyasi yathā arthopalabdhyā indriyānumāne ? ucyate ---- tatrāpi vikalpena yathā so'rthaḥ spṛśyate tathā anumeya iti sthitiḥ / vikalpaśca na indriyādikam arthaṃ kenacit saṃniveśaviśeṣādinā viśeṣātmanā spṛśati , api tu kiṃcidupalabdheḥ kāraṇam iti amunā svabhāvena , sa ca svabhāvaḥ kāraṇatālakṣaṇaḥ pratyakṣagṛhīta eva / tathā ca bījāt aṅkuraḥ tantubhyaḥ paṭa ityādau kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ pratyakṣānupalambhabalena tāvat niśceyaḥ / tatra ca pratyakṣaṃ pratyābhāsaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ bhajate , vimarśalakṣaṇasya pramitivyāpārasya ekaikaśabdavācye'rthe pravṛtteḥ tadanusāritvācca pramāṇasya iti vakṣyate /
children.translated_text: Not only is the external object not manifest through direct perception by the reasoning stated in the next verse — for direct perception is just this much: 'that blue appears,' which is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, nothing more — but it is also not established through inference: this is the purport of the word 'api' (also). Therein, inference cannot even venture to operate here; and even if it operates, it cannot bring about the establishment of the matter at hand — this is shown by these two <s>sūtras</s>. Therein, inference is conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>), and it is well-established that all conceptual cognition is rooted in experience. Therefore, regarding what has in every way never appeared before, never been within the range of experience — inference, which is the operation of conceptual cognition in its inferential function, is never accepted by any philosopher. But granted that this discussion concerns inference based on perception; what will you say about inference from general observation, such as the inference of sense organs from the perception of objects? We reply: Even there, whatever object is touched by conceptual thought in whatever manner, it is in that manner that it is established as the object of inference. And conceptual thought does not touch an object such as a sense organ with any particular distinguishing characteristic such as a specific arrangement; rather, it touches it as 'something is the cause of perception' — with this nature. And that nature, characterized by being a cause, is grasped by direct perception itself. Accordingly, in cases like 'from a seed, a sprout' and 'from threads, a cloth,' the cause-effect relation is to be ascertained first by the force of direct perception and non-apprehension. Therein, direct perception partakes of validity with respect to each appearance, since the operation of valid cognition characterized by reflective determination (<s>vimarśa</s>) proceeds with respect to the object denoted by a single word, and the means of valid knowledge follows that — as will be stated:
{A cognition with respect to an object denoted by a single expression, when uncontradicted, is valid. /}

children.text: iti / ābhāsamātraṃ ca sāmānyam iti nir.eṣuate / anupalambho'pi anyopalambharūpa ābhāsamātraviśrānta eva iti kāraṇābhāso viśeṣaśūnyaḥ parigṛhīta eva bījāt aṅkura iti pratītau / yat yasya niyamam anuvidhatte avyatiriktam tat tasya kāryam iti pratighaṭaṃ mṛttikādirūpahetutadvanmātrasya āmāsāt //8//
children.translated_text: Thus. And the universal is nothing but mere appearance — as is established. Non-apprehension too, being of the nature of the apprehension of something else, rests in mere appearance alone. Therefore, the appearance of the cause, devoid of particularity, is indeed grasped in the cognition 'from the seed, the sprout.' Whatever follows the invariable pattern of something else without deviation — that is the effect of that. And the sheer impression of the cause-form such as clay etc. is from every individual pot. // 8 //

children.text: ābhāsāt bāhyaḥ punarnābhāsarūpaḥ , sa ca ābhāsate iti vipratiṣiddham / anābhāse ca nāsti vikalparūpasya anumānasya vyāpāraḥ / grāmagṛhādestu yat bāhyaṃ tat agrāmādirūpaṃ na ucyate pratyekaṃ vāṭānūpakuṇyatulādeḥ bāhyatvaprasaṅgāt , api tu tatsaṃnikaṭam , tasmāt grāmabāhyam ābhāsabāhyam iti ca śabdasāmyamātram etat na vastusāmyam / evaṃ ye vikalpe vastu na ābhāti iti manyante teṣāmapi tāvat anumānavikalpo na bāhye upapannaḥ / asmābhistu upapāditam ---- adhyavasāyasyāpi ābhāsamānaviṣayatvam

children.translated_text: "and if determinate cognition were erroneous" —

children.text: iti sūtre / tena anumānavikalpātmanāpi prakāśena yadi anāviṣṭo nīlādiḥ arthaḥ tat na anumita eva syāt / atha āviṣṭa eva , tarhi
children.translated_text: in that <s>sūtra</s>. Therefore, if the object such as blue etc. is not pervaded by the luminosity that is the inferential conceptual cognition, then it would simply not be inferred. But if it is indeed pervaded, then,
"as before, the object would be non-luminous" —

children.text: iti nyāyena prakāśamātrasvabhāva eva , na bāhyaḥ / tena bāhye sādhye yat kiṃcit pramāṇam ānīyate , tadabāhyatāmeva pratyuta sādhayati iti viruddhameva , ata eva āha
children.translated_text: by this principle, it is of the nature of mere luminosity, not external. Therefore, whatever means of valid knowledge is brought to establish the external, it rather establishes its non-externality — and is thus contradictory. For this very reason, he says:
"somehow" (<s>kathaṃcana</s>) —

children.text: iti , kenāpi prakāreṇa pratyakṣātmanā anumeyātmanā vā ābhāsanam ābhāso bāhyasya anābhāsasya na kadācit abhūt iti , tasmāt siddham
children.translated_text: that is, by any manner whatsoever, whether in the form of direct perception or in the form of the inferable, an appearance — a manifestation of the external, of the non-appearing — has never occurred. Therefore, it is established:
"The Lord, whose nature is consciousness itself" (<s>cidātmaiva hi devaḥ</s>) —
thus. // 9 //

From an appearance, the external [object] is not of the nature of appearance; and if it appears — that is contradictory. And regarding the non-appearing, there is no scope for the operation of inference, which is of the nature of conceptual cognition. As for what is 'external' to a village, house, etc. — that is not said to be of the nature of non-village etc., since otherwise each enclosure, embankment, courtyard, balance, etc. would have the consequence of being 'external'; rather, it means 'near to it.' Therefore, 'external to the village' and 'external to appearance' — this is merely a similarity of words, not a similarity of things. Thus, even for those who hold that reality does not appear in conceptual cognition, inferential conceptual cognition regarding the external is not tenable. But we have established that even determinate cognition (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) has as its content what is being manifested —

children.text: nanu antaḥsthitaṃ bahiḥ prakāśayedityuktaṃ tat antaḥsthitatvam upapādanīyam iti āśaṅkya āha
children.translated_text: Objection: It has been said 'He would manifest externally what is situated within' — that state of being situated within needs to be demonstrated. Anticipating this, he says:
The manifestation of the collection of entities, which are situated in the self of the Lord,
certainly exists; without that, the reflective awareness of will (<s>icchā-vimarśa</s>) would not proceed. //
Even in manifestation as external, the 'I'-ness does not break off;
{The interiority is the identity with the perceiver} —

children.text: iti hi vakṣyate , tacca sadaiva , prakāśasya pramātṛtvāt , tadātmatayā ca vinā 'prakāśamānasya avastutvāt , kiṃ tu tatra aham iti ucite parāmarśe yo 'yam idantāparāmarśaḥ saiva bāhyatā , tacca iha antaḥsthitatvam ahamityetāvatā citsamucitenaiva bapuṣā parāmarśanameva , tacca iha nīlādīnāmastyeva , na tu nāsti iti , yadi hi na syāt kumbhakṛto

children.translated_text: "let me make a pot"

children.text: iti ya uttarakriyāmapekṣya icchāśabdavācyaḥ parāmarśaḥ , eṣaṇīyena sa parāmṛśyena aniyantritaḥ cet tataḥ paṭecchāpi sā na kasmāt iti saṃkīryeran vyavahārāḥ / atha tatrāpi ca eṣaṇīyaḥ tadānīmeva nirmitaḥ san tathā jātaḥ , tarhi tannirmāṇaṃ cidātmani vinecchayā nopapannam iti
children.translated_text: — this reflective awareness denoted by the word 'will' (<s>icchā</s>), which is relative to a subsequent action — if it were unrestricted by the desired object, then why would the desire for a cloth not also be that? And practical activities would become confused. But if, even there, the desired object is created at that very moment and then arises thus, then that creation within the consciousness-self without will is untenable — thus
"for one who wishes to remain, will itself is the cause" —

children.text: ityatra varṇayiṣyate / tacca icchāntaramapi viṣayaniyantritaṃ na vā iti vikalpe 'navasthā / viṣayaniyantritaṃ cet syāt ātmataiva jātā , na cet ghaṭe paṭecchā syāt / atha tatrāpi tadānīmeva iti kṛtvā anavasthā / tasmāt sarvo 'yaṃ bhāvarāśiḥ cidātmani aham ityeva vapuṣā satatāvabhāsuravapuḥ aiśvaryarūpācca svātantryalakṣaṇāt svāmibhāvāt vicitreṇa vapuṣā kramākramādinā saṃvit enaṃ bahiḥkaroti pramātṛprathanapūrvakam , tatrāpi kvacit ābhāse pramātḥn ekīkaroti nitambanīnṛtta iva prekṣakān / tāvati hi teṣām ābhāse aikyam / śarīraprāṇabuddhisukhādyābhāsāṃśeṣu tu bhedasya avigalanāt na sarvathā aikyam / ata eva pratikṣaṇaṃ pramātṛsaṃyojanaviyojanavaicitryeṇa parameśvaro viśvaṃ sṛṣṭisaṃhārādinā prapañcayati / taduktamācāryeṇa
children.translated_text: this will be elaborated there. And whether that further will too is restricted by its object or not — in this conceptual alternative lies an infinite regress. If it is restricted by the object, it has already arisen from the self; if not, there would be desire for a cloth in the case of a pot. But if even there [one says] 'at that very moment' — then there is an infinite regress. Therefore, this entire aggregate of entities, in the consciousness-self, with the form of 'I' alone, is a body that is constantly manifesting. And from the sovereignty that is the nature of freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) — the state of being the Lord — consciousness makes this [aggregate] external with a diverse body of sequential and non-sequential [forms], preceded by the manifestation of the perceiver. And even there, in some appearance, it unifies perceivers — like a dancer of the hip-movement dance [unifying] spectators. For to that extent, they have unity in that appearance. But in the aspects of appearances of body, vital breath, intellect, pleasure, and such, since difference does not dissolve, there is not unity in every respect. For this very reason, the Supreme Lord, through the varied sport of connecting and disconnecting perceivers at every moment, elaborates the universe through creation, dissolution, and such. As stated by the master:

thus it will be stated. And that is ever-present, since luminosity has the nature of being a perceiver, and since without its nature, what is not being manifested would be non-existent. However, in the reflective awareness properly called 'I,' this reflective awareness of 'this-ness' — that itself is externality. And the state of being situated within here means precisely the reflective awareness in the form of 'I' — with just the body appropriate to consciousness — and that certainly exists here with respect to blue etc.; it is not that it does not exist. For if it did not exist, then the potter's
{Always delighting in the play of creation, always seated in the bliss of sustenance,
always satisfied by devouring the three worlds — to <s>Bhava</s> (Śiva), obeisance! //}
And so forth. And by the illustrious <s>Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa</s> also:
{Incessantly, without rest, the three worlds with hundreds of imaginations,
fashioning and yet some one alone, free from conceptual construction, the Unborn is victorious! //}

children.text: iti / tasmāt sthitam antaḥsthitaṃ bhāvajātaṃ tena vinā tadviṣayasya parāmarśāyogāt iti //10//
children.translated_text: Thus. Therefore, it is established: the collection of entities is situated within; for without that, the reflective awareness regarding its object would be impossible. // 10 //

children.text: nanu parāmarśo nāma vikalpaḥ , sa ca avikalpaśuddhasaṃvidvapuṣi bhagavati kathaṃ syāt ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Reflective awareness (<s>parāmarśa</s>) is conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>); how can that exist in the Blessed One who is of the form of non-conceptual, pure consciousness? Anticipating this, he says:
They know reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) to be the very nature of appearance; otherwise,
even luminosity, though tinged by the object, would be like an inert crystal and such. //

children.text: iha avabhāvasya prakāśasya , anavabhāsasya ca aprakāśasya ghaṭādeḥ parasparaparihāreṇa dvayoḥ svātmani cet vyavasthānam , tat ghaṭapaṭayoḥ iva idamjaḍam idaṃ jaḍam iti durupapādaṃ vailakṣaṇyam / atha avabhāso yato 'rthasya saṃbamdhī , tato na jaḍaḥ , tarhi saṃbandhamātreṇa mṛt api ghaṭasya iti ajaḍā syāt / atha na svasaṃbandhamātram api tu avabhāso 'rthasya prakāśaḥ , tarhi arthātmanā sa prakāśa iti samāpatitam / na ca anyātmanā anyasya prakāśa upapannaḥ / atha anyasvabhāvo 'pi ghaṭo'vabhāsasya kāraṇam , tarhi avabhāso'pi ghaṭasya kāraṇam iti ghaṭo'pi ajaḍaḥ syāt / atha anyena satāpi ghaṭena yato 'vabhāsasya pratibimbarūpā cchāyā dattā , tām asau adabhāso bibhrat ghaṭasya iti ucyate , tataśca ajaḍaḥ , tarhi sphaṭikasalilamakurādiḥ api evaṃbhūta eva iti ajaḍa eva syāt / atha tathābhūtamapi ātmānaṃ taṃ ca ghaṭādikaṃ sphaṭikādiḥ na parāmraṣṭuṃ samartha iti jad.aḥ , tathāparāmarśanameva ajāḍyajīvitam antarbahiṣkaraṇasvātantryarūpaṃ svābhāvikam avabhāsasya svātmaviśrāntilakṣaṇam ananyamukhaprekṣitvaṃ nāma /

children.translated_text: 'I am thus, of the nature of luminosity, I shine' —

children.text: iti hi vimarśodaye svasaṃvideva pramātṛprameyapramāṇādi kṛtārtham abhimanyate na tu atiriktaṃ kāṅkṣati , sphaṭikādi hi gṛhītapratibimbamapi tathābhāvena siddhau pramātrantaram apekṣate iti nirvimarśatvāt jaḍam / sarvatra vastuto vimarśātmakapramātṛsvabhāvatādātmyāhaṃparāmarśaviśrānteḥ ajaḍatvameva pūrvāparakoṭyoḥ / yaduktam
children.translated_text: thus indeed, when reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) arises, self-awareness itself considers the knowing subject, the object, the means of knowledge, and such as fulfilled, and does not desire anything additional. For crystal and such, even though having received a reflection, require another knowing subject for their establishment as being of that nature — hence, due to being devoid of reflective awareness, they are insentient. Everywhere, in reality, non-insentience at both extremities [subject and object] is due to the resting in the reflective awareness of 'I' that consists in identity with the nature of the knowing subject characterized by reflective awareness. As stated:

Here, if the establishment of both — of appearance, which is luminosity, and of non-appearance, which is the non-luminosity of a pot and such — rests in their own selves through mutual exclusion, then, just as between a pot and a cloth, [saying] 'this is insentient, that is insentient' — such a hard-to-establish distinction [would obtain]. Now, if appearance is non-insentient because it is related to the object, then by mere relation, even clay would be non-insentient since it is [related to] the pot. Now, if it is not mere relation but rather appearance is the illumination of the object, then it has been arrived at that luminosity is of the nature of the object. Nor is the illumination of one thing by the nature of another tenable. Now, if the pot, though of a different nature, is the cause of appearance, then appearance too would be the cause of the pot, and so the pot too would be non-insentient. Now, if, although the pot exists as something different, it gives a shadow in the form of a reflection to appearance, and that appearance, bearing it, is called 'of the pot' — and is therefore non-insentient — then crystal, water, mirror, and such, being exactly of this kind, would also be non-insentient. Now, if crystal and such are insentient because, even though being of such a nature, they are unable to reflectively grasp themselves and the pot and such — then such reflective grasping alone is the life of non-insentience, being of the nature of the freedom of inner and outer faculties, the innate characteristic of appearance as resting in its own self, [its] not looking toward another's face.
{The fulfillment of the reflective awareness that has been severed as 'this' —
that resting in one's own essential nature, that reflective awareness is this 'I.' //}

children.text: iti / madhyāvasthaiva tu idantā vimṛśyamānaūrvāparakoṭiḥ vimūḍhānāṃ māyāpadaṃ saṃsāraḥ iti vimarśa eva pradhānaṃ bhagavata iti sthitam //11//
children.translated_text: Thus. But the middle state itself — the 'this-ness' whose prior and posterior extremities are being reflected upon — is, for the deluded, the domain of <s>Māyā</s>, which is <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly bondage). Thus it is established that reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) alone is the principal [nature] of the Blessed One. //11//

children.text: na kevalaṃ saṃvittattvasya asmābhiḥ eva vimarśaprādhānyam uktam yāvat āgamāntarairapi iti darśayati
children.translated_text: Not only has the primacy of reflective awareness for the principle of consciousness been stated by us, but also by other scriptural traditions — this he shows:
The Self itself is <s>caitanya</s> (consciousness); consciousness-action is consciousness-agenthood.
He is described with this purport; for thereby He is distinguished from the insentient. //

children.text: yato vimarśa eva pradhānam ātmano rūpam amumeva hetuṃ prayojanarūpam uddiśya ātmā dharmisvabhāvo dravyabhūto 'pi , caitantyam iti dharmavācinā śabdena sāmānādhikaraṇyam āśritya uditaḥ kathitaḥ , bhagavatā śivasūtreṣu
children.translated_text: Since reflective awareness alone is the principal form of the Self, having in view this very reason as the purpose — the Self, which is a substance (<s>dravya</s>) and a locus of properties (<s>dharmin</s>) in nature, has been described (<s>uditaḥ</s>) by resorting to co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with the word '<s>caitanya</s>' which denotes a property — by the Blessed One in the <s>Śiva Sūtras</s>:
{<s>Caitanyam ātmā</s>} (Consciousness is the Self.) (1-1)

children.text: iti paṭhitam / caitanyam iti hi dharmavācakopalakṣaṇam ,
children.translated_text: Thus it is stated. For '<s>caitanya</s>' is an implied marker of a property-denoting word,
{<s>Citi-śaktiḥ aparināminī</s>} (The power of consciousness is unchanging.)
{...the isolation of that seeing.} (<s>Yoga Sūtra</s> 2-25)
{The seer is mere seeing...} (<s>Yoga Sūtra</s> 2-20)

children.text: ityādau api hi dharmaśabdena sāmānādhikaraṇyam ātmano darśitaṃ guruṇā anantena / dravyaṃ hi tat ucyate yadviśrāntaḥ padārthavargaḥ sarvo bhāti ca arthyate ca arthakriyāyai , tad yadi na tat sakalo 'yaṃ tattvabhūtabhāvabhuvanasaṃbhāraḥ saṃvidi viśrāntaḥ tathā bhavati iti sa eva guṇakarmādidharmāśrayabhūtapadārthāntarasvabhāvaḥ tāmeva mukhyadravyasvarūpam āśrayate iti saiva dravyam / tat anantadharmarāśiviśramabhittibhūtāyāḥ tasyāḥ sa eva dharmaḥ caitanyam iti kartṛkṛdantāt utpannena bhāvapratyayena saṃbandhābhidhāyināpi prādhānyena darśitaḥ / tathā hi saṃbandhaviśrāntasya pratīteḥ , dravytarūpasya ca saṃbandhinaḥ prakṛtyā uktatvāt citikriyārūpaṃ dhramaṃ saṃbaddham avagamayatā ṣyañā niṣkṛṣṭāṃśaḥ pratyāyito bhavati / citikriyā ca cittau kartṛtā , svātaṃtryaṃ saṃyojanaviyojanānusaṃdhānādirūpam ātmamātratāyāmeva jaḍavat aviśrāntatvam aparicchinnaprakāśasāratvam ananyamukhaprekṣitvam iti / tadeva anātmarūpāt jaḍāt saṃyojanaviyojanādisvātaṃtryavikalāt vailakṣaṇyādāyi iti / tadevaṃ paratvena pradhānatayā abhisaṃdhāya ātmā cetana iti vaktavye dharmāntarādharīkaraṇāya vimarśadharmoddhurīkaraṇāya ca

children.translated_text: 'the Self is <s>caitanya</s> (consciousness)' —
thus it is said. 'With the purport of consciousness-action as consciousness-agenthood' — thus the compound [should be analyzed].
'A half-verse resting at the quarter' —

children.text: iti hi kāvye samayaḥ , na śāstre / yadi vā citkriyā ātmā ucitaḥ citikartṛtā ca iti pṛthageva / evaṃ tu na kvacit paṭhitam //12//
children.translated_text: this is a convention in poetry, not in treatises. Alternatively, 'consciousness-action is the Self' is fitting, and 'consciousness-agenthood' is separate. But this reading is not found anywhere. //12//

In these and other [texts] as well, the co-referentiality of the Self with the property-denoting word has been shown by the guru <s>Ananta</s>. For that is called substance (<s>dravya</s>) in which the entire class of categories rests, appears, and is sought for purposeful activity. If all this assemblage of principles, elements, and worlds were not resting in consciousness and thus existing, then that [consciousness] itself, being the essential nature of another category that is the substratum of properties such as qualities and actions, depends on that very thing which is the essential nature of principal substance — therefore, consciousness itself is substance. Then, of that [consciousness] which is the ground where the infinite mass of properties rests, that very property is '<s>caitanya</s>' — shown principally by the abstract suffix (<s>bhāvapratyaya</s>) derived from the agent-noun (<s>kartṛkṛdanta</s>) 'cetayati,' which also expresses relation. For since the cognition that rests in the relation has already been stated, and the relatum in the form of substance has been stated by its root, through the abstract suffix (<s>ṣyañ</s>) that conveys the property in the form of consciousness-action, the extracted aspect is indicated. And consciousness-action is agenthood in the act of being conscious — freedom consisting of connecting, separating, synthesizing, and such — which, when resting only in mere self-nature, is [characterized by] not resting like the insentient, being of the nature of unlimited luminosity, not looking toward another's face. That very thing, being different from the insentient self-nature that lacks the freedom of connecting, separating, and such, gives rise to distinction. Therefore, having aimed principally at this, instead of saying 'the Self is conscious,' in order to subordinate other properties and elevate the property of reflective awareness —

children.text: nanu yathā prakāśo 'prakāśaśca iti ybhayamapi svātmani , tataśca prakāśa iti ukte jaḍāt na vailakṣaṇyam uditaṃ syāt , tadvat vimarśo 'pi avimarśo 'pi ca svātmani, iti tenāpi kathaṃ vailakṣaṇyaṃ jaḍājaḍayoḥ ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Just as both luminosity and non-luminosity rest in the self, and therefore by saying 'luminosity,' distinction from the insentient would not be stated — similarly, both reflective awareness and non-reflective awareness rest in the self, so how could distinction between insentient and non-insentient be established even by that? Anticipating this, he says:
<s>Citi</s> (consciousness), whose nature is reflective awareness, arises as the supreme speech (<s>parā vāk</s>), the essence of autonomy;
this is the primary freedom — that is the sovereignty of the Supreme Self. //

children.text: cetayati ityatra yā citiḥ citikriyā tasyāḥ pratyavamarśaḥ svātmacamatkāralakṣaṇa ātmā svabhāvaḥ / tathā hi ---- ghaṭena svātmani na camatkriyate , svātmā na parāmṛśyate , na svātmani tena prakāśyate , na aparicchinnatayā bhāsyate , tato ca cetyata iti ucyate / caitreṇa tu svātmani ahamiti saṃrambhodyoyollāsavibhūtiyogāt camatkriyate , svātmā parāmṛśyate , svātmanyeva prakāśyate , idamiti yaḥ pariccheda etāvadrūpatayā tadvilakṣaṇībhāvena nīlapītasukhaduḥkhatacchūnyatādyasaṃkhyāvabhāsayogena avabhāsyate , tataḥ caitreṇa cetyate iti ucyate / evaṃ ca vimarśaḥ svātmani avimarśo 'pi svātmani ityasiddametat / vimarśo hi sarvaṃsahaḥ paramapi ātmīkaroti , ātmānaṃ ca parīkaroti , ubhayam ekīkaroti , ekīkṛtaṃ dvayamapi nyagbhāvayati ityevaṃsvabhāvaḥ / pratyavamarśāśca āntarābhilāpātmakaśabdanasvabhāvaḥ , tacca śabdanaṃ saṅketanirapekṣameva avicchinnacamatkārātmakam antarmukhaśironirdeśaprakhyam akārādimāyīyasāṅketikaśabdajīvitabhūta ---- nīlamidaṃcaitro 'hamityādipratyavamarśāntarabhittibhūtatvāt , pūrṇatvāt parā , vakti viśvam abhilapati pratyavamarśena iti ca vāk , ata eva sā svarasena cidrūpatayā svātmaviśrāntivapuṣā uditā sadānastamitā nityā ahamityeva / etadeva paramātmano mukhyaṃ svātantryam aiśvaryam īśitṛtvam ananyāpekṣitvam ucyate / parāparaṃ tu idaṃbhāvarūpasya pratyavamarśasya akhyātiprāṇasya udbodhamātre 'pi ahaṃbhāva eva viśrānteḥ śrīsadāśivādibhūmau paśyantīdaśāyām / aparaṃ tu idaṃbhāvasyaiva nirūḍhau māyāgarbhādhikṛtānāmeva viṣṇuviriñcendrādīnām , tattu teṣāṃ parameśvaraprasādajameva / iti anyanirapekṣataiva paramārthata ānandaḥ , aiśvaryam , svātanryam , caitanyam / tasmāt yuktamuktam
children.translated_text: 'Acts of being conscious' (<s>cetayati</s>) — the consciousness-action (<s>citikriyā</s>) therein, its reflective awareness (<s>pratyavamarśa</s>), characterized by self-wonder (<s>svātma-camatkāra</s>), is its essential nature (<s>ātmā</s>). For a pot does not wonder at its own self, does not reflectively grasp its own self, does not manifest in its own self, does not appear as unlimited — and therefore it is said to be 'that which is made conscious of.' But <s>Caitra</s>, through the connection with the glory of exuberant intensity, vigor, and power of 'I' in his own self, wonders at his own self, reflectively grasps his own self, manifests in his own self, and — the delimitation that is 'this,' [appearing] as being of just this extent, through becoming different from that, through the connection with innumerable appearances of blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, their void, and such — he is manifested. Therefore, it is said that '<s>Caitra</s> is made conscious of.' Thus, [the objection that] 'reflective awareness is in the self and non-reflective awareness is also in the self' — this is not established. For reflective awareness is all-encompassing — it makes even the supreme its own, makes its own self into another, unifies both, and also subordinates the unified pair — such is its nature. And the reflective grasping is of the nature of inner speech (<s>āntarābhilāpa</s>), of the nature of verbalization; and that verbalization, independent of convention, is of the nature of uninterrupted wonder, resembling the inner pointing of the head [in assent], being the life-force of the <s>Māyic</s> conventional sounds beginning with 'a' — because it is the ground underlying the reflective graspings such as 'this is blue,' 'this is <s>Caitra</s>,' 'I [am],' and the like. Because of its completeness, it is <s>parā</s> (supreme); because it speaks, articulates the universe through reflective grasping, it is <s>vāk</s> (speech). Therefore, it arises naturally (<s>svarasena</s>) as the nature of consciousness, with the form of resting in its own self, ever-risen, never-set, eternal — as 'I' alone. This alone is called the primary freedom, sovereignty, lordship, non-dependence-on-another of the Supreme Self. The intermediate [level] of freedom belongs to the reflective grasping whose form is 'this-ness' — [which is] the life-force of <s>akhyāti</s> (non-recognition) — even in the mere awakening of the 'I'-sense in which it rests, at the level of the glorious <s>Sadāśiva</s> and others, in the state of <s>paśyantī</s>. But the lower [level] belongs to those presiding within the womb of <s>Māyā</s> — <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Viriñca</s> (Brahmā), <s>Indra</s>, and others — where 'this-ness' itself has become fully developed; and that [freedom] of theirs is born solely from the grace of the Supreme Lord. Thus, non-dependence-on-another is in ultimate truth bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya</s>), freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>), consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>). Therefore, it is rightly said:
{...thereby He is distinguished from the insentient. /}
He demonstrates that this has been shown in the principal scriptures as well:
That scintillation (<s>sphurattā</s>) is the great existence (<s>mahāsattā</s>), not particularized by space and time;
that very thing is declared as the essence — the heart of the Supreme Lord. //

children.text: iha ghaṭaḥ kasmāt asti , svapuṣpaṃ kasmāt nāsti ityukta itivaktāro bhavanti ghaṭo hi sphurati mama na tu itarat iti / tadetat ghaṭatvameva yadi sphurattvaṃ sphuraṇasaṃbandhaḥ , tat sarvadā sarvasya sphuret na kasyacidvā , tasmāt mama sphurati iti ko'rthaḥ , madīyaṃ sphuraṇaṃ spandanam ādiṣṭam iti / spandanañca kiñciccalanam , eṣaiva ca kiñcidrūpatā yat acalamapi calamābhāsate iti , prakāśasvarūpaṃ hi manāgapi nātiricyate , atiricyate iva iti tat acalameva ābhāsabhedayuktamiva ca bhāti / tata uktam
children.translated_text: Here, 'why does the pot exist?' 'why does the sky-flower not exist?' — those who say this in response say: 'the pot scintillates to me, but not the other.' Now, if this 'pot-ness' itself is 'scintillation' — a relation with scintillation — then it would scintillate to everyone always, or to no one at all. Therefore, what does 'it scintillates to me' mean? — my scintillation, my vibration (<s>spanda</s>) is indicated. And vibration is a slight movement; and this very 'slight-ness' is that even the unmoving appears as moving — for the nature of luminosity does not increase even slightly; it appears as if increasing, and thus shines as unmoving yet as if possessing differences of appearance. Therefore it is stated:
{The Self itself, scintillating in all entities, of the nature of blissful consciousness,
with unobstructed flow of will, with expanding seeing and action — is <s>Śiva</s>. //}
Thus. And:

children.text: {atikruddhaḥ prahṛṣṭo vā kiṃ karomīti vā mṛśan /
children.translated_text: {Whether extremely angry, or greatly delighted, or deliberating 'what shall I do?',
or running — whatever state one reaches, there <s>spanda</s> (vibration) is established. //} (<s>Spandakārikā</s> 22)
Thus.
{...for the discernment of the <s>spanda</s> principle. /} (<s>Spandakārikā</s> 21)
Thus.
{The outpourings of the vibration of the <s>guṇas</s>... /} (<s>Spandakārikā</s> 19)

children.text: iti ca / loke 'pi vividhavaicitryayogena spandavattvam / sattā ca bhavanakartṛtā sarvakriyāṣu svātantryam / sā ca svapuṣpādikamapi vyāpnoti iti mahatī , deśakālau nīlādivat saiva sṛjati iti tābhyāṃ viśeṣaṇīyā na bhavati , yat kila yena tulyakakṣyatayā bhāti tat tasya viśeṣaṇaṃ kaṭaka iva caitrasya / na ca deśakālau vimarśena tulyakakṣyau bhātaḥ tayoḥ idantayā tasya ca ahantayā prakāśe tulyakakṣyatvānupapatteḥ / evaṃ deśakālāsparśāt vibhutvaṃ nityatvaṃ ca , sakaladeśakālasparśo '; pi tannirmāṇayogāt iti tato 'pi vyāpakatvanityatve / taduktam
children.translated_text: Thus too. In common life as well, vibrant-ness (<s>spandavattvam</s>) consists in the connection with various diversity. And existence (<s>sattā</s>) is the agenthood of being, freedom in all actions. And that pervades even sky-flowers and such, hence it is great (<s>mahatī</s>); space and time are created by it alone, like blue and such — hence it cannot be qualified by them. For that which appears to another as being of equal status is a qualifier of that other, like a bracelet of <s>Caitra</s>. But space and time do not appear as being of equal status with reflective awareness, since in their manifestation as 'this' and its [manifestation] as 'I,' the impossibility of equal status [is evident]. Thus, from not being touched by space and time, omnipresence (<s>vibhutva</s>) and eternality (<s>nityatva</s>) [follow]; and also from touching all space and time through manufacturing them — hence from that too, pervasiveness and eternality. As stated:
{The great existence is called the great goddess — the life of the universe. /}

children.text: iti / sāram iti yat atucchaṃ rūpaṃ tat iyameva vimarśaśaktiḥ , grāhyagrāhakāṇāṃ yat prakāśātmakaṃ rūpaṃ tasyāpi aprakāśavailakṣaṇyākṣepikā iyameva iti śrīsāraśāstre'pi nirūpitam
children.translated_text: Thus. The 'essence' (<s>sāra</s>) — that which is the non-empty form — is this very power of reflective awareness; for even the luminous form of the apprehended and the apprehender, its distinction from non-luminosity is cast by this alone — as demonstrated in the glorious <s>Sāra Śāstra</s> as well:
{That which is the essence of this world is the supreme power <s>Mālinī</s>. /}

children.text: iti / saiṣā iti śaktipratyabhijñānaṃ darśitam / hṛdayaṃ ca nāma pratiṣṭhāsthānamucyate , tacca uktanītyā jaḍānāṃ cetanam , tasyāpi prakāśātprakatvam , tasyāpi vimarśaśaktiḥ iti viśvasya parame pade tiṣṭhato viśrāntasya tasya idameva hṛdayaṃ vimarśarūpaṃ paramantrātmakaṃ yatra tatra abhidhīyate / sarvasya hi mantra eva hṛdayam , mantraśca vimarśanātmā , vimarśanaṃ ca parāvākchaktimayam / tata evoktam
children.translated_text: Thus. By 'that very' (<s>saiṣā</s>), the recognition of the power is shown. And 'heart' (<s>hṛdaya</s>) means the place of establishment — and that, in the manner stated, is consciousness for the insentient; even for that, luminosity is its nature; and even for that, the power of reflective awareness — thus, for the universe resting in the supreme state, this alone is the heart, of the nature of reflective awareness, consisting of the supreme <s>mantra</s>, wherever it is spoken of. For the heart of everything is indeed <s>mantra</s>, and <s>mantra</s> is of the nature of reflective awareness, and reflective awareness is constituted by the power of supreme speech (<s>parā vāk</s>). Therefore it is said:
{Without them there would be no word, no meaning, nor any movement of consciousness. /}
Thus.
{There, having first attained the state of the knower... /}
and so forth — thus in the scriptures. And by the revered <s>Bhartṛhari</s> as well:
{There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of word. /}
All knowledge, as if pervaded [by word], is apprehended through word.
If the eternal word-nature of awareness were to depart,

children.text: na prakāśaḥ prakāśeta sā hi pratyavamarśinī // }
children.translated_text: luminosity would not shine — for that [word-nature] is the reflective awareness (<s>pratyavamarśinī</s>).}
Thus.
{This very [word-awareness] is the consciousness of beings in <s>saṃsāra</s>, functioning both externally and internally;
upon its departure, this [being] appears unconscious, like a wooden puppet.}

children.text: ityādi ca / tat etena viduḥ ityetat nirvāhitam / bauddhairapi adhyavasāyāpekṣaṃ prakāśasya prāmāṇyaṃ vadadbhiḥ upagataprāya eva ayam arthaḥ , abhilāpātmakatvāt adhyavasāyasya iti //14//
children.translated_text: And so on. Thus by this, 'they know' — this has been established. Even by the Buddhists, who state that the validity of <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity) depends on <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination), this meaning has been nearly accepted, since determination is of the nature of verbal expression (<s>abhilāpa</s>). //14//

children.text: nanu asaṃkhyaśaktiśreṇośobhitavapuṣi paramaśive vimarśaśaktireva iyam itthaṃkāram abhiṣicyate kasmāt ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Now, when <s>Paramaśiva</s> (the Supreme <s>Śiva</s>) is adorned with a body of innumerable series of powers, why is this power of reflective awareness (<s>vimarśaśakti</s>) alone anointed in this manner? — anticipating this objection, he says:
For this very reason, He would make Himself an object of knowledge, being in a state of separation;
but the object of knowledge — by His turning toward it, His independence would not be impaired.
By His independence, the Lord — Himself unabandoned by independence, being of non-dual nature —
having created through conceptions such as 'Lord' and the like, would engage in worldly activity.

children.text: sarvāḥ śaktoḥ kartṛtvaśaktiḥ aiśvaryātmā samākṣipati / sā ca vimarśarūpā iti yuktam asyā eva prādhānyam iti tātparyeṇa uttaramuktam / śabdārthasya ayam , prakāśātmā parameśvaraḥ svātmānaṃ jñātrekarūpatvāt ajñeyamapi jñeyīkaroti iti yat saṃbhāvyate kāraṇāntarasya anupapatteḥ darśitatvāt dṛḍhena saṃbhāvanānumānena , tadata eva vimarśaśaktilakṣaṇāt kartṛtvāt hetoḥ bhavati , yato hi ayam ātmānaṃ parāmṛśati tato viśvanirbharatvāt tathā nīlāditvena cakāsti / nanu eṣaiva kutaḥ saṃbhāvanā , ātmānaṃ jñeyīkaroti iti ? āha, pṛthak prakāśāt bahirbhūtā sthitiḥ yasya tādṛk jñeyaṃ naiva bhavati / tuḥ avadhāreṇa / tatra ca uktā yuktayaḥ / abhyuccayayuktimapi āha , yadi vyatiriktaṃ jñeyaṃ syāt tat jñātṛrūpasya ātmano yat etat jñeyaviṣayam aunmukhyaṃ svasaṃvedanasiddhaṃ dṛśyate tat na asya syāt , tena vyatiriktaviṣayaunmukhyena anyādhīnatvaṃ nāma pāratantryam asya ānīyate / pāratantryaṃ ca svātantryasya viruddham / svātantryameva ca ananyamukhaprekṣitvam ātmanaḥ svarūpam , iti vyatiriktonmukha ātmā anātmaiva syāt / anātmā ca jaḍo jñeyaṃ prati na unmukhībhavati iti prasaṅgaḥ / tataḥ prasaṅgaviparyayāt idamāyātam ---- avyatiriktonmukhaḥ svatantraḥ san ātmānameva jñeyīkaroti iti //15//
children.translated_text: The power of agency (<s>kartṛtvaśakti</s>), which is the essence of sovereignty, encompasses all powers. And since that [power of agency] is of the nature of reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>), it is appropriate that this [vimarśaśakti] alone has primacy — this is the purport of the following reply. The meaning of the words is: the Supreme Lord, being of the nature of <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity), makes His own self — which is unknowable due to being of the sole nature of the knower — into an object of knowledge; this is inferred with strong presumptive inference, since the impossibility of any other cause has been shown. That happens precisely due to <s>kartṛtva</s> (agency), which is characterized by the power of reflective awareness — for since He apprehends Himself, therefore, due to being replete with the universe, He shines also as blue and the like. But whence this very presumption that He makes Himself an object of knowledge? He answers: that which has its existence externally, separate from <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity), does not become an object of knowledge at all. The word 'tu' is restrictive. And the reasoning for this has been stated. He also presents the argument by way of increasing force: if there were a separate object of knowledge, then the orientation toward the knowable object — this orientation of the self, whose nature is that of a knower, which is established through self-awareness — would not belong to it; and through that orientation toward a separate object, a dependence on another, which is bondage (<s>pāratantrya</s>), would be imposed upon it. And bondage is opposed to independence (<s>svātantrya</s>). And independence alone — not looking to the face of another — is the essential nature of the self. Thus a self oriented toward a separate [object] would be a non-self. And a non-self, being inert, would not turn toward an object of knowledge — this is the logical consequence (<s>prasaṅga</s>). Therefore, by the reversal of this consequence, this has been arrived at: being independent, with orientation not toward something separate, He makes His own self alone the object of knowledge. //15//

children.text: na ca kevalaṃ nīlādirūpameva jñeyam , yāvat atyaktakartṛsvabhāvaṃ svātantryeṇa aparityaktameva santam ātmānaṃ nirmāya vyavahāreṇa dhyānopāsanārcanopadeśādinā yojayati iti yat saṃbhāvyate tadapi ata eva iti saṃbandhaḥ / nanu svātantryayuktaṃ ca nirmīyate ca iti viruddham idam ? atrāha ,

children.translated_text: 'of non-dual nature' —

children.text: saṃvidekarūpasya svātantryāt hetoḥ idaṃ na na yujyate , yat kila māyāpade atidurghaṭaṃ pratibhāti , tatsaṃpādane yat apratihataṃ svātantryaṃ tadeva punaḥ svātantryaśabdena darśitam /
children.translated_text: due to <s>svātantrya</s> (independence), the cause, of one whose essential nature is unitary consciousness — what appears exceedingly difficult to accomplish at the level of <s>Māyā</s>, that very unobstructed independence which accomplishes it has been indicated again by the word <s>svātantrya</s>.
'for this very reason' —

children.text: ityanena tu vimarśaśaktirūpam iti apunaruktam / atha vā ata eva svātantryāt iti sāmānādhikaraṇyena ślokadvayena saṃbandhanīyam / udāharaṇam atrārthe darśayati , nīlādinirmāṇavat asya svatrantranirmāṇasya aprasiddhatvāt , īśvaro bhagavān ātmā nityo vibhuḥ svatantraḥ ityevamādau hi pramātuḥ , pūjayituḥ , dhyātuḥ vā 'pṛthagbhūtaṃ tat prameyam , pūjyam , dhyeyaṃ ca bhāti iti tat tāvat nirmitam , na ca anīśvaram / evaṃ hi īśvara iti , anīśvara iti saṃkalpadhyānādeḥ tulyatvaṃ syāt , na ca evam phalabhedasya upalabdheḥ iti , tasmāt svātantryaśūnyatābhāsanena svātantryayuktatābhāsanena ca yat idam ubhayaṃ jñeyam ātmarūpameva parameśvaro bhāsayati tat vimarśaśaktibalāt eva , iti saiva pradhānam iti //16//
children.translated_text: but by this [expression], [it is indicated] that it is of the nature of the power of reflective awareness — thus there is no repetition. Or else, 'for this very reason, due to independence' should be connected with both verses through co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>). He gives an example for this meaning, since this independent creation is not well-known like the creation of blue and the like: In 'the Lord, the Blessed One, the Self, eternal, all-pervading, independent' and such [statements], for the knower, the worshipper, or the meditator, the separate [entity] appears as the object of knowledge, the object of worship, the object of meditation — and to that extent it is created; but it is not non-sovereign. For otherwise, the conception 'Lord' and the conception 'non-Lord' would be equal in meditation and so forth; but that is not so, since a difference of result is perceived. Therefore, by manifesting both — the appearance of being devoid of independence and the appearance of being endowed with independence — that which the Supreme Lord manifests as this twofold object of knowledge, identical with His own self, is indeed by the force of the power of reflective awareness (<s>vimarśaśakti</s>) alone — and hence that [power] is primary. //16//

And it is not merely blue and such that is the object of knowledge; rather, without abandoning His nature as agent, by His independence (<s>svātantrya</s>), He creates Himself — who is indeed not abandoned [by independence] — and engages [Himself] in worldly activity through meditation, worship, ritual, instruction, and the like; that this is inferred — 'for this very reason' — this is the connection. But is it not contradictory that [what is] endowed with independence is also created? To this he responds:

children.text: nanu prakāśabalāt bhāvavyavasthā , sa ca prakāśo vimarśasāra iti vimarśābhede tadeva tat iti vaktuṃ yuktam , īśvara ātmā ityādisaṃkalpeṣu ca nirmitasya idantayā parāmarśaḥ , svātantryaṃ tu ahaṃparāmarśarūpam , iti nirmitasya tadrūpatvābhāve kathaṃ svātantryāmuktatvam iti ? tat etat parihartumāha
children.translated_text: Objection: The establishment of entities is by the force of <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity), and that luminosity has <s>vimarśa</s> as its essence — hence, since <s>vimarśa</s> is non-different [from <s>prakāśa</s>], it is proper to say 'that is that.' And in conceptions such as 'the Lord,' 'the Self,' etc., the created [entity] is apprehended as 'this' (in objectivity), whereas independence has the form of the 'I'-apprehension — so when the created lacks that [I-]form, how can it be said to be not abandoned by independence? To resolve this he says:
Due to the difference of apprehensions such as 'I' and others, there is no otherness of this [self] that is not of any other nature;
by the very fact of being apprehended as 'I,' the creation of this [self] is like the verbal ending and the action [it denotes].

children.text:
svarūpe bhāvapratyayaḥ , ādigrahaṇāt ātmeśvarādiparāmarśaḥ , tiṅgrahaṇaṃ kriyāvācipratyayopalakṣaṇam , karmagrahaṇam asattvabhūtaśaktirūpopalakṣaṇam / tat ayam arthaḥ , aham ityevaṃ svarūpo yaḥ parāmarśo yaśca īśvaraḥ pramātā ātmā śiva ityādiḥ anantaprakāraḥ parāmarśaḥ , tasya yadyapi bhedo 'nyonyarūpatā tathāpi tadbhedāt hetoḥ asya ātmano nirmātṛrūpasya ahaṃparāmarśamayasya nirmeyarūpasya ca īśvarādiparāmarśāspadasya yo bhedaḥ śaṅkitaḥ , sa na yuktaḥ / yata īśvara ityapi yaḥ parāmarśaḥ , sa īśanaśīle jñātṛtvakartṛtvatattve viśrānyati , jñātṛtvādi ca jñānādau svātantryam ananyamukhaprekṣitvam avicchinnajñānayogaḥ , avicchedaśca jānāmi karomi iti asmadarthaviśrāntiḥ iti asya īśvarasya ātmanaḥ sṛṣṭeḥ sṛjyamānasya ahaṃvimarśanīyatvameva / sṛṣṭeriti vā hetau pañcamī / asya īśvarasya yataḥ īśvarādisaṃkalpeṣu api ahaṃparāmarśanayogyasyaiva sṛṣṭiḥ /
arhe kṛtyaḥ / yathā kriyākārakasamuccayavikalpādiśaktayo yathāsvaṃ tiṅtṛtīyādicavādiprayogāvaseyaparāmarśaparamārthāḥ pākaḥ kartā samuccayo vikalpaḥ ityādiśabdaiḥ abhidhīyamānāḥ sattvabhāvamāpāditā api pacati caitreṇa ca vā ityevaṃrūpe mūlaparāmarśe viśrāmyanti , anyathā tu tāḥ pratītā naiva bhaveyuḥ / tadvat atrāpi / etaduktaṃ bhavati ---- parāmarśe nāma viśrāntisthānam , tacca pāryantikameva pāramārthikam , tacca ahamityevaṃrūpameva / madhyaviśrāntipadaṃ tu yat vṛkṣamūlasthānīyaṃ grāmagamane tasya tadapekṣayā sṛṣṭatvam ucyate iti ko virodhaḥ / anena nīlādeḥ api idaṃ nīlam iti madhyaparāmarśe 'pi mūlaparāmarśe ahamityeva viśrānteḥ ātmamayatvam upapāditameva /

children.translated_text: 'I know this blue' —
for even in this,
'I am luminosity' —
this alone is the truth. As has been stated:
'of this' —

children.text: ityādi / mūḍhastu nīlādivimarśāt eva arthakriyādiparitoṣābhimānī iti nīlādeḥ svātantryanirmuktatvam uktam / ātmādau tu tanmūlaparāmarśaviśrāntimantareṇa pratītiparisamāptim arthakriyāṃ ca mūḍho'pi na abhimanyata iti tasya nirmitau api anujjhitasvātantryam uktam //17//
children.translated_text: and so on. But the deluded one, being satisfied by the efficacy of objects and such from the reflective awareness of blue alone, — therefore it has been stated that blue and the like are released from independence. But regarding the Self and such, even the deluded one does not consider cognition complete or efficacy [achieved] without repose in that root-apprehension — therefore, even in what is created [as 'Lord' etc.], independence has been stated as not abandoned. //17//

The <s>bhāva</s> suffix is in the sense of essential nature. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the apprehensions 'self,' 'Lord,' and the like [are included]. The term 'tiṅ' (verbal ending) illustrates suffixes denoting action. The term 'karma' (object) illustrates the power in the form of a non-substantive entity. The meaning is this: the apprehension that is of the form 'I,' and the apprehension of infinite variety such as 'Lord,' 'knower,' 'Self,' '<s>Śiva</s>' — although there is difference among these, i.e., mutual distinctness of form, nevertheless, the difference that is suspected between this self in its nature as creator, which consists of the 'I'-apprehension, and in its nature as created, which is the locus of the 'Lord' and such apprehensions — that [difference] is not justified. For the apprehension 'Lord' too reposes in the principle of knower-and-agent that has the nature of sovereignty; and knower-hood and the like is independence (<s>svātantrya</s>) in knowledge and so forth — not looking to the face of another, the uninterrupted conjunction with knowledge; and the non-interruption is the repose in the first-person meaning (<s>asmad-artha</s>): 'I know,' 'I do' — thus, the creation of this Lord, the self, is necessarily to be apprehended by the 'I'-reflective awareness. Or the fifth case 'of creation' (<s>sṛṣṭeḥ</s>) is in the causal sense: because, for this Lord, even in conceptions such as 'Lord' and the like, creation is only of what is fit to be apprehended as 'I.' 'arhe kṛtyaḥ' (the gerundive suffix in the sense of fitness). Just as the powers of action-agent-aggregation-conceptual-construction and the like, whose ultimate reality is the apprehension to be ascertained by the usage of verbal endings, instrumental case-endings, 'and' particles, etc., — such as 'cooking,' 'agent,' 'aggregation,' 'conceptual construction' — even though elevated to the status of substantive entities by being denoted by these words, they ultimately repose in the root-apprehension of the form 'he cooks,' 'by <s>Caitra</s>,' 'and,' 'or' — otherwise, those [entities] would not be cognized at all. So too here. What is being said is this: the resting-place in the case of apprehension is the place of repose, and that which is ultimate is the one that is truly real, and that is of the form 'I' alone. But the intermediate resting-place, which is like a tree-root [rest stop] during a journey to a village — with respect to that, its being 'created' is said — so what contradiction is there? By this, even in the case of blue and the like, the 'this-ness' — 'this is blue' — even in this intermediate apprehension, since the repose in the root-apprehension is 'I' alone, the nature of being constituted by the Self has been established.

children.text: nanvevaṃ viśvaparāmarśanām aham ityeva viśuddhaikaparāmarśaviśrāntireva tattvam tat katham idam ucyate ---- jñānasmṛtyādikā asya śaktaya iti , jñānasya ca saṃśayanirṇayādibhedaḥ nīlādīnāṃ ca vaicitryam ? iti āśaṅkāyāṃ parihāramāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If the truth of all apprehension of the universe is nothing but repose in the single pure apprehension 'I,' then how is it said that knowledge, memory, and the like are its powers, and that knowledge has divisions such as doubt, ascertainment, and so on, and that blue and such have variety? In response to this doubt, he presents the resolution:
That very [awareness], by the <s>Māyā-śakti</s> (power of illusion) of the all-pervading Lord, having differentiated knowable objects as its domain,
is called by the names knowledge, conception, determination, and so on.

children.text: anupapannam avabhāsanaṃ māyā iti ucyate , tataśca bhinnaṃ prakāśāt sarvam avabhāsajātaṃ māyā , tatra ca cittattvasyaiva svātantryaṃ māyāśaktiḥ , tayā bhinnaṃ yat saṃvedyaṃ pramātuśca anyonyataśca , māyāśaktyā bhinnena pramātuḥ anyonyato vedyācca karaṇavargeṇa yat saṃvedyaṃ sa eva gocaro viśrāntipadaṃ yasyāḥ tādṛśī satī ,

children.translated_text: 'that very' —

children.text: pratyavamarśātmā citiḥ parāvāgrūpā jñānam iti , saṃkalpa iti , adhyavasāya iti ca ucyate , ādigrahaṇāt saṃśayaḥ smṛtiḥ ityādi / tathā hi ---- indtriyeṇa sphuṭagrāhiṇā bāhyena viṣayeṇa sphuṭena ca niyantritaṃ saṃvittattvaṃ tat jñānam / manasā viṣayeṇa ca apshuṭena saṃkalpaḥ / buddhyā viṣayeṇa ca viṣayatvaparyantabhājā adhyavasāyo niścayaḥ / viṣayasya ca yat bhinnatvaṃ bahirantaḥkaraṇānāṃ ca tatprakāśābhedāt anupapannaṃ cittattvena bhāsyate iti bhede yato viśrāntiḥ , na tu bhedasya abhede īśvarasadāśivādivat , tato jñānasaṃkalpādayo bhinnāḥ tasya apradhvastasvasvabhāvābhedasya saṃvittattvasya anusaṃdhātuḥ śaktaya iti uktāḥ , saṃśayādayaśca bhinnā nīlādivaicitryaṃ ca iti sarvam akhaṇḍitam //18//
children.translated_text: <s>citi</s> (consciousness), which is the supreme <s>vāk</s> (speech) of the nature of reflective awareness (<s>pratyavamarśa</s>), is called 'knowledge,' 'conception,' 'determination,' and so on — by the word 'ādi' (etc.), doubt, memory, and the like [are included]. For — the consciousness-principle, when regulated by the external sense organ that grasps clearly and by the external object that is clear, is knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>). When [regulated] by the mind and by an unclear object, it is conception (<s>saṃkalpa</s>). When [regulated] by the intellect and by an object that reaches the culmination of objecthood, it is determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>), i.e., ascertainment (<s>niścaya</s>). And the differentiation of the object and of the external and internal instruments — since it is not established as different from the consciousness-principle due to its non-difference from that luminosity — is manifested by the consciousness-principle itself; and since the repose is in differentiation, but the differentiation does not [repose] in non-differentiation as in the [levels of] <s>Īśvara</s>, <s>Sadāśiva</s>, and the like — therefore knowledge, conception, and so on are different, and are called the powers of the consciousness-principle — the connector (<s>anusaṃdhātṛ</s>) — whose non-difference of its own essential nature has not been destroyed; and doubt and the like are different, and the variety of blue and the like — all is unimpaired. //18//

Manifestation that is not established [as non-different from consciousness] is called <s>Māyā</s>; and therefore, all the host of manifestations that are differentiated from <s>prakāśa</s> (luminosity) constitute <s>Māyā</s>; and therein, the very independence of the consciousness-principle is the <s>Māyā-śakti</s>. By that [<s>Māyā-śakti</s>], what is differentiated — the knowable that is [separated] from the knower and mutually from one another — by the instrument-group that is differentiated by <s>Māyā-śakti</s> from the knower, from one another, and from the knowable, [the awareness] whose domain, whose resting-place, is that knowable — being such,

children.text: nanu pratyavamarśātmatvaṃ citiśakteḥ saṅkalpasmaraṇādiśaktiṣu sacikalpātmikāsu bhavatu / yā tu nirvikalparūpā sākṣātkaraṇalakṣaṇā anubahvaśaktiḥ , tatra katham / pratyabamarśo hi abhilāpaviśeṣayojanāmayaḥ , abhilāpaviśeṣayojanā ca saṅketasmaraṇam apekṣate / tacca saṃskāraprabodham / so 'pi tādṛśdṛśam , iti evaṃ prathamasamaye katham abhilāpayogaḥ iti parasya vyāmoham apohitumāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Let the nature of reflective awareness (<s>pratyavamarśa</s>) belong to the <s>citi-śakti</s> (consciousness-power) in the powers of conception, remembrance, and the like, which are of a conceptual (<s>savikalpa</s>) nature. But in the power of direct perception (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>), which is of a non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpa</s>) nature — how [does reflective awareness apply] there? For reflective awareness consists in the application of specific verbal expression (<s>abhilāpa</s>), and the application of specific verbal expression requires the recollection of convention (<s>saṅketa</s>); and that [requires] the awakening of an impression; and that too [requires] a similar prior perception — thus, at the very first moment, how can there be application of verbal expression? To dispel this confusion of the opponent, he says:
Even at the moment of direct perception there is reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>); how otherwise
could running and such be possible, being devoid of reconnection (<s>pratisaṃdhāna</s>)?

children.text: iha tāvat caitanyasya ātmabhūto 'ṅgulinirdeśādiprakhyo'bhilāpayogaḥ , anyathā bālasya prathamaṃ vyavahāre dṛśyamāne vyutpattireva na syāt / nirvikalpakajñānaparaṃparayā hi taṃ śabdaṃ śṛṇoti , tataḥ tamarthaṃ puraḥ paśyati , punastadviviktaṃ bhūtalaṃ paśyati iti ghaṭam ānaya naya iti vyavahārāt katham asya ayam artha iti hṛdi parisphuret , idam ghaṭa iti , idamānaya iti , idaṃ naya iti , itiyojanāprāṇo hi ayamarthaḥ , yojanā ca vikalpavyāpāraḥ / atra bālāsya prāgjanmānubhūtasaṅketasmṛteḥ evam , tathāpi saṅketakāle sa śabdo viṣayatvena idaṃbhāvena pratyavamṛśyamānatvāt bhedāt pracyutya nirbhāsamāno vijñānaśarīre viśrāntaḥ san vācaka iti bhavati , tad vijñānasya savarūpaṃ cet bhāti tat abhilāpamayameva iti , yathā viṣayasya sukharūpatvābhāve 'pi jñānaṃ sukhātmakaṃ bhāti tathā mā bhūt abhilāpātmā rūpādiḥ viṣayaḥ , tathāpi vijñānaṃ tadātmakaṃ avabhāsiṣyate / atra tu darśane viṣayasyāpi vimarśamayatvāt abhilāpamayatvameva vastutaḥ , staimityādyavasthāpi yadi na parāmarśamayī tarhi asyāṃ vikalpātmakapramātṛvyāpārānulāsāt saṃbhavaḥ śapathaparamārtha eva , smaraṇaṃ ca na syāt , rūpaviṣayādhyavasāyī hi yadi vikalpa udiyāt kimanyat , sarvacintāsaṃharaṇena staimityaṃ nāma na syāt , iti tatrāpi asti antaḥ parāmarśaḥ , sakalena ca śabdagrāmeṇa śabdanaṃ hi sahante vastūni , tatra ca niyataśabdayojanaṃ kriyate / tathā hi ---- bālasya puraḥ puṇḍe sahajo yaḥ parāmarśaḥ , aham ityavicchedena idam iti vicchedena vā tatpṛṣṭhe eva gaura iti gauḥ iti vā śabda āropyate , so 'pi abhyāsāt pramātṛmayo bhavati , tatpṛṣṭhe ca anyaḥ śukla iti , anyat balīvarda iti , ityevaṃ saṅketatattvam / tasmāt asti sākṣātkāre pratyavamarśaḥ / apiśabdasya ayamāśayaḥ / iha sākṣātkāro vastutaḥ

children.translated_text: 'I see' —

children.text: ityevaṃbhūtavikalpanavyāpāraparyanta eva / vikalpo hi pratyakṣasya vyāpāra iti paro 'pi manyate / na ca vyapāraḥ tadvato bhinno yuktaḥ , tatsvarūpabhūto hi saḥ / bhavatu vā kṣaṇamātrasvabhāvaḥ sākṣātkāraḥ , tatrāpi asti vimarśaḥ / avaśyaṃ caitat /
children.translated_text: of such a nature, extending up to the operation of conceptualization (<s>vikalpa</s>). For <s>vikalpa</s> is the operation of perception — even the other [school] accepts this. And it is not proper that the operation should be different from the possessor of the operation, for it is intrinsic to its nature. Or, even if direct perception is of momentary nature, even there reflective awareness exists. And this is necessarily so.
'How otherwise' —

children.text: iti / yadi sa na syāt tat ekābhisaṃdhānena javāt gacchan , tvaritaṃ ca varkṣān paṭhan , drutaṃ ca mantrapustakaṃ vācayan , na abhimatameva gacchet , uccārayet , vācayet vā / tathā hi ---- tasmin deśe jñānam -- ācikramiṣā -- ākramaṇam -- ākrāntatājñānam -- prayojanāntarānusaṃdhānam -- tityakṣā -- deśāntarānusaṃdhiḥ , tatrāpi ācikramiṣā ityādinā yojanaviyojanarūpeṇa pratyavamarśena vinābhimatadeśāvāptiḥ kathaṃ bhavet / evaṃ tvaritodgrahaṇavācanādau mantavyam / tatra viśe.ataḥ sthānakaraṇākramaṇādiyogaḥ / atra ca yataḥ paścādbhāvisthūlavikalpakalpanā na saṃvedyate , tata eva tvaritatvam iti sūkṣmeṇa pratyavamarśena saṃvartitaśabdabhāvanāmayena bhāvyameva / saṃvartitā hi śabdabhāvanā prasāraṇena vivartyamānā sthūlo vikalpaḥ , yathā idamityasya prasāraṇā ghaṭaḥ śkla ityādiḥ , tasyāpi pṛthubudhnodarākāraḥ śuklatvajātiyuktaguṇasamavāyī ityādiḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. For if it did not exist, then one going quickly with a single aim, or reading trees rapidly, or reciting a mantra-text swiftly, would not go, utter, or recite precisely the intended [thing]. For thus: knowledge of that place — desire to step — stepping — knowledge of having stepped — anticipation of the next purpose — desire to cross — awareness of the next place; and there too, desire to step, and so on — without reflective awareness in the form of combining and separating, how could the arrival at the intended place occur? The same should be considered regarding rapid grasping, recitation, and such. Therein, specifically, there is the conjunction of phonetic place, articulatory effort, sequencing, and such. And here, since the subsequent gross conceptual construction is not experienced [as such], that very swiftness [shows that] one must accept a subtle reflective awareness pervaded by contracted verbal contemplation (<s>śabdabhāvanā</s>). For contracted verbal contemplation, when expanded through unfolding, is gross <s>vikalpa</s> — just as the expansion of 'this' is 'pot,' 'white,' and such; and the expansion of that is 'having a broad base and belly,' 'possessing whiteness-universal and the inherence of qualities,' and so forth.
'Dhāvu' (the root meaning swift purification in motion) —

children.text: iti pāṭhāt dhāvistvaritagatau svaśaktivaśāt vartata iti //19//
children.translated_text: from this reading, one who runs swiftly moves by the power of his own capacity. // 19 //

Here, to begin with, the association with verbal expression (<s>abhilāpa</s>), resembling finger-pointing and such, is intrinsic to consciousness; otherwise, for a child first observed engaging in practical activity, linguistic comprehension would simply not occur. For through a succession of non-conceptual cognitions, the child hears that word, then sees that object before it, then again sees the ground devoid of it — so from the practical activity 'bring the pot, take it away,' how would it flash in the heart that 'this is the meaning of this' — 'this is pot,' 'this is bring,' 'this is take' — for the life of this meaning is combination, and combination is the operation of conceptual thought (<s>vikalpa</s>). Here, even if this is due to the child's memory of conventions experienced in prior births, nevertheless, at the time of the convention, that word, being reflectively grasped as an object with 'this-ness,' having fallen from differentiation, shining forth devoid of separate manifestation, resting in the body of cognition, becomes an expressive term. If that shines as identical with the nature of cognition, then it is nothing but of the nature of verbal expression — just as, even though the object does not have the form of pleasure, cognition appears as having the nature of pleasure; similarly, even if form and such objects are not of the nature of verbal expression, cognition will nonetheless appear as having that nature. But here, in perception, since even the object is of the nature of <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness), it is in reality of the nature of verbal expression. Even the state of stillness and such — if it were not of the nature of reflective awareness, then the occurrence of the operation of the perceiver, who is of the nature of <s>vikalpa</s>, therein would be impossible in the truest sense, and memory too would not occur; for if a <s>vikalpa</s> determining a form-object were to arise, what else [would be needed]? Without the withdrawal of all thought, the state called stillness would not exist — thus even there, inner reflective awareness exists. And objects tolerate verbalization by the entire mass of words, and therein the fixed association of words is accomplished. Thus: before a child, regarding a piebald bull, the innate reflective awareness — superimposed upon it is the word 'gaura' (light-colored) or 'gauḥ' (cow/bull) with unbroken 'I'-awareness or with broken 'this'-awareness, and even that [word], through practice, becomes fused with the perceiver; on top of that, another [word] 'śukla' (white), another 'balīvarda' (bull) — and such is the essence of convention. Therefore, reflective awareness exists in direct perception. This is the intention of the word 'api.' Here, direct perception is in reality

children.text: bhavatu evaṃ sūkṣmo vimarśaḥ prakāśaśarīrāveśī , yatra tu sthūlatvena vikalparūpatā sphuṭā , tatra śabdo nīlādivat eva pṛthak pratibhāsate ---- nīlam idam iti , sa kathaṃ prakāśasvarūpāt apṛthagbhūtaḥ syāt , śabdātmā ca vimarśaḥ , sa ca atra māyātmakaṃ bhedapade 'pi prakāśāpṛthagbhūto bhavadbhiḥ iṣṭaḥ , tat etat kathaṃ pratipattavyam ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Granted that there is such a subtle <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness) that pervades the body of luminosity; but where the conceptual nature (<s>vikalparūpatā</s>) is clearly manifest in gross form — there the word appears separately just like blue and such — 'this is blue' — so how could it be non-separate from the essential nature of luminosity? And <s>vimarśa</s> is of the nature of word, and that, even in the domain of differentiation which is of the nature of <s>Māyā</s>, is accepted by you as non-separate from luminosity — how then is this to be understood? Anticipating this, he says:
The determination 'this is a pot' — transcending name and form —
is the power of the Supreme Lord; it shines as the Self itself, not as 'this-ness.'

children.text: kena etat uktam ghaṭa iti yaḥ sthūlaḥ śabdaḥ sa prakāśajīvitasvabhāvo vimarśa iti / so'pi hi sthūlaḥ śabdo 'rthavat pṛthagbhūta eva bhāti / tau nāmakarūpalakṣaṇau śabdārthau ekarūpatayā

children.translated_text: 'this very one' —

children.text: ityevaṃrūpatvena parāmṛśantī adhyavasā yā sā parameśvaraśaktiḥ vimarśarūpā ātmavadeva ahamityanavacchinnatvena bhāti , na tu kadācit idantayā vicchinnatvena bhāti vicchinnatvena avabhāse parapratiṣṭhatvāt punarvimarśāntareṇa bhāvyam , tatrāpi evam iti anavasthāto nīlasya prakāśanameva na syāt pratiṣṭhālābhābhāvāt / tasmāt sarva eva vimarśaḥ prakāśāt avicchinna eva iti / adhyavasā iti , {ātaścopasarge}(pā. vyā. 3-3-16) ityaṅantaḥ striyām //20//
children.translated_text: as having such a nature, the determination (<s>adhyavasā</s>) that reflectively grasps them — that is the power of the Supreme Lord, of the nature of <s>vimarśa</s>, and it shines as the Self, with unlimited 'I'-awareness; it never appears as 'this-ness,' with limited [awareness]; for to appear with limitation would require being dependent on another and thus requiring yet another <s>vimarśa</s>, and there too the same [would apply] — leading to infinite regress — so that even the illumination of blue would not occur, for lack of a foundation. Therefore, all <s>vimarśa</s> is indeed non-separate from luminosity. 'Adhyavasā' — with the suffix under the rule {ātaścopasarge} (<s>Pāṇini</s> 3.3.16), feminine form. // 20 //

Who has said that the gross word 'pot' — that it is the <s>vimarśa</s> whose essential nature is the life of luminosity? For that gross word too, like an object, appears as utterly separate. Those two — word and meaning, characterized as name and form — in a unified manner,

children.text: nanu evaṃ sarvasyaiva jñānakalāpasya ahamityeva pratiṣṭhāne vedyabhūmisparśo nāsti vedyabhuvi ca deśakālayogaḥ na tu vedakāṃśe , deśakālayogābhāve ca yat idaṃ jñānāṃ deśāpekṣayā pramātrādyaṃśāpekṣayā ca sakramatvaṃ lakṣyate tat kathaṃ syāt , kramābhāve ca ekatvameva vastuto bhavet , tataśca

children.translated_text: 'He who possesses knowledge, memory, and such — the Supreme Lord' —

children.text: iti yat uktaṃ tat kathaṃ nirvahet ityāśaṅkāṃ śamayan pūrvoktamupasaṃharati
children.translated_text: how could what has been stated thus be coherent? — Pacifying this doubt, he concludes what was previously stated:

Objection: If thus the entire aggregate of cognitions has its foundation in 'I'-awareness alone, then there is no contact with the domain of the knowable; and in the domain of the knowable there is conjunction with space and time but not in the knower-aspect; and in the absence of conjunction with space and time, the sequentiality that is observed in cognitions — with respect to spatial position and with respect to the perceiver-aspect and such — how could it exist? And in the absence of sequence, there would in reality be only unity; and therefore,
Only due to conformity with the different knowables, space, and time,
do knowledge, memory, determination, and such appear as sequential.

children.text: satyam evam akramameva saṃvittattvam , kintu svaśaktivaśāt bhinnatvena bhāsitāni yāni vedyāni teṣāṃ mūrtibhedakṛto yo dūrādūravaitatyāvaitatyādiḥ deśaḥ , kriyābhedakṛtaśca yaḥ ciraśīghrakramādirūpaḥ kālaḥ , tau anurudhya chāyāmātreṇa abalambya, jñānasmaraṇādhyavasāyānāṃ svāṃśā iva bhānti niraṃśānāmapi , tadbhāsamānāṃśakṛtaśca sakramatvāvabhāsaḥ parasparāpekṣayā svāṃśāpekṣayā ca , yadyapi kālakrama eva sphuṭo vijñāneṣu bhāti na deśakramaḥ , tathāpi vimūḍhasya parvatasaṃvedanaṃ vitatamiva vadarasaṃvedanaṃ ca sūkṣmamiva bhāti iti deśakramo 'pi darśitaḥ , tena vedyagatakramasvīkārābhāsāt sakramatvam ābhāsamānamapi na apāramārthikam ābhāsamānasya parārthatvāt , tataśca yuktamuktam

children.translated_text: 'Knowledge and such are the powers of the Blessed Lord' —
thus.

True, the principle of consciousness (<s>saṃvit-tattva</s>) is indeed non-sequential; however, the knowables that have been manifested as different by its own power — the space that is constituted by the difference of forms, as distance and proximity and such extension or non-extension, and the time that is constituted by the difference of activities, in the form of slow, fast, sequential, and such — conforming to these two, by merely reflecting them as shadows, knowledge, memory, and determination appear as if they were parts of themselves even though they are partless; and the appearance of sequentiality, produced by those appearing parts, is in relation to one another and to their own parts. Although it is temporal sequence alone that shines clearly in cognitions and not spatial sequence, nevertheless, for a confused person the perception of a mountain appears as if extended and the perception of a small berry as if subtle — thus spatial sequence too has been shown. Therefore, the appearance of sequentiality through the assimilation of the sequence belonging to the knowable, even while appearing, is not ultimately unreal, since what appears has its purpose — and thus it was rightly said:
{By the <s>māyā-śakti</s> of the all-pervading Lord}

children.text: iti ślokena svarūpavaicitryaṃ jñānāṃ darśitam / anena tu deśakālavaicitryam iti viśeṣaḥ / iti śivam //21//
children.translated_text: — by that verse, the variety of cognitions in their essential nature was shown. But by this [verse], the variety in terms of space and time — this is the distinction. Thus, may there be auspiciousness. // 21 //

children.text: iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptaviracitāyāṃīśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinyāṃ prathame jñānādhikāre jñānaśaktinirūpaṇaṃ nāma pañcamāhnikam // 5 //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fifth daily lesson, entitled 'Investigation of the Power of Knowledge' (<s>Jñānaśaktinirūpaṇa</s>), in the first Knowledge Section (<s>Jñānādhikāra</s>) of the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 5 //
Now begins the sixth daily lesson.
{He who, with the chisel of exclusion (<s>apoha</s>), from entities that are the wealth of non-difference from His own Self,
cleaves by His own will, having assumed variegated forms — that <s>Śiva</s> we praise. //}

children.text: evaṃ smṛtiśaktirjñānaśaktiśca nirūpitā / atha tadubhayānuprāhiṇī apohanaśaktirvitatya ślokaikādaśakena

children.translated_text: 'The reflective awareness "I," whose nature is luminosity' —
beginning with this,
'it is established for every living being' —

children.text: ityantena nirṇīyate / tatra ślokena pratyavamarśe avikalpo viśeṣaḥ iti sūcyate / tataḥ ślokena śuddhe 'haṃpratyavamarśe 'pohanavyāpārāsaṃbhavaḥ ucyate / tataḥ svadṛṣṭāveva tadupapattiḥ iti ślokena / tato 'pi dvayena aśuddhasyāhamityavamarśasya vikalparūpatā / tataḥ ślokena anusaṃdhānasvāpi vikalparūpatā / evaṃrūpānusaṃdhānādirūpameva parameśvarasya sraṣṭṭatvam iti ślokena / tataḥ prakṛte cidātmanyarthāvabhāsasya sattopasaṃhiyate ślokena / tato dvayena tasmaivārthāvabhāsasyānubhavasmaraṇādau vaicitryamucyate , taduktiśca prakṛtāyāmīśvararūpasvātmapratyabhijñāyāmupayujyate iti ślokena / ityāhnikasya tātparyārthaḥ / atha granthārtho vyākhyāyate /
children.translated_text: ending with this. Therein, by one verse, the non-conceptual specific character of reflective awareness is indicated. Then, by one verse, the impossibility of the operation of exclusion in pure 'I'-reflective awareness is stated. Then, its possibility in our own system — by one verse. Then, by two verses, the conceptual nature (<s>vikalparūpatā</s>) of impure 'I'-reflective awareness. Then, by one verse, the conceptual nature even of recognition (<s>anusaṃdhāna</s>). That the very creation-nature of the Supreme Lord is of the form of recognition and such — by one verse. Then, in the present context, the existence of the appearance of objects in the consciousness-self is concluded — by one verse. Then, by two verses, the variety of that very object-appearance in experience, memory, and so forth is stated; and by one verse, it is said that statement too is useful in the recognition of one's own Self as the Lord that is the present subject. Such is the purport of the daily lesson. Now the meaning of the text is explained.

Thus, the power of memory (<s>smṛti-śakti</s>) and the power of knowledge (<s>jñāna-śakti</s>) have been investigated. Now, the power of exclusion (<s>apohana-śakti</s>), which accompanies both of these, is determined at length in eleven verses,
'This statement' —
{the <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness) that is the essential nature of appearance... /}

children.text: iti / tatra vimarśo 'bhilāpātmanā śabdena yojita eva , tadyojanākṛtaṃ ca vikalparūpatvaṃ śuddhe 'pi parameśvare prāptam , na caitadiṣṭaṃ tasya saṃsārapade māthātmanyupapatteḥ ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: thus. Therein, <s>vimarśa</s> is indeed associated with verbal expression (<s>abhilāpa</s>) in the form of words; and the conceptual nature produced by that association would apply even to the pure Supreme Lord; and this is not desired, since it would be possible only in the worldly state of <s>saṃsāra</s> — anticipating this, he says:
The reflective awareness 'I,' though having luminosity as its nature, has the body of speech (<s>vāk</s>);

children.text: nāsau vikalpaḥ sa hyukto dvayākṣepī viniścayaḥ //
children.translated_text: yet it is not <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition), for that [vikalpa] is defined as a determination that involves the apprehension of a pair.

children.text: prakāśasya śuddhasaṃvidrūpasya dehādisaṃsparśairanāvilībhūtasya yaḥ ātmā jīvitabhūtaḥ sārasvabhāvo vicchedaśūnyo 'ntarabhyupagamakalpo 'nanyamukhaprekṣitvarūpasvātantryaviśrāntirūpaḥ
iti pratyavamarśaḥ asau vikalpo na bhavati / vikalpatvāśaṅkāyāṃ bījaṃ darśayati
children.translated_text: that reflective awareness is not <s>vikalpa</s>. He shows the seed of the suspicion of its being <s>vikalpa</s>:
'even having the body of speech' (<s>vāgvapurapi</s>) —
