children.text: iti / viṣayarūpāt śrotragrāhyāt śabdādanya eva antaravabhāsamānaḥ saṃvidrūpāveśī śabdanātmābhilāpo vāgityanenoktaḥ ---- vakti arthaṃ svādhyāsena so 'yamityabhisaṃdhānena / yadi vāgvapuḥ , kasmānna vikalpaḥ ? āha ---- na hyasya vikalpalakṣaṇamasti , tathā hi ---- vividhā kalpanā vividhatvena ca śaṅkitasya kalpo 'nvavyavacchedanaṃ vikalpaḥ , vividhatvaṃ ca bahnāvanagnisaṃbhāvanāsamāropanirāse 'sati bhavat , dvayaṃ vahnyavahnirūpaṃ samākṣipati , tena vikalpe 'vaśyaṃ tacca niścetavyam atacca apohitavyaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: thus. Different from the word that is of the form of an object and graspable by the ear, the verbal expression (<s>abhilāpa</s>) that manifests internally, that pervades the nature of consciousness, whose essence is verbalization — that is called <s>vāk</s> (speech); it speaks the object through superimposition upon itself, through the intentional awareness 'this very one.' If it has the body of speech, why is it not <s>vikalpa</s>? He answers: it does not have the defining characteristic of <s>vikalpa</s>. For thus: <s>vikalpa</s> is variegated construction — the determining of what is doubted as being of variegated nature, where variegation exists when there is no removal of the superimposition of the possibility of fire and non-fire in smoke — it apprehends a pair of the form fire and non-fire; therefore, in <s>vikalpa</s>, there must necessarily be something to be determined and something else to be excluded.

Of luminosity — that is, of pure consciousness (<s>śuddha-saṃvid</s>), not sullied by contact with body and such — that which is the Self, the life-principle, the essential core, devoid of limitation, of the nature of internal acceptance without looking at another's face, of the nature of resting in autonomous freedom —
And thus,
For the appearance of two different [things] would occur — of pot and non-pot;
it is of luminosity alone, not of another, that there is no appearance of a divider.

children.text: ghaṭe hi dṛṣṭe ghaṭasthāna evāghaṭe 'pi yogyadeśābhimatasthānākramaṇaśīlo vijñānajanakaḥ svakāraṇopanītaḥ saṃbhāvyate paṭādisvabhāvaḥ , ato ghaṭāghaṭayordvayoravabhāvasasya saṃbhāvanāt samāropaḥ sāvakāśo bhavati , aghaṭasya satyārope niṣedhanalakṣaṇopohanavyāpāraḥ iti tadanuprāṇitā vikalparūpatā ghaṭa ityetasya niścayasya ,

children.translated_text: 'Liṅ' (the optative mood is used) in the sense of possibility —

children.text: / yastvayaṃ prakāśo nāma tasya sthāne yaḥ saṃbhāvyate sa tāvadaprakāśarūpo na bhavati tulyakakṣasya hi saṃbhāvanaṃ bhavati , na ca yatprakāśena kartavyaṃ tadaprakāśasya kadācit dṛṣṭam saṃbhāvanāropaṇādibalādeva ca asyāprakāśarūpatvaṃ vighaṭeta , ataḥ prakāśatulyasyānyasyāprakāśarūpasya bhedinastattulyakakṣyasyāpohanātmakabhedanavyāpārāsāhiṣṇoravabhāsanameva nāsti , tadabhāve kasyāpoṣṭhanam ? avabhāsasaṃbhave 'pi prakāśarūpatvameva / na ca prakāśasya svarūpadeśakālabhedo yena dvitīyaḥ prakāśa ekasmādapohyeteti / hīti , yasmādevaṃ tato dvayābhāvādpohāsaṃbhave vikalparūpatvābhāvāt cinmātre parāmarśātmani ahamiti pratyavamarśa eva , na tu vikalpaḥ //2//
children.translated_text: But as for what is called luminosity (<s>prakāśa</s>), that which is postulated in its place is certainly not of a non-luminous nature, for postulation applies only to what is of equal status; and what is to be accomplished by luminosity has never been seen as accomplished by non-luminosity; and its non-luminous nature would be undermined by the very force of postulation, superimposition, and such. Therefore, there is simply no manifestation of another that is non-luminous, different from luminosity yet of equal status, incapable of enduring the operation of differentiation in the form of exclusion. In the absence of that [manifestation], what is to be excluded? Even if manifestation is possible, it is of the nature of luminosity alone. And there is no difference of essential nature, space, or time in luminosity by which a second luminosity could be excluded from the first. 'Hi' (for): since this is so, therefore, in the absence of a duality, in the impossibility of exclusion, in the absence of the nature of conceptual construction, in pure consciousness whose nature is reflective awareness, there is only the self-reflective awareness 'I' — and not conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>). //2//

When a pot is seen, in the very place of the pot, even a non-pot — of the nature of cloth and such, having the character of occupying eligible desired positions — is postulated as a producer of cognition, brought by its own causes. Therefore, since the possibility of the appearance of both pot and non-pot exists, superimposition has scope, and when non-pot has been superimposed, the operation of exclusion in the form of negation [occurs] — thus the conceptual nature (<s>vikalparūpatā</s>) of the determination 'this is a pot' is animated by that [exclusion].

children.text:
nanu ghaṭe pariniṣthitarūpe dṛṣṭe taddarśanamupajīvatā vikalpena kathamaghaṭasya niṣedhanaṃ kriyate , na hyaghaṭasya kenacinnāmāpi gṛhītam ,
aghaṭavāsanāpi ghaṭe dṛṣṭe kathaṃkāraṃ prabudhyatām ? satyam , evaṃ śākyaḥ paryanuyojyo na tu vayam , yataḥ
children.translated_text:
Objection: When a pot of established form is seen, how can the conceptual cognition that depends on that perception negate what is not-a-pot? For no one has ever grasped even the name of a non-pot,
and how would the <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) of non-pot awaken when a pot is seen? True — thus the Buddhist is to be challenged, not we; because:
The perceiver who partakes of both 'that' and 'not-that' appearances — merely through the exclusion of what is not-that,
the conceptual cognition 'this is a pot' is said to be accompanied by the determination of that.

children.text: iha pramātā nāma pramāṇādatiriktaḥ pramāsu svatantraḥ saṃyojanaviyojanādyādhānavaśāt kartā darśitaḥ , tasya ca pramāturantaḥ sarvārthāvabhāsaḥ , cinmātraśarīro 'pi tatsāmānādhikaraṇyavṛttirapi darpaṇanagaranyāyenāsti ---- ityapi uktam / evaṃ ca tatpratibhāṃ ghaṭābhāsam , atatpratibhāṃ ca aghaṭābhāsaṃ pramātā bhajate ---- sevate tāvat , tadavikalpadaśāyāṃ citsvabhāvo 'sau ghaṭaḥ cidvadeva viśvaśarīraḥ pūrṇaḥ , na ca tena kaścidvyavahāraḥ , tat māyāvyāpāramukkāsayanpūrṇamapi khaṇḍayati bhāvam , tenāghaṭasyātmanaḥ paṭādeścāpohanaṃ kriyate niṣedhanarūpam , tadeva vyapohanamāśritya tasma ghaṭasya niścayanamucyate

children.translated_text: 'pot alone' —

children.text: iti , evārthasya saṃbhāvyamānāparavastuniṣedharūpatvāt , eṣa eva paritaśchedāttakṣaṇakalpāt paricchedaḥ , hīti ---- yata evam , tasmāt yuktaṃ
children.translated_text: thus; the word 'eva' having the nature of negation of other things that might be postulated. This very delimitation, arising from a limitation that is of the nature of that particular moment, is determination (<s>pariccheda</s>). 'Hi' (for): since this is so, therefore it is proper that
'conceptual cognition implies a duality' —

children.text: iti pūrvaślokoltena vastudvayena hetū krameṇoktau yasmādevaṃ vikalpaḥ tato 'hamiti śuddho vimarśaḥ na vikalpaḥ ---- iti ślokatraye mahāvākyārthaḥ / śākyairapi pramāturevāyaṃ vyāpāra uktaḥ
children.translated_text: thus, by the first verse, two realities are stated as reasons in sequence. Since conceptual cognition is thus, therefore the pure reflective awareness 'I' is not conceptual construction — this is the great thesis of the three verses. Even the Buddhists have stated this operation to belong to the perceiver:
'one, called self-reflective awareness' —
in that context,
'the apprehender' —
thus,
'by itself' —

children.text: iti ca vadadbhiḥ , sa tvetaiḥ kathaṃ samarthyaḥ ---- ityāstāmetat //3//
children.translated_text: thus they say. But how this can be sustained by them — let that be. //3//

Here, the perceiver (<s>pramātṛ</s>) has been shown to be distinct from the means of knowledge, independent in cognitions, and an agent by virtue of conferring conjunction, disjunction, and such. And it has also been stated that within the perceiver there is the manifestation of all objects; that even though his body is pure consciousness, there exists a co-located function according to the analogy of a city in a mirror. And thus the perceiver partakes of — experiences — both the appearance of a pot ('that') and the appearance of a non-pot ('not-that'). But in the non-conceptual state, that pot, being of the nature of consciousness, is complete and universal-bodied like consciousness itself, and there is no practical activity with it. Therefore, manifesting the operation of <s>Māyā</s>, he fragments even the complete entity; thereby the exclusion in the form of negation of non-pot, of oneself, of cloth, and such is accomplished. Relying on that very exclusion, the determination of that pot is expressed as

children.text: nanvevamahamityapi pratyavamarśe 'nahaṃrūpasya ghaṭādeḥ pratiyogino '; pohanīyasyāpohe vikalparūpatā kathaṃ na syāt ityāśayenāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If even in the self-reflective awareness 'I,' the counter-correlate of non-I nature such as a pot must be excluded, how can the nature of conceptual construction not apply? With this in mind, he says:

children.text: cittattvaṃ māyayā hitvā bhinna evāvabhāti yaḥ /
children.translated_text: He who, having abandoned the <s>cit-tattva</s> (consciousness-principle) through <s>Māyā</s>, manifests as differentiated —

children.text: dehe buddhāvatha prāṇe kalpite nabhasīva vā //
children.translated_text: whether in the body, in the intellect, in the vital breath, in the postulated void, or the like —
the reflective awareness 'I' that occurs as a perceiver, being born from the exclusion of the other,
and from the appearance of a counter-correlate, is indeed conceptual construction alone.

children.text: ahamityavamarśo dvidhā ---- śuddho māyīyaśca , tatra śuddho yaḥ saṃvinmātre viśvābhinne viśvacchāyācchuritācchātmani vā / aśuddhastu vedyarūpe śarīrādau / tatra śuddhe 'haṃpratyavamarśe pratiyogī na kaścidapohitavyaḥ saṃbhavati ghaṭāderapi prakāśasāratvenāpratiyogitvenānapohyatvāt , ityapohyābhāve kathaṃ tatra vikalparūpatā / aśuddhastu vedyarūpe śarīrādau anyasmād dehāderghaṭādeśca vyavacchedena bhavan vikalpa eva ---- iti vākyārthaḥ / akṣarārthastu ---- cittattvaṃ prakāśamātrarūpaṃ hitvā sadapyapahastanayā apradhānīkṛtya bhinne dehādāvahameva dehādiḥ nīlādau prameye pramātā ---- ityabhimānena

children.translated_text: the reflective awareness such as 'I am stout' —

children.text: ityādivimarśaḥ sa vikalpa eva , na tu śuddhaṃ pratyavamarśamātram / atra hetuḥ ---- paro dvitīyo dehādirghaṭādiśca yaḥ pratiyogī tulyakakṣyo 'nyonyaparihārācca viruddhastasya yo 'vabhāsaḥ ---- samāropaṇalakṣaṇaḥ , tasmādyato 'sāvatanniṣedhānuprāṇito '; hamityavamarśo jātaḥ
children.translated_text: and so on, is conceptual construction alone, not pure self-reflective awareness. The reason here is: the other, the second — the body, pot, etc. — which is the counter-correlate of equal status and mutually exclusive, and hence opposed — its appearance, which is of the nature of superimposition, from which and because of which, this reflective awareness 'I' has arisen as animated by the negation of that,

children.text: ahaṃ sthūlaḥ , na kṛśaḥ , na ghaṭādiḥ
children.translated_text: 'I am stout, not thin, not a pot, etc.' —

children.text:
iti , śuddhaprakāśarūpasya apahastanaiva dehāderbhedahetuḥ ,
tadapahastane tu parameśvarasya svātmapracchādanecchārūpā 'bhedāprakāśanaṃ bhrāntirūpaṃ prati svātantryarūpā māyāśaktirhetuḥ , cidrūpasya cāpahastanaṃ dehādereva atyaktavedyabhāvasya bhinnasyaiva upapattiśūnyatayaiva pramātṛtvābhimānaḥ / tathā ca dehābhimānabhūmikāyāṃ sthitāścārvākāḥ
children.translated_text:
thus. The very setting aside of what is of the nature of pure luminosity is the cause of differentiation of the body and such;
and in that setting aside, the <s>Māyā-śakti</s> (power of illusion) of the Supreme Lord — which is the Lord's will to conceal His own Self, which is of the nature of His absolute freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) toward the erroneous non-manifestation of non-difference — that is the cause. And the setting aside of the consciousness-nature, and the identification as perceiver of the body etc. which has not abandoned its nature as object and is differentiated — this occurs solely by reason of the impossibility [of it being otherwise]. And thus, those who stand on the level of identification with the body — the <s>Cārvākas</s>:
'The body qualified by consciousness is the person (<s>puruṣa</s>)' —

children.text: iti kāyameva prādhānyenāhuḥ / strībālamūrkhāṇāṃ tathābhimānāt tato 'pi vivekayuktāḥ pākajotpattipariṇāmādibalādasthiraṃ śarīraṃ manvānāḥ prāṇaśaktisamadhiṣṭhānena ca vinā vikāraśatāveśaṃ śarīrasya paśyanto bubhukṣāpipāsāyogayogyaṃ prāṇamevātmānaṃ kecana śrutyantavido manyante / tato 'pi samadhikavivekabhājaḥ prāṇasyāpi anityatvādanusaṃdhānayogyatāmapaśyanto jñānasukhādyāśrayabhūtāṃ buddhimeva kāṇādaprabhṛtaya ātmānamāhuḥ / apare tasyā api yogidśāyāṃ vedyabhāvādaparatvaṃ manyamānāḥ asaṃvedyaparvarūpaṃ yanna kiṃcidrūpaṃ sakalavedyarāśivinirmuktaṃ śūnyatvānnabhastulyaṃ na tu mahābhūtākāśasvabhāvaṃ tat pramātṛtattvaṃ śūnyabrahmavādinaḥ sāṃkhyaprabhṛtaya āhuḥ / tasminnapi vedye śunyāntaraṃ tatrāpi śūnyāntram ---- iti yāvadbhedaḥ tāvatkalpanā na truṭyatīti tadarthamāha
children.translated_text: thus they declare the body alone as primary. Since women, children, and the ignorant have such identification. More discriminating than those, considering the body to be unstable due to the force of digestive transformation, production, modification, etc., and seeing the body as subject to hundreds of changes without the support of the vital force (<s>prāṇa-śakti</s>), capable of hunger and thirst — some who know the culmination of the <s>Śruti</s> consider the vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>) alone to be the self. More discriminating even than those, seeing that even the vital breath, being impermanent, is incapable of connected awareness, <s>Kaṇāda</s> and others declare the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), which is the substratum of knowledge, pleasure, and such, to be the self. Others, considering even that to be inferior since it becomes an object in the yogic state, and [positing] a supreme nature that is unknowable, that has no particular form, that is free from the entire mass of knowable objects, that is equal to space due to its voidness but not of the nature of the great element space — this they call the perceiver-principle. The proponents of the void-<s>Brahman</s>, the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> and such, declare this. Even in that void, another void; in that, yet another void — as long as there is differentiation, the conceptual construction does not cease. To convey this, he says:
'kalpite' (in the postulated):

children.text: iti / na cānavasthā paramārthaprakāśabalena yataḥ sarvasya prakāśo na tu dehādivaśāt , tayā tvabhimānamātraṃ dehaḥ pramāteti , saṅkocamātrarūpaṃ cittattvaṃ śūnyam , bhūtalaṃ yathā ghaṭābhāvaḥ , saṅkocoparivedyāṃśacchāyācchuritaṃ tu cittattvameva buddhiprāṇadehādi iti / amī eva bhūmikāviśeṣā uttarottaramārohatāṃ yogināṃ jāgradāditayā piṇḍasthāditayā cāgameṣu bhaṇyante , apahastanaṃ ca vyākhyāsyateḥ
children.translated_text: thus. And there is no infinite regress, because by the power of ultimate luminosity, luminosity belongs to everything and not due to the body and such. Through that [Māyā], the identification 'the body is the perceiver' is a mere contraction; the <s>cit-tattva</s> (consciousness-principle) [is] the void, having the nature of mere contraction, as a ground is the absence of a pot. But the consciousness-principle itself, tinted with the reflection of the knowable aspect above the contraction, is the intellect, vital breath, body, and such. These very levels are described in the scriptures as the waking state etc. for yogins ascending ever higher, and also as <s>piṇḍastha</s> (established in the body) etc. And the 'setting aside' will be explained:

The reflective awareness 'I' is of two kinds — pure and <s>Māyic</s>. Therein, the pure one is that which occurs in pure consciousness, non-different from the universe, or in the self that is tinted with the reflection of the universe. The impure one is that which occurs in what is of the nature of an object — the body and such. In the pure self-reflective awareness 'I,' no counter-correlate to be excluded is possible, since even a pot and such, being of the essence of luminosity, are not counter-correlates and hence not excludable. In the absence of anything to be excluded, how can there be the nature of conceptual construction? But the impure one, occurring in what is of the nature of an object — the body and such — being accompanied by exclusion from another body, pot, and such, is indeed conceptual construction — this is the meaning of the statement. As for the literal meaning: having abandoned — even though existing, having set aside, having made non-primary — the <s>cit-tattva</s>, whose nature is pure luminosity, in the differentiated body and such, with the identification 'I am the body itself,' and in the knowable blue and such, 'the perceiver is the knower' — with this self-appropriation,
{And this consciousness-principle, brought forth by <s>kalā</s> (limited agency), is of the nature of agency;
it is established as a quality of what is of non-conscious nature, such as the void and others. //}
reflective awareness is conceptual construction alone. //5//
Thus, 'established therein' — the impure
'ahaṃ-pratyaya' (I-cognition):
is twofold — of the nature of mere experience and of the nature of connected awareness. In the <s>Śiva</s>-self,
thus. In the <s>Sadāśiva</s>-self,
'I am this' —

children.text: iti śuddho dvidhā / aśuddho 'pi ahaṃ sthūla iti , yo 'haṃ sthūlo 'bhavaṃ so 'haṃ kṛśa , bālo , yuvā , sthaviraḥ , sa eva aham iti ca aśuddho dvividhaḥ / tatra śuddhe vikalparūpatvamapratiṣṭhameva ityuktam , aśuddhe tu anubhavarūpe vikalpatvamupapāditam , aśuddhe 'pi tu anusaṃdhānātmakatayā abhedasya prasphuraṇāt kaścidavikalpakatvaṃ śaṅketa tasya vyāmohaṃ vyapohitumāha
children.translated_text: thus: the pure is twofold. The impure is also twofold: 'I am stout' — and 'I who was stout am now thin, child, youth, old man — that same I' — thus. Therein, that the pure [I-awareness] has the nature of conceptual construction has been shown to be groundless; but in the impure, when of the nature of experience, its nature as conceptual construction has been established. However, even in the impure [I-awareness], when of the nature of connected awareness, since non-difference flashes forth, someone might suspect it is non-conceptual. To dispel that delusion, he says:
And this [I-awareness] is also of two kinds:
The connection of a momentary appearance with a prior appearance and such,
arising from a latent impression, is declared to be conceptual construction — and that too in one who manifests as differentiated.
'Dehe' (in the body):

children.text: ityādi vartate , kādācitkaḥ kadācidbhavo niyatadeśakālākāro 'vabhāso yasya dehādeḥ svalakṣaṇarūpasya , tatra yā pūrvābhāsena bālādiśarīrāvabhāsena yojanā
children.translated_text: and so forth applies. 'Momentary' means occurring at a particular time; a manifestation of a definite place, time, and form belonging to the body etc. as its particular characteristic. Therein, the connection with a prior appearance — the appearance of the childhood body, etc. —
'I who was a child' —
'that same one today' —
'is a youth' —

children.text: ityanusaṃdhānam , ādigrahaṇāduttareṇa bhāvinā ābhāsena saha yojanā
children.translated_text: thus, connected awareness. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the connection with a subsequent, future appearance also:
'I shall become old' —

children.text: iti , sā yojanā sarvā kalpanā vikalpa eva , na tu śuddhaḥ pratyavamarśaḥ / atra dehāderviśeṣaṇaṃ hetutvāśayena ---- yato bhinnatāvabhāsitvameva dehādestadānīmapi avichinnam , yadi hi tasya dehādeḥ sarvataḥ pūrṇatvam avacchedahīnatvaṃ paśyan anusaṃdhānam
children.translated_text: thus. All that connection is conceptual construction, <s>vikalpa</s> alone, and not pure self-reflective awareness. Here, the qualification of the body etc. is with the intention of indicating the reason: because the body etc. manifests as differentiated even then, without interruption. For if one, seeing the body etc. as complete in all respects and devoid of limitation, were to perform the connected awareness
'I am this' —

children.text: iti vidadhyāt tadiyaṃ sadāśivabhūḥ kena vikalpātpadatvena bhaṇyeta yāvatā 'vicchinne eva so 'nusaṃdhiḥ / bhinnepi(KSS: hi) kathamanusaṃdhānam iti cedāha
children.translated_text: that would be the level of <s>Sadāśiva</s>; by what [criterion] could it be called conceptual construction? Inasmuch as that connected awareness is precisely of what is limited. If it be asked, how can there be connected awareness even in what is differentiated? — he says:
'saṃskārāt' (from the latent impression):

children.text: prāktanānubhavakṛtavāsanāprabodhajasmṛtivaśāt iti yāvat , prāṇe balābalavaśādanusaṃdhiḥ , buddhau jñānasukhāditāratamyāt , śūnye vaitatyāvaitatyayogāt , ayamapi vikalpa eva , evaṃ
children.translated_text: meaning, by the force of memory born from the awakening of the <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) produced by prior experience. In the vital breath, connected awareness is due to variations of strength and weakness; in the intellect, due to gradations of knowledge, pleasure, and such; in the void, due to the presence and absence of such-ness. This too is conceptual construction alone. Similarly,
'this is the same pot' —

children.text: iti ghaṭādyanusaṃdhāne 'pi vikalpatvaṃ mantavyam , kintu etāsu anusaṃdhānabhūmiṣu vidyāśaktirādhikyena aciradyutivaddīpyate iti tāsāṃ parapadapariśīlanaprathamakalpābhyupāyatvamabhyupāgaman guravaḥ //6//
children.translated_text: even in the connected awareness of pots and such, the nature of conceptual construction should be understood. However, in these levels of connected awareness, the power of knowledge (<s>vidyā-śakti</s>) shines with predominance, like a flash of lightning; therefore, the masters have accepted these as the initial stages of the path to the supreme state. //6//

children.text: na ca dehādīnāṃ pūrvapūrvapramātṛvedyatā yena pramāturaprakāśe prameyaṃ na bhāti tatprakāśaśca na pūrvaprakāśaṃ vinā , so 'pi na pramātrantaraprakāśaṃ vinā ityanavasthā syāt , api tu śuddhaprakāśa eva viśvasya prakāśa iti nirūpayan uktayuktyā sadaiva sṛṣṭyādiśaktyaviyogo bhagavata ukto bhavati , iti darśayati
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that the body and such have the nature of being objects of prior perceivers, such that in the absence of the perceiver's luminosity the knowable object would not shine; and that its luminosity would not exist without prior luminosity; and that [prior luminosity] would not exist without the luminosity of another perceiver — resulting in an infinite regress. Rather, it is pure luminosity alone that is the light of everything. Establishing this through the aforementioned reasoning, the author shows that the inseparability of the Lord from His powers of creation etc. has always been declared:
Thus even in worldly activity, the Lord, entering the body and such,
by His will manifests externally the flood of objects that shine within.
'in the body, in the intellect' —

children.text: ityādi tat evam upapadyate , katham ? yadi vyavahāre māyāpade dehaprāṇādimapi prabhureva prakāśaparamārtha icchayā māyāśaktirūpayā , āviśan dehaprāṇādiprādhānyena svarūpaṃ pradarśayan , antaḥ saṃbinmātre , bhāntam ahamityevaṃrūpam arthaugham icchayaiva bahiḥ idamiti bhāsayati tata etadupapadyate , anyathā tu anavasthā syāt / hetau liṅ / apiśabda evaśabdaśca bhinnakramau , yat etāvat uktam , taditi , tasmāt hetoḥ , evaṃ jātaṃ vakṣyamāṇarūpam , kiṃtat ? yat kila prabhuḥ parasparaṃ vyavahārakāle krayavikrayaprekṣāvyākhyādau caitramaitrādisaṃbandhino dehaprāṇādīn ekatayā tāvati vyavahāre āviśan antarbhāntameva anujjhitāntaḥprakāśameva santaṃ bahiḥ ekābhāsatayā bhāsayati iti saṃbhāvyate ityetajjātam , iti saṃbhāvanāyāṃ liṅ / tena tena pramātrā saha asminkāle aikyaṃ sṛjyate , anyena pramātrā aikyaṃ saṃhriyate , ghaṭādimātrarūpe sthitiḥ kriyate , pūrṇasvarūpanimīlanāt tirobhāva ādhīyate , tāvatyābhāse aikyāvabhāsapūrṇatvavitaraṇāt anugrahaḥ kriyate , tena na kevalaṃ mahāsṛṣṭiṣu mahāsthitiṣu mahāpralayeṣu prakopatirodhāneṣu dīkṣājñānādyanugraheṣu bhagavataḥ krṭyapañcakayogaḥ yāvat satatameva vyavahārepi / yaduktam
children.translated_text: and so forth — this is thus tenable. How? In worldly transaction, at the level of <s>Māyā</s>, even the body, vital breath, and such — the Lord Himself, whose ultimate reality is luminosity, entering [them] by His will, which is of the nature of the <s>Māyā-śakti</s>, manifesting His own essential nature with the body, vital breath, and such as predominant, internally in pure consciousness, the flood of objects that shines as 'I' — by His will alone He causes it to appear externally as 'this.' Otherwise there would be an infinite regress. The optative mood is used in the sense of a reason. The words 'api' and 'eva' have different sequences. What has been stated so far — 'that' — therefore, for that reason; 'thus arisen' means of the nature to be described. What is that? The Lord, during the time of [worldly] transactions — buying, selling, observing, explaining, and such — entering the bodies, vital breaths, and such related to <s>Caitra</s>, <s>Maitra</s>, and others, as a unity for the extent of that transaction, causes what is already shining within — what has not abandoned its inner luminosity — to appear externally as a single appearance. This is to be postulated — the optative is used in the sense of supposition. With this or that perceiver, at this time, unity is created; with another perceiver, unity is dissolved; in the mere form of a pot and such, persistence is accomplished; due to the closing of the full essential nature, concealment is imposed; in that extent of appearance, due to the bestowal of the fullness of the appearance of unity, grace is performed. Therefore, not only in the great creations, great persistences, great dissolutions, wrathful concealments, and gracious acts of initiation and knowledge does the Lord have the conjunction of the five acts — but constantly, even in [ordinary] worldly transaction. As stated:
What was previously shown —
{Always delighting in the sport of creation, always seated in the bliss of preservation,
always satiated by the devouring of the three worlds — to that Master, salutations. //}
Thus.
{Without rest at every moment, through hundreds of acts of imagination, creating the three worlds,
yet one, without conceptual construction, unborn — He alone is victorious. //}
and so forth. Likewise:
{...when You manifest the absolute sovereignty in Your own Self,
of the manifest... //}
thus. //7//

children.text: iha antararthābhāvabhāsaḥ sthita eva , tat kiṃ tatra kāraṇāntaracintayā iti prakṛtaṃ prameyam , tatsiddhaye upapattiḥ uktā , tena vinā icchārūpaḥ pratyavamarśo na syāt iti , tatprasaṅgāt pratyavamarśavikalpādisvarūpam upapāditam , iti śiṣyāṇāṃ dhiyaṃ samādhātuṃ prakṛtaṃ prameyam upapādayan upasaṃharati
children.translated_text: Here, the appearance of the internal objects is already established — so what is the need for thinking of another cause? This is the subject at hand. The reasoning for establishing it has been stated — without it, the reflective awareness that is of the nature of will would not be [possible]. In that connection, the essential nature of reflective awareness, conceptual construction, and such has been demonstrated. In order to settle the minds of the students, he summarizes by establishing the subject at hand:
Thus, whether in memory, or in conceptual construction that is devoted to exclusion,
or in [experiential] knowledge — it is certain that the internal appearance is already established.

children.text: prakāśātmā parameśvara eva yato dehādipramātṛtābhimānadaśāyāmapi vastutaḥ pramātā ,

children.translated_text: 'thus' —

children.text: iti , ato hetoḥ idaṃ siddhaṃ bhavati ---- smaraṇe apohanajīvite ca vikalpe anubhavajñāne ca antarābhāsaḥ prakāśaviśrāntaḥ sthita eva , nātra saṃśayaḥ kaścit , yadi hi dehādireva paramārthapramātā syāt tat śarīrasya prāṇasya dhiyaḥ śūnyasya vā antarghaṭādi iti na kiṃcit etat ---- ghaṭādiparihāreṇa dehādeḥ sthitatvāt / paramārthaprakāśastu sarvaṃsahaḥ iti tatrāntarviśvam , iti anāyāsasiddhametat //8//
children.translated_text: for this reason, this is established: in memory, in conceptual construction whose life is exclusion, and in experiential knowledge, the internal appearance — resting in luminosity — is already established. There is no doubt about this. For if the body and such were the ultimate perceiver, then the interior of the body, vital breath, intellect, or void would be [merely] a pot and such — that would be nothing at all, since the body and such stand with the exclusion of pots and such. But the ultimate luminosity is all-embracing — therefore the universe is within it. This is established effortlessly. //8//
Since the Supreme Lord, whose nature is luminosity, is in truth the perceiver even in the state of false identification with the body and such as the perceiver,

children.text: nanu antarābhāsavargasya bahirābhāsanaṃ yadi sarvatrāsti kastarhi smaraṇādau ābhāsabhedaḥ , na ca asau na saṃvedyate ---- sphuṭatāsphuṭatādiprasphuraṇasya anapahnavanīyatvāt ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If the external manifestation of the group of internal appearances is present everywhere, then what difference of appearance is there in memory and such? And that [difference] is certainly perceived — since the flashing forth of vividness and non-vividness is undeniable. Anticipating this, he says:
However, in experiential knowledge, which is of the nature of external manifestation, [the internal appearance] is natural;
but in memory and such, it has the form of prior experience as established [therein].
'this is blue' —
when it externally manifests the internal appearance, its own internal appearance is natural —
Of experiential knowledge —

children.text: nisṛṣṭeḥ svātantryāt āyāto na tu smaraṇāderiva anyajñānakṛtavāsanādibalāt / smaraṇe utprekṣaṇe pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvini adhyavasāye ca yo 'ntarnīlādyavabhāso bāhyatayā adhyavasāyitavyaḥ nāsau svātmoyaḥ api tu pūrvānubhavasaṃskārajo 'sau , tatra saṃskāro nāma anubhavasya kālāntare 'pi anuvartamānatā , ato 'sāvanuvartamāno 'nubhavo yato nīlādyābhāsasaṃbhinnaḥ tataḥ tattādātmyāpannaṃ smaraṇādyapi tathā nirbhāsate , tata eva smaraṇakālāsaṃbhavī ābhāsaḥ tadanubhavapūrvakālakalita eveti svayaṃ smaraṇādernirviṣayatvaṃ gṛhītagrāhitvaṃ ca uddhoṣyate / etadeva asphuṭatvam , iti siddho 'nubhavasmaraṇādau ābhāsabhedaḥ antarābhāsavargasya bahirābhāsanam anyāvyavadhānena sphuṭatā , vyavadhānena tu tātkālikatvābhāvāt asphuṭatā iti //9//
children.translated_text: arising from the freedom of emission itself, not, as in memory and such, from the force of latent impressions created by another cognition. In memory, in imaginative extrapolation, and in the post-determinative cognition that follows direct perception, the internal appearance of blue and such that is to be determined as external — that is not of its own arising; rather, it is born from the latent impressions of prior experience. Therein, the latent impression is the continuing of the experience even in subsequent time. Therefore, that continuing experience, since it is conjoined with appearances of blue and such, memory and such too, having attained identity with them, manifest in the same way. Therefore, the appearance that is impossible at the time of memory is tinged with the prior time of that experience — and thereby memory itself declares its own objectlessness and its having-been-grasped nature. This very thing is its non-vividness. Thus, the difference of appearance between experience and memory and such is established: the external manifestation of the group of internal appearances has vividness when without obstruction, and non-vividness when with obstruction, due to the absence of contemporaneity. //9//

children.text: nanu anubhavajñānāt aindriyakāt anyat sarvaṃ jñānaṃ vyavadhānena bahirābhāsanarūpaṃ prāptam ityāśaṅkya pravibhāgamāha
children.translated_text: Objection: All knowledge other than experiential perceptual knowledge has the nature of external manifestation through obstruction. Anticipating this, he states a distinction:
That [natural external manifestation] exists even in free-roaming conceptual construction,
in the domain of the intellect, due to the manifesting of appearances of whatever form is desired.

children.text: yaḥ pratyakṣavyāpāram anupajīvan vyākṣepasāratayā manorājyasaṅkalpādivikalpaḥ sa svaraṃ kṛtvā svapreraṇena prapreraṇanairapekṣyeṇa svātantryeṇa carati udeti vyayate ca , tatra yo bahirābhāso nīlādeḥ antarābhāsamayasya sa naisargika eva , tathā hi aparidṛṣṭapūrvamapi śvetaṃ daśanaśatakalotakarayugalayuktaṃ dantinam antaḥ pramātṛbhūmau sthitaṃ bahiḥ antaḥkaraṇabhūmau svacchadhīdarpaṇātmikāyāṃ sa vikalpaḥ tātkālikameva bhāsayati //10//
children.translated_text: The conceptual construction that does not depend on perceptual operation — daydreaming, fantasy, and such — moves, arises, and ceases freely, by its own impulsion, independently of external stimulation. Therein, the external appearance of what is of the nature of internal appearance, such as blue and the like — that is natural. For: even a white elephant with a hundred tusks, adorned with a pair of trunk-tips, never before seen — established within the perceiver-level, externally on the level of the internal organ, in the mirror-like transparent intellect — that conceptual construction manifests as contemporary alone. //10//

children.text: asmācca antarābhāsasaṃbhavasamarthanaprasaṅgāgatāt ābhāsabhedavicārāt śāstre yat prayoanaṃ mukhyatayā abhisaṃhitaṃ svātmani īśvarapratyabhijñānarūpaṃ tadadhikaraṇasiddhāntanītyā anāyāsasiddham iti darśayati
children.translated_text: And from this investigation of the differentiation of appearances, which has come up in the context of establishing the possibility of internal appearances, what the treatise primarily intends — the recognition of Lordship in one's own Self — is shown to be established effortlessly by the principle of the thesis being proved incidentally:
For this very reason, from the manifesting of whatever desired impressions as appearances,

children.text: jñānakriye sphuṭe eva siddhe sarvasya jīvataḥ //
children.translated_text: the powers of knowledge and action are clearly established as belonging to every living being.
'A pot appears' —

children.text: iti yadyapi viṣayopaśliṣṭameva pratibhānaṃ bhāti tathāpi na tadviṣayasya svakaṃ vapuḥ , api tu saṃvedanameva tat tathā cakāsti
children.translated_text: although the appearing seems to be attached to the object, nevertheless that is not the object's own body; rather, it is awareness itself that so shines —
'it appears to me' —
since it is attached to the perceiver. And likewise, the <s>Veda</s> states:

children.text: {tameva bhāntamanu bhāti sarvaṃ tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti /}
children.translated_text: {Everything shines following Him alone who shines; by His light all this is illuminated. /}

children.text: iti / śatrā aviratasphuraṇatvaṃ karmapravacanīyena tadīyasvātantryopakalpitanirmāṇakriyājanito vedyavedakabhāvarūpo lakṣaṇātmā saṃbandho dyotitaḥ , kevalaṃ viṣayollekhanabalāt bahiḥ kramāvabhāsaḥ samarthitaḥ , sa sa kramayaugapadyādivicitrarūpo yaḥ padārthānāṃ vakṣyamāṇeśvarasvātantryarūpadeśakālaśaktyupakalpitaḥ kramaḥ deśakālaparipāṭī , tena rūṣitā pratibimbakalpatayā uparaktā , yā pratibhā uktā
children.translated_text: Thus. By the present participle [in the verse], the unceasing luminosity is indicated; by the preposition, the relation — whose nature is the definitional characteristic consisting of the knowable-knower relationship, born of the creative action fashioned by His own freedom — is indicated. Merely by the force of the delineation of the object, the external sequential appearance is established. That sequence — the ordering of space and time, fashioned by the Lord's freedom in the form of the power of space and time, which will be described — being colored, i.e., tinted as if by a reflection, the intuitive flash (<s>pratibhā</s>) that was described as
{'Merely with a differentiated knowable...' /}

children.text: ityādinā / eṣā iti ca sarvasya svakāśarūpā , paramārthataśca antarmukhatvena prakāśamātraparamārthatayā bhedābhāvāt akramā , saiva maheśvaraḥ , avidyamāno 'ntaḥ paricchedo deśataḥ kālataḥ svarūpataśca yasyāḥ cittaḥ saṃvidaḥ tadeva rūpaṃ yasya iti , ata eva bahirmukhaprakāśātmakavijñānasvabhāvasya pramāṇavargasya yo 'ntaḥ pratyābhāsam

children.translated_text: 'this, this' —

children.text: iti ananta ---- kalpaḥ vikalpamayo vimarśātmā pramāsamūhaḥ , tatra saṃyojanaviyojanaviśramādirūpānekaprakārasvātantryaparipūrṇaḥ śuddhāhaṃpratyavamarśamayaḥ pramātā sa bhaṇyate , ataśca bahirghaṭaprakāśaḥ
children.translated_text: an almost infinite, conceptual-construction-filled, reflective-awareness-natured aggregate of cognitions. Therein, the perceiver is he who is filled with manifold freedom of the nature of conjoining, disjoining, resting, and such — who is of the nature of the pure self-reflective awareness 'I.' And therefore, the external luminosity of the pot,
'this is a pot' —
the internal conceptual construction, having accepted the prior form,

children.text: iti tadubhayaviśrāntisthānam , itīyat pūrṇaṃ prakāśasya svarūpam //1//
children.translated_text: that which is the resting-ground of both — this much is the full essential nature of luminosity. //1//

and so forth. And 'this' [refers to] what is of the nature of one's own luminosity for everyone. And in ultimate truth, by being inward-facing, having the ultimate reality of mere luminosity, due to the absence of difference — it is non-sequential. That itself is <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord). That whose inner delimitation by space, time, and essential nature is non-existent — whose form is that of undivided consciousness — therefore, the aggregate of valid cognitions, which is of the nature of the outward-facing luminosity — of the group of valid means of knowledge — has per-appearance, internally,
To show the reasoning for this very point, he first states the positive concomitance:
When entities are established in a single perceiver through the various faces of distinct cognitions,
this kinship (<s>jñāteya</s>) becomes tenable.
'The determinations of objects rest in consciousness' —

children.text: iti yat ucyate tat na bhinnarūpaprakātmakasaṃvinmātraviśrāntyā siddhyati api tu tāstā vibhinnāḥ saṃvido niścayarūpāḥ pramātmāno yāḥ tāni eva mukhāni dvārāṇi upāyā mārgāḥ taiḥ mukhaiḥ nadīsrotaḥsthānīyaiḥ yadi amī bhāvā nīlasukhādaya uhyamānā ekasmin
children.translated_text: what is stated thus is not established merely by resting in mere consciousness of differentiated luminous form; rather, the distinct cognitions of the nature of determination — the valid cognitions — those very things are the faces, doors, means, and paths. If through those faces — which are like channels of a river — these entities such as blue, pleasure, and the like, being carried, are established in the one

children.text: iti pramātṛrūpe mahāsaṃvitsamudre pratitiṣṭhanti ābhimukhyena viśrāntiṃ bhajante , tata eṣu parasparaṃ samanvayarūpaṃ tat jñāteyaṃ tat upapattyā ghaṭate , jñātīnāṃ bhāvaḥ tacchabdapravṛttinimittaṃ parasparaṃ jānīyuḥ iti , karma ca anyonyayogakṣemodvahanātmakaṃ jñāteyam , tacca samanvayābhiprāyeṇa iha darśitam , na jaḍānāṃ svataḥ samanvayaḥ kadācidapi iti pratipādayitum //2//
children.translated_text: perceiver-nature, the great ocean of consciousness — if they rest there with full orientation — then in those [entities], the mutual connection (<s>samanvaya</s>) that constitutes kinship (<s>jñāteya</s>) becomes tenable through reasoning. Kinship (<s>jñāteya</s>) is the state of kinsmen — the ground for the use of that word — 'they know one another mutually.' And kinship also means the action of mutual bearing-of-fortune-and-misfortune. That has been shown here with the intention of [establishing] connection, since insentient things never have connection of their own. //2//
And he states this same point through negative concomitance:
Of objects that occupy the sequence of space and time and are fulfilled in themselves,
what connection could there be that is accomplishable by a single appearance? Otherwise, [there would be] none.

children.text: arthānāṃ jaḍānām , tajjñānāṃ tadvikalpānāṃ tanniścayānāṃ ca deśakramaṃ kālakramaṃ cātyajatām , svasamāpinām ---- svarūpamātrapratiṣṭhānām , kaḥ samanvayaḥ , na kaścit ityarthaḥ , yato hi asau samanvayaḥ sakṛdābhāsena deśakālākāramiśrīkaraṇātmanā yojanābhāsena sādhayituṃ śakyaḥ nānyathā , na hi pṛthakpṛthak parikṣīṇeṣu srotaḥsu taduhyamānāḥ tṛṇolapādayaḥ samanvayaṃ kaṃcit yānti iti / anekatvena deśakālādibheda ityāśayena sakṛcchabdaḥ tanniṣedhatātparyeṇa prayuktaḥ //3//
children.translated_text: Of insentient objects, of their cognitions, of their conceptual constructions, and of their determinations — which do not abandon the sequence of space and time — of those that are fulfilled in themselves, resting in their own form alone — what connection? None whatsoever: this is the meaning. For that connection is accomplishable only by a single appearance that is of the nature of mixing together the [factors of] space, time, and form — a connecting appearance — and not otherwise. For when separate streams are individually exhausted, the grasses, lotuses, and such carried by them do not attain any connection. The word 'sakṛt' (single/simultaneous) is used with the intention of [indicating] plurality, i.e., difference of space and time, and is employed with the purport of negating that. //3//

children.text: tatra ko 'sau samanvaya ityāśaṅkya bahutaravyāpakaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvaṃ tāvat darśayati
children.translated_text: Therein, what is that connection? — anticipating this, he shows the more extensive cause-and-effect relation first:
The fact that perception and non-apprehension, falling upon different respective portions,
are the reasons for establishing the cause-and-effect relation — that arises from a single perceiver.

children.text: iha anubhūto viṣayaḥ prakāśate smṛtau , tatra viṣayasyāsau smṛtiḥ na nūtanaḥ prakāśaḥ api tu asya sa prakāśaḥ prācyo 'nubhava eva , sa cānubhavo jñānarūpatvena jñeyarūpatvābhāvāt na jñānāntarasaṃvedyaḥ api tu svaprakāśaḥ , sa ca smṛtikāle yadi asan tat kathaṃ prakāśatām , bhavatu vā asau tathāpi smṛtiḥ syāt , tasmāt etat evamupapadyate , yadeva smṛtisvasaṃvedanam , tadeva anubhavasya svasaṃvedanam , na tu aparaṃ svasaṃvedanavyatiriktaṃ pratyakṣam anumānādikaṃ vā tatra kramate , tataśca tāvatkālāpi avichinnamekaṃ yat svasaṃvedanaṃ tadeva

children.translated_text: 'perceiver-hood' —

children.text: iti siddham / anyatra anubhavitari smartā anyo na upapadyate , ityanayā chāyayā smṛtyā pramātṛsiddhiḥ pūrvamuktā , idānīṃ tu svasaṃvedanaikībhāvena bhaṅgyantareṇa iti viśeṣaḥ //5//
children.translated_text: Thus it is established. Elsewhere, the position that the rememberer is different from the experiencer is untenable — in this vein, the establishment of the perceiver through memory was stated earlier. But now [it is established] through identity with self-awareness, by a different approach — this is the distinction. //5//

Here, the experienced object appears in memory. Therein, that memory of the object is not a new luminosity of it; rather, its luminosity is the prior experience itself. And that experience, being of the nature of knowledge, and being devoid of the nature of the knowable, is not perceivable by another cognition; rather, it is self-luminous. And if at the time of memory it were non-existent, then how could it be luminous? Or even if it does exist [at that time], still it would be the memory [that is operative]. Therefore, this is tenable in the following way alone: the very self-awareness of memory is itself the self-awareness of experience — and no other thing, whether a direct perception or inference separate from self-awareness, extends there. And therefore, the self-awareness that has been unbroken for that long — that itself is

children.text: nanvanubhavātirikte 'pi arthe santu vikalpāḥ pramāṇam , aprāmāṇyaṃ hi bādhabalāt bhavati , bādhābhāve tat kathaṃ syād ityāśaṅkya so 'pi ayaṃ bādhyabādhakabhāvaḥ satyāsatyapravibhājanayā viśveṣāṃ vyavahārāṇāṃ jīvitabhūto na ekena pramātṛtattvena vinā ghaṭata iti vitatya darśayati
children.translated_text: Objection: Even regarding objects beyond experience, let conceptual cognitions be valid means of knowledge, for invalidity arises from the force of invalidation, and in the absence of invalidation, how could it be? Anticipating this, he shows at length that even this relation of invalidated and invalidating, through the discrimination of true and false, which is the life-breath of all practical activities, is not possible without a single perceiver-principle:
Even the relation of invalidated and invalidating, of cognitions that in themselves are mutually non-contradictory,
would arise only from the establishment of a single perceiver.
'Validity in the absence of invalidation' —

children.text: ityetadartham avaśyasamarthyo yo bādhavyavahāraḥ so 'pi katham iti
children.translated_text: for the purpose of establishing this, the relation of invalidation that must necessarily be justified — how [is it possible]? That is the meaning of the word
'api' (even).

children.text: śabdasyārthaḥ / iha śuktyā tāvat rajatasya na kācit bādhā nāma kriyamāṇā dṛśyate , śuktijñānena rajatajñānaṃ bādhyate ityapi na yuktam , svasmin viṣaye ātmani ca svarūpe dvayoḥ jñānayoḥ pariniṣṭhitayoḥ viśr|antayoḥ anyonyaṃ virodhasya abhāvāt / atha ayaṃ parasparaparihāra eva virodhaḥ tarhi sarveṣāṃ jñānānāṃ virodhāt bādhyabādhakabhāvasya svātmani pariniṣṭhaiva na labhyeti sutarāṃ vighaṭeta satyetarapravibhāgaḥ / nañapi atra tantreṇa vyākhyeyaḥ / etaduktaṃ bhavati ---- yadi jñānaṃ svayaṃ naśyati tadā kiṃ jñānāntareṇa asya kṛtam , na hi tena tatkāle 'saṃbhavatā tasya viṣayāpahāraḥ kartuṃ śakyaḥ , na rājatam ityapi jñānaṃ svaṃ rajatābhāvaṃ viṣayīkurvat na viṣayam apaharet rajatajñānasya / athāpi jñānāntareṇa nāśyate ityapi pakṣaḥ , tatrāpi sarveṣāṃ jñānām iyameva saraṇiriti kiṃcideva bādhyam iti kathaṃ syāt ? yadā tu rajatajñānaṃ śuktijñānaṃ ca ekatra svasaṃvedane viśrānyataḥ tadā etat upapadyate , tathā hi ---- ekatrāpi pramātṛtattve viśrāmyatāṃ jñānānāṃ naikaprakāraiva viśrāntiḥ api tu vicitratayaiva sā saṃvedyate , tathā hi ---- nīlam iti utpalam iti jñāne pramātari viśrāmyantī parasparoparāgābhāsena viśrāmyataḥ / ghaṭa iti paṭa iti parasparānāśkeṣeṇa , śuktikā iti na rajatam iti vā jñānaṃ rajatam iti jñānasya unmūlanaṃ tadīyavimarśātmakapramārūpavyāpārānuvartanavidhvaṃsaṃ kurvat pramātari pratiṣṭhāṃ bhajate / evaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvādau viśrāntivaicitryaṃ prameyāsaṃbhavi pramātrā svātantryeṇa nirmitaṃ tata eva asya pramāsvatantratādāyi vācyam / evamekatra pramātari pūrvajñānasya parivarjanena yato niścitā sthitiḥ , iti bādhyabādhakavyavahāra upapannaḥ , nīlādivat kila tānapi vyavahārān sa eva parameśvaraḥ svātantryāt ābhāsayati tat te 'pi satyā eveti //6//
children.translated_text: Here, first of all, no invalidation of silver by nacre is seen as being performed. 'The cognition of silver is invalidated by the cognition of nacre' — this too is not proper, since there is no mutual contradiction between two cognitions that are established and resting in their own respective objects and in their own essential natures. If this very mutual exclusion is what is meant by contradiction, then since all cognitions would contradict each other, the establishment of the relation of invalidated and invalidating in itself would not be obtainable — and the discrimination of true and false would be all the more undermined. The negative particle here too should be explained in the same manner. What is being said is this: if a cognition perishes on its own, then what has another cognition done to it? For that [other cognition], being impossible at that time, cannot rob it of its object. And the cognition 'this is not silver' too, while objectifying its own [content of] absence-of-silver, does not rob the cognition of silver of its object. Even if the alternative position is that it is destroyed by another cognition, even then, since this is the path of all cognitions, how could only some particular [cognition] be invalidated? But when the cognition of silver and the cognition of nacre both rest in a single self-awareness, then this is tenable. For even when cognitions rest in a single perceiver-principle, their resting is not of one kind alone; rather, it is experienced as of a varied nature. Thus: the cognitions 'this is blue' and 'this is a lotus' rest in the perceiver with the appearance of mutual coloring. 'This is a pot' and 'this is a cloth' — without mutual destruction. But 'this is nacre' or 'this is not silver' — this cognition, uprooting the cognition 'this is silver' and destroying the continuation of the operation of valid cognition that is of the nature of reflective awareness belonging to it, takes its stand in the perceiver. Thus, the variety of resting — such as in the relation of cause and effect and such — which is impossible in mere objects, is fashioned by the perceiver through his freedom; therefore, this very thing must be declared as bestowing upon him the autonomy of valid cognition. In this way, since the prior cognition is established with certainty in a single perceiver through exclusion, the relation of invalidated and invalidating is tenable. Indeed, just like blue and such, that very Supreme Lord manifests even those practical activities through His freedom; therefore, they too are real. //6//
Here, anticipating the opponent's view with the intention of refuting it:
Just as the cognition of bare ground establishes the absence of a pot,
so too, if the cognition of nacre knows the invalidity of the cognition of silver.

children.text: iha śuktikājñānaṃ svātmānaṃ saṃvidat svātmābhinnaṃ pramāṇatvaṃ budhyate ,

children.translated_text: 'it determines that' —

children.text: iti nyāyāt , tatparicchedanāntarīyakaśca anyavyavaccheda ityaśuktijñānarūpasya rajatajñānasya apramāṇatvavedanaṃ tadeva ucyate yat etat śuktikāsaṃvedanābhinnapramāṇatvavedanam , na ca etat apūrvaṃ yat vastvantarajñānameva vastvantarābhāvajñānam iti , śuddhabhūbhāgagrahaṇameva hi ghaṭābhāvagrahaṇam iti prasiddhametat / evam apramāṇatvasaṃvedanameva rajatajñānasya bādhyatvam ucyate , ataśca bādhyabādhakatvam evaṃ siddham iti cet asmābhiḥ ucyate ---- tat kiṃ pramātraikyeneti //7//
children.translated_text: by this principle. And the exclusion of what is other is inseparable from that determination. Therefore, the awareness of the invalidity of the cognition of silver, which is of the nature of non-nacre-cognition, is none other than the awareness of validity that is non-different from the self-awareness of nacre. And this is nothing new — that the cognition of one thing is itself the cognition of the absence of another thing — for it is well known that the grasping of a clean ground-surface is itself the grasping of the absence of a pot. Thus, the awareness of invalidity of the cognition of silver is itself what is called its being invalidated, and thereby the relation of invalidated and invalidating is established — if this be said, we reply: then what about the unity of the perceiver? //7//
Here, the cognition of nacre, being aware of itself, knows its own validity as non-different from itself —

children.text: atra prasaṅgāt abhāvavyavahārasya siddhau tattvamupapādayiṣyan dṛṣṭāntameva tāvat paradarśane dūṣayati
children.translated_text: Here, incidentally, wishing to establish the true nature of the practical activity of absence, he first refutes the example in the opponent's system:
It is not so: from the cognition of bare ground, [the absence of the pot] would not be established, since that [ground] is not of the nature of non-pot;
nor [is there established] the absence of a pot, which is [actually] fit to be perceived, here.

children.text: yo dṛṣṭānta uktaḥ sa eva na , kuta iti cet ucyate

children.translated_text: Here, 'the ground is not a pot' —

children.text: iti tādātmyena abhāvo vyavahartavyaḥ kadācit , kadācit vyatirekeṇa
children.translated_text: sometimes absence is to be expressed through identity [negation]; and sometimes through difference [negation]:
'here on the ground there is no pot' —

children.text: iti / tatra śuddhabhūtalajñānāt ādyo 'yaṃ vyavahāraḥ sidhyati , yatra dṛśyatvaṃ na upayogi , upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptirapi hi yasya nāsti piśācādeḥ svabhāvabalāt , yasya vā śabdādeḥ tadgāhakaśrotrādisāmagrīsākalyasya tatra ekajñānasaṃsargivastvantarapratipattyabhāvenāniścayāt tasyāpi tādātmyenāyamabhāvo gṛhyate
children.translated_text: thus. Therein, from the cognition of bare ground, the first practical activity is established — where perceptibility is not relevant. For even [the absence of] a ghost (<s>piśāca</s>) and such, which by its very nature does not possess fitness for perception, or [the absence of] sound and such, for which the complete aggregate of the grasping instrument, the ear, etc. is present there — due to the absence of apprehension of any other thing associated with a single cognition, and hence due to uncertainty — even its absence is grasped through identity [negation]:
'The ground is not a ghost, not a sound' —

children.text: iti , yatra tu dṛśyatvaṃ viśeṣaṇam avaśyam apayogi tatra vyatirekeṇa abhāve vyavahartavye na eṣo 'bhyupāyaḥ //8//
children.translated_text: thus. But where perceptibility must necessarily be employed as a qualifier, there, when the absence is to be expressed through difference [negation], this approach does not work. //8//
The very example that was cited is untenable. If asked why, we reply:

children.text: kuta iti cet ---- atiaprasaṅgāditi brūmaḥ / tameva darśayati
children.translated_text: If asked why — we say: because of overextension. He shows that very thing:
The ground is always distinct from entities, since they are established in their own nature;
so how could that cognition [of bare ground] ever be the means of establishing the absence of a separate [entity]?

children.text: vidyamāne 'pi ghaṭe bhūtalaṃ śuddhameva , na hi bhāvā miśrībhavanti , tataśca tadāpi śuddhabhūtalajñānam asti , iti satyapi ghaṭe katham abhāvo vyatirekeṇa na vyavahriyate

children.translated_text: 'Here on the ground there is no pot' —
thus.
'tajjñānam' (that cognition):
means the cognition of the distinct portion of the ground;
'jātu' (ever):

children.text: iti kasyāṃcideva daśāyāṃ ghaṭāsaṃnidhānarūpāyām , bhinnasya ghaṭasya abhāvaṃ sādhayati na tu sarvadā iti kena prakāreṇa bhavet , etena atra bhūtale piśāco nāsti ityapi syāditi āpatitaṃ mantavyam //9//
children.translated_text: in a certain state alone, characterized by the non-proximity of the pot — it establishes the absence of the separate pot, but not in all circumstances — by what means could it be so? By this, one should understand that the consequence also follows that 'here on the ground there is no ghost.' //9//

Even when a pot is present, the ground is pure [i.e., ground] alone — for entities do not intermingle. And therefore, even then the cognition of bare ground exists. Hence, even when the pot exists, how is absence not expressed through difference [negation]?

children.text: nanvevaṃ vyatirekābhāvaniṣṭho vyavahāro loke tāvat avigītaḥ asyāṃcideva daśāyāṃ dṛṣṭaḥ , tatra kā gatirityāśaṅkya cirantanairaparidṛṣṭaṃ tatsiddhiprakāraṃ darśayati
children.translated_text: Objection: The practical activity of absence established through difference [negation] is indeed uncontested in the world and is seen in a certain state alone. What is the way out here? Anticipating this, he shows the mode of establishing it, unseen by the ancients:
But rather, a mass of light, or for the blind, a touch such as warm or soft —
that which exists there — its own cognition would establish it as having the nature of non-pot.

children.text: iha bhāva eva bhāvāntarasya abhāva iti vyavahartavyaḥ iti ayaṃ tāvat aparityājyaḥ prātītikaḥ panthāḥ , tatra bhāvasya bhāvāntareṇa ya ādhāryādhārabhāvaḥ sa eva bhāvatadabhāvayoḥ , tataśca bhūtale ghaṭavyatiriktaṃ vastvantaraṃ śilādikam ālokapuñjādikaṃ vā yat cākṣuṣe jñāne bhāti tadeva vyavahriyate

children.translated_text: 'the absence of a pot on the ground' or 'there is no pot on the ground' —

children.text: iti vā , yatrāpi nāsti cakṣurvyāpāro netranimīlanasaṃtamasādau tatrāpi bhūtale ghaṭocitakaṭhinasparśaviviktaṃ mṛdum uṣṇaṃ śītam anuṣṇāśītaṃ vā gṛhṇan tameva atra ghaṭābhāva iti vyavaharati vāyusparśasya sarvagasya avaśyaṃbhāvāt , iti vākyārthaḥ / padārthastu ----
children.translated_text: thus. Even where there is no operation of the eye — in the darkness of closing the eyes and such — even there, on the ground, one who grasps touch that is soft, warm, cold, or neither warm nor cold, being free from the hardness appropriate to a pot, expresses that very thing as 'here is the absence of a pot' — since the touch of wind is necessarily omnipresent. This is the meaning of the statement. As for the word-by-word meaning:
'kiṃ tu' (but rather):

children.text: iti svamatopakṣepāya svapratibhāpraśnaparāmarśaḥ , kiṃ punaratra nyāyyamiti tatrāha
children.translated_text: introduces one's own view — a reflection in the form of a question arising from one's own insight: 'what then is proper here?' — to that he says:
'tatra' (there):
on the ground,
'ālokacayaḥ' (a mass of light):
is to be known as existing;
'for the blind, touch such as warmth and the like' —
exists;
'tasya' (of that):
of the mass of light or of the touch,
'svajñānam' (its own cognition):

children.text: anyaghaṭādiviviktena svena rūpeṇa jñānam tat kartṛ ,
children.translated_text: cognition through its own form, distinct from any other [thing such as] a pot and the like — that is the agent;
'tasya' (of that):
of the light and such, the nature of being non-pot, the nature of being the absence of a pot —
'tatra' (there):

children.text: bhūtale sādhayati iti śakyo '; yamarthaḥ / {śaki liṅ ca}(pā. sū. 3-3-172) iti liṅ / āntaraprāṇaspandanajanitasūkṣmaśabdākarṇanācca śrotrādisākalyaṃ saṃbhavāyamānaḥ tameva śabdam ekajñānasaṃsargiṇaṃ śṛṇvan śabdāntaraṃ niṣedhayati
children.translated_text: on the ground, it establishes — this is the possible meaning. The optative is by the rule '{śaki liṅ ca}' (<s>Pāṇini</s> 3.3.172). And from the non-hearing of a subtle sound generated by the internal pulsation of the vital breath, while being possible for the complete aggregate including the ear and such, one who hears that very sound as associated with a single cognition negates another sound:
'There is no other sound here' —

children.text: iti / tatsūkṣmaśabdābhāvamapi sūkṣmatamāntarnādāvahitaśrotro vedayate , rasagandhasparśābhāvo 'pi dantodakarasaṃ tripuṭikāgandhaṃ kāyīyaṃ ca sparśaṃ saṃvedayamānenaiva rasābhāvo vedyaḥ , na hi ekajñānasaṃsargayogyavastvantaropalambhena vinā upalabdhikāraṇasākalyaniścayo 'sti , iti ekānta eṣaḥ / acirapravṛttatattadviṣayānubhavakalpitasya tadaiva dhvaṃsānāśaṅkanāt karaṇasya kāraṇasākalyaniścayaḥ kim ekajñānasaṃsargitayā iti cet na , tattvabhāvopalipsurhi prayatnena tattadindriyādhiṣṭhānaṃ vyāpārayanneva lakṣyate //10//
children.translated_text: thus. One whose ear is attentive to the subtlest internal resonance also perceives even the absence of that subtle sound. And the absence of taste, smell, and touch too is to be perceived only by one who is perceiving the taste of the teeth-water, the smell of the nostrils' cavity, and the bodily touch. For without the apprehension of another thing fit for association with a single cognition, there is no certainty of the completeness of the conditions of perception — this is the definitive position. [Objection:] The instrument whose certainty regarding the completeness of conditions arises from the recently commenced experience of this or that object, which has been posited just at that moment with no suspicion of destruction — [why should it be] through association with a single cognition? Not so, for one who desires to ascertain the reality of things is observed to make efforts precisely by operating the various respective sense-faculties. //10//

Here, the position that a positive entity alone is the absence of another entity — this practical path grounded in experience is not to be abandoned. Therein, the container-contained relation that a positive entity has with another entity is the same as that between an entity and the absence of that [other entity]. Therefore, on the ground, another thing distinct from the pot — stone or the like, or a mass of light, or the like — that which appears in visual cognition, that alone is expressed in practice as

children.text: nanvevam adṛśyāsyāpi piśācādeḥ niṣedhavyavahāro vyatirekeṇāpi prāpnoti , sa hi ālokapuñjo yathā ghaṭāt anyaḥ tadvat piśācāderapi / tadetat āśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If so, then the negation in the form of difference [negation] would also apply even to an invisible entity such as a ghost and such — for the mass of light is other than a pot, and similarly other than a ghost. Anticipating this, he says:
A ghost (<s>piśāca</s>) might be non-luminous and yet exist within the luminous [space], just as
it is invisible within the ground — it cannot be negated in every respect.

children.text: ālokapuñjo yadyapi piśācād vyatirikto yadyapi ca āloko 'sti apiśācātmā ityetāvat siddhyati tathāpi atra

children.translated_text: 'there is no ghost' —

children.text:
ityetat aśakyam adhyavasātum ,
ghaṭo hi ālokapūramadhye 'pi asaṃbhāvyaḥ , ghaṭasaṃnidhau tatra ālokapūrāsamarpaṇāt , ataśca siddhyatīdam
children.translated_text:
this cannot be determined;
for a pot is inconceivable even within a flood of light — since in the proximity of a pot, the flood of light is not furnished there. And therefore this is established:
'there is no pot here' —

children.text: iti , piśācastu tādṛksvabhāvo yo bhūtalamadhye ālokamadhye 'pi vā bhavan bhūtalasya ālokasya vā tāṃ nibiḍatāṃ na vihanti , tataśca ālokamadhye tasya saṃbhāvanāt kathaṃ vyatirekeṇa niṣedhavyavahāraḥ , evaṃ rūpamadhye rasādeḥ saṃbhāvanāt tasyāpi aniṣedhaḥ / yadyapi anālokaḥ ālokāt anyaḥ piśācaḥ tathāpi asau bhūtalasya antarmadhye 'dṛśyo bhavati iti saṃbhāvyate yathā , tadvadeva ālokasyābhyantarepi so'sti iti saṃbhāvyata eva , tataśca yadyapi ālokastato 'nyaḥ ityanena pathā niṣiddhaḥ piśācaḥ tathāpi sarvaprakāreṇa na niṣiddhaḥ iti tadabhāvanibandhanāḥ kathaṃ tatra vyavahārāḥ pravartantām iti ślokārthaḥ //11//
children.translated_text: thus. But a ghost is of such a nature that even while existing within the ground or within the light, it does not disturb the density of the ground or the light. And therefore, since a ghost is possible even within the light, how can there be a practical activity of negation through difference? Similarly, since taste and such are possible within form, their negation too is not [established]. Although a ghost, being non-luminous and different from light, is thus — nevertheless, it is postulated that it could be invisible within the interior of the ground; and in just the same way, it is postulated that it could exist within the interior of the light. And therefore, although the ghost has been negated by the path 'the light is other than it,' nevertheless it has not been negated in every respect — so how could practical activities grounded in its absence proceed there? — this is the meaning of the verse. //11//
Although the mass of light is different from a ghost, and although the light is established as being of non-ghost nature — nevertheless, here

children.text: evaṃ prasaṅgāt abhāvavyavahārasya tattvam upadarśya prakṛte yojayati
children.translated_text: Having thus shown incidentally the true nature of the practical activity of absence, he connects it to the main topic:
Thus, the cognition of nacre would be of the nature of the absence of silver;
but it cannot be the knower of the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver.

children.text: yathā āloko ghaṭābhāva iti āloke gṛhīte prāk gṛhītasya ghaṭasya na kiṃcit āyātam tathaiva śuktijñānaṃ rūpyajñānābhāva iti iyat saṃbhāvyate / yathā ghaṭajñānaṃ ghaṭajñānaprāmāṇyasaṃvit paṭajñānābhāvaḥ paṭajñānābhāvaprāmāṇyasaṃvit iyatā ca na pūrvapravṛttaṃ paṭajñānam apramāṇībhavati , eṣā hi tasya ghaṭajñānasya svarūpacintā sarvā na jñānāntarasya ādyasya kimapi ato jātam / evaṃ śuktiriyam iti , na rajatam idam iti ca jñānameva svātmanā prakāśatām , ahaṃ śuktau rajatābhāve ca pramāṇaṃ na tu rajate iti , tāvatā tu prāktanasya rajatajñānasya na kiṃcit vṛttam iti tadviṣayīkṛtaṃ rajataṃ katham asatyaṃ syāt //12//
children.translated_text: Just as when 'light is the absence of the pot,' upon grasping the light, nothing has happened to the pot previously grasped — in the same way, it can be supposed that 'the cognition of shell is the absence of the cognition of silver.' Just as the cognition of a pot is [accompanied by] the self-awareness of the validity of the pot-cognition, and is the absence of the cloth-cognition and [accompanied by] the self-awareness of the validity of the absence of cloth-cognition — yet by that much, the previously existing cloth-cognition does not become invalid — for this entire investigation is of the nature of that pot-cognition itself, and nothing has arisen regarding the other, earlier cognition. Similarly, let the cognition 'this is shell' and 'this is not silver' shine by its own nature — 'I am a valid means of knowledge regarding the shell and the absence of silver, but not regarding silver' — yet by that much, nothing has befallen the prior cognition of silver, so how could the silver that was its object become unreal? //12//

children.text: nanvidamityanena tadeva parāmṛśyate yatra rajatajñānam abhūt tatraiva idānīṃ

children.translated_text: 'not silver' —
thus,
'shell' —

children.text: iti ca jñānaṃ pramāṇabhūtaṃ jātam , tat ato 'numīyate ---- tat
children.translated_text: thus — a cognition that is a valid means of knowledge has arisen. From that, it is inferred that
'the prior silver-cognition is not a valid means of knowledge' —

children.text: iti , na hi etat saṃbhavati ---- viruddhaviṣayadvayāvagāhi jñānadvayaṃ pramāṇam ekatra viṣayībhavati iti , tadayam ānumāniko bādhavyavahāro bhaviṣyati ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: thus. For this is not possible — that two cognitions apprehending two contradictory objects should both be valid with respect to a single [thing]. This sublation-transaction will be inferential — anticipating this [objection], he says:
Objection: By [the demonstrative] 'this,' that very thing is reflectively grasped where the silver-cognition occurred; in that very [place], now,
Sublation cannot be from inference either, due to the non-establishment of the locus of properties;
but [sublation] established through self-awareness is proper, since it arises from a single knowing subject. //

children.text: na kevalaṃ svasaṃvedanāt na siddhyati bādhā , yāvat anumānato 'pi na siddhyati , dharmiṇo 'siddheḥ , apiśabdāt hetoḥ vyāpteśca , apiḥ ubhayatra neyaḥ , iha dharmiṇi siddhe siddhena hetunā smaryamāṇavyāptikena sādhyadharmāyogavyavacchedo 'numānavyāpāraḥ , iha ca prācye rūpyajñāne dharmiṇi aprāmāṇyaṃ sādhyo dharmaḥ tatra śuktikājñānaṃ vā , na rajatam iti jñānaṃ vā , tajjñānaviṣayīkāryatvaṃ vā viṣayagataṃ hetūkriyeta , na caitat yuktam tatkāle prācyarūpyabodhasya dharmiṇo 'bhāvāt , na cāpi tasya śuktijñānādayo dharmāḥ , na ca apakṣadharmāt sādhyasiddhiḥ , ataḥ smaryamāṇaṃ taddharmi syāt ityapi asat / atha śuktiḥ na rajatajñānasya viṣaya iti sādhyate śuktikājñānaviṣayatvāt iti , tat yadi idānīm tadā siddhasādhanam , atha pūrvam tadā tatpūrvasvasaṃvedanena bādhyaviṣayatā / kena caivaṃ vyāptirgṛhītā ---- yatra idānīm anyat jñānam tatra pūrvam anyat na bhavati iti , anumānantareṇa iti cet , ananvasthā / etena etat pratyuktam ---- ekasmin viṣaye kathaṃ jñānadvayaṃ syāt iti , ko hi ekaviṣayatāṃ tayorjñānayoḥ jānīyāt , te hi tāvat svātmani svaviṣaye ca viśrāmyate iti uktam , iti anumānato 'pi na bādhā , na ca tathābhūtamapi vyavadhānam atra pratītau saṃvedyate , svasaṃvedanasiddhatayā jhaṭiti bhāsanāt / ata eva etadapi aśakyaṃ vaktum ---- mā bhūt bādhā nāma iti /
children.translated_text: Not only is sublation not established through self-awareness, but it is not established even through inference, due to the non-establishment of the locus of properties (<s>dharmin</s>). By the word 'api' (also), [the non-establishment] of the reason (<s>hetu</s>) and its invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) [is indicated]; the word 'api' should be applied to both. Here, when the locus of properties is established, the operation of inference is the exclusion of the non-connection of the property to be proven, through a reason that is established and whose concomitance is remembered. And here, the prior silver-cognition is the locus of properties; invalidity is the property to be proven; therein, either the shell-cognition, or the cognition 'not silver,' or the objectifiability by that cognition as pertaining to the object — [any of] these would be made the reason. But this is not proper, since at that time the locus of properties — the prior silver-cognition — is absent. Nor are the shell-cognition and such properties of that [prior cognition]. Nor can there be establishment of the property to be proven from what is not a property of the thesis-locus. Therefore, [the suggestion] that the remembered thing would be the locus of properties is also wrong. If what is being proven is 'the shell is not the object of the silver-cognition, because it is the object of the shell-cognition' — if [this is said about] the present [shell], then it is already-established-as-proven (<s>siddhasādhana</s>); if about the past, then the sublatable-objecthood is [contradicted] by the self-awareness of the prior [cognition] itself. And by whom has this concomitance been grasped — namely, 'where there is now a different cognition, there was not previously a different one'? — if by another inference, then there is infinite regress. By this, the following is also answered: 'how can there be two cognitions regarding a single object?' — for who could know the single-object-ness of those two cognitions? For they rest in their own selves and their own objects — this has been stated. Therefore, sublation is not [established] even through inference. Nor is any such intervening [process] experienced in this cognition as having the nature of self-awareness-establishment, since it flashes forth instantaneously as established by self-awareness. For this very reason, it is also impossible to say 'let there be no such thing as sublation!'

children.text: evaṃ parapakṣe 'nupapattiṃ pradarśya svapakṣe ekapramātṛpariniṣṭhiteḥ udiyāt bādhyabādhakabhāva iti vākyena pratijñātaṃ nigamayati ---- yuktā sā ekasmāt pramātuḥ yadi jāyeta iti , sa eva hi tathā nirmātā iti vyākhyātameva , sthite caivaṃ yadi vyavahārasiddhaye 'nyathānupapattirapyucyate tat ucyatāṃ kāmam , adhunā sarvaṃ siddhyati , iti //13//
children.translated_text: Having thus shown the impossibility in the opponent's position, he concludes by demonstrating what was proposed by the [previous] verse — that the sublating-sublated relationship would arise if [cognitions are] established in a single knowing subject: it is proper if it arises from a single knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>) — for He alone is the creator in that way, as has been explained. And this being established, if it is also said that it cannot be otherwise for the establishment of practical activity, let it be said as desired — now everything is established. //13//

children.text: na kevalamete kāryakāraṇabhāvasmaraṇabādhāvyavahārāḥ sakalalokayātrāsāmānyavyavahārabhūtā ekapramātṛpratiṣṭhāḥ , yāvat avāntaravyavahārā api ye krayavikrayādayaḥ samalāḥ , upadeśyopadeśabhāvādayaśca nirmalāḥ , tepi ekapramātṛniṣṭhā eva bhavanti , vyavahārā hi sarve samanvayaprāṇāḥ iti upasaṃhārakrameṇa darśayati
children.translated_text: Not only are these transactions of cause-and-effect, memory, and sublation — which are common general transactions of all worldly life — established in a single knowing subject, but even particular transactions such as buying and selling, which are impure, and the relationship of teacher and pupil, which is pure — these too are established in a single knowing subject alone. For all transactions are animated by synthesis (<s>samanvaya</s>) — this he shows by way of conclusion:
Thus, in the all-pervading One who is studded with appearances of extremely differentiated objects,
practical activity — whether impure or pure — is experienced. //
'Differentiated in various ways' (<s>tattadvibhinna</s>) —

children.text: iti ślokadvayoktena anena upapattiprakāreṇa , anvayavyatirekātmanā , tathā ślokāntarairuktena vyavahārodāharaṇaprakāreṇa idamapi mantavyam ---- yat vibhau deśakālānavacchinne , ata eva atyarthabhinnaiḥ māyābalāt bhedaikaprāṇitaiḥ nīlasukhādyābhāsaiḥ pratibimbakalpaiḥ anatiriktatayā vartamānaiḥ , khacite svarūpānanyathābhāvena uparakte , viśrāntaḥ sarvo vyavahāro 'nubhūyate , anubhava eva atra dṛḍhatamaṃ pramāṇam iti yāvat , anubhūyate ca sopadeśaiḥ avadhānaparaiḥ yena eṣāṃ yaiva saṃsāradaśāsaṃmatā vyavahāradaśā saiva pramātṛtattvaprakhyātmikā śivabhūmiḥ / yaduktam
children.translated_text: by this mode of reasoning stated in the two verses, of the nature of positive and negative concomitance, and also by the mode of illustration of practical activity stated in other verses, this too should be understood: that in the all-pervading One (<s>vibhu</s>) who is unlimited by space and time — and therefore studded with appearances of blue, pleasure, and such that are extremely differentiated, that are animated solely by difference through the force of <s>Māyā</s>, that are like reflections, existing without being additional [to consciousness] — [the One who is] tinted by them without any alteration of His own nature — in Him, all practical activity is experienced as resting. Experience itself is the most firm means of valid knowledge here — this is the import. And it is experienced by those who are instructed and attentive, for whom this very state of practical activity, accepted in the condition of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), is itself the ground of <s>Śiva</s>, of the nature of the manifestation of the principle of the knowing subject. As stated:
{...attentiveness regarding the relation. //}

children.text: iti / apratyabhijñātātmaparamārthānāṃ samalo vyavahāraḥ , anyeṣāṃ sa eva nirmalaḥ // iti śivam //14// āditaḥ //77//
children.translated_text: Thus. For those whose ultimate reality of the Self is unrecognized, the practical activity is impure; for others, that very same [practical activity] is pure. // Thus, auspiciousness! //14// From the beginning, 77 [verses]. //

children.text: iti śrīmanmāheśvarācāryavaryotpaladevapādaviratitāyāmīśvarapratyabhijñāyāṃ śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptakṛtavimarśinyākhyavyākhyopetāyāṃ prathame jñānādhikāre ekāśrayanirūpaṇaṃ nāma saptamamāhnikam // 7 //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the seventh chapter named 'The Determination of the Single Substratum' in the first Section on Knowledge, in the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñā</s> composed by the eminent master <s>Utpaladeva</s>, accompanied by the commentary called <s>Vimarśinī</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 7 //
Now begins the eighth chapter named 'The Determination of Sovereignty' in the Section on Knowledge.
{He who is eternally established as <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) through practical activity

children.text: nityaṃ maheśvaraḥ siddhaḥ siddhānāṃ taṃ stumaḥ śivam //}
children.translated_text: established by self-awareness — we praise Him, <s>Śiva</s>, the accomplished among the accomplished. //}

children.text: evaṃ jñānasmaraṇāpohanāni vyutpādya eṣāmekamāśrayaṃ vinā vyavahāro na yuktaḥ iti nirūpitam etāvatā ,
children.translated_text: Thus, having expounded knowledge, memory, and exclusion, it has been determined through that much that practical activity is not proper without a single substratum for these. In that [verse]:
{'Unless, having made within...' /}
'one' (<s>ekaḥ</s>) —
that has been established. Through the justification of internal appearances,
'having made the infinite universe His inner content' —
this too has been determined. What was stated in that very [context] as
'<s>Maheśvara</s>' (the Great Lord) —

children.text: iti uktam tanmāheśvaryaṃ svātantryarūpamupapādayitavyam , tacca jñānaviṣayaṃ kriyā ---- viṣayaṃ ca ityubhayaprakāram , tatra yato bhagavān jñātā kartā ca , yadyapi ca prakāśavimarśātmakaṃ cidekaghanam ekameva saṃvidrūpam , tathāpi vyutpādanāya tatparighaṭita eva ayaṃ vibhāgaḥ , tena jñānātmakakriyāviṣayaṃ svātantryaṃ yadyapi kriyāśaktirūpaṃ tathāpi tat jñānādhikāra eva nirṇetavyaṃ tadviṣayatvāt / evaṃ ca jñātṛśabdārthaḥ prakṛtitaḥ pratyayataśca saṃpūrṇatayā nirṇīto bhavati / tatra jñānaṃ nāma svayaṃbheditābhāsabhedopāśrayaniyantraṇāsaṃkucitam
children.translated_text: the sovereignty (<s>māheśvarya</s>) of that, which is of the nature of freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>), is to be demonstrated. And that is of two kinds: pertaining to knowledge and pertaining to action. Therein, since the Blessed One is both knower and agent, and although the consciousness-reality (<s>cid</s>), which is a compact mass of luminosity and reflective awareness, is one and the same, still, for the purpose of exposition, this division is established within it. Therefore, the freedom pertaining to action as it relates to knowledge, although being of the nature of the power of action (<s>kriyā-śakti</s>), is nevertheless to be determined in the Section on Knowledge itself, since it pertains to that. And thus, the meaning of the word 'knower' (<s>jñātṛ</s>) will have been completely determined both from the root and from the suffix. Therein, knowledge is the awareness

children.text: saṃvedanam / tatrābhāseṣu yat svātantryaṃ tadeva jñānaśaktiviṣayaṃ svātantryaṃ saṃpadyate iti /
children.translated_text: which is not contracted by the constraint of the support of the self-manifested difference of appearances. The freedom with respect to those appearances is precisely the freedom that pertains to the power of knowledge.
what was stated there as
{'The contemporaneity of sense-proximity...' /}
beginning with this, up to
{'...since knowledge and action are pure. /'}

children.text: ityantena ślokaikādaśakena tat nirūpyate / tatra abhāsāntarāpekṣī ca ābhāso 'nyathā vā iti ślokena uktvā , sa eva ābhāsa eka iti ślokāntareṇa ucyate / arthakriyābhāso 'pi tathaiva ābhāsaniyata iti ślokadvayena uktvā kasmin ābhāse sā arthakriyā iti punaḥ ślokadvayena / ābhāsāntaravicitritābhāsabhittisthānīyam āntaratvam iti ślokena / tato bāhyatvaṃ svarūpato vibhāgataśveti ślokayugmena / tataḥ ślokena jñānādiśaktyāśrayasya ekasya upasaṃhāraḥ / ślokāntareṇa maheśvaratvam upasaṃharatā bhāvinaḥ kriyādhikārasya upakṣepa iti saṅkṣepārtha āhnikasya / atha ślokārtho nirūpyate /
children.translated_text: — by eleven verses, that is determined. Therein, having stated by one verse that an appearance depends on another appearance or is otherwise, by another verse it is said that that appearance itself is one. Having stated by two verses that even the appearance of purposeful activity is likewise appearance-determined, then by two more verses [he treats] in which appearance that purposeful activity [resides]. By one verse, the internality that is the ground, the position of the wall that is diversified by other appearances.
