Then by a pair of verses, externality from the standpoint of its own nature and from the standpoint of division. Then by one verse, the conclusion regarding the one [consciousness] that is the substratum of the powers of knowledge and such. By another verse, concluding with sovereignty, the introduction of the forthcoming Section on Action — this is the summary meaning of the chapter. Now the meaning of the verses is examined.

children.text: nanu yadi parameśvaraniṣṭhatayaiva samasto 'yaṃ vyavahāraḥ tat asya sphuṭatvāsphuṭatvaprāyaprasiddhavaicitryānupapattiḥ , yena kila ayam anuprāṇitaḥ sa eka eva bhagavān , na ca tadvyatirekeṇa vyavahārasya nijaṃ kiṃcana tattvam utpaśyāma ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If this entire practical activity is based solely on the Supreme Lord, then its well-known variety characterized by clarity and obscurity would be impossible — for the one who animates it is the single Blessed Lord alone, and we do not perceive any independent reality of practical activity apart from Him. Anticipating this, he says:
Appearances are, in some cases, solely dependent on contemporaneous proximity to the senses;
but in other cases, such as [objects of] the blind and pitch darkness, they are otherwise. //
There is a distinction in the appearance of objects with respect to their being; but in none of
the conceptual constructions — whether pertaining to future, present, or past objects — [is there such a distinction]. //

children.text: kevalam etāvatā ābhāsānāṃ bhedo na punararthāvabhāsasya svātmagataḥ kvacidapi bheda iti ślokadvayasya saṃmelitasya saṃbandhaḥ / yasminneva kāle sa ābhāsa ābhāti tatkāle eva bhavati , yat akṣasāmakṣyaṃ bāhyendriyapratyakṣatvaṃ nāma ābhāsāntaraṃ paśyāmītyevaṃrūpaṃ tatsāpekṣāḥ tadvyāmiśrāḥ kvacit ābhāsā bhavanti , yatra sphuṭatāvyavahāraḥ / andhaviṣayaḥ andhakārasthapramātṛviṣayaḥ punaḥ yo 'nyo vyavahārosphuṭatāmayaḥ tatra te ābhāsā anyathā , tathā hi jātyandhasya bāhyendriyapratyakṣatvalakṣaṇam ābhāsāntaraṃ naivāsti , dṛṣṭavatastu andhībhūtasya saṃtamasashtitasya ca tātkālikaṃ tat nāsti api tu prāktanameva bāhyendriyapratyakṣatvam anusaṃdhatte //1//
children.translated_text: 'Solely by this much there is difference of appearances, but there is no difference anywhere belonging to the self of the appearance of objects' — this is the connection of the two verses taken together. At whatever time that appearance appears, it exists at that time; what is called 'sense-proximity' — direct perceptibility by the external senses — is another appearance of the form 'I see'; dependent on that, mixed with that, some appearances exist — [those] where the transaction of clarity [obtains]. But in the domain of the blind, the domain of a knowing subject situated in darkness — the other transaction that is characterized by obscurity — there, those appearances are otherwise. For a person blind from birth, the other appearance characterized by direct perceptibility by the external senses simply does not exist; but for one who has seen and then become blind, or for one situated in utter darkness, that contemporaneous [sense-proximity] does not exist, but one synthesizes precisely the prior direct perceptibility by the external senses. //1//

children.text: tasmāt arthāvabhāsasya keṣucidapi vikalpeṣu sattāyāṃ svarūpe viśeṣo 'sti iti saṃbhāvanā na kartavyā / te hi vikalpā bhāvivastugāmino vā bhaviṣyanniṣṭhā vā bhavantu avrtamānaniṣṭhā vā atītavastuviśrāntā vā / etaduktaṃ bhavati ---- nīlamidaṃ paśyāmi , saṅkalpayāmi , utprekṣe , smarāmi , karomi vacmi ityādau nīlābhāso 'sau svarūpato 'nūnādhikaḥ / evaṃ paśyāmītyapi yaḥ pītādiṣu / te punarābhāsāḥ svātantryeṇa yadā bhagavatā saṃyojyante viyojyante ca tadā ayaṃ sphuṭatvādirvyavahāraḥ , nīlamityābhāsasya utprekṣe ityādyābhāsāntaravyavacchedanena paśyāmīti ābhāsavyāmiśraṇāyāṃ sphuṭatāvyavahāraḥ / evaṃ traikālikavyavahāravaicitryopapattiḥ / parameśvarasvarūpāntarbhūtatve punarābhāsānāṃ na kutaścit vyavacchedaḥ na kenacit vyāmiśraṇā iti //2//
children.translated_text: Therefore, the supposition should not be entertained that there is a distinction in the being, the essential nature, of the appearance of objects in some conceptual constructions. For those conceptual constructions may be directed toward future objects, or established in the future, or established in the present, or resting in past objects. What is meant is this: in 'I see this blue,' 'I imagine [it],' 'I fancy [it],' 'I remember [it],' 'I make [it],' 'I say [it],' and so forth, that appearance of blue is neither diminished nor increased in its essential nature. Similarly with 'I see' regarding yellow and such. But those appearances — when they are conjoined and disjoined by the Blessed One through His freedom — then this transaction of clarity and such [arises]. When the appearance 'blue' is delimited by another appearance such as 'I fancy,' the transaction of clarity [arises] through admixture with the appearance 'I see.' Thus, the possibility of the variety of transactions across the three times [is established]. But when appearances are included within the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, there is no delimitation from anything, nor admixture with anything. //2//

children.text: nanvetat nīlādiṣu upapadyatāṃ yatra bāhyendriyavyāpāro 'sti sukhādau tu tadabhāvāt kathaṃ vaicitryamityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Let this be possible with regard to blue and such, where the operation of the external senses exists; but in pleasure and such, where that [sense-operation] is absent, how can there be variety? Anticipating this, he says:
With regard to pleasure and such, and even in things that are causes of pleasure and so forth,
though the appearance exists, the situation is the same due to its having passed. //
But when pleasure and such are being vividly delineated by conceptual construction,
the situation would be just the same, due to the clear apprehension of it. //

children.text: sukhe srakcandanādike ca tatkāraṇe , duḥkhe ahikaṇṭakādau ca taddhetau atīte 'nāgate vā yadyapi ābhāsaḥ sa eva tathāpi atītamidam anāgatamidam iti ābhāsāntareṇa yato vyāmiśraṇā anubhavāmīti ābhāsācca yato vyavacchedaḥ tena vidyamāneṣvapi teṣu tasya pramātuḥ tena prakāreṇa sthitirna bhavati yathā pūrvan abhūt aham adhunā sukho duḥkhīti samarjitatattannimitasāmagrīko vā iti //3//
children.translated_text: In the case of pleasure, and in garlands, sandalwood, and such that cause it; and in the case of pain, and in snakes, thorns, and such that cause it — whether past or future — although the appearance is the same [as the present], still, since by mixture with another appearance — 'this is past,' 'this is future' — and since by delimitation from the appearance 'I am experiencing' — even though those [pleasures and pains] exist, the perceiver does not abide in them in that manner as before — [for example:] 'Previously I was not [happy]; now I am happy, or unhappy' — or 'the aggregate of conditions for this or that has been accomplished.' // 3 //

children.text: yadā tu vikalpena tāni vastūni bāḍham ullikhati tadā paunaḥpunyaviśiṣṭasukhataddhetūllekhanābhidhānakāraṇābhāsānupraveśāt ābhāsāntaravyāmiśraṇātmanā tenaiva asmaduktena prakāreṇa na punaranyena ,

children.translated_text: 'in that way' —

children.text: iti , sukhī ahamityādikena sthitiḥ bhavati iti saṃbhāvyam / ucitametat yatastadānīṃ sphuṭatvābhāsamiśraṃ sukhābhāsam upalakṣayati asau / atītagrahaṇaṃ bhāvino 'pi upalakṣaṇam //4//
children.translated_text: thus — abiding occurs through [cognitions such as] 'I am happy' and the like: this is conceivable. This is appropriate, since at that time one perceives the pleasure-appearance mixed with the clarity-appearance. The word 'past' is also illustrative of the future. // 4 //

But when through <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition) one vividly delineates those objects, then — due to the entry of appearances of the cause of the repetition-qualified delineation of pleasure and its cause, and of the verbalization [thereof] — through the very admixture with other appearances, by this very mode that we have described and not by any other —

children.text: nanu iyatā kimuktam bhavati ---- bāhyarūpāḥ sragādayaḥ sukhādihetavo bāhyajanitāśca sukhādayaḥ sukhyahamiti abhimānahetavaḥ iti , tataśca bāhyatvābhāve tajjanyatvābhāve ca na tathā uktaṃ syāt , tatra ca ta eva na kecit , tataśca kathamuktam arthāvabhāsasya sattāyāṃ na kvāpi viśeṣa iti sattāyā eva abhāvāt ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: What has been said by all this? — that garlands and such, of external form, are causes of pleasure and such; and pleasures and such, produced by external [objects], are causes of the conceit 'I am happy.' And therefore, in the absence of externality, and in the absence of being produced by that, what has been stated would not hold. And therein, those [external objects] simply do not exist, and hence there is nothing at all. So how has it been said that there is no special distinction anywhere regarding the existence of the appearance of objects — since existence itself is absent? Anticipating this, he says:
Externality is held to be a mere limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) of the appearances of existent and non-existent things;
it is not their essential nature — the existence of those that are internal is perpetual.

children.text: iha sukhamasti mama , duḥkhaṃ nāsti mameti ye bhāvābhāsā abhāvābhāsāśca teṣāṃ bāhyatvaṃ nāma ātmā svarūpaṃ na bhavati , na hi sukhamityasya svarūpaṃ

children.translated_text: 'as external' —

children.text: iti vapuṣā bhāti , sukhasya hi sukhameva svarūpam kevalaṃ bāhyatvaṃ nāma abhāsāntaram īśvareṇa svātantryabalādeva yadā tatra sukhābhāse miśratayā bhāsyate tadā tat tasya upādhirūpatām uparañcakatāṃ viśeṣaṇatvaṃ gacchati , tataśca yathā nīlābhāsābhāve utpalābhāsasya na kiṃcit vṛttaṃ svarūpato rājābhāsābhāve vā puruṣābhāsasya , tathā bāhyatvābhāsābhāve 'pi sukhābhāsasya duḥkhābhāvābhāsasya kāntābhāsasya ca na svarūpataḥ kācana mlānatā iti āntarāṇāṃ sadaiva sthitiḥ eṣām //5//
children.translated_text: in such a form. For pleasure's own form is simply pleasure. Only externality — another appearance — when the Lord, by the force of His freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) alone, manifests it as mixed with that pleasure-appearance, then it assumes the status of a limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>), a tinting, a qualification of it. And therefore, just as the lotus-appearance [is not affected] in its own nature by the absence of the blue-appearance, or the person-appearance by the absence of the king-appearance — so too the pleasure-appearance, the non-pain-appearance, and the beloved-appearance [are not affected] in their own nature by the absence of the externality-appearance. Thus, the existence of those that are internal is perpetual. // 5 //

Here, 'I have pleasure,' 'I do not have pain' — the appearances of entities and the appearances of non-entities — their externality is not their essential nature, their own form; for the own-form of 'pleasure' does not appear

children.text: iha antaḥkaraṇe buddhidarpaṇātmani nīlādīnāmavabhāsānām āntaratvamapyasti antaḥkaraṇamadhyebhavatvāt , bāhyatvamapi grāhyatārūpaṃ pramātuḥ vicchedenāvabhāsāt , bāhyatvaṃ ca kevalaṃ bāhyapratyakṣatā , atra ca avasthādvaye 'pi arthakriyām amī kurvantyeva antato jñānaṃ svaviṣayam / yat punaḥ pramātṛtādātmyalakṣaṇam āntaratvaṃ tatra amī kathaṃ na kāṃcit arthakriyāṃ vidadhīran ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Here, even for the appearances of blue and such in the internal organ — whose nature is the mirror of the intellect — there is internality, since they exist within the internal organ; and there is also externality in the form of graspability, since they appear as delimited from the perceiver. And externality is merely external perceptibility. In both these states, these [appearances] do produce purposeful activity (<s>arthakriyā</s>) — at least knowledge regarding their own object, minimally. But in the internality that is characterized by identity with the perceiver — how could these not produce some purposeful activity? Anticipating this, he says:
Due to internality, in the unity of the perceiver, there is no purposeful activity of these that is based on difference;
but in externality, that [purposeful activity] arises from the difference of different appearances.
'In the unity of the perceiver' —

children.text: iti , tannimittakaṃ yat ānantaratvaṃ tasmāddhetoḥ , eṣām ābhāsānām arthakriyā na kācit asti , sā hi arthakriyā bhede sati bhavati , sa hi nīlābhāsaḥ pītābhāsāt yato bhidyate yataśca pramāturbhidyate tataḥ svena sādhyāṃ bhinnam arthakriyāṃ tasya pramātuḥ kuryāt , na ca eṣa tadā bhede 'sti pramātraikyāt / sā hi arthakriyābhāsabhedaniyatā , tathā ca kāntābhāsasya bāhyatve 'pi sati ābhāsāntarasya āliṅganalakṣaṇasya vyapagame dūrībhavati , iyam iti ca ābhāsāntarasya upagame 'nyaiva prāktanāhlādaviparītā dṛśyate arthakriyā , ata ābhāsabhedābhāvaḥ yataḥ pramātraikyakṛte āntaratve tasmāt na arthakriyā iti / arthakriyābhāso 'pi ca ābhāsāntarameva iti arthakriyākāritvamapi na bhāvānāṃ sattvam , yena tadabhāve svarūpato 'bhāvaḥ syāt //6//
children.translated_text: thus — from the internality caused by that [unity], for these appearances, there is no purposeful activity whatsoever. For purposeful activity occurs when there is difference. For the blue-appearance, insofar as it differs from the yellow-appearance and insofar as it differs from the perceiver — to that extent it would produce for that perceiver a different purposeful activity that is to be accomplished by its own [nature]. But it does not exist in difference at that time, due to the unity of the perceiver. For purposeful activity is fixed by the difference of appearances. Similarly, even when the beloved-appearance has externality, when another appearance — that of embracing — is absent, it becomes remote; and when another appearance — 'this one' — approaches, an entirely different purposeful activity, opposite to the previous delight, is observed. Therefore, since there is no difference of appearances due to the internality produced by the unity of the perceiver, there is no purposeful activity. And even the appearance of purposeful activity is itself just another appearance — therefore, causal efficacy is not the existence of entities, such that its absence would mean the absence of their own nature. // 6 //

children.text: nanu ca bāhyābhāsavyatibhedanakāle āntarābhāso virodhāt vicchinna iti katham idam uktam

children.translated_text: 'The appearance of those that are internal — that is perpetual' —
thus? He resolves this:
Objection: At the time of the separation by the external appearance, the internal appearance is interrupted due to contradiction — so how has this been said:
Since appearances are of the nature of consciousness, their abiding is always internal;
for those that appear through <s>Māyā</s>, due to externality, it is external as well.

children.text: iha avabhāsānāṃ sadaiva bāhyatābhāsatadabhāvayoḥ api antareva pramātṛprakāśa eva sthitiḥ , yata ete cinmayāḥ , anyathā naiva prakāśeran iti uktaṃ yataḥ / yadā tu māyāśaktyā vicchedāvabhāsanasvātantryarūpayā bāhyatvam eṣām ābhāsyate tadā tat avalambya avabhāsamānānām asau sthitiḥ bahirapi antarapi / nāyam antarābhāso bāhyatvasya virodho pratyuta sarvābhāsabhittibhūto 'sau , tat kathaṃ virodhaḥ iti yuktamuktam

children.translated_text: 'The existence of those that are internal is perpetual' —
thus. // 7 //

Here, the abiding of appearances is always internal alone — in the perceiver's luminosity itself — even when there is or is not the externality-appearance; since they are of the nature of consciousness — for otherwise they would not appear at all, as has been stated. But when, through <s>māyā-śakti</s> (the power of illusion) — whose nature is the freedom of manifesting delimitation — the externality of these is manifested, then for those appearing while relying on that, the abiding is external as well, and internal as well. This internal appearance is not contradictory to externality; rather, it is the ground-surface of all appearances — so how could there be contradiction? Therefore, it was rightly said:

children.text: nanu bāhyatve sati arthakriyā , tacca bāhyendriyagamyatvam , na ca vikalpollikhitānāṃ tat saṃbhavati , tat katham amīṣām arthakriyā syāt , dṛśyate ca vikalpollikhitaḥ piśācādiḥ trāsādividhāyī ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Purposeful activity occurs when there is externality, and that means graspability by the external senses; but that is not possible for things delineated by <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition) — so how could there be purposeful activity for these? And yet a <s>piśāca</s> (demon) and such, delineated by <s>vikalpa</s>, is observed to produce fear and such. Anticipating this, he says:
Even the delineation that occurs in <s>vikalpa</s> is external, appearing as separate;
the identity with the perceiver is internality; difference from that is externality.

children.text: vimarśaviśeṣarūpe vikalpajñāne ya ullikhyamānaḥ kāntācaurādiḥ arthaḥ sopi bāhyaḥ , na kevalaṃ bahiravalokyamānaḥ , yasmāt so 'pi pramātuḥ sakāśāt pṛthageva prathate

children.translated_text: 'This one' —

children.text: iti , yacca pramātari ahamityeva viśrāntatvaṃ tat āntaratvam , antariti nikaṭam , tacca kiṃcit apekṣya , apekṣaṇīyaśca sarvatra pramātaiva apekṣaṇīyāntaraābhāve , tataśca pramātari nikaṭaṃ tādātmya ---- prāptameva iti , tato yat bhinnaṃ tat bāhyameva iti yuktā ullekhasyāpi arthakriyā //8//
children.translated_text: thus. And what is resting in the perceiver as 'I' alone — that is internality; 'internal' means proximate; and that [proximity] is relative to something; and the reference-point everywhere is the perceiver alone, in the absence of another reference-point. And therefore, proximity to the perceiver means having attained identity with it. What is different from that is external. Thus, purposeful activity even of delineation [in vikalpa] is justified. // 8 //

The object — beloved, thief, and such — that is delineated in <s>vikalpa</s>-knowledge, which is of the nature of a specific <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness), is also external — not merely what is observed externally [by the senses] — since it too appears as utterly separate from the perceiver:

children.text: nanu kumbhakārādivyāpāreṇa ghaṭādeḥ astu bāhyatvam , antaḥkaraṇagocarasya tu kiṃ kṛtaṃ tat ityāśaṅkya āha
children.translated_text: Objection: Let the pot and such have externality through the operation of the potter and such; but what produces the externality of what is within the range of the internal organ? Anticipating this, he says:
The illumination of delineation [in vikalpa] and of pleasure and such, with an external nature,
is through the will of the Lord, in the form of direct perception — just as [the illumination] of things produced by the senses and such.

children.text: antarvikalpapratibimbatasya nīlādeḥ yo bahirātmanā pramātṛvicchinnena svabhāvena prakāśaḥ , sa bhartuḥ antarābhāsān bibhrato bahiḥ sṛṣṭiṃ ca puṣṇataḥ īśvarasyaiva icchayā , yathaiva cakṣurādiviṣayabhūtānāṃ pratyakṣajñānaśabdavācyo bāhyātmanā prakāśo nīlādīnām / etaduktaṃ bhavati ---- kumbhakāravyāpāro nāma paramārthataḥ īśvarecchaiva tadabhāsitakāyaspandaparyantā , na punaranyaḥkaścana saḥ , tataśca tathā īśvarecchayā prakāśāt avahirbhūtā api nīlādyā bāhyakaraṇagocarībhūtāḥ kalpitāt pramātuḥ vicchinnarūpatvena bāhyatvena bhāsante , tathā antaḥkaraṇagocarībhūtā api iti ko viśeṣaḥ / sukhaduḥkhaprāyāstu bharatādyuktarūpāḥ sthāyivyabhicārirūpā ritinirvedādayo 'ntaḥkaraṇaikagocarībhūtā bahirātmanā bhānti , saṅkalpeṣu yadyapi kṣetraJñasyaiva svātantryam tathāpi citparamārthatāyā nyagbhāvayitum aśakyatvāt īśvarasyaiva tat vastutaḥ , yathoktaṃ granthakṛtaiva
children.translated_text: For blue and such, which are internally reflections in <s>vikalpa</s>, the illumination with an external nature — a nature delimited from the perceiver — is through the will of the Lord, who sustains the internal appearances and also nourishes external creation. Just as the illumination with an external nature of blue and such that are objects of the senses, which is designated by the word 'direct perception,' is [through the Lord's will]. What is being said is this: the operation of the potter is, in ultimate reality, nothing but the will of the Lord, extending up to the manifested bodily movement — and it is not something else. Therefore, just as blue and such, though not external to luminosity, appear as external through the externality of being within the range of the external senses — appearing with the form of delimitation from the constructed perceiver — so too [those within the range of] the internal organ. What difference is there? And pleasures, pains, and similar [emotions] — which are predominantly of the forms described by <s>Bharata</s> and others as permanent and transitory emotions such as <s>rati</s> (love), <s>nirveda</s> (disgust), and such — even though within the range of the internal organ alone, appear with an external nature. And in mental constructions, although the freedom belongs to the <s>kṣetrajña</s> (field-knower/individual soul), still, since the ultimate reality of consciousness cannot be subordinated, it belongs in truth to the Lord alone. As stated by the author of the treatise himself:
{Although the abiding of objects is restricted in the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul),

children.text: jīve niruddhā tatrāpi paramātmani sā sthitā //
children.translated_text: which is controlled by <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and <s>puryaṣṭaka</s> (subtle body), even there it rests in the Supreme Self.
How could there be control by <s>prāṇa</s> of one whose very nature is that [Supreme Self]? /}

children.text: iti / yatra tu anicchoreva kṣetrajñasya svarasavāhivyākṣepasārā sāṅkalpikī sṛṣṭiḥ tatra sphuṭaḥ īśvarasyaiva vyāpāraḥ / tasmāt sāṅkalpikānāmapi bahirbhāve parameśvarecchiava heturiti siddhāntaḥ //9//
children.translated_text: Thus. And where the imaginative creation of the <s>kṣetrajña</s> — which is not willed [by him], whose essence is involuntary agitation and flowing — occurs, there the operation is clearly that of the Lord alone. Therefore, the established conclusion is that even for imaginatively constructed [objects], the Lord's will alone is the cause of externality. // 9 //

children.text: adhunā pūrvoktam aikyaṃ māheśvaryaṃ ca nigamayati
children.translated_text: Now he concludes the previously stated unity and sovereignty (<s>māheśvarya</s>):
Without that unity, the practical conduct of the world through cognitions would not be possible;
due to the unity of luminosity, that unity [of cognitions] — the perceiver is one — this is established.
He alone, through the specific nature of reflecting, is <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord);

children.text: vimarśa eva devasya śuddhe jñānakriye yataḥ //
children.translated_text: for the reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) is the Lord's pure knowledge and action.
'that' —

children.text: iti , tasmāt hetoḥ , saṃvidāṃ jñānām aikyena vinā , lokapaddhatiḥ lokamārgaḥ sarvo vyavahāro na saṃbhavet , saṃbhavati ca ayam , tasmāt aikyam āsām / na caitat durghaṭam yato viṣayaprakāśa eva saṃvit ucyate , kevalaṃ viṣayoparāgamahmnā bahirmukhatayā nīlaprakāśo 'nyaḥ , pītaprakāśaścānyaḥ , pramārthatastu prakāśasya deśakālākārasaṅkocavaikalyāt ekatvameva , ityeka eva prakāśo'ntarviśrāntaḥ , sa eva ca pramātā ucyate iti sthitam idānīmupapattitaḥ //10//
children.translated_text: therefore, for that reason: without the unity of cognitions — of knowledges — the practical conduct of the world, the path of the world, all practical activity, would not be possible. And it is possible. Therefore, there is unity of these. And this is not difficult to maintain, since cognition is simply called the illumination of the object; only, through the glory of the tinting by the object, in an outward-facing manner, the blue-illumination is different and the yellow-illumination is different; but in ultimate reality, due to the absence of contraction of space, time, and form, luminosity is one alone. Thus, a single luminosity, resting internally — that alone is called the perceiver. This is now established through reasoning. // 10 //
What has been demonstrated by the text previously stated —

children.text: na ca asya asau prakāśalakṣaṇaḥ svātmā nīlādyuparāgaśca parāmarśan śūnya eva āste sphaṭikrama.eriva , api tu sadaiva vimṛśyamānarūpaḥ , iti vimṛśadrūpatvam anavacchinnavimarśatā ananyonmukhatvam ānandaikaghanatvam , tadevāsya māheśvaryam / sa eva hi ahaṃbhāvātmā vimarśo devasya krīḍādimayasya śuddhe pāramārthikyau jñānakriye , prakāśarūpatā jñānaṃ tatraiva svātantryātmā vimarśaḥ kriyā , vimarśaśca antaḥkṛtaprakāśaḥ , iti vimarśa eva parāvasthāyāṃ jñānakriye , parāparāvasthāyāṃ tu bhagavatsadāśivabhuvi idantāsāmānādhikaraṇyāpannāhatāvimarśasvabhāve , aparāvasthāyāṃ ca māyāpade idaṃbhāvaprādhānyena vartamāne iti viśeṣaḥ / sarvathā tu vimarśa eva jñānaṃ tena vinā hi jaḍabhāvo 'sya syāt iti uktam , sa eva ca kriyā iti bhāvinaḥ kriyādhikārasya upakṣepaṃ karoti iti śivam //11// āditaḥ //89//
children.translated_text: And His self, characterized as luminosity, and the tinting by blue and such — He does not sit empty while reflecting on these, like a crystal-gem. Rather, He is of a nature that is perpetually being reflected upon. And this reflecting-nature, this unrestricted reflective awareness, this non-looking-at-another, this being-a-solid-mass-of-bliss — that itself is His sovereignty (<s>māheśvarya</s>). For that very reflective awareness, whose nature is the 'I'-sense, of the Lord — who is of the nature of play — constitutes the pure, ultimate knowledge and action. Luminosity-nature is knowledge; therein itself, reflective awareness whose nature is freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) is action. And reflective awareness has luminosity internalized within it. Thus, in the supreme state, reflective awareness alone is knowledge and action. But in the supreme-non-supreme state — in the level of the Blessed <s>Sadāśiva</s> — where the 'I'-reflective awareness has assumed the co-location with 'this-ness.' And in the non-supreme state — in the level of <s>Māyā</s>, where the 'this-ness' predominates — this is the distinction. But in every case, reflective awareness alone is knowledge; for without it, there would be insentience — as has been stated. And that alone is action — thus he introduces the forthcoming Action Section (<s>Kriyādhikāra</s>). May there be auspiciousness! // 11 // From the beginning, [this covers] 89 [verses]. //

Thus ends the eighth daily lesson, entitled 'Determination of Sovereignty' (<s>Māheśvaryanirūpaṇa</s>), in the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñā</s> composed by the venerable <s>Māheśvara</s> master <s>Utpaladeva</s>, accompanied by the commentary called <s>Vimarśinī</s> composed by the venerable master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 8 //
And the first Knowledge Section (<s>Jñānādhikāra</s>) is complete.
Now, of the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñā</s>,
the section called the Action Section (<s>Kriyādhikāra</s>),
the second section.
<s>Vimarśinī</s>
on the two banks of the perceiver-aspect and the knowable-aspect,
{He who, in the broad and clear mirror of His own Self, displays the radiant stream of His own power

children.text: prakaṭayatu naḥ śrīmāngaurīpatiḥ sa ṛtaṃ param //
children.translated_text: may the glorious Lord of <s>Gaurī</s> reveal to us the supreme truth. //
the supreme river of action, whose ground consists of extremely numerous states of becoming —
{In whom, having found rest, action-power reveals the variegated display of play —
to that <s>Śiva</s> we offer praise. //

children.text: atha kriyāśaktisvarūpaṃ vitasya nirṇetum adhikārāntaram ārabhyate /
children.translated_text: Now, in order to determine the nature of <s>kriyā-śakti</s> (power of action) at length, a new section is commenced.
Therein, in eight verses,
{Therefore... /}
beginning with this,
{Whatever is manifested... /}

children.text: ityantena parameśvare paramārthato'kramā kriyā , parimitasāṃsārikapramātṛkramāvabhāsanayogāt sakramāpi ca , ityupapādyate / tathāhi ślokena uktapūrvapakṣapratikṣepaḥ / tataḥ ślokena sakramatvākramatvavivekaḥ / tataḥ ślokatrayeṇa kramasvarūpanirūpaṇam / tataḥ ślokadvayena sakramatvākramatvayorviṣayavibhāgaḥ , viṣayavibhāge ca sati vastutaḥ ekatraiva tayoḥ viśrāntiḥ , iti ślokena nirūpyate , iti tātparyaṃ āhnikasya /
children.translated_text: ending with this — it is established that in the Supreme Lord, action is ultimately non-sequential, and yet also sequential due to the manifestation of the sequence of the limited worldly perceiver. For thus: by one verse, the refutation of the previously stated opponent's position. Then, by one verse, the discrimination between sequentiality and non-sequentiality. Then, by three verses, the determination of the nature of sequence itself. Then, by two verses, the distribution of the domains of sequentiality and non-sequentiality, and when that distribution is made, both [sequentiality and non-sequentiality] in reality rest in one and the same [Lord] — this is determined by one verse. Such is the purport of the daily lesson.

children.text: atha ślokārtho vibhajyate / tatra pūrvokte jñānaśaktisamarthanopayoganimeye siddhe prameyāntaramapi ayatnataḥ siddham , iti adhikaraṇasiddhāntadiśā darśayati
children.translated_text: Now the meaning of the verses is analyzed. Therein, when the previously stated matter — established for the purpose of supporting the power of knowledge — is established, another matter to be proven is also effortlessly established. He shows this in the manner of a supplementary conclusion (<s>adhikaraṇasiddhānta</s>):

children.text: ata eva yadapyuktaṃ kriyā naikasya sakramā /
children.translated_text: Therefore, what was also stated — 'sequential action is impossible for one [entity]' —
and so forth — that has been refuted, through the establishment of that one [entity's nature].

children.text: jñānānyeva anubhavavikalparūpādibhinnāni na teṣām āśrayo 'sti kaścit , saṃskārācca smṛtiḥ siddhā jñānaṃ ca jaḍaṃ cet na arthasya prakāśaḥ , ajaḍaṃ cet deśakālasaṃkocavaikalyāt ātmatattvāt abhinnam
children.translated_text: that cognitions alone, differentiated as experience, <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition), and such, exist; that there is no substratum for them; that memory is established from latent impressions; and that if knowledge is insentient, there is no illumination of the object, while if non-insentient, it is non-different from the self-principle due to the absence of contraction of place and time —

children.text: iti , tat tāvat pratikṣiptaṃ bhinnānāmanubhavādīnāmanupapatteḥ vitatya darśitatvāt /
children.translated_text: that has been refuted, since the impossibility of differentiated experiences and such [without a substratum] has been shown at length.
'And memory does not arise from mere latent impressions alone' —

children.text: ityetadapyuktam , ajaḍameva ca asaṃkucitarūpaṃ jñānam , tatsvātantryāvabhāsitajñeyoparāgavaśāt tu tasya saṃkocāvabhāsa ityapi darśitaṃ yataḥ , na kevalam ato hetukalāpāt jñānaśakticodyāni nidāritāni , yāvat kriyāśaktiviṣayāṇyapi dūṣaṇāni ata eva hetukalāpāt apasāritāni iti apiśabdaḥ /
children.translated_text: this too has been stated; and that knowledge is indeed non-insentient and of non-contracted form, but that the appearance of its contraction is due to the tinting by the knowable manifested through its own freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) — this too has been shown. Therefore, not only have the objections pertaining to <s>jñāna-śakti</s> (power of knowledge) been dispelled by this aggregate of reasons, but the criticisms pertaining to <s>kriyā-śakti</s> (power of action) too have been removed by this very aggregate of reasons — this is the meaning of the word 'api.'

children.text: ekā kriyā kramikā katham āśrayasya ekasvabhāvatve sati ghaṭate ?
children.translated_text: How can a single sequential action be possible when the substratum has a single nature?
This is reasonable. Likewise,
What was first stated —
{When that which abides in each... /}
thus, and
{Because of the many-formed nature of what abides in two... /}

children.text:
iti ca yaduktaṃ tadapi pratikṣiptameva , yataḥ iyati pūrvapakṣe iyadeva jīvitamekamanekasvabhāvaṃ kathaṃ syāt iti /
atra ca uktaṃ citsvabhāvasya darpaṇasyeva ekatānapabādhanena ābhāsabhedasaṃbhave ka iva dhirodha iti , tasmāt pratyabhijñānabalāt eko 'pi asau padārthātmā svabhāvabhedān viruddhān yāvat aṅgīkurute tāvat te virodhādeva kramarūpatayā nirbhāsamānāḥ tamekaṃ kriyāśrayaṃ saṃpādayanti iti , tataśca saṃbandhādīnāmapi upapattiriti //1//
children.translated_text:
— what was thus stated has also been refuted. For the entire life of this opponent's position is just this: how can one thing have many natures?
And to this it has been said: when consciousness, like a mirror, without sublation of its unity, allows the possibility of difference of appearances — what possible hindrance could there be? Therefore, by the force of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), even though this entity-self is one, insofar as it accepts contradictory differences of nature, those very [differences], precisely because of their contradiction, shining as sequential in nature, establish that one [entity] as the substratum of action. And from that, the possibility of connection and the rest also follows. // 1 //

children.text: nanu ca kramikatvameva kriyāyāḥ svarūpam , kramaśca kālakalanāhīne cinmaye bhagavati nāsti , iti katham asya sā bhavedityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: But sequentiality is the very nature of action, and sequence does not exist in the Blessed Lord who is of the nature of consciousness and free from the artifice of time — so how could action belong to Him? Anticipating this, he says:
The sequentiality of mundane action is possible due to <s>kāla-śakti</s> (the power of time);

children.text: ghaṭate na tu śāśvatyāḥ prābhavyāḥ syātprabhor iva //
children.translated_text: but for the eternal [action] that belongs to the Lord, which is [His] sovereign power, it would not be [sequential] — just as [sequence does not apply to] the Lord [Himself].

children.text: utkṣipati apakṣipati hastam iti ye pūrvottare kṣaṇāḥ te kramavantaḥ , tatra yeṣāṃ ta eva kriyā kāṇādādīnāmiva teṣāṃ sā sakramā pratyakṣeṇaiva bhāti / ye tu manyante tathābhūtapratyakṣaparidṛśyamānarūpabhedasaṃpādikā yā asau kācit atīntriyā hastagatā śaktirvyāpārodbodharūpā nityānumeyā tasyāḥ kevalaṃ pūrvāparībhūtatvam anumīyate , iti laukikyāḥ kriyāyāḥ sakramatvaṃ kālaśakteḥ ābhāsavicchedanapradarśanasāmārthyarūpāt pārameśvarāt śaktiviśeṣāt ghaṭate upapadyate , yā tu prabhoḥ saṃbandhinī tadavyatiriktā kriyāśaktiḥ śāśvatī kālena aspṛṣṭā tasyāḥ sakramatvam asti iti saṃbhāvanā'pi nāsti , yathā prabhoḥ sakramatvamasaṃbhāvyaṃ tathā asyā api / uktaṃ hi ----
children.translated_text: 'He raises, he lowers the hand' — the prior and subsequent moments are sequential. Therein, for those for whom these very [moments] are action, like the followers of <s>Kaṇāda</s> and such, that [action] appears as sequential through direct perception itself. But for those who think that a certain extra-sensory power residing in the hand — of the nature of the awakening of function — which produces the difference of forms seen through such direct perception, and which is always inferable — for them, only the prior-and-posterior-ness of that [power] is inferred. Thus, the sequentiality of mundane action is possible — i.e., is tenable — due to <s>kāla-śakti</s> (the power of time), a specific power of the Supreme Lord whose nature is the capacity to display the differentiation of appearances. But the <s>kriyā-śakti</s> that belongs to the Lord, that is non-different from Him, that is eternal, untouched by time — there is not even the possibility that it could be sequential, just as sequentiality is inconceivable for the Lord Himself. For it has been said:
{If the hand has sequentiality, the action residing in it would also be thus} —
thus. // 2 //

children.text: nanu kālo viśeṣa bhāvam upagacchan bhāvaṃ svena rūpeṇa avacchinatti tatra ko'sau kālo nāma ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Time, when it assumes a particular modification, delimits an entity by its own form — what then is this thing called time? Anticipating this, he says:
Time is the movement of the sun and such, or the birth of such-and-such flowers and the like,

children.text: śītoṣṇe vātha tallakṣyaḥ krama eva sa tattvataḥ //
children.translated_text: or heat and cold — it is to be defined by those. In reality, it is nothing but sequence.

children.text: ye iyattayā pariniṣṭhitā ābhāsāḥ siddhāḥ , tadyathā candrasūryādīnāṃ sahakāramallikākuṭajādīnāṃ śītoṣṇādeḥ parabhṛtamadavilāsādeḥ ta eva

children.translated_text: 'time' —

children.text: yato'pariniṣṭhitaṃ gamanapaṭhanādi tairiyattayā pariniṣṭhīyate parivartakairiva kanakam / sa eva ca sūryādīnāṃ svabhāvaviśeṣastattvataḥ paramāśrataḥ kramo nānyaḥ kaścit kramo nāma , krama eva ca kālo nānyo'sau kaścit , iti evakāro bhinnābhinnakramo yojyaḥ , yaugapadyamapi dvayorābhāsayoḥ aparābhāsāpekṣayā krama eva , cirakṣiprādidhīrapi vitatānyatvavaśāt ābhāsabhede krama eva , paratvāparatvabuddhirapi sphuṭatvādinā tatraiva , iti tena tena pratimānavartakatulyena sūryasaṃcārādinā saha mīyamāno hemasthānīyo devadattābhāsasya vaicitryabheda ittham ucyate
children.translated_text: because that which is without definite measure — walking, reading, and such — is measured by those, as gold is [measured] by standards. And that very specific nature of the sun and such, in its ultimate dependence, is sequence and nothing else — there is no other entity called sequence. And sequence alone is time — there is no other entity that [time] is. The word 'eva' should be applied to both [krama and kāla], separately and jointly. Even simultaneity — as the [relation of] two appearances in reference to another appearance — is itself sequence. Even the cognition of fast and slow, due to extended and non-extended appearance-difference, is itself sequence. Even the cognition of remote and proximate, through clarity and such, rests in that alone. Thus, measured against the movement of the sun and such — which serves as a standard like a standard-weight — the variety-difference in the appearance of <s>Devadatta</s>, like gold, is expressed thus:
'A day passes' —
thus. // 3 //

Those appearances that are established with a definite measure — such as the [movements of] the moon, sun, and such; the [blooming of] mango, jasmine, <s>kuṭaja</s> (Wrightia), and such; heat and cold; the amorous play of cuckoos and such — they themselves are

children.text: nanu evaṃ kālo nāma bhāvasvabhāva eva astu , kā asau kālaśaktiḥ ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Let time be the very nature of entities; what then is <s>kāla-śakti</s> (the power of time)? Anticipating this, he says:
Sequence depends on difference, and difference arises from the being and non-being of appearances;
but the being and non-being of appearances is produced by the Lord's variegated manifestation.

children.text: iha svabhāvabhedamātraṃ yadi kramātmā kālaḥ , tadāṅgulīcatuṣṭayaṃ bhonnasvabhāvam iti bhinnakālaṃ bhavet , tasmāt aruṇābhāsasya sadbhāvaḥ sphuṭaprabhāpuñjasya ca asadbhāvaḥ ityevaṃbhūto yo bheda ābhāsasadbhāvāsadbhāvābhyanuprāṇitaḥ tatkṛtaḥ kramaḥ kālātmā , tau ca ābhāsānāṃ bhāvābhāvau na bāhyahetukṛtau iti vistārya upapāditam , iti ya eva saṃvitsvabhāva ātmā svaprasaṃkalpādau ābhāsavacitryanirmāṇe prabhuḥ prabhaviṣṇuḥ iti svasaṃviditastata eva tau bhavataḥ , sa hi ātmani nīlādīn ābhāsān ābhāsayan citratayā aparimeyayā bhāsayati , tathāhi ---- lohitābhāsaṃ ghaṭābhāsam unnatābhāsaṃ dṛḍhābhāsaṃ ca sāmānādhikaraṇyena ghaṭābhāsaṃ paṭābhāsaṃ ca pṛthaktvāvabhāsena anyonyatra ābhāsābhāvena , svātmani tu ekarasenābhāsena , iyati ca na kramasya udayaḥ , yadā tu śaradābhāsaṃ hemantābhāsena ca sarvathaiva śūnyamābhāsayati hemantābhāsaṃ ca śāradābhāsena tadā kālātmā krama uttiṣṭhati , iti seyam itthaṃbhūtā bhāvavaicitryaprathanaśaktiḥ bhagavataḥ

children.translated_text: 'kāla-śakti' (the power of time) —
thus. // 4 //

Here, if time as the nature of sequence is mere difference of nature, then four fingers, being of different nature, would be of different times. Therefore, the difference that is animated by the being and non-being — the existence and non-existence — of appearances; and the sequence constituted by that difference, which has time as its essence — and those being and non-being of appearances are not caused by external factors, as has been established at length — therefore, the Self whose nature is consciousness, who is capable — i.e., sovereign — in the creation of variety of appearances in His own volition and such, who is self-known — from Him alone do these two [being and non-being] arise. For He, manifesting in Himself appearances of blue and such, manifests them with immeasurable variety: the red appearance, the pot-appearance, the tall appearance, the firm appearance — as co-located with the pot-appearance; and the pot-appearance and cloth-appearance — with the manifestation of separateness, with the absence of appearance in each other; but in His own Self, with the manifestation of a single essence. And in all this, sequence does not arise. But when He manifests the autumn-appearance as completely devoid of the winter-appearance, and the winter-appearance as devoid of the autumn-appearance — then the sequence whose nature is time arises. Thus, this power of the Lord — of such a nature — the capacity to manifest the variety of entities — is called
He clarifies the very fact that [sequence] is produced by variegated manifestation:
From the variety of forms, He manifests spatial sequence;
from the manifestation of the variety of activities, the Lord [manifests] temporal sequence also.

children.text: padārthasya svaṃ rūpaṃ mūrtiḥ , tasyāḥ yat vaicitryaṃ vibhedaḥ , tadyathā gṛhamiti anyat svarūpam , prāṅgaṇamiti anyat , vipaṇiriti anyat , devakulamiti aparam , udyānamiti anyat , araṇyamiti tadanyatarat , tasmāt vaicitryāt ābhāsyamānāt deśarūpo dūrādūravitatatvāvitatatvādiḥ kramo bhagavatā avabhāsyate / yadā tu gāḍhapratyabhijñāprakāśabalāt tadeva idaṃ hastasvarūpam iti pratipattau mūrterna bhedaḥ , atha ca anyānyarūpatvaṃ bhāti tadaikasmin svarūpe yadanyat anyat rūpaṃ tadvirodhavaśāt asahabhavatkriyā ucyate , tasyā yat vaicitryaṃ parimitāparimitātmakaṃ tadekānusandhānena phalasiddhyādinibandhanavaśāt yathāruci carcitena nirbhāsayan kālarūpaṃ kramamevāvabhāsayati / na caitat vācyam ---- ekasvarūpasya katham anyat anyadrūpamiti ? yato na asau kaścit bhāvo ya evaṃ kalpyate ; saṃvideva hi tathā bhāti , tathā bhānameva ca tasyā aiśvaryam , na hi bhāsane virodhaḥ kaścit prabhavati , sa hi sukhaduḥkhāderbhāsanakṛta eva , tathā bhāsanābhāva eva hi virodhatattvam , etat apiśabdena īśvaraśabdena ca darśitam //5//
children.translated_text: The 'form' (<s>mūrti</s>) of an entity is its own nature; its 'variety' is differentiation — such as: a house is one nature, a courtyard another, a market another, a temple yet another, a garden another, a forest yet another — from that variety being manifested, spatial sequence, consisting of far and near, extended and non-extended, and such, is manifested by the Blessed Lord. But when, due to the force of the light of firm recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), in the cognition 'this is the very same hand-nature,' there is no difference of form, and yet difference of other-and-other-ness appears — the otherness of form in one single nature, by force of its contradiction, is called action that cannot co-exist [in a single moment]; and its variety, consisting of limited and unlimited, by unified recognition, based on considerations such as the accomplishment of purpose, manifested as one pleases — [the Lord] manifests temporal sequence alone. And this should not be objected: 'how can one single nature have other-and-other forms?' — for there is no entity whatsoever that is thus conceived [as unchanging]. It is consciousness alone that appears thus, and appearing thus is itself its sovereignty. For no contradiction has power over manifestation — for [contradiction] is produced precisely by the manifestation of pleasure, pain, and such; and the very non-manifestation [of contradictories together] is indeed the essence of contradiction. This is shown by the words 'api' and 'Īśvara' (Lord). // 5 //

children.text: nanu evam ābhāsaviṣayābhyāmeva deśakālakramābhyāṃ bhavitavyam , anābhāsaśca pramātā , sa hi na kasyacit ābhāsate , tasya sarvam ābhāti yataḥ , tataśca tau pramātari katham , dṛśyete ca

children.translated_text: 'I was, I am, I shall be' —
thus, and
'I stand at home, in the forest, at the temple' —

children.text: iti ca , kiṃ ca svayaṃ deśakālakramaśūnyasya kiṃ dūraṃ kim antikaṃ kiṃ vartamānaṃ kim atītaṃ kiṃ bhāvi , iti pramātrāśrayo bhāveṣvapi kramo na yuktaḥ , na ca pramātṛnirapekṣeṣvapi teṣu svātmani dūratvādi bhūtatvādi vā , tadetat samarthayitum āha
children.translated_text: thus. Moreover, for one who is himself devoid of spatial and temporal sequence — what is far? what is near? what is present? what is past? what is future? — thus, sequence in entities is also not tenable if dependent on the perceiver; nor do those entities, even independently of the perceiver, have far-ness and such, or past-ness and such, in their own selves. To establish this, he says:

Objection: Thus, spatial and temporal sequence must belong only to appearances, while the perceiver does not appear [to others]; for He does not appear to anyone, since everything appears to Him. And therefore, how can those two [types of sequence] apply to the perceiver? Yet they are observed:
Everywhere, the difference of appearances may be the source of temporal sequence;
[but only] for the perceiver of the void and such, whose manifestation is intermittent, not for [the perceiver who shines] at once.
Spatial sequence also appears in entities for the perceiver of limited self;

children.text: svātmeva svātmanā pūrṇā bhāvā bhāntyamitasya tu //
children.translated_text: but for the unlimited [Lord], entities shine as the Self itself, complete in themselves.

children.text: sarveṣu vastuṣu ekānekarūpeṣu yaḥ kālātmā kramaḥ tasya ya ākaraḥ ---- utpattinibandhanam iti vyākhyātaḥ , ābhāsasya bhāvābhāvakṛto bhedaḥ sa śūnyaprāṇabuddhidehādeḥ bhavati , iti saṃbhāvyati , yataḥ sa śūnyādiḥ vicchinnabhāḥ , na hi tasya bhāsanaṃ svarūpaṃ nīlādivat jaḍatvāt , api tu saṃvitsphuraṇamasya bhāsanam , tat yadā asya nāsti , yathā supto dehasya saṃsārayātrāpatitatve śūnyasya prāṇādeḥ , tadā asya bhāsanaṃ vicchidyate , iti ābhāsasadbhāvāsadbhāvakṛtaḥ kālakramo 'sti ,

children.translated_text: 'I in the past had the appearance of a child's body; I am [now] having the appearance of a youth's body' —

children.text: iti / sa ca yataḥ pramātā ahaṃbhāvasamāveśanāt aparipūrṇāt ata eva udriktakālakramavattvāt bhāveṣvapi kālakramam ābhāsayati ,
children.translated_text: thus. And because such a perceiver, due to the imperfect absorption in 'I'-awareness, and hence because of the predominance of temporal sequence, manifests temporal sequence even in entities —
'I who was a child — the banyan-tree appearance that co-existed [with me] also existed then' —
thus; but he who
'has shone at once,' —

children.text: iti anayā vācoyuktyā avicchinnabhāsanaḥ pramātā saṃvidrūpaḥ , tasya svātmani kālakramaḥ , nāpi tadapekṣayā vedye bhāvajāte , taddhi tatra abhedena bhāti iti /
children.translated_text: i.e., the perceiver whose nature is consciousness and whose manifestation is uninterrupted — as indicated by this expression — for him there is no temporal sequence in his own self, nor in the mass of knowable entities relative to him, for they shine in him as non-different.

In all things, whether of single or manifold nature, the temporal sequence — its 'source,' explained as the basis of origination — is the difference produced by the being and non-being of appearance. This is conceivable for the void, vital breath, intellect, body, and such, because that void and such has intermittent manifestation; for its shining is not its own nature, like blue and such, since it is insentient; rather, its shining is the flashing of consciousness. When that [flashing] does not exist for it — as when the body that has fallen into the course of worldly existence is asleep, and the void, vital breath, and such [appear not] — then its manifestation is interrupted. Thus, temporal sequence, produced by the being and non-being of appearance, exists [for such a limited perceiver] —

children.text: evaṃ deśakramo'pi mitātmanaḥ paricchinnasvarūpasya śūnyādeḥ dehāntasya svātmani bhāti

children.translated_text: 'I stand here' —
thus; and relative to himself, in entities also —

children.text: yat mama saṃyogapārimityena vartate tadantikam itarat dūram
children.translated_text: 'That which exists for me through the limit of conjunction is near; the other is far' —

children.text: iti / amitasya svarūpeyattāśūnyasya tu saṃvittattvasya bhāvāḥ svātmanā ahaṃbhāvena yato bhānti tataḥ pūrṇāḥ ---- aparicchinnasvarūpeyattākāḥ , yataḥ svātmā tasya tathābhūta eva iti samuccayopamā , taduktam ----
children.translated_text: thus. But for the consciousness-principle, which is immeasurable, devoid of delimited self-extent, since entities shine by its own self, through 'I'-awareness, they are therefore complete — of the form of unlimited self-extent. Since its own self is of precisely such a nature, this is a cumulative simile. As stated:
Similarly, spatial sequence also appears in one's own self for the limited one — the void and such, up to the body — whose nature is delimited:

children.text: {apūrvāparaṃ hi idaṃ mūrtitaḥ kriyātaśca sarvaṃ sarvataḥ pūrṇam}
children.translated_text: {For this [universe] is without prior or posterior, in form and in action, full in every way from all directions.}

children.text: iti / kriyāprasaṅgāt iha kālakramaḥ prākarṇiko dṛṣṭāntatvena tatprasaṅgāt deśakramo nirūpitaḥ , dṛṣṭāntaśca pūrvaṃ vācya iti vaicitryanirūpaṇāvasare deśakramasya ādau abhidhānaṃ nyāyyam , upasaṃhāre tu prākaraṇikasya kālakramasyaiva ādau nirdeśaḥ , paścāttu prāsaṅgikasya deśakramasya iti //6 ; 7//
children.translated_text: Thus. Since the discussion pertains to action, the temporal sequence is the primary topic; [but] since the illustration relates to spatial sequence, spatial sequence has been examined. Since the illustration should be stated first, it is proper to describe the spatial sequence first at the occasion of examining variety; but in the conclusion, the temporal sequence — which is the primary topic — is stated first, and afterwards the spatial sequence, which is incidental. //6; 7//

children.text: nanu evaṃ satyapramātari bhagavati nāstyeva kriyā iti āyātaṃ kālakramābhāvāt kramāśrayeṇa ca tasyā avasthānāt ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If so, then in the Blessed One who is the true knowing subject, there is simply no action — this has been arrived at, since there is no temporal sequence, and since action subsists depending on sequence. Anticipating this, he says:

children.text: kintu nirmāṇaśaktiḥ sāpy evaṃ viduṣa īśituḥ /
children.translated_text: But even the power of creation — thus, of the knowledgeable sovereign,
is that by which the difference of unknowing and known is manifested. //

children.text: iha tattvataḥ parameśvarasya apratihatasvātantryarūpāvicchinnasvātmaparāmarśamayī ananyonmukhatārūpā icchaiva kriyā iti upasaṃhariṣyate adhikārāntare

children.translated_text: 'Thus, will itself is causality, agenthood, and action.' —

children.text: iti / caitramaitrāderapi pacāmi iti yaiva antaricchā saiva kriyā , tathā ca adhiśrayaṇādibahutaraspandanasaṃbandhe 'pi pacāmi iti nāsya vicchidyate , yattu pacāmi iti icchārūpaṃ tadeva tathāspandanātmatayā bhāti , tatra tu na ko'pi kramaḥ tattvataḥ / evam īśvarasyāpi
children.translated_text: thus. Even for <s>Caitra</s>, <s>Maitra</s>, and others, the very inner will 'I cook' is itself action. And thus, even when connected with the many movements of placing-on-fire and such, the [awareness] 'I cook' is not interrupted. But what is of the form of will 'I cook' — that very thing appears as being of the nature of those movements. There, however, there is no sequence in ultimate reality. Similarly, for the Lord too —
'I rule, I shine, I scintillate, I whirl, I reflectively grasp' —
whatever reflective awareness of this form is of the nature of will,

children.text: ityetāvanmātratattvaṃ na tatra kaścit kramaḥ , etadeva ca ucyate
children.translated_text: the ultimate reality of just this much — there is no sequence in that. And this itself is expressed by the statement
'let the sequence of the variety of knowing subjects and known objects flash forth' —

children.text: ityamunā vākyena , tadatrāpi na kaścit kramaḥ , yathā tu icchārūpaṃ
children.translated_text: by this sentence. Therefore, even there, there is no sequence. But just as the will of the form
'I cook' —

children.text: iti spandanātmatāṃ kāyāparyantāṃ gataṃ kramārūpitam ābhāti tadā bhagavadicchā pramātṛprameyabhedaparyavasitā tatkramopaśliṣṭā bhāti darpaṇatalamiva vitataprabahannadīprabāhakramasamāśliṣṭam , atra ca kevalaṃ darpaṇasya tathā icchā nāsti , parameśvarasya tu sā asti ---- iti ubhayathā asya kriyāśaktiḥ
children.translated_text: having assumed the nature of movements extending to the body, appears as invested with sequence — so too, the will of the Blessed One, having culminated in the difference of knowing subjects and known objects, appears as embraced by the sequence of those [manifestations] — like a mirror-surface embraced by the sequence of the stream of a great flowing river. But here, the mirror has no such will; the Supreme Lord, however, does have it — thus His power of action is twofold:
'the capacity to create action in the form of sequence, and the connection with the coloring of action in the form of sequence' —

children.text: iti / evaṃ deśakrame'pi vācyam , tatra tu asya cicchaktiḥ ucyate anyaiḥ , iha tu kriyāśaktireva sā svīkṛtā iti piṇḍārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: thus. The same should be said regarding spatial sequence as well; but there, others call it His power of consciousness (<s>cit-śakti</s>), whereas here, that very thing is accepted as the power of action (<s>kriyā-śakti</s>) — this is the summary meaning.

Here, it will be concluded in the other section [on Action] that, in ultimate truth, the will (<s>icchā</s>) of the Supreme Lord — consisting of uninterrupted self-reflective awareness that has the form of unobstructed freedom, whose nature is not looking toward another — is itself action:

children.text: akṣarārthastu ---- tathā iti svarūpabhedena deśakramakāriṇā kriyābhedena ca kālakramasaṃpādakena upalakṣito yo vijñātuḥ śūnyādeḥ pramātuḥ bhedo'nyonyaṃ jñeyācca , evaṃ ghaṭādeḥ parasparaṃ jñātuśca sa bhagavatā avabhāsyate , yat tadavabhāsanaṃ sā īśiturapi nirmāṇaśaktiḥ kriyāśaktiḥ na tu kevalaṃ śūnyādereva kriyā , yataśca tannirmitaṃ jñātṛjñeyakriyāvaicitryabhedam asau vidvān vetti aviratam tatraiva hi tat sphurati tato'pi tasya sā kriyāśaktiḥ / ato bhāsanavicchedanābhāvāt kramābhāve sthūladṛṣṭyā yadyapi asya bhavet kriyānupapattiśaṅkā , kiṃ tu evamasya kriyāśaktirūpapannā ---- iti saṃgatiḥ / iti śivam //8// āditaḥ 97//
children.translated_text: The literal meaning, however, is: 'tathā' (thus) — the difference that is characterized by the form-difference that produces spatial sequence and the action-difference that accomplishes temporal sequence — the mutual difference of perceivers such as the void-self and such from each other and from the knowable, and similarly the mutual [difference] of knowable [objects] such as pots and such from each other and from the knower — that is manifested by the Blessed One. The manifestation of that is the power of creation, the power of action, of the sovereign — and action does not belong to the void-self and such alone. And since He, the knower, knows the variety of the difference of knower, known, and action that He has created — for it scintillates in Him alone — therefore too His power of action [is established]. Therefore, even though from a gross perspective one might entertain the doubt that action is impossible for Him due to the absence of interruption in manifestation and hence the absence of sequence, the connection is: but His power of action is established in this way. // Thus, auspiciousness! //8// From the beginning, 97 [verses]. //

Thus ends the first chapter named 'The Determination of the Power of Action' in the Section on Action, in the <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñā</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Utpaladeva</s>, accompanied by the commentary called <s>Vimarśinī</s> composed by the illustrious master <s>Abhinavagupta</s>. // 1 //
The second chapter of the Section on Action.
{Demonstrating contradiction and non-contradiction by His own will alone,

children.text: bhedābhedau ca yo mantratattvavittaṃ stumaḥ śivam //
children.translated_text: as well as difference and non-difference — we praise <s>Śiva</s>, the knower of the <s>mantra</s>-reality. //
'due to the unobstructed capacity of the Blessed One, the power of creation' —
that very thing, in order to sustain through justifying the categories of action, relation, universal, and such, whose connection is impossible in the view of the proponent of external objects —
What was stated —
{'Action, relation, universal...' /}
beginning with this, up to
{'...therefore, such error does not exist. /'}

children.text: ityantaṃ ślokasaptakena āhnikaṃ prastūyate / tatra prathamaślokena sūtrakalpena ekānekarūpasya kriyādeḥ bāhyavāde viruddhadharmādhyāsadūṣaṇena anupapadyamānasyāpyavaśyasamarthanīyaṃ vapuḥ iti darśayate / dvitīyena tatra upapattiḥ sūcyate / tṛtīyena nirvikalpakasaṃvedanasaṃvedyatve 'pi vikalpakāle eva sphuṭameṣāṃ rūpam ityucyate / caturthapañcamābhyām ekānekasvarūpatāyā vi.ayavibhāgaḥ cintyate / ṣaṣṭhena prahaṇakasūtrasūcitasaṃbandhasvīkṛtānāṃ kriyākārakabhāvādīnāṃ svarūpam ucyate / saptamena arthakriyopayoga iti saṃkṣepaḥ /
children.translated_text: — the chapter is introduced through seven verses. Therein, by the first verse, which is like a <s>sūtra</s>, it is shown that action and such, which have a one-and-many form, though impossible [to account for] in the view of external objects due to the fault of superimposition of contradictory properties, nevertheless have a form that must necessarily be justified. By the second, the justification therein is indicated. By the third, it is said that even though perceivable in non-conceptual awareness, the clear form of these [categories] exists only at the time of conceptual construction. By the fourth and fifth, the domain-division of the one-and-many nature is considered. By the sixth, the essential nature of action, agent-patient relations, and such — indicated by the refuting <s>sūtra</s> — and of the accepted relations is stated. By the seventh, the utility for purposeful activity — this is the summary.

children.text: nanvevaṃ tathā nirmāṇaśaktyā avabhāsanārūpayā yat nirmīyate tasyāvabhāsanaiva nirmāṇam , nānyat , sā ca dvicandrāderapi asti , nīlāderapi , nīlādiniṣṭhasya karmasāmānyasaṃbandhāderapi , tataśca asatyaṃ satyaṃ saṃvṛtisatyamiti ya evaṃprāyeṣu vyavahāraḥ sa kathaṃ saṃgaccheta nirmeyatvāviśeṣāt ityāśaṃkya

children.translated_text: 'the non-reality of action and such is thus established' —

children.text: iti vadan dvicandrādīnāṃ tu itthamapi asatyatvam iti sūcayan āha ----
children.translated_text: saying this, while indicating that the unreality of two moons and such is [of a different kind] even in this way, he says:

Objection: If what is created by the power of creation — which is of the nature of manifestation — is nothing but manifestation itself, and that [manifestation] exists for two moons and such as well, and for blue and such, and for the action-universal-relation and such that rest in blue and such — then how could the transaction of 'unreal,' 'real,' 'conventionally real' and the like be coherent, given that there is no difference in being-created? Anticipating this,
Action, relation, universal, substance, direction, time, and cognitions —
these are considered real, through [possessing] stability and utility, and as having both one and many substrata. //
'<s>Caitra</s> cooks,'
'the rice grains soften,'
'the fuel burns' —

children.text: iti , tasyā ekānekarūpaścaitrādyartha āśrayaḥ ālambanam / tathāhi ---- tattaddeśakālākārabhinnaḥ tatra caitradeho'nekasvabhāvo'pi
children.translated_text: thus — its substratum, the object such as <s>Caitra</s> and others, is of one-and-many form. For the body of <s>Caitra</s> there, though differentiated by various places, times, and forms and hence of many natures,
'that very one is this' —

children.text: iti ekarūpatām aparityajanneva nirbhāsate , sa eva ca ekānekarūpā kriyā tathaiva pratibhāsanācca pāramārthikī , dvicandrādi tu tathābhāsamānamapi uttarakālaṃ pramāvyāpārānuvṛttirūpasya sthairyasya unmūlanena
children.translated_text: thus, shines without abandoning its one-form. That very thing is action of one-and-many form; and since it appears precisely thus, it is ultimately real. But the two moons and such, even though appearing thus, [are unreal because] at a subsequent time, through the uprooting of stability that has the form of the continuation of the operation of valid means of knowledge,
'the two moons do not exist' —
in this form, it is unreal. But here,
'<s>Caitra</s> moves' —

children.text: ityevaṃbhūto vimarśaḥ anuvartamāno na kenacit unmūlyamānaḥ saṃvedyate , dvicandrādi ca yadyapi hlādodvegayoḥ upayujyate , tathāpi dvicandrābhimānī na tāvatīṃ tatra arthakriyām abhimanyate , api tu yādṛśī ekena śaśinā kartavyā timirāpasāraṇādirūpā , tādṛśyeva apareṇa , iti na taddviguṇām arthakriyāṃ tatra adhyavasyati , tasyāṃ ca asau na upayujyate , brajyāyāṃ tu yāmeva grāmaprāptim adhyavasyati tasyām avikalāyām upayogo 'syā iti sthairyāt upayogācca ekānekarūpakriyātattvālambanabuddhiḥ satyaiva , evaṃ saṃbandhādiṣu kālaparyanteṣu vācyam uttarakārikāsu sphuṭīkariṣyati //1//
children.translated_text: the reflective awareness of this form is experienced as continuing, not being uprooted by anything. And although the two moons and such are useful for pleasure and dismay, still, the one who believes in two moons does not claim that much purposeful activity there — rather, whatever purposeful activity such as dispelling darkness and such is to be accomplished by one moon, exactly the same by the other — thus he does not determine doubled purposeful activity there, and for that [doubled activity] the [second moon] is not useful. But in walking, the very arrival at the village that one determines — in that being unimpaired, this [walking-cognition] is useful. Therefore, through stability and utility, the cognition that rests on the reality of action and such of one-and-many form is indeed real. The same should be said regarding relation and the rest up to time — this will be clarified in the subsequent verses. //1//
Apart from the consciousness-principle, the cognition of action in agents, patients, instruments, and such —

children.text: nanvekatvam anekatvaṃ ca parasparaṃ viruddhe , katham ekatra vastuni syātām , tataścāyaṃ bādhakapramāṇakṛtaḥ sthairyonmūlanaprakāra ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Unity and multiplicity are mutually contradictory — how can they exist in a single thing? And thus this mode of uprooting stability is created by a sublating means of valid knowledge. Anticipating this, he says:
Therein, the one is the inner reality; that very thing, attaining perceptibility by the senses,
becomes many, by reason of [differences of] space, time, and nature. //

children.text: iha tāvat caitre calati dṛṣṭe na jātucit

children.translated_text: 'he does not move' —

children.text: iti buddhiḥ jāyate ---- na rajatam itivat , dvicandro 'pi nāyaṃ dvicandraḥ timiravaśāt aham upaplutanayanaḥ param evaṃ vedmi iti bhavati unmūlanābuddhiḥ / yattu uktam ---- ekameva katham anekaṃ bhavati iti , tatra ucyate ---- iha kāraṇameva katham akāraṇaṃ bhavati atha ucyate ---- viṣayabhedāt tathā iti , tadviṣayabhede etat na virudhyate iti kena ayaṃ vitīrṇo'vasaraḥ ? saṃvedanena iti cet
children.translated_text: never arises — unlike 'this is not silver.' Even in the case of two moons, the uprooting cognition arises: 'this is not a two-moon [situation]; I, with afflicted eyes, perceive it thus due to an eye-defect.' But as for what was said — 'how can the one become many?' — to that, the reply: here, how does a cause become a non-cause? If it is said 'due to the difference of objects' — then, if it is not contradictory where there is difference of objects, who has granted the occasion [to object]? If it is said 'by awareness' —
'moves' —

children.text: ityādau saṃvedanameva asmāmiḥ pramāṇīkṛtaṃ kimiti na sahyate , viṣayabhedo 'pi ca atra vaktuṃ na na śakyate ; tathāhi ---- ābhāsāntareṇa asaṃbhedane tadekābhāsamātram , ata eva anyāpekṣāviyogāt antaraṅgatvāt āntaram anuvartamānaṃ tathābhūtābhāsamātragrahaṇocitāntaḥkaraṇavedyatayā ca āntaraṃ tathāsvarūpāparicyuteḥ tattvam ābhāsāntarayogena tananasahiṣṇutvācca tattvam
children.translated_text: the awareness in such [cases] has been accepted by us as a valid means of knowledge; why is it not tolerated? And a difference of objects can indeed be stated here as well. For: when not mixed with another appearance, it is the mere appearance of just that one; and for that very reason, being free from dependence on another, being internal — it is inner, continuing, and perceived as merely grasping an appearance of that nature by the internal organ; and being inner due to non-deviation from its true nature — that is the reality. Through connection with other appearances — and through intolerance of that [connection] — the reality
'is one' —

children.text: iti pratīyate , tadeva deśābhāsena iha amutra iti , kālābhāsena adhunā tadānīmiti , svabhāvābhāsena kṛśaḥ sthūla ityādinā , miśritayā anekamiti bāhyendriyavedyatāyāṃ pratīyate / tathā
children.translated_text: thus it is cognized. That very thing, through the appearance of space as 'here' and 'there,' through the appearance of time as 'now' and 'then,' through the appearance of nature as 'thin' and 'stout,' and so forth — through admixture, it is cognized as many in the domain of perceptibility by the external senses. Similarly,
Here, when <s>Caitra</s> is seen moving, the cognition
{of the master resting in himself...}

children.text: iti uktanītyā viśvameva ānantaraṃ sat ekam , tadeva
children.translated_text: in the manner stated, even the universe, being immediately present, is one; that very thing,
{'the perceptibility by both [inner and outer] senses of what is internally changing'}

children.text: iti vakṣyamāṇakāryakāraṇabhāvatattvadṛṣṭyā intriyavedyatāyāmanekam , deśādyābhāsamiśraṇāt iti / ekatvam ---- ābhāsāntarāmiśratāyāmantaḥkaraṇaikavedyatve cinmātratāyām , anekatvaṃ punar ---- ābhāsāntaramiśratāyām uvhayakaraṇavedyatve cidatiriktatābhāsane ca , iti sphuṭo viṣayabhedaḥ , tasyaiva ca tathātvam iti parāmarśabalādeva kāraṇākāraṇavat upādānasahakārivat / atha vyapadeśamātram etat

children.translated_text: 'cause and non-cause' —

children.text: ityādi , tadihāpi ekamanekamiti vyavahāramātram , nīlaṃ pītam avikalpakaṃ savikalpakam ityapi sarvaṃ māyāpade vyavahāramātram iti sarvaṃ samānam , tasmāt ekatvānekatvavirodho na bādhakaḥ , tadetat evakāreṇa uktam / tatra iti , teṣu kriyādiṣu yat āntaraṃ tattvaṃ tadekam , tadeva indriyavedyatāṃ prāpya deśādibhedāt anekatāṃ yāti iti saṃbandhaḥ , tatra iti satyatve sthite , tayorvā ekatvānekatvayoḥ madhye
children.translated_text: and so forth — then here too, 'one and many' is mere transaction, and 'blue,' 'yellow,' 'non-conceptual,' 'conceptual' — all of this too is mere transaction in the domain of <s>Māyā</s>; thus everything is the same. Therefore, the contradiction of unity and multiplicity is not a sublator. This is stated by the word 'eva' (alone). 'Therein' — in those [categories of] action and such, the inner reality is one; that very thing, attaining perceptibility by the senses, becomes many due to differences of space and such — this is the connection. 'Therein' — with reality being established; or among the two — unity and multiplicity —
'unity is thus, multiplicity is thus' —
thus is also a possible construal. //2//

— from the perspective of the principle of cause-and-effect to be stated, in perceptibility by the senses it is many, due to admixture with appearances of space and such. Unity — when unmixed with other appearances, in perceptibility by the internal organ alone, in mere consciousness-nature. Multiplicity — when mixed with other appearances, in perceptibility by both organs, in the appearance of what transcends consciousness. Thus, the difference of domain is clear. And its being precisely thus — by the force of reflective grasping alone, like cause and non-cause, like material cause and auxiliary cause. If it be said that all this is mere designation —

children.text: nanu evaṃ viṣayabhede abhyupagamyamāne yadā ekaṃ pratibhātaṃ bhavati tadā na anekam , anekapratibhāse ca na ekaṃ pratibhātam , iti katham ekānekarūpaṃ vastu syāt , tathāhi bāhyena indriyeṇa caitro vicitradeśakaḥ param anubhūyate , na tu anekābhāsasaṃmiśrīkāre bāhyendriyajasya avikalpakasya vyāpāraḥ ---- saṃnihitaviṣayabalotpatteḥ avicārakatvāt ityāhuḥ , vikalpenāpi mānasena tathābhūtaṃ vastu naiva spṛśyate iti kayā dhiyā vastu ekānekarūpaṃ gṛhyeta ? iti paravyāmohanibarhaṇāya āha ----
children.translated_text: Objection: If a difference of domain is accepted in this way, then when the one appears, the many does not [appear], and when the many-appearance [occurs], the one does not appear — so how could a thing be of one-and-many form? For indeed, by the external sense, <s>Caitra</s> with diverse locations is merely experienced, but the operation of the non-conceptual [cognition] born of the external sense is not applicable to the mixing-together of many appearances — since it arises from the force of the proximate object and is non-discriminating, so they say. And by the mental conceptual construction too, a thing of such nature is simply not touched. By what cognition, then, is the thing of one-and-many form grasped? To dispel the confusion of the opponent, he says:
The mind, which is post-determinative awareness (<s>anuvyavasāyin</s>), being real and taking that pair as its support,
produces these conceptual constructions of action and such, which consist of the operations of the knowing subject. //

children.text: iha jñānamālāyā antaḥsūtrakalpaḥ svasaṃvedanātmā pramātā jīvitabhūtaḥ iti upapāditaṃ prāk , sa ca svatantra ityapi nirṇītam , sa tu viśuddhasvabhāvaḥ śivātmā , māyāpade tu saṃkucitasvabhāvaḥ paśuḥ , tadasya manaḥsamullāsāvasare vikalpabhūmikāyāṃ sphuṭa ullāsaḥ , aindriyake nirvikalpake sadāśiveśvaradaśābhyudayāt , avikalpabodhābahirbhūtasya vimarśavyāpāraḥ / paścādbhāvinaṃ vyavasāyaṃ niścayātmakaṃ vikalpakam anuvyavasāyaśabdavācyaṃ vidadhadantaḥkaraṇam etān kriyāsaṃbandhādivikalpān saṃpādayati / te ca vikalpāḥ taddvayam ekatvānekatvarūpam avalambante , nahi vikalpeṣu pratibhāsamānam avastusat iti hi uktam

children.translated_text: 'From the very fact of appearing, it is a real thing' —

children.text: iti / na ca vikalpasya prakāśarūpatāṃ muktvā āropaṇādhyavasāyābhimānādināmadheyaṃ vyāpārāntaraṃ yuktam , tato 'bāhye bāhyam āropayanti ityādi vaco vastuśūnyam , tacca etat uktam
children.translated_text: thus. Nor is it proper that conceptual construction should have any other operation named superimposition, determination, identification, or such, apart from its nature of luminosity. Therefore, statements like 'they superimpose the external upon the external' are devoid of reality. And this has been stated

Here, it has been demonstrated earlier that the knowing subject, who is like the inner thread of the garland of cognitions, being of the nature of self-awareness, is its life-force, and it has also been determined that he is free. But in his pure nature he is of the essence of <s>Śiva</s>; in the domain of <s>Māyā</s>, however, having a contracted nature, he is a bound soul (<s>paśu</s>). So, at the occasion of the arising of the mind, at the level of conceptual construction, his manifestation is clear; in the non-conceptual [cognition] born of the senses, due to the emergence of the <s>Sadāśiva</s>-<s>Īśvara</s> level, the operation of reflective awareness — which is beyond non-conceptual cognition — [occurs]. The internal organ, producing the subsequent determination — the conceptual construction that is of the nature of definite ascertainment, called <s>anuvyavasāya</s> (post-determinative awareness) — accomplishes these conceptual constructions of action, relation, and such. And those conceptual constructions take that pair — unity and multiplicity — as their support. For what appears in conceptual constructions is not a non-real thing — as has been said:
{'And if determination is erroneous...' /}

children.text: ityatra / atha brūyāt paro yat indriyajñānena prakāśanīyaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ tat kathaṃ vikalpaḥ spṛśediti , bhavedevaṃ ---- yadi vikalpo nāma svatantro bhavet , yāvatā pramāturasau vyāpāraḥ pramātā ca pūrvānubhavāntaḥsvasaṃvedanarūpaḥ tadasya ca ayameva pūrvānubhavasaṃskāro yat vikalpanavyāpārakāle 'pi pūvānubhavātmatvam anujjhanneva āste , tataḥ pūrvānubhavo yāvat svalakṣaṇakāśanātmā tāvat pūrvānubhavatādātmyāpannapramātṛtattvavyāpāro 'pi vikalpastadviṣaya eva , ata evamuktam ācāryeṇa
children.translated_text: in that context. Now, the opponent might say: 'How could conceptual construction touch the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), which is to be illuminated by sense-cognition?' — this would be so if conceptual construction were independent; but inasmuch as it is the operation of the knowing subject, and the knowing subject is of the form of the self-awareness within prior experience, and this very impression of prior experience is such that even at the time of the operation of conceptual construction, it remains without abandoning its identity with prior experience — therefore, prior experience being of the nature of illuminating the particular, the conceptual construction too, being the operation of the principle of the knowing subject that has attained identity with prior experience, has the very same particular as its object. Therefore, it has been stated by the master:
{This impression of prior experience belongs to the knowing subject itself;
for even at the time of exclusion, that prior experience remains established. //}

children.text: iti / tasmāt pramātuḥ yo vyāpāra ekatvānekatvasaṃyojanātmā sa eva prakṛto tatra tādṛśīḥ kriyādikalpanā ekānekavastuviṣayā

children.translated_text: 'these' (<s>etāḥ</s>) —

children.text: iti grahaṇakavākyasūcitā mana eva karoti iti sthitam , yadyapi avikalpe'pi sāmānyādyavabhāso ghaṭamātrāvabhāsādau , tathāpi na tadā sāmānyādi sphuṭam , samānoparañjakatve saṃbandhidvayodbhave kramikakṣaṇasaṃtānātyāge avayavakadambakasvīkāre avadhyavadhimatparigrahādau sāmānyasaṃbandhakriyādravyadigādipadārthasya paramārthataḥ sphuraṇāt , iti
children.translated_text: as indicated by the correlative clause. It is established that the mind alone produces [them]. Although even in the non-conceptual [cognition], the appearance of the universal and such exists in the mere-pot-appearance and such, nevertheless, the universal and such are not clear then — for the category of universal, relation, action, substance, direction, and such truly scintillates [only] when there is coloring by what is similar, when the two relata have arisen, when the continuous momentary series is not abandoned, when the aggregate of parts is accepted, when the limit-possessing and limiter are grasped, and so forth. Thus —
'universals and such, having one-and-many form, are graspable by mental conceptual construction' —

children.text: iti sthitam / evaṃ ca saṃvṛttiḥ vikalpabuddhiḥ , tadvaśāt ucyatāṃ saṃvṛtisatyatvaṃ satyatvasyaiva tu prakāraḥ tat , iti dvicandrādivat na asatyatā //3//
children.translated_text: this is established. And thus, <s>saṃvṛtti</s> (convention) is conceptual cognition; on account of that, let it be called conventionally real — but that is a mode of reality itself. Therefore, unlike two moons and such, there is no unreality. //3//

Therefore, the operation of the knowing subject that consists of conjoining unity and multiplicity — that very thing, being the primary [subject], produces those conceptual constructions of action and such, having as their object things of one-and-many [form] —

children.text: tatra ca ayaṃ saṃvidavataraṇakramo yat kriyāśaktereva ayaṃ sarvo visphāraḥ , tatrāpi sambandha eva mūlabhūtaḥ , tathāhi ---- samānānāṃ yat ekaṃ bhāti tat sāmānyam , devadattasya yat vaitatyaṃ sā kriyā , avayavānāṃ yadaikyaṃ vaitatyaṃ ca deśataḥ so'vayavī , imam avadhiṃ kṛtvā ayam ittham tato 'sya ayaṃ purastāt ityādirdik , asyāyaṃ kriyāpratānaḥ sahabhāvena āste vinābhāvena vā iti vartamānādiḥ kālaḥ , yāvat hi prātipadikārthasya pṛṣṭapāti vapuḥ bhāti tadatiriktaṃ sarvaṃ saṃbandha eva iti kārakāṇāmapi saṃbandharūpataiva , kevalaṃ kvacit asau saṃbandho vyapadeśāntaragranthiṃ sahate , yathā sāsrādimatāṃ saṃbandho

children.translated_text: 'cows' —

children.text: iti ekavyapadeśasahiṣṇuḥ tatra sāmānyādivyavahāraḥ , vyapadeśāntaragranthibhaṅge tu saṃbandhācoyuktireva , ata eva diṣṭiprasthapalādipramāṇaparimāṇonmānarūpaṃ tatra antargataṃ vā aṇumahadādi saṃkhyāpṛthaktvādi ca yat tat sarvaṃ saṃbandhasyaiva vijṛmbhitam , ye 'pi sāmānyādi vastvantaram amaṃsata te 'pi tatra samavāyam abhyupajagmuḥ jīvitatvena , samavāyaśca saṃbandhātmā tadanugrāhyo vā keṣāṃcit , yata āhuḥ ----
children.translated_text: tolerates a single designation — there the transaction of universal and such [applies]. But when the knot of additional designation is broken, there is simply relation. For this very reason, what is included therein — measurement in the form of <s>diṣṭi</s>, <s>prastha</s>, <s>pala</s>, and such, and size in the form of atoms, large, and such, and also number, separateness, and such — all of that is a display of relation itself. Even those who considered the universal and such to be a different reality accepted <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) therein as its life-force; and <s>samavāya</s> is of the nature of relation, or is assisted by relation, according to some. For they say:

And therein, this is the order of the descent of consciousness — that all this effulgence belongs to the power of action alone, and within that, relation is the fundamental one. For: the one that appears among similars is the universal; the traversal of <s>Devadatta</s> is action; the unity and spatial traversal of parts is the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>); making this the limit, this one is thus in relation to that — 'in front of this,' and so forth — is direction; 'this chain of action of his exists with co-presence or co-absence' — this is time, such as present and such; for as far as the form that follows the meaning of the nominal stem appears as something more than it, all of that is nothing but relation. Therefore, even the <s>kārakas</s> (agent-factors) are of the nature of relation. Only in some cases, that relation tolerates being tied to another designation; just as the relation of those that possess the universal and such —
{Relation assists that power called <s>samavāya</s>. /}
Thus.

children.text: yadapi ca kārakaṃ tadapi kriyāmukhaprekṣi , sāpi kālaṃ prāṇeśvaram āśrayati , so 'pi kriyādvāreṇa sarvabhāvātmā sambandham uddhurayati iti saṃbandhādhīnaiva iyaṃ citrā lokayātrā / yadāha ācārya eva
