children.text: iti tadvimarśavimarśanīyam yat tatpūrvavimarśakālasamucitameva rūpaṃ tat tasmin pūrvavimarśakāle naivāmṛśyate , bhāvyaṃ ca tenāmarśanīyena / tatraiva kāle
children.translated_text: the form that should be reflectively grasped by that [subsequent] reflective grasping, and that is suited to the time of the prior reflective grasping — that is simply not grasped at the time of the prior reflective grasping; and it should have been grasped by that which was to be grasped. At that very time,
'this was not silver' —

children.text: iti hi uttaraḥ parāmarśo na tu uditapratyastamitāyāṃ śatahradāyāmiva idānīmeva
children.translated_text: this is the subsequent reflective grasping; it is not the case that — like a lightning flash that has arisen and set — even now,
'this is not' —

children.text: iti vimarśaḥ ; tato yāvatā pūrṇena rūpeṇa prakhyātavyaṃ vimarśaparyantaṃ tāvat na prakhyāti , ityapūrṇakhyātirūpā akhyātireva bhrāntitattvam / tadvaśena hyasadviparītānirvācyādikhyātayo'pi ucyantām /
children.translated_text: such a reflective grasping [occurs simultaneously]. Therefore, to the extent that the full form, up to the completion of reflective grasping, should have been manifest — to that extent it does not manifest. Thus, error is in truth incomplete manifestation (<s>apūrṇakhyāti</s>) — non-manifestation in the form of incomplete manifestation. By its force, let the manifestations called 'of the non-existent,' 'of the contrary,' 'of the indescribable,' and such also be spoken of.

children.text: nanu satyarūpyajñānamapi apūrṇakhyātiḥ / tatastarhi kim ? / idam , ataḥ sarvaṃ bhrāntiḥ , ---- ityāgacchet / diṣṭyā dṛṣṭirunmīliṣyati āyuṣmataḥ , māyāpadaṃ hi sarvaṃ bhrāntiḥ , tatrāpi tu svapne svapna iva gaṇḍe sphoṭa iva apareyaṃ bhrāntirucyate , anuvṛttyucitasyāpi vimarśasyāshtairyāt / ataśca pṛthak idantādyābhāseṣu na kācana bhrāntiḥ , mekanāṃśe tu vimarśānuvṛttinirmūlanaṃ vimarśodayakālādeva ārabhya bādhakena kriyate , iti tatraiva bhrāntibhāvaḥ , ---- iti siddham / rajatasya śuktikayā saha yadyapi eko vimarśaḥ tathāpi śuktau rajatasya jñānena yā dattā sthitiḥ

children.translated_text: 'this is silver' —

children.text: iti , sā na , yata upādhirūpo yo deśaḥ
children.translated_text: that [stability] does not [endure], because the locus which is of the nature of an adventitious condition (<s>upādhi</s>) —
'silver here' —

children.text: iti rajatacchāyām ātmanoparañjayan śuktideśaḥ , tasyāsaṃvādāt , samyagvimarśānuvṛttyābhāsanaṃ saṃvādanam
children.translated_text: the shell-locus, tinting itself with the hue of silver — due to its non-concordance. Concordance means the appearance of the continuation of correct reflective grasping.
'Vad' (<s>vadiḥ</s>) —
has 'appearance' as its object here; due to its absence, which is the cause.

Objection: But even the cognition of real silver is incomplete manifestation. Then what follows? This: therefore everything is error — this would follow. Fortunately, the vision of the long-lived one is about to open! For everything in the domain of <s>Māyā</s> is indeed error. But even therein — like a dream within a dream, like a boil upon a boil — this is called the additional error, due to the instability of the reflective grasping whose continuance was expected. Therefore, in the separate appearances of 'this'-ness and such, there is no error whatsoever; but in the combination-aspect, the uprooting of the continuance of reflective grasping is accomplished by the sublator from the very time of the arising of the reflective grasping — thus, error resides precisely there. This is established. Although there is a single reflective grasping of silver together with the shell, nevertheless, the stability granted by the cognition to silver in the shell —
'two moons' —

children.text: ityābhāse śuktikayeva melanaṃ na kenacitsākamābhāsate yatra bādhaḥ syāt , ekābhāsāṃśe ca na bādhaḥ , ---- ityuktaṃ bhavataiva / ka etadāha --- melanaṃ na kenacitsaha iti / evaṃ hi sati svālakṣaṇyena niyatadeśakālatayā kathamābhāsaḥ , ? taddeśakālābhyāṃ saha tatrāpi asti melanābhāso yadvimarśo'nuvivṛtsurnirudhyate , dvitvābhāsacandrābhāsayorapi melanābhāse vimarśānuvṛttivyāvartanaṃ vācyam / tadetadāha --- dvirūpe candre'pi , na kevalaṃ rajata eva /
children.translated_text: in this appearance, combination with something, as in the case of the shell, does not appear — [where] sublation could [occur]; and in the single-appearance-aspect, there is no sublation — as you yourself have stated. Who says there is no combination with something? For if that were so, then how could an appearance be [constituted] as a particular, with fixed space and time? With that space and time, even there the combination-appearance exists — whose reflective grasping, wishing to continue, is obstructed. Even in the combination-appearance of the duality-appearance and the moon-appearance, the obstruction of the continuance of reflective grasping is to be stated. This he states: even in the case of two moons — not only in the case of silver alone —
'the sky' (<s>nabhaḥ</s>) —
is some particular locus.
'Otherwise' (<s>anyathā</s>) —

children.text: iti dvicandrāvaruddho yovimṛṣṭaḥ sa na tathā , ---- iti bādhakena unmūlitaprācyavimarśānuvṛttikaḥ kriyate , ---- iti / evamābhāsastanmelanaṃ ca niyamānuprāṇitam ---- ityetāvadeva prameyam / etānyeva āgame tattvāni vakṣyante / vastu tattvaṃ prameyam ---- iti paryāyāḥ / tathā ca kāṭhinyābhāsa iti pṛthivī , lohitābhāsa iti rūpaṃ tejaśca , melanābhāso rajaḥ , saṃniveśastu niyatirūpaḥ , niyatirhi niyamaḥ , sa ca abhāvaprāṇaḥ , abhāvasphuraṇameva ca pṛthivyābhāsasya vicitratayā cakāsat pṛthubudhnodarākāratā , bhedābhāsaśca māyā , tatpṛṣṭhe satyaprakāśābhāsaśca śivatattvam, ---- ityāstāṃ tāvat / agre bhaviṣyati etat / sarvathā tāvadatra prameye bhagavata eva bhedane ca abhedane ca svātantryaṃ ghaṭagatābhāsabhedābhedadṛṣṭireva ca paramārthādvayadṛṣṭipraveśe upāyaḥ samavalamvanīyaḥ , na tu vyavahāro'pi ayaṃ parameśvarasvarūpānupraveśavirodhī , iti pratipāditam //13//
children.translated_text: that which is reflectively grasped as encompassed by two moons is not so — it is made [such that] the continuance of the prior reflective grasping has been uprooted by the sublator. Thus, the appearance and its combination are animated by regulation (<s>niyama</s>) — this alone is what is to be known (<s>prameya</s>). These very principles (<s>tattvas</s>) will be stated in the <s>Āgama</s> [section]. 'Entity,' 'principle,' 'knowable' — are synonyms. And thus: the hardness-appearance is earth; the red-appearance is form and fire; the combination-appearance is <s>rajas</s>; arrangement is of the nature of regulation; for regulation is restriction, and that is animated by absence; the scintillation of absence itself, shining as the variegation of the earth-appearance, is the broad-based form with base and belly; the difference-appearance is <s>Māyā</s>; behind that, the appearance of true luminosity is the <s>Śiva</s>-principle. But let this rest for now — it will come later. In every case, regarding this knowable, it is the Blessed One's freedom alone in differentiating and non-differentiating — and the perception of the difference and non-difference of appearances within a pot itself is the means of entry into the vision of ultimate non-duality. And this practical activity too has been shown to be not contrary to the entry into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord. //13//
Objection: Let this be so in the case of shell-silver; but in the cognition of two moons,

children.text: etadeva sphuṭayan sakalaprameyasiddhiḥ parameśvara eva āyattā , iti nirūpayati /
children.translated_text: Making this very point explicit — that the establishment of all knowables depends on the Supreme Lord alone — he demonstrates:
By qualities such as sound and such, difference; by universal and such, non-difference —
of entities, in this way, is accounted for in a single knowing subject. //

children.text: iha anuvṛttaṃ vyāvṛttaṃ ca cakāsadvastu katareṇa vapuṣā na satyamucyatām ubhayatrāpi bādhakābhāvāt , satyato hi yadi bādhaka eva ekatarasya syāt tattadudaye sa eva bhāgaḥ punarunmajjanasahiṣṇutārahito vidyudvilāyaṃ vilīyeta ; na caivam , ata eva bhedābhedayorvirodhaṃ duḥsamarthamabhimanyamānairekairavidyātvena anirvācyatvam , aparaiśca ābhāsalagnatayā sāṃvṛtatvam abhidadhadbhiḥ ātmā paraśca vañcitaḥ / saṃvedanaviśrāntaṃ tu dvayamapi bhāti saṃvedanasya svātantryaāt / sarvasya hi tiraśco'pi etat svasaṃvedanasiddhaṃ ---- yat saṃvidantarviśrāntamekatāmāpādyamānaṃ jalajvalanamapi aviruddham , tata eva uktam
children.translated_text: Here, a thing that shines as both persisting and excluded — by whichever form should it not be called real? — since there is no sublator in either case. For if, in reality, there were a sublator of one of the two, then upon the arising of that [sublator], that very portion, incapable of tolerating re-emergence, would dissolve like a flash of lightning. But this is not the case. For this very reason, those who consider the contradiction of difference and non-difference to be difficult to justify and [therefore posit] the nature of <s>avidyā</s> (nescience) and inexpressibility — and others who, by [saying it is] attached to appearance, declare conventionality — by both, the self and the other have been deceived. But both [difference and non-difference] shine as resting in awareness, due to the freedom of awareness. For even the most ordinary person has this established through self-awareness — that what rests within awareness, being brought to unity, even water and fire are non-contradictory. Therefore it is said:
{'Therefore, the delineation according to one's wish...' /} (<s>Īpk</s> 1,6.11)

children.text: iti / ataśca guṇairupādhirūpairupādhitayā vivakṣitaiḥ śabdādibhirvā daṇḍādibhirapi vā yo bhedaḥ , jātivaśāt sādṛśyāt bhedāgrahaṇādvā , yaśca abhedo bhāvānām itthamityuktanītyā {kriyāsaṃbandha}(2,2.1) ityataḥ prabhṛti nirūpitaḥ , sa ekatrapramātari sakalapramāpramāṇasaṃyojanaviyojanādivicitrāsaṃkhyakṛtyaprapañcocitasvātantrye bhagavatyasmadīyahṛdayaikāntaśāyini śivaśabdavyapadeśye sati upapadyate , nānyathā / viśeṣaṇānyeva ca bhedakāni ---- iti kimantyairanyairviśeṣaiḥ ayaṃ sa paramāṇurya etaddeśādiviśiṣṭaghaṭārambhaṇakālasthitapaścāttanasaṃghaṭitadvyaṇukārambhakāle pūrvaṃ militaḥ / ayaṃ sa ātmā , yaḥ purā svargasadane surayoṣitamimāmitthaṃ parirabdhavān , ---- iti iyataiva yogisarvajñādīnāṃ siddhaḥ paramāṇvātmādiṣu bhedāvabhāsaḥ , ---- ityalamavāntareṇa / siddhaṃ tāvat bhedābhedarūpaṃ prameyatattvam ekapramātṛviśrāntyā niḥśaṅkatāṃ śrayati , iti //14//
children.translated_text: thus. And therefore, the difference that is through qualities — which are of the nature of adventitious conditions, intended as such — whether through sound and such, or through a staff and such — and the non-difference that is through universal and such, through similarity, or through non-apprehension of difference — of entities, in this manner as has been explained, examined from {'action-relation'} (2,2.1) onward — is accounted for in a single knowing subject, in the Blessed One whose freedom is fit for the innumerable play of wondrous acts of conjoining and disjoining all valid cognitions and means of knowledge, who reclines in the innermost chamber of our heart, who is designated by the word <s>Śiva</s> — and not otherwise. And the qualifiers alone are the differentiators — so what use of ultimate, other specific [differentiators]? 'This is that very atom which, at the time of being situated in the production of this pot specified by this place and such, was previously combined in the dyad-production-time with the subsequently joined [atom]'; 'this is that very self who formerly in the heavenly abode embraced this celestial woman in this way' — to just this extent, the appearance of difference in atoms, selves, and such is established for <s>yogins</s>, omniscients, and such. Enough of further discussion. It is established that the knowable reality, of the nature of difference and non-difference, attains fearlessness through resting in a single knowing subject. //14//

children.text: nanvevaṃbhūto yadyayaṃ pramātā tatrava tarhi pramāṇopanyāse prayatanīyaṃ na prameye , yadāha

children.translated_text: 'For effort in what is primary is fruitful' —

children.text: iti / tadetadāśaṅkya prathamopakṣiptameva prameyaṃ smārayatyācāryaḥ / tathā hi /
children.translated_text: Thus. Anticipating this [objection], the master reminds [us] of the very knowable object that was introduced at the outset. For indeed:
Objection: If the knowing subject is of such a nature, then effort should be directed toward the means of valid knowledge, not toward the knowable. As it is said:

children.text: {ajaḍātmā miṣedhaṃ vā siddhiṃ vā vidadhīta kaḥ /}(Ipk 1,1.2)
children.translated_text: {Who, being of a non-inert nature, could bring about either negation or establishment?} (<s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.1.2)

children.text: iti / yadvastu tadevedānīṃ jñāte pramāṇasvarūpe parameśvarasvarūpe ca nirvāhaṇārham , evaṃ bhūtaṃ hi pramāṇaṃ tadevaṃbhūte hi bhagavati kathaṃ kramatām , iti / tadetat sphuṭayitumāha
children.translated_text: Thus. The very subject-matter that was [introduced there] is now, when the essential nature of the valid means and of the Supreme Lord is known, worthy of being carried through. For how could a valid means of such a nature proceed toward a Lord of such a nature? To make this explicit, he says:
In the Lord, who is like a level wall-surface for the painting of the variegated diversity of the universe,
who in ultimate reality is touched by the contact of contradictory appearances,
who is the primordial perceiver whose body is eternally manifest,
what valid means — a novel appearance partaking of all cognitions — [could apply]?

children.text: parimitapramātṛlagno navanavābhāsaḥ prameyonmukhaḥ pramāṇam ityuktam / tatra prakāśavauṣi prakāśamātrasvabhāve pūrvasiddhe kaḥ pramāṇasyopayogaḥ saṃbhāvanā vā / tathā ca pūrvasiddhe pramātari sati tallagnaprakāśāntarbhūtavimarśamayīm abhūtapūrvāṃ prameyasya siddhiṃ vitarati pramāṇam / pramātuścāsiddhasya kiṃ lagnā siddhirastu / viśvavaicitryaṃ hi tarta parameśvare prakāśaikātmani sati bhāti yathā citraṃ bhittau / yadi hi nīlapītādikaṃ pṛthageva parāmṛśyate tadā svātmaviśrānteṣu teṣu tataiva anyonyaviṣaye jaḍāndhabadhirakalpāni jñānāni svaviṣayamātraniṣṭhitāni , vikalpāśca tadanusāreṇa bhavantaḥ tathaiva , iti

children.translated_text: 'this is a painting' —

children.text: iti kathaṃkāraṃ pratipattiḥ / ekatra tu nimnonnatādirahite bhittitale rekhāvibhaktanimnonnatā divibhāgajuṣi

'deep navel, elevated breasts' —

children.text: iti citrāvabhāso yuktaḥ , tadvat ekaprakāśabhittilagnatvena vaicitryātmakabhedopapattiḥ , iti bhāvabhedagrahaṇaprakāśabhitteranapāyinīṃ svaprakāśatāmāha / tatra svaprakāśe kiṃ pramāṇena ? / athocyate pūrvamasya prakāśo na bhavati , tarhi sa eva nāsti iti syāt prakāśamātrarūpatvāt tasya / na ca asya nāsti , ityabhāvena sparśa upapannaḥ , yato hi asāveva paramārthataḥ san , prakāśasyaiva sattvāt , sataśca asadrūpatvāyogāt / athocyate ---- īśvaratā tasyāpramitā pramāsyate tadapi na , yato hi asau pramātṛtvena cet na cakāsyāt kasyāyamucyamaḥ , cakāsti cet tarhi pramātṛtaiva īśvaratā , tadāha
children.translated_text: such an appearance as a painting is appropriate. Similarly, due to attachment to a single wall of luminosity, the establishment of diversity in the form of differentiation is tenable. Thus, he states the self-luminosity that never departs from the wall of luminosity, which is the ground of grasping the differentiation of entities. Therein, what [need is there] of a valid means for what is self-luminous? But if one says: 'Previously, his luminosity did not exist' — then he simply does not exist, since his nature is nothing but luminosity. Nor is it tenable that he is touched by non-existence — since he alone exists in ultimate reality, because only luminosity exists, and what exists cannot be of the nature of the non-existent. But if one says: 'His Lordship, being unascertained, will be ascertained [by a valid means]' — even that is not so, for if he did not shine as a perceiver, for whom would this be uttered? And if he does shine, then perceivership itself is Lordship. Therefore he says:
'in the Lord who is the perceiver, whose body is eternally manifest' —

children.text: iti / viśeṣeṇa gṛhyate iti vigraho'sādhāraṇaṃ svarūpam , ata eva svatantraprakāśarūpatvāt abhāvasparśāyogenābhāvānupraveśanena yaḥ kālavyavahāraḥ so'tra nāsti , ---- iti
children.translated_text: thus. That which is particularly grasped — the <s>vigraha</s> (body) — is the distinctive essential nature. Therefore, precisely because it is of the nature of independent luminosity, since the contact with non-existence is impossible and since there is no entry of non-existence — the temporal transaction [of 'before' and 'after'] does not apply here. Hence
'purāṇe' (primordial) —

children.text: ityuktam / tatra kiṃ pramāṇaṃ , kutaḥ prayojanātpramāṇaṃ , kastatra pramāṇasyopayogaḥ , ---- iti , tatra ca kiṃ pramāṇam na kiñcit upapattyā ghaṭate ityarthaḥ / yataḥ pramāṇaṃ nāma navābhāsarūpaṃ pramātari pramitilakṣaṇāṃ viśrāntiṃ vidadhat pramāṇaṃ bhavati , pramātā cāvicchinnābhāsaḥ sarvāśca pramitīḥ svātmani antarmukharūpe bhajate / tat tasmin kathamabhinavābhāsastatpramitiśca kutra viśrāmyatu tasmāt dehaprāṇapuryaṣṭakaśūnyaprāya eva pramātari pramāṇamucyatām / tatrāpi ca vedyāṃśe yadi nāma , na tu kathaṃcit saṃvidaṃśe , tatrāpi viṣayonmukhe tata eva saṃkucitatvāt abhinavābhāse saṃkocavihīnasatyapramātṛlagnatāpekṣayā kathyatāṃ svasaṃvedanaṃ pramāṇam / saugatenāpi
children.translated_text: is stated. What valid means [could apply] therein? From what motive could there be a valid means? What use of a valid means could there be? — Thus, 'what valid means [could apply] therein?' — nothing can be coherently established: this is the meaning. For what is called a valid means, being of the nature of a novel appearance and producing a resting of the nature of cognition in the perceiver, becomes a valid means. But the perceiver has an unbroken appearance and partakes of all cognitions within himself in his inward-facing form. Therefore, how could there be a novel appearance in him, and where could that cognition rest? Therefore, let the valid means be spoken of only with respect to a perceiver who is of the nature of body, vital breath, subtle body, or void. And even there, if only with respect to the knowable aspect — but in no way with respect to the consciousness aspect. And even there, with respect to what is directed toward the object — since it is contracted precisely from that [consciousness] — in the novel appearance, with reference to attachment to the true perceiver who is devoid of contraction, let self-awareness be called the valid means. Even by the Buddhist,
'this cognition is mine' —

children.text: iti kalpitapramātṛlagnameva tadupetyam na tu paramārthapramātari pramāṇena kiṃcit / uktaṃ ca mayaiva
children.translated_text: it is accepted as attached precisely to a postulated perceiver, and not that a valid means accomplishes anything with respect to the ultimate perceiver. And it has been stated by me:

It has been stated that a novel appearance, ever-new, attached to a limited perceiver and directed toward the knowable, is the valid means. In that case, for one whose nature is mere luminosity and who is already established, what use or even possibility is there of a valid means? And thus, when the perceiver is already established, the valid means delivers an unprecedented establishment of the knowable that consists of reflective awareness included within the luminosity attached to him. But for one who is not established as a perceiver, how could there be an establishment attached [to him]? For the diversity of the universe shines in that Supreme Lord, whose sole essence is luminosity, just as a painting on a wall. If blue, yellow, and such are each reflectively grasped separately, then those cognitions, resting in their own selves, would be inert-blind-deaf-like with respect to each other's domains, resting only in their own objects; and conceptual constructions following them would be likewise — so
{Every self is embarrassed [to be told] 'you have been made an object of knowledge';
how could <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) tolerate being made an object of knowledge? //}

children.translated_text: as stated in that text. What is the purpose for the other? It is for the other's understanding. And that [understanding arises] from inference-for-the-sake-of-another. And therein, the thesis and such are useful. Therefore, all scripture that produces complete understanding in the other is, in ultimate truth, entirely inference-for-the-sake-of-another — as established by the architect of logic, <s>Akṣapāda</s>, distinct from <s>āgama</s> (revelation). And so, even here, to remind [us] of what was stated earlier — {but due to delusion} (<s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.1.3) — he says:

Objection: If the valid means is thus inapplicable and untenable with respect to the Lord, then for what purpose is a treatise concerning Him? For that [treatise] is itself a valid means — scripture being of the nature of inference-for-the-sake-of-another. And therein, the ultimate truth consists in the reality of the sixteen categories beginning with valid means and such. As for what is criticized by the Buddhists — the doctrine of five members and such — that is mere failure to grasp [the true intent]. For when the sixteen categories are properly examined, what is to be taught is communicated to the other,
What has never been set in motion before — merely due to the force of bewilderment —
is set in motion as the transaction of Lord and such, through the illumination of the powers.

children.text: iha parameśvarasyedameva paraṃ svātantryaṃ ---- yat asmādṛkprācyapaśudaśāviśeṣāsaṃbhāvyamānātiduṣkaravastusaṃpādanaṃ nāma / itaśca kim atiduṣkaraṃ bhaviṣyati , ---- yatprakāśātmani akhaṇḍitatādrūpye eva prakāśamāne prakāśananiṣadhāvabhāsaḥ prakāśamānaḥ / tasmāt parameśvarasya tatparaṃ svātantryaṃ yat tathānavabhāsanaṃ paśurūpatāvabhāsanaṃ nāma grāhakāṃśasamutthāpanaṃ taddvāreṇa ca grāhyollāsanamapi / saiṣā bhagavato māyāśaktirucyate / yathoktam /
children.translated_text: Here, this is the supreme freedom of the Supreme Lord — namely, the accomplishment of something extremely difficult, inconceivable from a prior state of bondage such as ours. And what could be more difficult than this: that in what is of the nature of luminosity, even while shining in unbroken identity, the appearance of the negation of luminosity is manifest! Therefore, the supreme freedom of the Supreme Lord is this: the very non-manifestation of that [luminosity], the manifestation of the state of a bound soul — namely, the raising up of the perceiver-aspect and, through that, also the efflorescence of the knowable. This is called the <s>Māyā-śakti</s> (power of illusion) of the Lord. As stated:
{<s>Māyā</s>, the bewildering one by name... /}

What is being said is this: just as for an embodied person, even when his own self is manifest,

children.translated_text: and such, when through delusion one falsely identifies — the delusion is dispelled. 'He who possesses the freedom of knowledge and action is the Lord — as is well known in the <s>Siddhānta</s>, <s>Purāṇas</s>, and such — and so are you.' Or: 'He in whom whatever depends is the lord thereof, like a king in his domain — and so the universe [depends] on you.' Thus, the transaction of Lordship has no other cause — this is the universal concomitance. 'Whatever shines as attached to something is filled by it, like a treasury by gems — and the universe is attached to you.' 'He within whom something shines is pervading that much, like a box containing gems — and in you, who are of the nature of consciousness, the entire universe from earth to <s>Sadāśiva</s> as described in the scriptural tradition [shines].' 'That in which something arises and dissolves — that pervades the prior and posterior parts of it, as a sprout in the earth — and so the universe [rests] in you, who are of the nature of luminosity.' Similarly, thousands of other properties established by scripture and such should be applied. Thus, when the delusion is dispelled, even while the body and such remain — sustained by mere residual impressions — even when there is the false identification of non-selfhood in the body, preceded by [what previously was] the false identification of selfhood [therein], and even when in pots and such, which are already manifest, there is the false identification of non-selfhood — just as for one who has recognized the truth of a magical illusion, even though the illusion appears, there is no real delusion — similarly, for one who has recognized the essential nature of the Self. Therefore, upon the departure and completion of the body, there is indeed the state of the Supreme Lord. But through the power of practice and cultivation, following the instruction of <s>Śiva</s>'s teaching, for one who contemplates and sees the entry of the Supreme Lord's nature even in the body, pot, and such, right here in this body there arises the manifestation of aspects of the Lord's qualities — but not fullness in reality, since [that comes] upon the dissolution of the very nature of embodiment, which is the vital principle of contraction, whereupon the state of being the universe as it truly is is attained. For one who has the false identification of non-establishment even regarding the aggregate of reasons that serve to establish the transaction, for that person too the delusion is to be removed by those very means of establishing the transaction. But for one whose [delusion] is in no way removed, there the bewilderment is by the force of the Lord's power; and even for that person, since the sound has reached the ear, through the ripening of impressions, there will certainly at some time be the attainment of one's own essential nature. Thus,
'kartari' (in the agent) —
what was stated by the verse-pair beginning with (<s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.1.2) — that very thing
'viśvavaicitrya' (the diversity of the universe) —

From such freedom, which is of the nature of the <s>Māyā-śakti</s>, the bewilderment — the destruction of complete consciousness — which is the false identification as non-manifest of what is in fact manifest: the fullness that consists in the luminous bursting forth of the entire universe through the arising of the pulsation of will residing in one's own Self, the freedom that is of the nature of powers of memory and such, and the properties of effortlessly established glory, eternality, and such — by the power and capacity of that [bewilderment], the transaction that was not set in motion before, concerning the perceiver who is the Lord, whose nature was stated in the preceding two verses — the transaction with Lordship and such, with the very fullness and such already mentioned — namely, what indeed shines as
