'evamicchaiva hetutā kartṛtā kriyā' (thus will itself is causality, agency, and action) —

children.text: ityantam / tatra ślokena svamate kartṛkarmabhāva eva kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ , ---- ityupakṣipyate / tataḥ ślokatrayeṇa jaḍasya kāraṇatvaṃ parākriyate / tataḥ ślokaṣaṭkena cetanasyaiva kartṛtārūpā kāraṇatā prasādhyate / tataḥ prasaṅgādanumāne niyatiśaktiravaśyopajīvyā , ---- iti ślokatrayeṇocyate / tataḥ saugatoktakāryakāraṇaparamārtho'pi asmanmatamevāvalambate , no cet na kiñcit , ---- iti tribhiḥ ślokaiḥ / sāṃkhyopadarśito 'pi kāryakāraṇabhāvo nopapadyate , yadyasmaduktaṃ cetanasya kartṛtvaṃ nāṅgīkriyate , ---- iti tribhiḥ / cetanasyāpi anīśvaratāyāṃ naitadghaṭate , ---- iti dvābhyāmiti saṃkṣepārthaḥ / granthastu vyākhyāyate /
children.translated_text: ending with that. Therein, by one verse, in our view the cause-and-effect relation is nothing but the agent-object relation — thus it is introduced. Then, by three verses, the causality of the insentient is refuted. Then, by six verses, the causality in the form of agency belonging to the conscious alone is established. Then, incidentally, <s>niyati-śakti</s> (the power of regulation) must necessarily be relied upon in inference — this is stated in three verses. Then, even the ultimate reality of cause and effect as stated by the Buddhists rests upon our view; otherwise, there is nothing at all — in three verses. Even the cause-and-effect relation as presented by the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> is untenable if the agency of the conscious that we have stated is not accepted — in three [verses]. Even for the conscious, if sovereignty is denied, this does not hold — in two [verses]. This is the summary meaning. The text is now explained.

Having established, in the context of relation — which is primarily an expansion of the power of action — the nature of the revealer-revealed relation, in order to establish the nature of the cause-and-effect relation, a new chapter is begun with twenty-one verses —

children.text: evaṃ kriyāśaktimukhena pramātrekarūpatāṃ bhagavati vyavahartavyāṃ prasādhya , kartṛrūpatāpi tata evāyatnasiddhā , ---- iti darśayitumāha
children.translated_text: Having thus established, through the medium of <s>kriyā-śakti</s> (power of action), that the unity of the perceiver with the Blessed Lord must be transacted, he shows that agency-nature too is effortlessly established from that very [premise]:
And this [Lord], due to possessing infinite powers, manifests in this way these
entities by the force of [His] will — this is action, this is His creatorship.

children.text: co 'vadhāraṇe / eṣa eva purāṇaḥ pramātā amūn bhāvān ābhāsitapūrvān ābhāsān ābhāsayati avicchinnena prabandhena / katham , icchāyā īśiturabhinnāyā avikalparūpāyā akramāyā vaśena sāmarthyena kutrāsya te bhāvāḥ sthitāḥ ? āha ,

children.translated_text: 'Due to possessing infinite powers' —

children.text: iti / viśve hi bhāvāstasyaiva śaktirūpeṇa svarūpātmatvena sthitāḥ ; ityuktaṃ
children.translated_text: thus. For all entities in the universe reside in Him alone in the form of powers, as being of the nature of His own essence. As has been stated,

The word 'ca' is used for emphasis. This very ancient perceiver manifests these entities — previously manifested appearances — in an unbroken continuum. How? By the force, i.e., the capacity, of <s>icchā</s> (will), which is non-different from the Lord, non-conceptual in nature, and non-sequential. Where do those entities reside in Him? He says:
{And of the non-different, abiding in the Self... /} (<s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.5.10)

children.text: ityatra / yadetadābhāsanaṃ yāsāvicchā , sā kriyā , asya bhagavato nirmātṛtvam //1//
children.translated_text: in that context. This very manifesting, this very will — that is action, that is the creatorship of this Blessed Lord. // 1 //

children.text: nanu bījādaṅkura udbhavan dṛśyate , na ca atra kaściccetano 'nupraviśan dṛṣṭaḥ , tatkathametaduktam ? , ---- ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: A sprout is seen arising from a seed, and no conscious being is observed entering there — so how can this be stated? Anticipating this, he says:

children.text: jaḍasya tu na sā śaktiḥ sattā yadasataḥ sataḥ /
children.translated_text: But the insentient does not have that power — existence — namely, [the power] that from the non-existent, [brings about] the existent.
The cause-and-effect relation is nothing but the essence of the agent-object relation; therefore...

children.text: sadvā kāryamasadvā saṃbhāvyate / ubhayātmakam anubhayātmakamanirvācyam , iti tu svavācaiva virudhyate tat kimanena / yadi asan ghaṭaḥ , tarhi tasyāsadrūpataiva paramārthaḥ iti kathaṃ svarūpaviruddhaṃ sattvamabhyupagacchet , na hi pādapatanaśatairapi nīlamātmani pītimānaṃ mṛṣyate / atha sanneva ghaṭastarhi kimanyat upayācyate daṇḍacakrasūtrāt / abhivyaktiviṣayatvasphuṭatvādayo'pi sadasadrūpatayā cintyāḥ //
children.translated_text: The effect — a pot — is either existent [before production] or non-existent. 'Both-natured,' 'neither-natured,' 'indescribable' — these are contradicted by their very words, so what use is that? If the pot is non-existent, then its nature is precisely non-existence — how then could it accept existence, which contradicts its nature? For not even by hundreds of prostrations would blue tolerate yellowness in itself. But if the pot already exists, then what else is sought from the wheel, stick, and thread? And the theories of manifestation, clarity, and such should also be considered as of existent-or-non-existent form.
Objection: Then let one remain silent [on the matter]. He says: even that is not proper —
... But if it is said... // <s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 2.4.3 //
[The meaning is:] this [being] necessarily has the capacity for [producing] the object — to that extent. // 3 //
And so, he shows that it is tenable in this way:
The cause-and-effect relation in the world is the internal-external abiding of what revolves within;
its being cognizable by both [internal and external] faculties is due to the power of some [conscious being].

children.text: kumbhakārahṛdaye antarmanogocaratvāt pūrvamapi svasaṃvidekātmatayā vicitratvena viśvasya bhedābhedātmanā parivartamānasya spandanena sphurato yat antaḥkaraṇahiṣkaraṇadvayavedyatvamābhāsyate , eṣaiva sākāryakāraṇatā / ubhayagrahaṇamupalakṣaṇam , yasya yāvati pūrṇārthakriyā samāptiriti yāvat / sukhādīnām antaḥkaraṇaikavedyatāpādanameva nirmāṇam / na ca kumbhakāre prāṇapuryaṣṭabuddhiśūnyadehaprāye tadetat sthitam , etasyāpi jaḍatvāt / tataḥ saṃvideva viśvamātmani bhāsayati śaktivaicitryāt / tasya kasyāpi iti pūrvamuktasya acintyāparyanuyojyamahimna ityarthaḥ / naca vācyam ubhayendriyavedyatvamapi sadasad vā iti / yato'yamatra paramārthaḥ ---- yathā darpaṇāntaḥ kumbhakāranirvartyamānaghaṭādipratibimbe darpaṇasyaiva tathābhāsanamahimā , tathā svapnadarśane saṃvidaḥ , tathāpi tanmahimnaiva etena idaṃ bahiḥ sphuṭarūpaṃ kriyata ityabhimāna ullasati / evaṃ saṃvinmahimnā kumbhakṛti daṇḍacakrādau ghaṭe sthite tanmahimnaiva abhimāno jāyate ; yathā mayā idaṃ kṛtam , anena idaṃ kṛtam , mama hṛdaye sphuritam , asya hṛdaye sphuritamiti / tatra jaḍasya mṛdāderdūrāpeto'bhimāna iti saṃvitsvabhāve kartṛtvaṃ vyavasthāpyate / nanu bhāvarūpameva itthaṃ bhāsyatāṃ kiṃ dvayendriyavedyatvenoktamatra , sphuṭamarthakriyākṣamaṃ rūpamanenoktam , ---- iti ko virodhaḥ //4//
children.translated_text: Even before [the external production], in the heart of the potter — due to being within the range of the internal organ — with the sole identity of self-awareness, the universe that revolves in a differentiated-yet-non-differentiated manner, pulsating variously — the being-cognizable by both the internal and external faculties that is manifested — this alone is the cause-and-effect relation. The word 'ubhaya' (both) is illustrative, meaning: [the process continues] until the complete accomplishment of purposeful activity. The mere bringing into cognizability by the internal organ alone of pleasure and such is [itself] creation. And this does not rest in the potter, who consists mostly of <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), <s>puryaṣṭaka</s> (subtle body), intellect, void, and body — since even he is insentient. Therefore, consciousness alone manifests the universe in itself, through the variety of its powers. 'Tasya kasyāpi' (of some [being]) means: of the one previously described, whose glory is inconceivable and unquestionable. And it should not be objected that the being-cognizable-by-both-faculties is also either existent or non-existent. For this is the ultimate truth here: just as in the reflection of a pot being fashioned within a mirror, it is the glory of the mirror alone that appears thus; and just as in dream-vision it is [the glory] of consciousness — yet even so, by that very glory, the conceit arises that 'this is being made externally in clear form by this [agent].' Similarly, by the glory of consciousness, when the pot stands in the potter's wheel, stick, and such, by that very glory the conceit arises: 'this was made by me,' 'this was made by him,' 'it flashed in my heart,' 'it flashed in his heart.' Therein, since the conceit is far removed from the insentient clay and such, agency is established in what has consciousness as its nature. Objection: Let the nature of entities be manifested just so — what is the point of stating 'cognizability by both faculties'? He has stated the form that is clearly capable of purposeful activity — so what contradiction is there? // 4 //

children.text: anena ca vicāreṇa prakṛtamapi kriyāsvarūpaṃ siddhaṃ bhavati , ---- iti darśayati
children.translated_text: And he shows that by this very investigation, the nature of action that is the present subject is also established:

children.text: evam ekā kriyā saiṣā sakramāntarbahiḥ sthitiḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, this one action — the internal-external abiding with sequence —
has been established as belonging to one and the same [being] who is capable of bearing both forms.
'it is untenable both in its own nature and in its substratum' —

children.text: iti upālambhaḥ kṛtaḥ , sā upapattyā sthāpitā / yataḥ saṃvidrūpādāntarāt prabhṛti indriyagocaratayā bahiṣparyantatayā sthitirābhāsanārūpā , tata eva vedyātmakakarmāliṅganena sakramā tāvadupapannā , kartṛkarmaikāśrayatādātmyācca ekā / sa caika āśrayaḥ saṃvidrūpatvena svacchatvasvatantratvābhyāmubhayamapyantarbahīrūpaṃ sahata iti //5//
children.translated_text: this censure was made — that [action] has been established by reasoning. Since the abiding, which is of the nature of manifestation, extends from the internal — which is of the nature of consciousness — up to the external, as cognizable by the sense organs; and therefore, through the embrace of the object that has the nature of the knowable, it is first of all sequential; and due to the identity of the single substratum of agent and object, it is one. And that single substratum, being of the nature of consciousness, through transparency and independence, tolerates both forms — the internal and the external. // 5 //
'Saiṣā' (this very one) — that of which

children.text: nanu bhavatu ghaṭādāvevaṃ , yatra tu bījāṅjurādau cetanānupraveśo na dṛśyate tatra kathaṃ bījasyaivāṅkuraḥ kāryo na bhavati ? ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Let it be so in the case of the pot and such, but where, as in the seed-sprout case, the entry of a conscious being is not observed — how can the sprout not be the effect of the seed itself? Anticipating this, he says:
Externally, that very thing's effect is what was internally, relative to what [it depends on];
and the twofold internal-external abiding is stated relative to the perceiver.
The perceiver alone is the cause; therefore, he, being established in the abiding of the twofold appearance,
is the single one established even of the effect — thus, the action of that single [being] has been set forth.

children.text: antarābhāsamānasya tathārūpāparityāgenaiva bahirābhāsanaṃ nirmāṇam / tataśca yad vastu yamapekṣya antarityuktaṃ tad vastu tasyaiva āntararūpaviparivṛttimātrasya bahiṣkāryaṃ bahiṣkaraṇārhaṃ bhavati / saṃvidrūpaṃ ca pramātāramapekṣya antarābhāsino bhāvāstadapekṣayaiva bāhyābhāsā iti tenaiva eteṣāṃ bahiṣkaraṇābhāsanaṃ yuktam /
children.translated_text: The external manifestation of what is being internally manifested is creation, without the abandonment of that very form. And therefore, whatever entity, in relation to whatever [other entity], is called 'internal' — the external effect of that very entity is nothing but the transformation of that internal form, worthy of being externalized. And relative to the perceiver, who is of the nature of consciousness, entities that are internally manifesting — relative to him alone they are externally manifesting — therefore, by him alone is their externalization and manifestation appropriate.

children.text: tataśca pramātaiva kāraṇaṃ bhavati na jaḍaḥ / hyarthe caḥ / yasmāt sa pramātā kāryasyāntarbahirābhāsanadvayanimittatayā sthitastena vinā tadapekṣasyābhāsadvayasyānupapatteḥ , tasmādekasya pramātureva na tu kathaṃcit jaḍasya uditā prasādhitarūpā kriyā nirmātṛtā bhavatīti //7//
children.translated_text: And therefore, the perceiver alone is the cause, not the insentient. The word 'hi' is in the sense of 'ca.' Since the perceiver is established as the ground of the twofold appearance — internal and external — of the effect, since the twofold appearance relative to him would be untenable without him — therefore, the action, i.e., creatorship, whose nature has been established, belongs to the one perceiver alone and not in any way to the insentient. // 7 //
He reinforces this very point:
For this very reason, even in the sprout, the Supreme Lord is accepted as the efficient cause;
and the causality of anything other than Him — such as the seed — is untenable.

children.text: yata evaṃ cetana eva nirmātā , ata eva naiyāyikādibhiraṅkurādau buddimāneva parameśvaro hetutvena iṣṭaḥ / nanu taiḥ nimittakāraṇatāsya aṅgīkṛtā kriyāvibhāgādikramāyātaparamāṇvādidvārakatayā , samavāyikāraṇanijāvayavārambhaparamparayā tu tata īśvarādanyasyāpi bījabhūmijalāderhetutā kathitā / satyam kathitā , sā tu nopapadyate , uktayuktyā jaḍasya hetutāyogāt ; tataśceśvara eva bījabhūmijalābhāsasāhityenāṅkurātmanā bhāsate , ---- itīyānatra paramārthaḥ //8//
children.translated_text: Since it is thus that only a conscious being is the creator, for this very reason, even the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others have accepted that the Supreme Lord, an intelligent being, is the cause of the sprout and such. Objection: By them, His efficient causality has been accepted through the intermediary of the material atoms and such, arrived at through the sequence of action-specific-quality and such; and through the succession of the material cause — the construction of parts from their own constituents — the causality of entities other than the Lord, such as the seed, soil, water, and such, has been stated. True, it has been stated; but that is untenable, since by the reasoning already given, the insentient cannot be a cause. And therefore, the Lord alone appears as the sprout, together with the appearances of seed, soil, and water — this is the ultimate truth here. // 8 //

children.text: nanuparidṛṣṭabījādivyatiriktabuddhimatkāraṇakalpanena vinā kimuparudhyata iti parasya bhrāntiṃ bhindannāha
children.translated_text: Now, without postulating an intelligent cause beyond the observed seed and such, what is impeded? — shattering the opponent's delusion, he says:
For thus, this potter, precisely by the arrangement that is sovereignty,
through the sequence of processing such-and-such clay and other [materials], would produce a pot.
'For thus' —

children.text: iti nidarśanopakrameṇa vyāptirevaṃbhūtaiva dṛṣṭā , ---- iti draḍhayati / jaḍā hetavaścetanapreritāḥ kāryaṃ kurvanti , mṛdādayo yadi hi sannidhānamātreṇa vidadhyuḥ kumbhakāreṇa kimatra kṛtyam / śivikastūpakādiparamparayā te janayanti ; sā ca kumbhakārāyattā iti cet siddhaṃ naḥ sādhyam ---- śivikasaṃpādane 'pi te cetanapreraṇāmapekṣante iti / tajjaḍakāraṇānāṃ cetanapreraṇāmantareṇa na kvacit kāryakāritvam / yadi hi syāt mṛdādīnāmapi syāt , iti ekānta eṣaḥ / tataśca yat acetanaṃ kāryakāri tat cetanāpekṣaṃ mṛdādaya iva , tathā ca vījādi , ---- iti svabhāvaḥ / acetanakāryakāritvaṃ hi kādācitkatvāt sanimittam , na cānyadasya nimittamupapadyate anupalambhāt , iti tat cetanapreraṇaṃ yadi na nimittīkuryāt vyāpakaviruddhamanimittakatvaṃ prasajyeta ; na ca yuktaṃ tat , mṛdādāvapi tasyaiva prasaṅgāt , iti siddhā vyāptiḥ / ataśca kumbhakadeva tatreśvaraḥ / tadetadāha ---- īśvararūpayā vyavasthayā yaḥ sa sa mṛddaṇḍacakrādīnāṃ saṃskāraḥ , mṛdo mardanaṃ , daṇḍasya praguṇatvaṃ , cakrasya parivartanam ityādiḥ , tadārambho yaḥ kramaḥ śivikastūpakādirūpaḥ , tena ghaṭaṃ niyogato janayati , nānyathā , ---- niyoge liṅ / kiṃ ca yadi na krudhyate vastutaḥ kumbhakāro'pi aiśvaryaiva svatantraviśvātmatārūpayā vyavasthayā mṛdādisaṃskārāpekṣayā pradarśitaniyatyabhidhānanijaśaktivijṛmbhāto janayet ; anyathā acetanā mṛdādayaḥ kathaṃ kumbhakārecchāmanurudhyeran ,
children.translated_text: by way of commencing an illustration, he reinforces that the pervasion has been observed to be precisely of this form. Insentient causes, being impelled by a conscious being, produce the effect. For if clay and such were to produce [the pot] by mere proximity alone, what role would the potter have here? They produce through the succession of <s>śivikā</s> (base-form), <s>stūpaka</s> (dome), and such. If it be said that this succession depends on the potter — then our thesis is established: even in accomplishing the <s>śivikā</s>, they require the impulsion of a conscious being. Therefore, insentient causes never produce effects without the impulsion of a conscious being. For if they could, then even clay and such on their own would do so — this is an absolute [rule]. And therefore: whatever insentient thing produces an effect requires a conscious agent, like clay and such — and so too seed and such — this is the invariable nature. For the causal efficacy of the insentient, being occasional, has a cause; and no other cause of it is tenable, since it is not perceived. Therefore, if it does not accept the impulsion of a conscious being as its cause, the consequence of causelessness — which pervades the contradictory — would follow. And that is not proper, since it would apply even to clay and such. Thus, the pervasion is established. And therefore, the potter-like [conscious being] there is the Lord. He states this: by the arrangement that is of the nature of the Lord — whatever that processing of clay, stick, wheel, and such is — the kneading of clay, the straightening of the stick, the revolving of the wheel, and such — that initiation of processing which has the form of <s>śivikā</s>, <s>stūpaka</s>, and such — by that sequence, he necessarily produces the pot, not otherwise — the optative mood is used in the sense of necessity. Moreover, if one does not become angry [at this analysis], in reality the potter too, precisely by the arrangement that is sovereignty — of the nature of independent universal selfhood — with dependence on the processing of clay and such, by the play of his own power described as the displayed regulation — would produce [the pot]; otherwise, how would the insentient clay and such conform to the potter's will?
Or would even threads not respect the desire for producing cloth?
And this too has been stated by this very <s>sūtra</s>:
'For thus' —

children.text: iti / nanvevaṃ kumbhakṛto nāsti kartṛtvam , ---- iti samutsīdet dharmādharmavyavasthā / yadi pratyeṣi yuktyāgamayoḥ tadevameva / tathāpi samastetaranirmāṇamadhya eva idamapi parameśvareṇaiva nirmitaṃ yadavicalastasya kumbhakārapaśormithyākartṛtvābhimānaḥ pratibhuva iva adhamarṇatābhimānaḥ / yadi punarīśvarasyecchaiva iyamīdṛśī
children.translated_text: thus. Objection: If so, the potter has no agency — and thus the system of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit) would collapse. If you attend to both reasoning and scripture, it is indeed so. Even so, in the midst of all other creation, this too has been created by the Supreme Lord alone — namely, the unwavering false conceit of agency in this bound soul the potter, like the false conceit of being a debtor in a guarantor. But if the Lord's will itself is such —
'Let this conceit not arise in him' —

children.text: iti , tadā nāsau kartā kaścit / tadidamapi uktaṃ sūterṇaiva
children.translated_text: then there is no agent whatsoever. And this too has been stated by the <s>sūtra</s> itself:
'For thus' —
thus. Even for the potter,

children.text: mṛdādisaṃskāra krameṇa kiṃ ghaṭaṃ janayāmi , uta na janayāmi
children.translated_text: 'Shall I produce a pot through the sequence of processing clay and such, or shall I not produce it?' —

children.text: iti ya ekapakṣaniścayāya saṃpraśnātmā vicāraḥ , sa īśvarasaṃnamdhina eva vividhāt svarūpāvacchādanatattvaprakāśanarūpāt avasthānāt , ---- iti saṃpraśne liṅ / tasmāt vastuta
children.translated_text: this deliberation, which is a questioning for the purpose of determining one position — that arises from the Lord's connection alone, from the variegated condition whose nature is the concealment and revelation of one's own true nature — the optative mood is used in the sense of questioning. Therefore, in reality,

children.text: īśvara eva sarvatra kartā , ahaṃ ca sa eva
children.translated_text: the Lord alone is the agent everywhere, and I am He.

children.text: iti na parimite kartā , api tu sarvatra kartā , ---- iti etāvati sarvathā hṛdayena avadhātavyam iti sthitam //9//
children.translated_text: thus, he is not an agent in a limited [domain], but rather an agent everywhere — to this extent one must attend with full heart from all sides. This is established. //9//

children.text: dṛśyate 'sya cetanasya svātantryameva sarvatra jambhamāṇaṃ jaḍānapi yat svātmatāmāpādayati , na tu jaḍānāṃ vastvantarāviṣkaraṇe sāmarthyam , ---- iti yaduktaṃ , tat sarvavādiprasiddhanidarśanena draḍhayati
children.translated_text: The freedom of this conscious being, which yawns forth everywhere and brings even the insentient to the status of being its own self, is seen; but the insentient have no capacity to reveal another entity — what has been stated [thus], that he strengthens through an illustration well-known to all philosophical schools:
Even for <s>yogins</s>, by the force of will alone, without clay or seed,
pots and such are born — producing stable, specific causal efficacies. //

children.text: yadiha cetanapreritaṃ kāraṇam iti prasiddhaṃ mṛdādi , yacca tadanapekṣaṃ bījādi ghaṭaāderaṅkurādeśca janakaṃ , tadeva yadi paramārthataḥ kāraṇaṃ syāt tat tadvyatirekeṇa ghaṭāṅkurādeḥ kathaṃ yogīcchāmātreṇa janma syāt , akāraṇakatvaprasaṅgāt teṣāṃ vā akāraṇatvaprasaṃgāt / athocyate ---- anye eva te ghaṭāṅkurādayo mṛddhījādijanyāḥ , anye eva ca yogīcchādijanyāḥ , ---- iti , tatrāpi prabodhyase ---- vimarśābhedāt tāvadabheda , ---- iti pūrvameva uktam ; tatrāpi yogī khalu apratihatecchaḥ , tasya ca icchā tādṛgeva ghaṭo bhavatu yo mṛdādikṛtakumbhasaṃbhavabhūryarthakriyākaraṇacaturavṛttiriti / tadetadāha ---- tasya tasya sthirasya arthakriyāviśeṣasya karaṇe hetutacchīlānukūlarūpaṃ ghaṭādi jāyate , ---- iti / ye tvāhuḥ ---- nopādānaṃ vinā ghaṭādyutpattiḥ , yogī tu icchayā paramāṇūn paśyan saṃghaṭṭayatīti / te vācyāḥ ---- yadi khalu anvayavyatirekāgamādiparidṛṣṭaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo yogiṣu na viparyeti , ---- iti hṛdayamāvarjayati vaḥ tat kiṃ paramāṇugraheṇa ; no cet ghaṭasya kapālāni śarīrasya svāvayavāḥ , teṣāṃ nijaṃ nijaṃ prasiddhaṃ tṛṇaśastilaśo 'pi anyathābhavabanasahamānaṃ laukikameva kāraṇam , iti ghaṭe mṛddaṇḍacakrādi , dehe strīpuruṣasaṃyogādi ubhayamapekṣyaṃ dehādisaṃbhavo duḥsamartha eva / cetana eva tu tathā tathā bhavati / bhagavān bhūribhargo mahādevo niyatyanuvartanollaṅghanatarasvātantryaḥ , ---- ityatra pakṣe niyatyanuvartinaḥ laukike prasiddhe kāryakāraṇabhāve svātantryaṃ , tadullaṅghanamādriyamāṇasya tu yogiprāyaprasiddhe lokottare , ---- iti na kaścit virodhaḥ / iyāṃśca loke eva / paramārthatastu sa eva kramākramarūpaviśvasṛṣṭyādikrṭyapañcakaprapañcasvabhāvaḥ prakāśate / cetano hi svātmadarpaṇe bhāvān pratibimbavadābhāsayati iti siddhāntaḥ / yadāha pūrvaguruḥ
children.translated_text: Here, if what is well-known — clay and such — is a cause set in motion by a conscious being, and if seed and such, which produce sprouts independently of that [clay], are indeed the ultimate cause of pots and sprouts — then how, without those, could pots and sprouts be born by the mere will of a <s>yogin</s>? — since the unwanted consequence of being without a cause would arise for them, or the unwanted consequence of those [materials] being non-causes. And if it is said 'the pots and sprouts born from clay, seeds, and such are entirely different from those born from a <s>yogin</s>'s will' — even there, you are to be informed: 'due to the non-difference of reflective grasping, there is non-difference' — as was stated earlier. And moreover, the <s>yogin</s> has unobstructed will, and his will is: 'let there be a pot exactly like one produced from clay by a potter, one that has stable and abundant causal efficacy.' This he states: pots and such are born that are of a form favorable to producing that particular stable causal efficacy. But those who say 'without a material cause, the production of pots and such is impossible; the <s>yogin</s> merely sees the atoms through his will and makes them combine' — they are to be addressed: if indeed the cause-effect relation observed through positive and negative concomitance, scripture, and such does not reverse in the case of <s>yogins</s> — if this wins your heart, then what need of grasping atoms? If not — the pot's sherds, the body's own parts — each of these has its own well-known mundane cause, which does not tolerate being otherwise even to the extent of a blade of grass or a sesame seed — thus, for the pot, clay, rod, wheel, and such; for the body, the union of man and woman and such — both must be relied upon, and the possibility of production of the body and such is quite impossible [without them]. But the conscious being alone becomes thus and thus. The Blessed One, <s>Mahādeva</s> (the Great God), of most brilliant splendor, has the supreme freedom of both following and transgressing regulation (<s>niyati</s>). In this position — for the mundane, well-known cause-effect relation that follows regulation, there is freedom; and for the extraordinary [cause-effect relation] well-known through <s>yogin</s>-like cases, which favors the transgression of regulation — there is no contradiction whatsoever. And this [distinction exists] only in the world. In ultimate truth, He alone shines, His essential nature being the fivefold display of creative activities — sequential and non-sequential — of universal creation and such. For the established doctrine is: the conscious being manifests entities in the mirror of His own Self, like reflections. As the former guru stated:
{To Him who, without material cause or auxiliary,
paints the variegated universe upon a wall-less [surface] — to that glorious trident-bearer, obeisance! //} (<s>Stavacintāmaṇi</s>, verse 9)

children.text: nanu yadi prasiddhakāraṇollaṅghanenāpi tatkāryaviśeṣatulyavṛttānyeva kāryāṇi jāyante , bhagnāstarhi anumānakathāḥ / tathā hi mathamanyadanyatra niyamavadbhavet ityāśaṅkya prāmāṇikatarammanyaistādātmyatadutpattī niyamanidānamupagate / na hi niḥsvabhāvaṃ vastu bhavati , nāpi bhinnasvabhāvaṃ svabhāvabhedena bhedāt / paryāyaśastatsvabhāvadvayābhāve ca niḥsvabhāvatāprasaṅgāt / evaṃ nirhetuke bhinnahetuke ca kārye vācyam / ubhayatrāpi ca hetukṛtaiva vyavasthā / svahetuta eva hi śiṃśapā vṛkṣasvabhāvāvyabhicāriṇī jātā , svahetutaśca hutabhugdhūmajananasvabhāvaḥ , tadidānīṃ niyatyullaṅghini kāryakāraṇabhāve sarvamidaṃ vighaṭeta / yogīcchayā hi śiṃśapāpi avṛkṣasvabhāvā bhavet , dhūme tu dviguṇaṃ codyam ; agnyādisāmagrī yogīcchodbhūtā dhūmaṃ na janayet , yogīcchā vā anagnikaṃ dhūmam , ---- iti na syādanumānam , asti ca talloke , ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If products of the very same kind as those specific effects are born even through transgression of the well-known cause, then the discourse of inference is broken! For what obtains here in one way should obtain elsewhere in the same way, with the same restriction. Anticipating this — identity and origination-from-that are accepted by those who consider themselves most authoritative as the basis of restriction. For an entity cannot be without essential nature, nor can it have a different essential nature, since difference [would follow] from difference of essential nature. And in the absence of both those essential natures through interchangeability, the unwanted consequence of having no essential nature [would follow]. The same should be said regarding an effect that is without cause or with a different cause. And in both cases, the determination is caused by the cause alone. For the <s>śiṃśapā</s> (rosewood) tree is born from its own cause as invariably concomitant with the tree-nature, and fire from its own cause is of the nature of generating smoke. Now, if the cause-effect relation transgresses regulation, all this would be destroyed. For by a <s>yogin</s>'s will, even a <s>śiṃśapā</s> could become non-tree-natured; and regarding smoke, the objection is twofold — the aggregate of fire and such produced by a <s>yogin</s>'s will might not produce smoke, or a <s>yogin</s>'s will might produce fireless smoke — and so there would be no inference. But inference does exist in the world — anticipating this, he says:
In the absence of yogic creation, ascertained by other means of valid knowledge,
the effect is the logical reason; or the essential nature — that itself, born from the root of origination. //

children.text: yogīcchāpi sarvathā tādṛśameva na tu vṛścikagomayādisaṃbhūtavṛścikādinyāyena kathaṃcit rasavīryādinā bhinnaṃ kāryaṃ janayati , ---- iti yat kathitamata evāsymādeva hetoḥ kāryaṃ vā dhūmādi agnyādyanumāne , śiṃśapātvādisvabhāvo vā vṛkṣatvādyanumāne evaṃ heturbhavati / yadi pramāṇāntareṇa evānumāne janmāntarābhyāsalokaprasiddhyādikamavaśyopajīvyam , sā ca śrutānumānaprajñayorbījam , ---- iti ca ṛtaṃbharāviṣayamuvāca patañjaliḥ / anye ca yauktikā yogipratyakṣakalpapratyakṣasadbhāvaṃ samastavastugrahaṇāya kalpitavantaḥ / sāṃvyavahārike ca pramāṇe nāsmākaṃ bharaḥ , prakṛtaṃ hi asmākamīśvarasvarūpam , tacca svaprakāśameva , prameyoparodhe 'pi noparudhyata ityuktamasakṛt / nanu svabhāvahetau kimanyā cintayā ? , āha ---- vṛkṣatvāvyabhicāriṇyāḥ śiṃśapāyā utpatteryanmūlaṃ kāraṇaṃ tata eva sa sanmātrānubandhī svabhāvo jāyate , ---- iti ; tataśca
children.translated_text: A <s>yogin</s>'s will does not, in any case, produce an effect that is somehow different — as in the case of scorpions born from cow-dung, where there is a difference of taste, potency, and such — this has been stated; from this very cause, the effect such as smoke is a [logical] reason in the inference of fire; or the essential nature such as <s>śiṃśapā</s>-hood is a reason in the inference of tree-hood — and thus becomes a logical reason. If, for the validity of inference, one must necessarily rely upon another means of valid knowledge — such as the practice from other births, common worldly knowledge, and such — then that is the seed of the knowledge [arising from] heard tradition and inference, as <s>Patañjali</s> stated regarding the domain of <s>ṛtaṃbharā</s> (truth-bearing wisdom). And others, the logicians, have postulated the existence of quasi-perceptual <s>yogic</s> perception for the grasping of all entities. And with regard to conventional valid cognition, we bear no burden, for our topic is the essential nature of the Lord; and that is self-luminous — even when the knowable is obstructed, it is not obstructed, as has been stated repeatedly. Objection: In the case of the essential-nature reason, what need of further inquiry? Reply: The root, the cause, of the origination of the <s>śiṃśapā</s>, which is invariably concomitant with tree-nature — from that very thing, that essential nature, connected with mere existence, is born. And therefore:
{The transition from form and such, which depend on a single aggregate, to taste —
is through inference by the essential-nature-based logical reason — like the transformation of smoke and fuel. //}

children.text: iti svabhāvaheturnyāyaḥ / nanu ca vṛścikādīnāṃ kīṭagomayādyanekakāraṇakatvaṃ tāvat dṛṣṭaṃ , rasavīryādibhedastu tatra , ---- ityanyadetat / tadyogijanyatvamvahnikasyāpi dhūmasya sahyaṃ nāma , svabhāvasya tu kathaṃ viparyāsasaṃbhāvanā / na hi nīlaṃ sadevānīlaṃ yogīcchayā bhavati , ---- iti kaścit prāmāṇikaḥ pratīyāt / ucyate / iha dvividho hi svabhāvaheturantarlīnakāryakāraṇabhāvastadviparītaśca ; vahnimānayaṃ parvato dhūmavattvāt iti , anityo 'yaṃ kṛtakatvāt iti / tatra ādyasya tāvat kāryakāraṇabhāva eṣa mūlam ---- iti kiṃ tatrocyate / aparastu vicāryate , yadi tāvat kṛtakatvasya kāraṇāyattatvaṃ nāma svabhāvaḥ katham abhavanaparicchinnabhavanasvabhāvatā nāmānityatvaṃ svabhāvaḥ syāt ābhāsabhedāt / abhede tu ābhāsasya hetusiddhāveva sādhyasya siddhatvāt , yadi paraṃ vyavahāraḥ sādhyate , tarurayaṃ vṛkṣatvāt , ---- iti nyāyena , vyavahāraśca jñānābhidhānātmā kāryaṃ eva , tatra ca niyatiśaktiraṅgīkrṭā bhavatāpi / tasmāt sarveṣu svabhāvahetuṣvābhāsabhedaṃ vinā vyavahāramātrasādhanameva , hetvābhāsamayatvādevānadhiko hi tatra sādhyābhāsaḥ , vyāvṛttīnāmeṣaiva vārtā , sāmānyānāmiyameva saraṇiḥ / tasmāt niyataḥ śiṃśapābhāsavṛkṣābhāsayoḥ pūrvanītyā sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāso hetubalāt ! tataḥ svabhāvo'yaṃ hetuhetumadbhāvamūla eva , tata eva sāmānyenedamuktaṃ draṣṭavyaṃ ---- sarvaḥ svabhāvaheturutpattimūlajaḥ , ---- iti / ābhāsā eva ca vastu , ---- iti ca samarthitaṃ prāk / tataśca śiṃśapāyāmekasyāmeva sṛjyamānāyāṃ śākhādimadarthāntarāṇāmasṛṣṭervṛkṣābhāsasya sāmānyātmanaḥ sādhyasya nāmāpi nāsti , ---- iti saṃbhāvyata eva / yattu tadekarūpaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ vṛkṣatvaṃ tat khalu śiṃśapātvameva tacca siddham , ---- iti na sādhyam / kāraṇāyattamidam , ---- ityābhāse 'pi na syādanityatābhāsaḥ / evamarthakriyākāritvābhāve 'pi kṣaṇikatvābhāsābhāvaḥ iti niyatyapekṣayaiva sarve svabhāvahetavo nānyathā , ---- ityekānta eṣaḥ //11//
children.translated_text: — this is the method of the essential-nature reason. Objection: But for scorpions and such, multiple causation from insects, cow-dung, and such is indeed observed; the difference of taste and potency is there — but that is another matter. Let the fire born from a <s>yogin</s> also produce smoke — that can be tolerated; but how can there be a supposition of reversal of essential nature? For no authoritative person would accept that what is blue could become non-blue by a <s>yogin</s>'s will. Reply: Here, the essential-nature reason is of two kinds — one with a concealed cause-effect relation, and its opposite. 'This mountain possesses fire, because of having smoke' — and 'this is impermanent, because of being produced.' Therein, the first has as its root this cause-effect relation — so what is to be said about it? But the second is examined: if the essential nature of being-produced is having-a-cause, how can the essential nature of impermanence — the nature of being delimited by non-existence — be its essential nature, given the difference of appearances? But if there is non-difference of appearance, then the thesis is established upon the establishment of the reason — and if only practical transaction is to be proven, then by the method 'this is a tree, because of tree-ness,' practical transaction — which is of the nature of knowledge and designation — is itself an effect, and therein the power of regulation (<s>niyati-śakti</s>) is accepted even by you. Therefore, in all essential-nature reasons, without the difference of appearances, it is merely practical transaction that is proven. For the thesis-appearance, being constituted by the reason-appearance alone, is nothing more than it. This is the account of exclusions (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>); this is the path of universals. Therefore, the co-referentiality-appearance of the <s>śiṃśapā</s>-appearance and the tree-appearance is regulated in the previously stated manner, by the force of the reason! Therefore, this essential-nature [reason] is rooted in the cause-reason relation itself, and therefore what was stated should be understood as applying generally — 'every essential-nature reason is born from the root of origination.' And appearances alone are the real thing — this too has been justified earlier. Therefore, when a single <s>śiṃśapā</s> is being created, since other entities such as branches and such are not created, the tree-appearance — which is of the nature of a universal and is the thesis — does not even have a name, and this is to be expected. But the specific tree-nature that is of one form — that is indeed <s>śiṃśapā</s>-nature itself, and that is already established — so it is not the thesis. 'This is dependent on the cause' — even this appearance of impermanence would not exist. Similarly, even in the absence of the appearance of causal efficacy, the appearance of momentariness would not exist. Thus, all essential-nature reasons are dependent on the power of regulation alone, and not otherwise — this is the definitive conclusion. //11//

children.text: nanvābhāsavastutvavāde 'nābhātasay agneravastutvam , ---- ityanābhātena kathaṃ dhūmo janyate , tataśca dhūmādagneḥ kāraṇasya kathamanumānam ? ityāśaṅkya samrathayitumāha
children.translated_text: Objection: In the doctrine that appearances are the real thing, fire that has not appeared is unreal — so how is smoke produced from unappeared fire? And thus, how can fire as the cause be inferred from smoke? Anticipating this, in order to justify [it], he says:
Repeatedly, from a single fire-appearance in such-and-such perceivers,
the new smoke-appearance and such would arise — even from the hidden [fire-appearance] of the sovereign. //

children.text: ekavāraṃ tāvat mahānase pratyakṣānupalambhabalenāgnyābhāsadhūmābhāsayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo gṛhītaḥ / tatra vijñānavādino darśane pratisantānamanyaścānyaścābhāsaḥ , ---- iti svābhāsayoreva kāryakāraṇatā gṛhītā na tu santānāntaragatayostadīyavṛttāntasyāsaṃvedanāt / tataścedānīmanumānaṃ na bhavet svasantānagatāt dhūmābhāsāt krimisarvajñādipramātṛsantānāntaraniṣṭhasyāgnyābhāsasya iti niścayaḥ / iha tu darśane vyāptigrahaṇāvasthāyāṃ yāvantastaddeśasaṃbhāvyamānasadbhāvāḥ pramātārastāvatāmeko'sau dhūmābhāsaśca vahnyābhāsaśca vāhyanaye iva , tāvati teṣāṃ parameśvareṇaikyaṃ nirmitam , ---- iti hi uktam / tataḥ svaparasantānaviśeṣatyāgena dhūmābhāsamātraṃ vahnyābhāsamātrasya kāryam , ---- iti vyāptau gṛhītāyāṃ bhūyo'pi parvate yo dhūmābhāsaḥ so 'pi agnyābhāsādeva iti vyāptiṃ smṛtvānuimimīte

children.translated_text: 'there is a fire-appearance here on the mountain.' —

children.text: iti / tāvati dhūmābhāsaviśeṣe pramātrantaraiḥ sahaikībhūya vahnyābhāsasāmānyāṃśe parokṣarūpāṃśasahite viśeṣābhāsāntaravivikte pramātrantaraiḥ sākamekībhavati , iti yāvat /
children.translated_text: To that extent — in the specific smoke-appearance, one who has become unified with other perceivers — with respect to the general aspect of the fire-appearance which includes the hidden aspect, being distinguished from other specific appearances — becomes unified with other perceivers. This is the import.
'Repeatedly' (<s>bhūyaḥ</s>) —

children.text: iti vyāptiṃ gṛhītvā punarapi yo dhūmābhāsaḥ , ādigrahaṇādaṅkurābhāsādirgṛhyate so'pyābhāso nūtano 'pūrvo na tu dhūmajadhūmavadapratyagraḥ / sa ca adhipaterasaṃcetyamānāt vahnyābhāsāt bījābhāsādeva vā bhavet tata eva janituṃ śaknoti nānyataḥ / śaki liṅ / sa cābhāsasteṣu teṣu pramātṛṣveka eva , anekatve na tu yujyate evaitadityāśayaḥ / yataśca sa eko'dhipatiśca vahnyābhāso dhūmakāraṇaṃ , tato dhūmābhāso'syaivāgnyābhāsasyāvyabhicāritaṃ kāryaṃ liṅgaṃ yogikṛtatvābhāve niścite sati , ---- iti tasmāt kāryāt so 'numīyate yataḥ parokṣo 'sāvadhipatitvādeva //12//
children.translated_text: having grasped the concomitance, the smoke-appearance that [arises] again — and by the word 'ādi' (etc.), the sprout-appearance and such — that appearance too is new, unprecedented — not stale like smoke born from [previous] smoke. And it would arise from the fire-appearance of the sovereign [Lord] that is not perceived — or from the seed-appearance — from that alone it is capable of being born, not from anything else. And that appearance is one and the same in all those perceivers; in multiplicity, this would not be tenable — this is the intention. And since that one fire-appearance which is the sovereign is the cause of smoke, therefore the smoke-appearance is the invariable effect — the logical reason (<s>liṅga</s>) — of this very fire-appearance, when the absence of yogic creation has been ascertained. Therefore, from that effect, it is inferred — since it is hidden, precisely because it is the sovereign. //12//

At one time in the kitchen, through the force of direct perception and non-perception, the cause-effect relation of fire-appearance and smoke-appearance has been grasped. Therein, in the Buddhist idealist view, since one appearance after another is distinct in each continuum, the cause-effect relation is grasped only between one's own appearances — not between those belonging to another continuum, since one is not aware of their state of affairs. And therefore, at this time, there would be no inference — from a smoke-appearance in one's own continuum — of a fire-appearance belonging to the continuum of another perceiver such as an insect, an omniscient being, and such — this is the conclusion. But in our view, at the stage of grasping the invariable concomitance, all the perceivers whose existence is supposed at that place — for all of them, that smoke-appearance and fire-appearance are one and the same, just as in the doctrine of external objects. For that many [perceivers], their unity has been created by the Supreme Lord — this has been stated. Therefore, abandoning the specification of one's own or another's continuum, having grasped the concomitance that the mere smoke-appearance is the effect of the mere fire-appearance — subsequently, that smoke-appearance on the mountain too is from the fire-appearance alone — remembering the concomitance, one infers:

children.text: nanvevaṃ gopālaghaṭikāntarālaciroṣitanirgatādapi dhūmābhāsāt syāt vahnyābhāsānumānam , ---- ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: In this case, even from a smoke-appearance [coming] from within an enclosed <s>gopāla</s> pot where [fire has] long resided and been extinguished, there would be an inference of a fire-appearance. Anticipating this, he says:
The effect of what is invariable is a logical reason; belonging to another perceiver,
that appearance [arises] from that very [cause-]appearance of the sovereign, which is other [than what is perceived]. //

children.text: paro nūtanādanyo yo dhūmābhāsaḥ sa dhūmābhāsādeva pramātrantaravartino'dhipatirūpāt parokṣāt , ---- iti tathābhūtāt dhūmābhāsāt kathamakāraṇabhūto vahnyābhāso'numīyatām ityabhiprāyaśeṣaḥ / kuśalāśca lakṣayantyeva vivekam , asyārthasyānumānikathahutaravyavahāropayogino yatnena vyutpattiḥ kāryā , ---- ityāśayena nūtanamiti yatsūcitaṃ tadeva vyavacchedyadvāreṇa sphuṭīkṛtam //13//
children.translated_text: The other — the smoke-appearance that is different from the new one — is one residing in another perceiver, of the nature of a sovereign, and not directly perceived. Thus, how could a fire-appearance that is not a cause be inferred from a smoke-appearance of such a nature? — this is the remainder of the intention. And the skillful indeed discern the distinction: 'The understanding of this matter, which is useful for the practical application of inferring fire, must be carefully cultivated' — with this intention, what was hinted at by the word 'novel' has been made explicit through what is to be excluded. //13//

children.text: nanu caivaṃ dhūmābhāso vahnyābhāsāt , ---- ityaṅgīkṛtaṃ cet tarhi cetanasyaiva kartṛtvam , ---- iti yaduktaṃ tat kathaṃ ? tathāhi

children.translated_text: 'When the seed exists, the sprout arises' —

children.text: iti yadetat dṛṣṭaṃ dhūmāgnivadeva tat kathamanādarāspadam ? ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: this which is observed — just like smoke and fire — how can it be disregarded? Anticipating this, he says:

Objection: If the smoke-appearance [is accepted as arising] from the fire-appearance — if this is accepted, then how can it be that agency belongs to a conscious being alone, as was stated? For indeed,
Even the causality of the form 'when this exists, that exists'
is not tenable for insentient things that are devoid of mutual dependence.

children.text: eka eva bhāvastāvat na kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ , bhāvadvayamapi ca na yugapadbhāvi kāryakāra.anarūpaṃ ghaṭapaṭavat , kramabhāvyapi nāniyatakramakaṃ nīlapītādijñānavat , niyatakramikatve 'pi na pūrvabhāvi kāryamuttarakālabhāvi ca kāraṇam , ---- ityevaṃ niyatapūrvabhāvaṃ kāraṇaṃ niyataparabhāvaṃ ca kāryam , ---- iti parasya tāvanmatam / tatra svarūpādanadhikā cet pūrvatā paratā ca tat bhāvadvayamātraṃ sa ca sa ca , ---- iti / cārtho 'pi vā na kaścit tasyāpyapekṣārūpatvāt sa sa ityeva hi syāt / atha pūrvatā nāma prayojakasattākatvaṃ paratā ca prayojyasattākatvaṃ tarhi vījasyāṅkuraprayoktrī sattā aṅkuraviśrāntā aṅkurāntarbhāvamātmanyānayati , aṅkurābhāve prayoktṛtvamātraṃ syāt tadapi na kiṃcit anyāpekṣatvāt tasya / evaṃ prayojyasattāke'pi vaktavyam / evaṃ na kevalaṃ bhāvamātrameva kāryakāraṇatā ityādayaḥ pakṣā nopapannā , yāvat

children.translated_text: 'this exists' —

children.text: iti bhāvyamānavibhaktyā prayojyasattākatvam , ---- ityevaṃ rūpāpi yā kāryakāraṇatā sāpi nopapadyate pramāṇena na saṃbhavati jaḍānām , anyonyāpekṣā hi atra jīvitaṃ sā ca jaḍānāṃ na saṃbhavati //14//
children.translated_text: the cause-and-effect relation expressed through the locative case-ending indicating the nature of produced existence — even that is not tenable, it is not possible through a valid means of knowledge, for insentient things. For the life-principle here is mutual dependence (<s>apekṣā</s>), and that is not possible for insentient things. //14//

A single entity, to begin with, is not the cause-and-effect relation. And even two entities do not exist simultaneously as cause and effect, like a pot and a cloth. Even if they exist in sequence, they are not of an indeterminate sequence, like the cognitions of blue and yellow. Even when the sequence is fixed, the effect is not the prior one and the cause is not the subsequent one. Thus, the cause is of a fixed prior nature and the effect is of a fixed posterior nature — this is the opponent's view. Therein, if priority and posteriority are nothing more than their own essential nature, then [there are] merely two entities — that one and that one — and nothing more. Or even the word 'and' [connecting them] would be nothing, since even that is of the nature of mutual dependence — [there would be] merely 'that, that.' If priority means having the nature of productive existence and posteriority means having the nature of produced existence, then the existence of the seed that is productive of the sprout, resting in the sprout, brings the sprout's inclusion into itself. In the absence of the sprout, there would be mere productive-ness — and even that would be nothing, since it depends on another [i.e., the product]. Similarly, this should be stated regarding what has the nature of produced existence. Thus, not only is the position that mere being alone is the cause-and-effect relation untenable, but even
How so? If asked, it is said:
For of those that rest solely in their own selves and are devoid of connected awareness,
even in the case of existence and non-existence, this locative meaning cannot be postulated.

children.text: jaḍāḥ kilānyonyarūpamanusandhātumaprabhaviṣṇavaḥ , anyonyānusaṃdhānarūpatvaṃ jaḍaviruddhena caitanyena vyāptam , anusaṃdhānaṃ cāpekṣā caitanyasvarūpameva , anyatra tu sopacaritā / ato 'nusandhānavihīnatvājjaḍo bhāvaḥ svātmamātraviśrāntisantoṣasaṃkucitaśarīraḥ kathaṃ paratra prasaret / tataśca yadi bījaṃ sadaṅkuro'san athāpi viparyaya ubhayamapi vā sat yadi vāsat , athāpi ekaṃ sopākhyamanyat nirupākhyam , dvayamapi vā sopākhyaṃ nirupākhyaṃ vā , tathāpi prātipadikārthamātraṃ dharmāntarreṇa samuccayādināpyanāliṅgitamavatiṣṭhate , tasya samastasyāpekṣārūpatvena caitanyaviśrāntatvāt //15//
children.translated_text: Insentient things, indeed, are incapable of connecting awareness of each other's nature. The nature of being a mutual connection is pervaded by consciousness, which is opposed to inertness. Connected awareness and dependence are of the very nature of consciousness, while in other [insentient] things they are merely figurative. Therefore, an insentient entity, being devoid of connected awareness, with its body contracted in the satisfaction of resting in its own self alone — how could it extend to another? And therefore, whether the seed exists and the sprout does not exist, or the reverse, or both exist, or both do not exist; or one has a name and the other is nameless, or both have names or both are nameless — even so, it remains merely the nominal-stem meaning, standing without being embraced by conjunction with any other property or such. For all of this, being of the nature of dependence, rests in consciousness. //15//
since dependence does not apply to the insentient —
for this very reason, the case-ending meaning, whose sole ground is the perceiver,
the connection of entities called the relation of action and case-relations (<s>kriyā-kāraka</s>) — that alone is proper.

children.text: saptamīrūpāyā vibhakteranyasyā api vā yo'rthaḥ kriyākārakabhāvalakṣaṇaḥ sa eva tāvadbhāvānāṃ samanvayo nānyaḥ śuṣkaḥ kaścit / sa ca yadi svatantre cidrūpe bhāvadvayaṃ viśrāmyati tadopapadyate , anyathā tu na kathaṃcit / tathā hi vikalpenāpi asau vyavahriyamāṇo na vastuniṣṭhatayopapadyate , vastvanusaraṇaprāṇo hi vikalpo 'nubhavānusāritayaiva bhavati , sā ceha nāsti vastvaprabhavatvena , vastvanusārī hi anubhavo , vastu ca syātmaniṣṭham ---- ityuktam / tasmāt bīje sati aṅkuro , bahnau sati dhūmaḥ , ---- iti ca svatrantracidrūpapramātṛviśrāntatve sarvametadyujyate nānyathā , iti //16//
children.translated_text: The meaning of the locative case-ending or of any other case-ending, whose nature is the relation of action and case-factors — that alone is the connection of entities, and nothing else devoid of content. And that is tenable if the two entities rest in an independent [being] whose nature is consciousness; otherwise, it is in no way possible. For even when that [causality] is expressed through conceptual construction, it is not tenable as resting in a real thing — since conceptual construction, whose life-force is following reality, exists only insofar as it follows experience, and that [experience-grounding] does not exist here, since it does not originate from a [real] thing. For experience follows reality, and reality rests solely in its own self — as has been stated. Therefore, 'when the seed exists, the sprout [arises],' 'when the fire exists, smoke [arises]' — all of this is proper when resting in an independent perceiver whose nature is consciousness, and not otherwise. //16//

children.text: nanu prayojyaprayojakasattākatālakṣaṇāpekṣā yadi svātmaikaniṣṭhatve nopapadyate , tarhi kāryakāraṇayostādātmyavādināṃ sāṃkhyānāṃ mate sā saṃbhavatyeva , tat kiṃ caitamyavijṛmbhātmakakartṛvādasamarthanena ? ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: If the dependence characterized by having the nature of productive and produced existence is not tenable when [things] rest solely in their own selves, then for the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> who hold the doctrine of identity of cause and effect, that dependence is indeed possible — so what is the need for justifying the doctrine of agency characterized by the display of consciousness? Anticipating this, he says:
Even in the mutual identity of cause and effect,
there would be mere unity; for in difference, there is simply no mutual identity.

children.text: yadi bījasyāṅkuraḥ svbhāvastarhi aṅkura eva na bījaṃ syāt kiṃcit viparyayo vā syāt , ---- iti kiṃ kāraṇaṃ kiṃ vā kāryam ; atha anyadvījamaṅkuro'nyaḥ , tarhi na parasparātmakatvam , bhedābhedau hi ekadaikaviṣayau viruddhāveva //17//
children.translated_text: If the sprout is the very nature of the seed, then there would be only a sprout and no seed at all — or the reverse — so what is the cause and what the effect? And if the seed is one thing and the sprout another, then there is no mutual identity. For difference and non-difference, [applied] simultaneously to a single object, are indeed contradictory. //17//

children.text: nanvevamapi bījamaṅkurādivicitramavabhātaṃ dīrghadīrghaparāmarśaśālibhiḥ srotovadavicchinnasvarūpameva nirbādhaṃ pratyavamṛśyate / tathā ca kva gataṃ vījam , ---- iti praśne vaktāro bhavanti , na kutracit gatamaṅkurātmanā vartate , aṅkurībhūtamayamaṅkurastat iti / evaṃ pradhānaṃ mahadādidharāntībhūtaṃ yāvadvitatībhūtamanantasargapralayaparamparātmatāṃ prāptam , ---- iti vitatagrāhiṇī pratītiḥ / bhāgābhiniveśavaśāt tu kāraṇakāryatāparikalpanaṃ tasyaiva bhāvasya viśasanaprāyam , ---- ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Even so, the seed, appearing variously as sprout and such, is unrestrainedly reflected upon by those of long and extended reflective awareness as having a nature continuous like a stream. And thus, to the question 'where has the seed gone?' — they answer: 'It has not gone anywhere; it exists in the form of the sprout; it has become a sprout — this sprout is that [seed].' Similarly, <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial nature), having become <s>Mahat</s> (great principle) and so on up to earth, as far as it has extended, having attained the identity of an infinite series of creations and dissolutions — this is the cognition of those who grasp the extended [continuum]. But the postulation of cause and effect due to attachment to parts is virtually a dissection of that very entity — anticipating this, he says:
The differentiation of what is of one nature is action, which follows the sequence of time;
and thus there would be agency — of that which transforms in such a way by that [action].

children.text: iha dīrghadarśinā pratyakṣānumānāgamānyatamapramāṇamūlāṃ pratyabhijñāmāśritya tadevedaṃ sukhaduḥkhamohasāmyamanantaprakāravaiṣamyāvalambanena viśvībhūtam , ---- iti samarthyate / tatra pratyabhijñānabalena yadekātmakamekasvabhāvaṃ tasya yo bhedo'nyānyarūpatā iyameva sā kriyocyate , yataḥ kālalakṣaṇena krameṇānugatā , te hi anyānyasvabhāvā yugapat na bhānti , pūrvāparībhūtarūpataiva ca kriyocyate / yata evaṃ kriyā

children.translated_text: 'tathā' (in that manner) —

children.text: iti tena prakāreṇa pradhānādeḥ kriyāviśeṣalakṣaṇena kartṛtaiva syāt , natu śuṣkaṃ kāraṇatāmātraṃ , yato hetoḥ
children.translated_text: by that manner, through the particular action characterizing <s>Pradhāna</s> and such, there would be agency — not mere dry causality alone. Because,
'tathā' (thus) —

children.text: iti tena tena mahadādiprakāreṇa satatameva krimikāṃ tathābhāsanarūpāṃ pariṇāmalakṣaṇāṃ kriyāmāviśataḥ pariṇamattā kiṃcidrūpaṃ parivarjya tyaktvā vyāvartyamanuvartanīyaṃ ca vyavasthāpya nirvartyamānatṛtīyarūpaprahvatā pradhānādestathā hetubhūtayā //18//
children.translated_text: by entering, in this and that manner of <s>Mahat</s> and such, the constantly sequential action characterized by transformation — the appearance of becoming-thus — the state of transforming: abandoning — i.e., relinquishing, i.e., separating from — a certain form, and establishing what is to be continued, the devotion to the third form that is being brought about — this [agency] belongs to <s>Pradhāna</s> and such as so caused. //18//

Here, by one of long vision, relying on recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) grounded in one or another valid means — perception, inference, or scripture — it is argued: 'This very thing has become the universe, resting upon pleasure, pain, delusion, equilibrium, and the infinite modes of disequilibrium.' Therein, by the force of recognition, the differentiation — the becoming-of-another-nature — of what is of one essence and one nature: this is called action (<s>kriyā</s>). Because it is accompanied by the sequence characterized by time. For those [forms] of mutually different natures do not shine simultaneously; and the very state of having become prior-and-posterior is called action. Since action is thus,

children.text: nanu pradhānaṃ pariṇāmakriyāyāṃ kartṛrūpamiyatā samarthitam , ---- iti ko doṣo , na hi puruṣavadasyākartṛtvamiṣyate ? ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: <s>Pradhāna</s> has been thus justified as having the form of an agent in the action of transformation — so what is the fault? For its non-agency is not asserted as with <s>Puruṣa</s>. Anticipating this, he says:
And it is not proper for the insentient, due to the contradiction of difference and non-difference;
but in a single [entity] whose nature is consciousness, it is proper, due to the differentiation of appearances.

children.text: evamityabhinnarūpasya dharmiṇaḥ satatapravahaddharmabhedasaṃbhedasvātantryalakṣaṇaṃ pariṇamanakriyākartṛkatvaṃ yaduktaṃ tat pradhānāderna yuktaṃ jaḍatvāt , jaḍo hi nāma pariniṣṭhitasvabhāvaḥ prameyapadapatitaḥ sa ca rūpabhedādbhinno vyavasthāpanīyo nīlapītādivat , ekasyabhāvavattvāccābhinno nīlavat , na tu sa eva svabhāvo bhinnaścābhinnaśca bhavitumarhati vidhiniṣedhayorekatraikadā virodhāt / kaścit svabhāvo bhinnaḥ kaścit tvabhinnaḥ , ---- iti cet , dvau tarhi imau svabhāvāvekasya svabhāvasya bhavetām , na caivaṃ yuktaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Thus' — that what was stated as the agency in the action of transformation, characterized by the freedom of constantly flowing differentiation and confluence of properties in a single undifferentiated property-possessor — that is not proper for <s>Pradhāna</s> and such, since they are insentient. For what is called insentient has a fixed nature, falls under the category of the knowable, and must be determined as different due to the differentiation of form — like blue and yellow — and as non-different due to not being a second thing — like blue. But that very same nature cannot be both different and non-different, since affirmation and negation are contradictory when [applied] to one [thing] at one [time]. [Objection:] Some nature is different, some is non-different. Then there would be two natures of a single nature — and even that is not proper, by the reasoning:
{The establishment of difference and non-difference would be undermined in all entities. /}
'this' —

children.text: iti pariniṣṭhitāmāsatayā sarvataḥ paricchinnarūpatvena prameyapadapatitasya nāyaṃ svabhāvabheda ekatve satyupapadyate / yattu prameyadaśāpatitaṃ na bhavati kiṃ tu cidrūpatayā prakāśaparamārtharūpaṃ cidekasvabhāvaṃ svaccham , tatra bhedābhedarūpatopalabhyate ; anubhavādeva hi svacchasyādarśāderakhaṇḍitasvasvabhāvasyaiva parvatamataṅgajādirūpasahasrasaṃbhinnaṃ vapurupapadyate / na ca rajatadvicandrādi yathā śuktikaikacandrarūpatirodhānena vartate , tathā darpaṇe parvatādi / darpaṇasya hi tathāvabhāse darpaṇataiva sutarāmunmīlati ----
children.translated_text: having a fixed identity with the word 'this,' having a form delimited in every respect, and falling under the category of the knowable — this differentiation of nature while maintaining unity is not tenable. But what does not fall under the state of the knowable, but rather, being of the nature of consciousness, has the ultimate reality of luminosity, with a single nature that is consciousness, and is transparent — therein, the nature of both difference and non-difference is apprehended. For from experience itself, a transparent thing like a mirror, even while its own nature is unbroken, admits of a form pierced by thousands of forms such as mountains, elephants, and the like. And it is not the case that, as silver and the two moons [in illusion] exist through the concealment of the form of nacre and the single moon, so too mountains and such [exist] in the mirror. For when the mirror manifests in such a way, the mirror-nature itself becomes all the more unveiled —
'This mirror is clear, this mirror is excellent' —

children.text: ityabhimānāt / na hi parvato bāhyastatra saṃkrāmati svadeśatyāgaprasaṅgādasya , na cāsya pṛṣṭhe'sau bhāti darpaṇānavabhāsapraṅgāt , na ca madhye niviḍakaṭhinasapratidhasvabhāvasya tatrānupraveśasaṃbhāvanābhāvāt , na paścāt tatrādarśanāt dūratayaiva ca bhāsanāt , na ca tannipatanotphalitapratyāvṛttāścākṣuṣā mayūsvāḥ parvatameva gṛhṇanti , bimbapratibimbayorubhayorapi parvatapārśvagatadarpaṇābhāse 'valokanāt / tasmāt nirmalatāmāhātmyametat yadanantāvabhāsasaṃbhedaścaikatā ca / giriśikharoparivartinaścaikatraiva bodhe nagaragataparārthasahasrābhāsaḥ , ---- iti cidrūpasyaiva kartṛtvamupapannam . abhinnasya bhedāveśasahiṣṇutvena kriyāśaktyāveśasaṃbhavāt //19//
children.translated_text: due to such a judgment. For the external mountain does not migrate into it — since the consequence would be its abandonment of its own location; nor does it appear on its back — since there would be the consequence of non-manifestation of the mirror; nor in the middle — since there is no possibility of entry into what is of a dense, hard, and resistant nature; nor behind — since it is not seen there, and because it appears precisely from a distance. Nor do the visual rays, produced by the impact, turned back from that [mirror], grasp the mountain alone — since both the image and its reflection are observed in the appearance of the mirror situated beside the mountain. Therefore, this glory of transparency is: the confluence of infinite appearances and yet unity. And on a single cognition perched on a mountain peak, thousands of objects belonging to the city [below] appear. Thus, agency is tenable precisely for what is of the nature of consciousness — since what is non-different can tolerate the entry of differentiation and hence the entry of the power of action. //19//
Thus, for the insentient,

children.text: nanvetāvatā vijñānameva brahmarūpamimāṃ viśvarūpatāvaicitrīṃ parigṛhṇātu kimīśvaratākalpanena ityāśaṅkyāha
children.translated_text: Objection: Let mere cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>) itself, as Brahman-nature, embrace this variegated universality — what need is there of postulating Lordship? Anticipating this, he says:
Even in the real unity of consciousness, there would be no action of what is differentiated in appearance
without the reflective grasping of unity characterized by the desire to act.

children.text: cidrūpasyaikatvaṃ yadi vāstavaṃ bhedaḥ punarayamavidyopaplavāt , ---- ityucyate tadā kasyāyamavidyopaplavaḥ , ---- iti na saṃgacchate brahmaṇo hi vidyaikarūpasya kathamavidyārūpatā , na cānyaḥ kaścitasti vastuto jīvādiryasyāvidyā bhavet / anirvācyeyamavidyā , ---- iti cet , kasya anirvācyā , ---- iti na vidmaḥ ; svarūpeṇa ca bhāti , na cānirvācyā , ---- iti kimetat ? ; yuktyā nopapadyate , ---- iti cet saṃvedatiraskāriṇī kā khalu yuktirnāma , anupapattiśca bhāsamānasya kānyā bhaviṣyati / sadrūpameva brahmābhinnaṃ cakāstyavikalpake , vikalpabalāttu bhedo 'yam , ---- iti cet , kasyāyaṃ vikalpanavyāpāro nāma ? brahmaṇaścet , avidyāyoge na ca anyo'sti ; avikalpalaṃ ca satyaṃ vikalpakamasatyam , ---- iti kuto vibhāgo bhāsamānatvasyāviśeṣāt / bhāsamāno'pi bhedo bādhitaḥ , ---- iti cet , abhedo'pi evam , bhedabhāsanena tasya bādhāt / viparītasaṃvedanodaya eva hi bādho nānyaḥ kaścit / bādho'pi ca bhāsamānatvādeva san nānyataḥ , ---- iti bhedo'pi bhāsamānaḥ kathamavidyā / bhāsanamavadhīrya āgamapramāṇako 'yamabhedaḥ ---- iti cet āgamo 'pi bhedātmaka eva vastubhūtaḥ pramātṛpramāṇaprameyavibhāgaśca , ---- iti na kiṃcidetat / tasmāt vāstavaṃ cidekatvamabhyupagamyāpi tasya kartṛtvalaks.aṇā bhinnarūpasamāveśātmikā kriyā nopapadyate ; parāmarśasvarūpaṃ tu svātantryaṃ yadi bhavati tadopapadyate sarvam / parāmarśo hi cikīrṣārūpecchā , tasyāṃ ca sarvamantarbhūtaṃ nirmātavyamabhedakalpenāste , ---- ityuktaṃ
children.translated_text: If the unity of consciousness is real but this difference is due to the error of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — then to whom does this error of <s>avidyā</s> belong? This does not cohere. For how can <s>Brahman</s>, whose sole nature is knowledge, have the nature of <s>avidyā</s>? And there is no other entity whatsoever — no <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) and such — to whom <s>avidyā</s> could belong. If [it is said] this <s>avidyā</s> is indescribable — to whom is it indescribable? We do not know. And it appears in its own form; and it is not indescribable — so what is this? If [it is said] it is untenable by reasoning — what kind of reasoning is this that overrides direct experience? And what other untenability could there be for what is manifest? In the non-conceptual [cognition], <s>Brahman</s> alone shines as of the nature of existence and as non-different; and this difference is due to the force of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition) — if so, to whom does this operation of conceptualization belong? If to <s>Brahman</s>, [that is untenable] since [Brahman's] conjunction with <s>avidyā</s> [would follow]; and there is no other [entity]. And the non-conceptual is real and the conceptual is unreal — whence this distinction, given that both are equally manifest? If [it is said] difference, though manifest, is sublated — then non-difference too [is sublated] in the same way, since it is sublated by the manifestation of difference. For sublation is nothing but the arising of a contrary cognition. And even sublation, being real precisely because it is manifest — from what other [source could it derive]? — so how can difference too, being manifest, be <s>avidyā</s>? If [it is said] disregarding manifestation, this non-difference is established by the valid means of <s>āgama</s> (scripture) — scripture too, as an actual entity, is of the nature of difference, being divided into perceiver, means of knowing, and object of knowledge — so this amounts to nothing. Therefore, even accepting the real unity of consciousness, the action characterized by engagement with different forms — the agency-nature — is not tenable for it. But if there exists the freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>) whose nature is reflective awareness (<s>parāmarśa</s>), then everything is tenable. For <s>parāmarśa</s> is the will in the form of desire to act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>); and in that, everything to be created rests in an internalized, non-differentiated mode — as has been stated,
{Of the master, abiding in the Self... /} (<s>Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā</s> 1.5.10)

children.text: ityatra / tena svātmarūpameva viśvaṃ satyarūpaṃ prakāśātmatāparamārthamatruṭitaprakāśābhedameva sat prakāśaparamārthenaiva bhedena bhāsayati maheśvaraḥ , ---- iti tadevāsyātidurghaṭakāritvalakṣaṇaṃ svātantryamaiśvaryamucyate / ābhāsabhinnayoriti kriyāpekṣā saṃbandhasāmānye ṣaṣṭhī , paścādyayocitaṃ vibhajyate / ābhāsena bhinnau jaḍājaḍābhāsau , jaḍo ghaṭādiḥ karmarūpaścidābhāsaḥ kartṛrūpaḥ , ---- iti tayoḥ kriyā , ekasya kriyamāṇatvamaparasya kartṛtvaṃ na bhavet / cikīrṣārūpeṇa nirmātavyābhedaparāmarśātmanā vinā ekā cāsau kriyā kathaṃ bhinnayoḥ svabhāvabhūtā bhavet / kāryakāraṇatāprastāvāt kartṛkarmaṇī ukte , kārakāntarāṇyapi tu ekakartṛtvānupraveśīni paramārthato'nyathā karaṇādau bhinne kārakavrāte kathamabhinnā sā / yadi vā ābhāsena yau bhinnau jaḍacetanau tayoryā cikīrṣā ekasyeṣyamāṇatā , parasyaiṣitṛtā tassvabhāvamekatvaparāmarśaṃ vinā , ---- iti / yadvā ābhāsabhinnayoḥ

children.translated_text: 'I — this' —

children.text: iti yaḥ parāmarśa ekaviśrāntirūpaścikīrṣātmā taṃ vinā , ---- iti / ābhāsabhinnayorekaparāmarśaṃ vinā cikīrṣālakṣaṇā kathaṃ kriyā , ---- iti vā / evaṃ kriyāṃ vā cikīrṣāṃ vā parāmarśaṃ vā apekṣya ṣ.aṣṭhī , nityasāpekṣatvācca samāsaḥ //20//
children.translated_text: without the reflective grasping that is of the form of resting in unity, whose nature is desire to act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>) — [it is untenable]. Without the single reflective grasping of those that are different in appearance, how could there be action in the form of <s>cikīrṣā</s>? — this too [is a possible construal]. Thus, the genitive may refer to action, or to <s>cikīrṣā</s>, or to reflective grasping; and because of constant dependence, [it is expressed as] a compound. // 20 //

Therefore, the universe that is of the nature of His own Self, that is of a real form, whose ultimate reality is luminosity, whose unbroken non-difference from luminosity has not been severed — that very [universe], with difference that is real in its ultimate luminosity alone, <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) manifests. And this alone is called His sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya</s>), His freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>), characterized by accomplishing the supremely difficult. 'Of the two that are different in appearance' — the genitive is in the general sense of relation with reference to action, [and] is later analyzed as appropriate. Those that are made different by appearance are the insentient and sentient appearances — the insentient, such as a pot, is of the nature of the object; the consciousness-appearance is of the nature of the agent. Of those two, [there is] action — one's being-acted-upon and the other's agency — this would not be possible without the reflective awareness of the nature of desire to act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>), which is the reflective grasping of non-difference with the to-be-created. And how could that one action, being the nature of both, belong to two that are different? Since the context is cause-and-effect, agent and object are stated; but the other <s>kārakas</s> (case-relations) too enter into the single agency — for ultimately, if the instrument and other separate case-relations were different, how could [action] be non-different? Alternatively, of the two — insentient and conscious — that are made different by appearance, the desire (<s>cikīrṣā</s>) wherein one is the desired and the other the desirer — without the reflective grasping of their unity, which is their nature, [it is untenable]. Or, of the two that are different in appearance —
He summarizes this:
Thus, for one who wishes to abide with a world-nature consisting of appearances of pot, cloth, and such —
this very will is the causality, the agency, the action.

The world, which is of the nature of appearances of pot, cloth, and such — having that as His self, one who

This is the connection. Therefore, the Blessed <s>Maheśvara</s> alone is the creator of the universe. Thus, may there be auspiciousness! // 21 //

Just as the insentient has no causality and no agency, so too the conscious being who is not the Lord — by this very mode of causality, what has arisen is this: for the very one who thus desires to create, that very <s>cikīrṣā</s> (desire to act), having reached the culmination of externality, is called

And the Action Section, the second investigation, is hereby complete. // 2 //
